cards.mean: to be on one's mind, to find oneself curious about
cards.lit: to come onto the mind: something lands in your thoughts and stays there

use.how: Xが気になる: X draws your attention by itself and won't let go (a worry, a curiosity, a person you like). It happens to you; you don't do it.

near.diff: 気にする is actively minding or worrying about something (を気にする); 気になる is something catching your attention on its own (が気になる).

cards.cue: You keep glancing at your phone because the exam results come out today and you can't stop thinking about them.

ctx.s: 明日[あした]の天気[てんき]が{気[き]になる}。
ctx.en: I keep wondering about tomorrow's weather.

ctx.s: テストの結果[けっか]が{気[き]になって}、夜[よる]よく眠[ねむ]れなかった。
ctx.en: The test results were on my mind, so I couldn't sleep well.

ctx.s: 「あの映画[えいが]、ずっと{気[き]になってた}んだ。一緒[いっしょ]に行[い]かない？」
ctx.en: "I've been curious about that film for ages. Want to go together?"

ctx.s: 「何[なに]か{気[き]になる}ことがあったら、遠慮[えんりょ]なく聞[き]いてください。」
ctx.en: "If anything bothers you or you're unsure about something, please don't hesitate to ask."

ctx.s: 最近[さいきん]、同[おな]じクラスに{気[き]になる}人[ひと]がいる。
ctx.en: Lately there's someone in my class I can't stop thinking about.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]{気[き]になりだす}と、壁[かべ]の小[ちい]さな傷[きず]まで目[め]につく。
ctx.en: Once it starts to bother you, you notice even the tiny scratches on the wall.

bad.s: 人[ひと]の目[め]を{気[き]になる}のはやめよう。
bad.en: (meant: let's stop worrying about what people think)
bad.why: Ki ni naru takes ga, not o. For actively minding what others think, the verb is ki ni suru: hito no me o ki ni suru.

bad.s: 「大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]、{気[き]にならないで}ください。」
bad.en: (meant: it's fine, please don't worry about it)
bad.why: You cannot ask someone not to have a thing catch their mind. The fixed reassurance is ki ni shinaide kudasai.

cards.mean: to be careful, to watch out
cards.lit: to attach one's mind (to something): keep your attention fixed on it

use.how: Xに気をつける: watch out for X; ～ように気をつける: take care to do ～. 気をつけて is the everyday 'take care' said when someone leaves.

near.diff: 気にする is worrying about something; 気をつける is taking care so that something bad does not happen.

cards.cue: Your friend is heading out into an icy night and you want to tell them to watch their step.

ctx.s: 道[みち]が凍[こお]っているから、{気[き]をつけて}ね。
ctx.en: The roads are icy, so be careful.

ctx.s: 熱[あつ]いので、やけどに{気[き]をつけて}ください。
ctx.en: It's hot, so be careful not to burn yourself.

ctx.s: 「寒[さむ]くなりますので、お体[からだ]に{気[き]をつけて}ください。」
ctx.en: "It's getting cold, so please take care of yourself."

ctx.s: 最近[さいきん]は食[た]べ過[す]ぎないように{気[き]をつけて}いる。
ctx.en: These days I make a point of not overeating.

ctx.s: 「申[もう]し訳[わけ]ありません。次[つぎ]から{気[き]をつけます}。」
ctx.en: "I'm very sorry. I'll be more careful from now on."

ctx.s: 「足元[あしもと]に{気[き]をつけて}お降[お]りください。」
ctx.en: "Please mind your step as you get off."

bad.s: 駅[えき]に着[つ]いてから、財布[さいふ]がないことに{気[き]をつけた}。
bad.en: (meant: when I got to the station, I noticed my wallet was gone)
bad.why: Ki o tsukeru is taking care beforehand, not noticing. Noticing something is ki ga tsuku: saifu ga nai koto ni ki ga tsuita.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の試験[しけん]を{気[き]をつけて}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I'm worried about tomorrow's exam)
bad.why: Ki o tsukeru already has its o and means being careful, not worrying. Say shiken ga ki ni naru, or shiken o ki ni shite iru.

cards.mean: to feel angry or offended at something
cards.lit: the belly stands up: anger rising in the gut, the old seat of feelings

use.how: Xに腹が立つ: to be angry at X (a person, behaviour, or oneself). Mostly the speaker's own anger; for someone else's, 腹を立てる is usual.

near.diff: 頭に来る is casual and sudden, anger flaring up; 腹が立つ is the plain, all-purpose way to say something makes you angry.

cards.cue: In calm, polite speech, tell a colleague how you felt when a friend cancelled by text an hour late without apologising.

ctx.s: 約束[やくそく]を破[やぶ]られて、本当[ほんとう]に{腹[はら]が立[た]った}。
ctx.en: He broke his promise and I was really angry.

ctx.s: 「このような対応[たいおう]をされて、正直[しょうじき]{腹[はら]が立[た]ちました}。」
ctx.en: "To be honest, being treated like this made me angry."

ctx.s: 「ねえ、何[なに]がそんなに{腹[はら]が立[た]つ}の？」
ctx.en: "Hey, what is it that's making you so angry?"

ctx.s: 今[いま]でも、あの時[とき]のことを思[おも]い出[だ]すと{腹[はら]が立[た]って}くる。
ctx.en: Even now, when I remember that time I start to get angry.

ctx.s: 同[おな]じミスを繰[く]り返[かえ]す自分[じぶん]に{腹[はら]が立[た]って}、しばらく黙[だま]っていた。
ctx.en: I was angry with myself for making the same mistake again, and stayed silent for a while.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の言[い]い方[かた]には{腹[はら]が立[た]った}が、言[い]っていることは正[ただ]しかった。
ctx.en: His way of putting it made me angry, but what he said was right.

bad.s: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べなかったので、{腹[はら]が立[た]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I skipped breakfast, so I got hungry)
bad.why: Hara ga tatsu is anger, not the stomach. Getting hungry is onaka ga suku.

bad.s: 遅[おく]れて来[き]た彼[かれ]を{腹[はら]が立[た]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I got angry at him for being late)
bad.why: The target of the anger takes ni, not o: okurete kita kare ni hara ga tatta.

cards.mean: to have a feeling that something is so
cards.lit: a feeling does (it): the mind senses something without proof

use.how: A clause goes before it: 雨が降る気がする, 会ったような気がする. A soft, unsure way to state a hunch or impression.

near.diff: 気がする puts forward a hunch; 気のせい dismisses a feeling as having no basis.

cards.cue: You're not sure, but that stranger's face seems familiar. Say so without claiming you know them.

ctx.s: 明日[あした]は雨[あめ]が降[ふ]るような{気[き]がする}。
ctx.en: I have a feeling it's going to rain tomorrow.

ctx.s: この人[ひと]、どこかで会[あ]った{気[き]がする}。
ctx.en: I feel like I've met this person somewhere.

ctx.s: 「なんだか今日[きょう]はいいことがありそうな{気[き]がする}ね。」
ctx.en: "Somehow I feel like something good is going to happen today."

ctx.s: 鍵[かぎ]をかけ忘[わす]れた{気[き]がして}、家[いえ]に戻[もど]った。
ctx.en: I had a feeling I'd forgotten to lock up, so I went back home.

ctx.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]してから、時間[じかん]が経[た]つのが早[はや]くなった{気[き]がする}。
ctx.en: Since I moved, it feels like time passes faster.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の話[はなし]を聞[き]いて、少[すこ]し救[すく]われたような{気[き]がした}。
ctx.en: Hearing her story, I felt a little as if I'd been rescued.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は{気[き]がする}、彼[かれ]は来[こ]ない。
bad.en: (meant: I have a feeling he won't come)
bad.why: The content of the feeling must come before ki ga suru: kare wa konai ki ga suru.

bad.s: あの人[ひと]は先生[せんせい]の{気[き]がする}。
bad.en: (meant: I have a feeling that person is a teacher)
bad.why: A noun cannot join with no here. Say sensei no you na ki ga suru, or sensei da to iu ki ga suru.

cards.mean: to take a liking to, to be pleased with
cards.lit: to enter the mind: something fits your taste and is let in

use.how: Xが/を気に入る: to come to like a particular thing you have met or chosen. A lasting liking is 気に入っている; a long-held general taste is 好き.

cards.cue: You gave your niece a scarf, and she has worn it every day since. Tell her parents you're glad.

ctx.s: このかばん、とても{気[き]に入[い]って}いる。
ctx.en: I really love this bag.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい部屋[へや]が{気[き]に入[い]った}ので、すぐに契約[けいやく]した。
ctx.en: I liked the new flat, so I signed the contract straight away.

ctx.s: 「プレゼント、{気[き]に入[い]って}もらえてよかった。」
ctx.en: "I'm so glad you liked the present."

ctx.s: 「どれでも{気[き]に入[い]った}ものを選[えら]んでください。」
ctx.en: "Please choose whichever one you like."

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]描[か]き直[なお]しても、自分[じぶん]の絵[え]が{気[き]に入[い]らない}。
ctx.en: No matter how many times I redraw it, I'm not happy with my picture.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は社長[しゃちょう]に{気[き]に入[い]られて}、すぐに昇進[しょうしん]した。
ctx.en: The company president took a liking to him, and he was soon promoted.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は子[こ]どもの時[とき]から寿司[すし]が{気[き]に入[い]る}。
bad.en: (meant: I've liked sushi since I was a child)
bad.why: The plain form ki ni iru is not a lasting state, and a lifelong taste is suki: sushi ga suki da.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]の説明[せつめい]に{気[き]に入[い]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I liked the teacher's explanation)
bad.why: The thing liked takes ga or o, not ni: sensei no setsumei ga ki ni itta.

cards.mean: to worry about something, to take it to heart
cards.lit: to make (something) into the mind: put your thoughts on it on purpose

use.how: Xを気にする: to mind or fret about X (looks, others' opinions, a mistake). 気にしないで is the everyday 'don't worry about it'.

near.diff: 気になる is something catching your attention by itself (が); 気にする is you dwelling on it (を), often more than you should.

cards.cue: A friend apologises again and again for spilling a drop of tea on your table. Tell them it's nothing.

ctx.s: 「大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]、{気[き]にしないで}。」
ctx.en: "It's fine, don't worry about it."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は人[ひと]の目[め]をとても{気[き]にする}。
ctx.en: She worries a lot about what other people think.

ctx.s: 年齢[ねんれい]なんて{気[き]にする}必要[ひつよう]はないよ。
ctx.en: There's no need to worry about your age.

ctx.s: 「体重[たいじゅう]、{気[き]にしてる}の？全然[ぜんぜん]太[ふと]ってないよ。」
ctx.en: "Are you worried about your weight? You haven't put on any at all."

ctx.s: 小[ちい]さなミスをいつまでも{気[き]にして}いたら、前[まえ]に進[すす]めない。
ctx.en: If you keep dwelling on small mistakes forever, you can't move forward.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は値段[ねだん]を{気[き]にせず}、一番[いちばん]いいワインを注文[ちゅうもん]した。
ctx.en: Without caring about the price, my father ordered the best wine.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の天気[てんき]が{気[き]にする}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm wondering about tomorrow's weather)
bad.why: Ki ni suru takes o, with a person as subject. With ga, use ki ni naru: ashita no tenki ga ki ni naru.

bad.s: 雪[ゆき]だから、運転[うんてん]は{気[き]にして}ね。
bad.en: (meant: it's snowing, so drive carefully)
bad.why: Ki ni suru is worrying, not taking care. Being careful is ki o tsukeru: unten ni ki o tsukete ne.

cards.mean: to notice, to realise
cards.lit: the mind gets attached: your attention suddenly lands on something

use.how: Xに気がつく: to notice or realise X; same as 気づく. 気がつくと／気がついたら also means 'before I knew it' or 'when I came to'.

near.diff: 気が利く praises someone for thoughtfully doing what others need; 気がつく is simply noticing.

cards.cue: Halfway to the station you realise your wallet is still on the kitchen table. Say when it struck you.

ctx.s: 財布[さいふ]を忘[わす]れたことに、駅[えき]で{気[き]がついた}。
ctx.en: I realised at the station that I'd forgotten my wallet.

ctx.s: 髪[かみ]を切[き]ったのに、誰[だれ]も{気[き]がつかなかった}。
ctx.en: I'd had my hair cut, but nobody noticed.

ctx.s: 「間違[まちが]いに{気[き]がついたら}、教[おし]えてください。」
ctx.en: "If you notice any mistakes, please let me know."

ctx.s: ゲームをしていて、{気[き]がついたら}もう夜中[よなか]の二時[にじ]だった。
ctx.en: I was playing a game, and before I knew it, it was two in the morning.

ctx.s: 事故[じこ]のあと、{気[き]がつくと}病院[びょういん]のベッドの上[うえ]だった。
ctx.en: After the accident, when I came to, I was lying in a hospital bed.

ctx.s: 失[うしな]って初[はじ]めて、家族[かぞく]の大切[たいせつ]さに{気[き]がついた}。
ctx.en: Only after losing them did I realise how precious my family was.

bad.s: 授業[じゅぎょう]では先生[せんせい]の話[はなし]をよく{気[き]がついて}ください。
bad.en: (meant: in class, please listen carefully to the teacher)
bad.why: Ki ga tsuku is noticing that happens to you; it cannot take o or be a deliberate effort. Say sensei no hanashi o yoku kiite kudasai.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は毎朝[まいあさ]七時[しちじ]に{気[き]がつく}。
bad.en: (meant: I wake up at seven every morning)
bad.why: Coming to is only after fainting or the like. Waking up normally is me ga sameru or okiru.

cards.mean: just one's imagination
cards.lit: the fault of the mind: blame the feeling, not the facts

use.how: A noun phrase: 気のせいだ, 気のせいじゃない？. 気のせいか、～ opens a remark the speaker is not sure of.

near.diff: 気がする states a hunch; 気のせい says a feeling is groundless.

cards.cue: Your friend jumps at a creak in the dark flat and asks if someone's there. Reassure them it's nothing.

ctx.s: 「今[いま]、誰[だれ]かいなかった？」「{気[き]のせい}だよ。」
ctx.en: "Wasn't someone there just now?" "You're imagining things."

ctx.s: 「ちょっと痩[や]せた？」「{気[き]のせい}じゃない？変[か]わってないよ。」
ctx.en: "Have you lost weight?" "Isn't that just your imagination? I haven't changed."

ctx.s: {気[き]のせい}か、今日[きょう]は駅[えき]がいつもより静[しず]かだ。
ctx.en: Maybe it's just me, but the station seems quieter than usual today.

ctx.s: 物音[ものおと]が聞[き]こえたと思[おも]ったが、{気[き]のせい}だったようだ。
ctx.en: I thought I heard a noise, but it seems it was just my imagination.

ctx.s: 「{気[き]のせい}かもしれないけど、最近[さいきん]元気[げんき]ないね。」
ctx.en: "Maybe I'm imagining it, but you've seemed down lately."

ctx.s: 熱[ねつ]っぽいのは{気[き]のせい}ではなかった。体温計[たいおんけい]は三十八度[さんじゅうはちど]だった。
ctx.en: Feeling feverish wasn't just my imagination: the thermometer read thirty-eight degrees.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]に落[お]ちたのは私[わたし]の{気[き]のせい}だ。
bad.en: (meant: failing the exam is my own fault)
bad.why: Ki no sei means a feeling is imagined, not blame. 'My fault' is watashi no sei.

bad.s: この部屋[へや]は{気[き]のせい}が悪[わる]い。
bad.en: (meant: this room has a bad atmosphere)
bad.why: Ki no sei is a fixed phrase for imagination, not atmosphere. Say fun'iki ga warui.

cards.mean: to lend a hand, to help someone with a task
cards.lit: to lend one's hand: give someone the use of your hands for a while

use.how: Xに手を貸す: help X with a task, often physical. 手を貸してくれない？ asks for help; Xに手を貸す can also mean being complicit in something bad.

near.diff: 手を出す is getting involved in something, meddling, or hitting someone; 手を貸す is helping.

cards.cue: You're struggling to carry a heavy box up the stairs and your flatmate walks past. Ask them for help.

ctx.s: 「ちょっと{手[て]を貸[か]して}くれない？この箱[はこ]、重[おも]くて。」
ctx.en: "Could you give me a hand? This box is heavy."

ctx.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの時[とき]、友達[ともだち]が{手[て]を貸[か]して}くれた。
ctx.en: When I moved, my friends lent a hand.

ctx.s: 階段[かいだん]の前[まえ]でお年寄[としよ]りが困[こま]っていたので、{手[て]を貸[か]した}。
ctx.en: An elderly person was having trouble at the stairs, so I helped them.

ctx.s: 「一人[ひとり]で大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]？」「うん、でも後[あと]で{手[て]を貸[か]して}もらうかも。」
ctx.en: "Can you manage on your own?" "Yes, but I might need your help later."

ctx.s: 困[こま]っている人[ひと]がいたら、{手[て]を貸[か]す}のは当然[とうぜん]だ。
ctx.en: If someone is in trouble, helping them is only natural.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は知[し]らないうちに詐欺[さぎ]に{手[て]を貸[か]して}いた。
ctx.en: Without realising it, he had been helping with a fraud.

bad.s: 宿題[しゅくだい]は兄[あに]に{手[て]を貸[か]した}。
bad.en: (meant: my older brother helped me with my homework)
bad.why: This says I helped my brother. Being helped is ani ni te o kashite moratta, or simply tetsudatte moratta.

bad.s: 財布[さいふ]を忘[わす]れたので、友達[ともだち]が千円[せんえん]{手[て]を貸[か]して}くれた。
bad.en: (meant: I forgot my wallet, so a friend lent me a thousand yen)
bad.why: Te o kasu is help with a task, never money. Lending money is okane o kasu: sen'en kashite kureta.

cards.mean: to show up, to put in an appearance
cards.lit: to put out one's face: let people see you there, if only for a moment

use.how: Xに顔を出す: to drop in at a gathering or place, often briefly or out of goodwill. Not for formal attendance where you play the main part.

near.diff: 足を運ぶ stresses making the trip to a place on purpose; 顔を出す is showing up at a gathering, often just briefly.

cards.cue: You're busy on the night of your old school reunion, but you plan to drop in for half an hour to say hello.

ctx.s: 「時間[じかん]があったら、パーティーに{顔[かお]を出[だ]して}ね。」
ctx.en: "If you have time, do drop by the party."

ctx.s: 忙[いそが]しいけど、同窓会[どうそうかい]には少[すこ]しだけ{顔[かお]を出[だ]す}つもりだ。
ctx.en: I'm busy, but I plan to show up at the reunion for a little while.

ctx.s: 最近[さいきん]、全然[ぜんぜん]実家[じっか]に{顔[かお]を出[だ]して}いない。
ctx.en: Lately I haven't been home to see my parents at all.

ctx.s: 「たまには部活[ぶかつ]に{顔[かお]を出[だ]せ}よ。みんな待[ま]ってるぞ。」
ctx.en: "Show up at club practice once in a while. Everyone's waiting for you."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は仕事[しごと]帰[がえ]りに、よくこの居酒屋[いざかや]に{顔[かお]を出[だ]す}。
ctx.en: He often drops in at this pub on his way home from work.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい店長[てんちょう]は、近[ちか]くに来[き]たついでに取引先[とりひきさき]へ{顔[かお]を出[だ]した}。
ctx.en: Since he was in the area anyway, the new manager dropped in on a supplier.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]、会社[かいしゃ]の飲[の]み会[かい]を{顔[かお]を出[だ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I showed up at the office drinks)
bad.why: Kao o dasu already has its o; the place you show up at takes ni: nomikai ni kao o dashita.

bad.s: 明日[あした]は大事[だいじ]な面接[めんせつ]なので、必[かなら]ず{顔[かお]を出[だ]します}。
bad.en: (meant: tomorrow is an important interview, so I'll definitely attend)
bad.why: Kao o dasu suggests a casual, brief appearance, wrong for your own job interview. Say mensetsu o ukemasu, or kanarazu ikimasu.

cards.mean: to be infuriated, to blow one's top
cards.lit: (anger) comes up to one's head

use.how: Intransitive; the cause takes に or は, often in the past: あいつの態度には頭に来た。 Casual talk about one's own sudden, strong anger.

near.diff: 腹が立つ is ordinary anger and fits any register; 頭に来る is more casual and more explosive, anger that flares up at once.

cards.cue: Your roommate ate the cake you had saved, then lied about it. Chatting with a friend, you say it made you absolutely furious.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]にゲームのデータを消[け]されて、{頭[あたま]に来[き]た}。
ctx.en: My little brother deleted my game data, and I was furious.

ctx.s: あの店員[てんいん]の態度[たいど]、ほんっと{頭[あたま]に来[く]る}！
ctx.en: That shop assistant's attitude, it really makes my blood boil!

ctx.s: 何[なに]をそんなに{頭[あたま]に来[き]てる}の？
ctx.en: What are you so mad about?

ctx.s: 約束[やくそく]を三回[さんかい]も破[やぶ]られたら、さすがに{頭[あたま]に来[く]る}。
ctx.en: If someone breaks a promise to you three times, of course you're going to lose it.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{頭[あたま]に来[き]て}、何[なに]も言[い]わずに電話[でんわ]を切[き]った。
ctx.en: He was so angry he hung up without a word.

ctx.s: 最初[さいしょ]は我慢[がまん]していたが、最後[さいご]の一言[ひとこと]でついに{頭[あたま]に来[き]た}。
ctx.en: I held it in at first, but that last remark finally made me snap.

bad.s: シャワーを浴[あ]びていたら、いいアイデアが{頭[あたま]に来[き]た}。
bad.en: (meant: a good idea came to me in the shower)
bad.why: It only means getting angry. An idea that comes to mind is atama ni ukabu or omoitsuku.

bad.s: 本日[ほんじつ]のご対応[たいおう]には、大変[たいへん]{頭[あたま]に来[き]ております}。
bad.en: (meant, in a formal complaint: I am most displeased with your handling today)
bad.why: It is casual speech and sounds childish in a formal complaint; write taihen fukai ni kanjite orimasu instead.

cards.mean: to get along well, to hit it off
cards.lit: two people's spirits fit together

use.how: Said of people: AとBは気が合う, Aと気が合う, or before a noun (気が合う友達). Describes a natural match of temperament, not agreement on one issue.

near.diff: 話が合う means you share topics and interests to talk about; 気が合う is a deeper match of temperament, being comfortable together.

cards.cue: You met someone at a party, and within ten minutes you were laughing at the same things as if you had known each other for years.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]とは初[はじ]めて会[あ]った日[ひ]から{気[き]が合[あ]った}。
ctx.en: She and I hit it off from the day we first met.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいルームメイトとは{気[き]が合[あ]いそう}ですか。
ctx.en: Do you think you'll get on with your new roommate?

ctx.s: 兄[あに]と僕[ぼく]は性格[せいかく]が全然[ぜんぜん]違[ちが]うのに、なぜか{気[き]が合[あ]う}。
ctx.en: My brother and I have completely different personalities, but for some reason we get along.

ctx.s: {気[き]が合[あ]う}仲間[なかま]と旅行[りょこう]するのが一番[いちばん]楽[たの]しい。
ctx.en: Travelling with friends you really click with is the most fun.

ctx.s: 「あの二人[ふたり]、いつも一緒[いっしょ]だね。」「昔[むかし]から{気[き]が合[あ]う}んだよ。」
ctx.en: "Those two are always together." "They've always got on well."

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい上司[じょうし]とどうも{気[き]が合[あ]わなくて}、毎日[まいにち]疲[つか]れる。
ctx.en: I just don't get along with my new boss, and it wears me out every day.

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]で全員[ぜんいん]の{気[き]が合[あ]って}、すぐに計画[けいかく]が決[き]まった。
bad.en: (meant: everyone agreed at the meeting, so the plan was decided quickly)
bad.why: It is about people's temperaments suiting each other, not agreeing on a decision; say iken ga icchi shite.

bad.s: この服[ふく]は私[わたし]によく{気[き]が合[あ]う}。
bad.en: (meant: these clothes suit me well)
bad.why: It is only used between people. Clothes that suit you are niau; things you like are ki ni iru.

cards.mean: to be quick to notice and do what others need
cards.lit: one's attention works well

use.how: Praises a person: 気が利く人, 気が利きますね. 気の利いた + noun means thoughtful or apt (気の利いた一言). 気が利かない is criticism.

near.diff: 気を遣う is the effort of being considerate, often tiring; 気が利く is the knack of spotting a need and acting on it, praised as a trait.
気がつく is mainly to notice something (気がつく人 can also mean attentive); 気が利く is specifically spotting what others need and doing it.

cards.cue: At dinner, a junior colleague refills everyone's glass and passes the soy sauce before anyone asks. How do you praise them?

ctx.s: 佐藤[さとう]さんは本当[ほんとう]に{気[き]が利[き]く}ね。
ctx.en: Sato is really thoughtful, isn't she?

ctx.s: お茶[ちゃ]がなくなる前[まえ]に注[つ]いでくれるなんて、{気[き]が利[き]きます}ね。
ctx.en: Topping up my tea before it runs out, how thoughtful of you.

ctx.s: 寒[さむ]そうにしていたら、彼[かれ]がすぐ毛布[もうふ]を持[も]ってきてくれた。{気[き]が利[き]く}人[ひと]だ。
ctx.en: When I looked cold, he brought me a blanket right away. He's so attentive.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]なのに、言[い]われる前[まえ]に資料[しりょう]を用意[ようい]するとは{気[き]が利[き]いている}。
ctx.en: She's new, yet she had the documents ready before being asked. Very sharp of her.

ctx.s: うちの夫[おっと]は{気[き]が利[き]かなくて}、言[い]わないと何[なに]もしてくれない。
ctx.en: My husband never picks up on things; unless I tell him, he does nothing.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]の{気[き]の利[き]いた}一言[ひとこと]で、会議[かいぎ]の雰囲気[ふんいき]が明[あか]るくなった。
ctx.en: One well-judged remark from the manager lightened the mood of the meeting.

bad.s: 駅[えき]に着[つ]いてから、財布[さいふ]を忘[わす]れたことに{気[き]が利[き]いた}。
bad.en: (meant: when I reached the station I noticed I had forgotten my wallet)
bad.why: Noticing a fact is ki ga tsuku. Ki ga kiku is attentiveness to other people's needs and cannot take koto ni.

bad.s: この薬[くすり]は頭痛[ずつう]によく{気[き]が利[き]く}。
bad.en: (meant: this medicine works well for headaches)
bad.why: A medicine that works is kiku written with a different kanji. Ki ga kiku is only said of people's thoughtfulness.

cards.mean: to take pains to be considerate of others' feelings
cards.lit: to spend one's attention (on someone)

use.how: The person cared for takes に: 周りに気を遣う. Often implies effort or strain (気を遣って疲れる); 気を遣わないで politely declines care. Also written 気を使う.

near.diff: 気が利く praises a knack for doing the right thing; 気を遣う is the effort of being careful with others, which can be a burden.
気にする is worrying about something; 気を遣う is acting considerately toward someone.

cards.cue: Staying with your partner's parents, you watch every word and help with every dish, and come home exhausted from being so careful with them.

ctx.s: 私[わたし]にそんなに{気[き]を遣[つか]わなくて}いいよ。
ctx.en: You don't have to go to so much trouble for me.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は周[まわ]りに{気[き]を遣[つか]い}すぎて、自分[じぶん]の意見[いけん]が言[い]えない。
ctx.en: She worries so much about other people's feelings that she can't voice her own opinion.

ctx.s: 「お土産[みやげ]、どうぞ。」「わざわざ{気[き]を遣[つか]って}くれてありがとう。」
ctx.en: "Here's a little gift." "Oh, you shouldn't have. Thank you."

ctx.s: 夫[おっと]の実家[じっか]に行[い]くと、{気[き]を遣[つか]って}すごく疲[つか]れる。
ctx.en: Whenever I visit my husband's family, I'm so careful about everything that it wears me out.

ctx.s: 入院中[にゅういんちゅう]の友達[ともだち]に{気[き]を遣[つか]わせない}ように、明[あか]るく話[はな]した。
ctx.en: I kept my tone cheerful so that my friend in hospital wouldn't feel she had to make an effort for me.

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]に{気[き]を遣[つか]って}、飲[の]み会[かい]を先[さき]に帰[かえ]れなかった。
ctx.en: I didn't want to upset my boss, so I couldn't leave the drinks party early.

bad.s: 道[みち]が凍[こお]っているから、{気[き]を遣[つか]って}歩[ある]いてね。
bad.en: (meant: the road is icy, so walk carefully)
bad.why: Watching out for danger is ki o tsukeru. Ki o tsukau is consideration for people's feelings.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の結果[けっか]をずっと{気[き]を遣[つか]って}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I keep worrying about my exam results)
bad.why: Worrying about something is ki ni suru or ki ni naru. Ki o tsukau is directed at people, not at results.

cards.mean: to dread something, to feel heavy-hearted about it
cards.lit: one's spirit is heavy

use.how: Predicate about something unpleasant one has to face: 明日の面接は気が重い, ～と思うと気が重い. Said of one's own feelings.

near.diff: 気が進まない is not wanting to do something; 気が重い is the gloomy weight of an unpleasant thing ahead, even one you will certainly do.

cards.cue: Tomorrow you must tell your team that the project you all worked on has been cancelled, and the thought has weighed on you all evening.

ctx.s: 明日[あした]は月曜日[げつようび]だと思[おも]うと{気[き]が重[おも]い}。
ctx.en: The thought that tomorrow is Monday gets me down.

ctx.s: 明日[あした]は断[ことわ]りの電話[でんわ]をかけなきゃいけない。{気[き]が重[おも]い}なあ。
ctx.en: Tomorrow I have to make the call turning them down. I'm dreading it.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]にミスを報告[ほうこく]しなければならず、{気[き]が重[おも]かった}。
ctx.en: I had to report the mistake to my manager, and I was dreading it.

ctx.s: 歯医者[はいしゃ]の予約[よやく]が近[ちか]づいて、だんだん{気[き]が重[おも]く}なってきた。
ctx.en: As my dentist appointment gets closer, I'm starting to dread it more and more.

ctx.s: 「元気[げんき]ないね。」「来週[らいしゅう]の発表[はっぴょう]のことを考[かんが]えると{気[き]が重[おも]くて}。」
ctx.en: "You look down." "Thinking about next week's presentation is weighing on me."

ctx.s: {気[き]が重[おも]い}仕事[しごと]ほど、早[はや]めに片付[かたづ]けたほうがいい。
ctx.en: The tasks you dread most are the ones best dealt with early.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]飲[の]みすぎて、今朝[けさ]は{気[き]が重[おも]い}。
bad.en: (meant: I drank too much last night and my head feels heavy this morning)
bad.why: A physical heaviness is atama ga omoi or karada ga darui. Ki ga omoi is dread of something ahead.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は来週[らいしゅう]の試験[しけん]を{気[き]が重[おも]い}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm dreading next week's exam)
bad.why: It takes no object with o. Say shiken no koto o kangaeru to ki ga omoi, or shiken wa ki ga omoi.

cards.mean: (of food) to suit one's taste
cards.lit: (food) fits one's mouth

use.how: Subject is food or drink, the eater takes の: 私の口に合う. Very common in polite offers and questions: お口に合うかどうか, お口に合いましたか.

near.diff: 気に入る is liking anything at all; 口に合う is only food and drink suiting one's palate, and is the polite way to ask a guest.

cards.cue: You have cooked a dish from your home town for a guest and, setting it down, politely say you hope the flavour will suit them.

ctx.s: 日本[にほん]の料理[りょうり]は{口[くち]に合[あ]います}か。
ctx.en: Do you like Japanese food?

ctx.s: お{口[くち]に合[あ]う}かどうか分[わ]かりませんが、どうぞ召[め]し上[あ]がってください。
ctx.en: I'm not sure it will be to your taste, but please help yourself.

ctx.s: このスープは少[すこ]し辛[から]すぎて、私[わたし]の{口[くち]には合[あ]わなかった}。
ctx.en: This soup was a bit too spicy for my taste.

ctx.s: 留学中[りゅうがくちゅう]は、現地[げんち]の食事[しょくじ]が{口[くち]に合[あ]わなくて}苦労[くろう]した。
ctx.en: When I studied abroad, I struggled because the local food didn't agree with my palate.

ctx.s: 「このケーキ、どう？」「甘[あま]さ控[ひか]えめで、僕[ぼく]の{口[くち]に合[あ]う}よ。」
ctx.en: "How's the cake?" "It's not too sweet, just how I like it."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]の煮物[にもの]は、子供[こども]の{口[くち]にも合[あ]う}優[やさ]しい味[あじ]だ。
ctx.en: My grandmother's simmered dishes have a gentle flavour that even children enjoy.

bad.s: この映画[えいが]は私[わたし]の{口[くち]に合[あ]わなかった}。
bad.en: (meant: this film wasn't to my taste)
bad.why: It is only for food and drink. For films, music or style say konomi ni awanakatta.

bad.s: 私[わたし]はこの料理[りょうり]を{口[くち]に合[あ]う}。
bad.en: (meant: this dish suits my taste)
bad.why: The food is the subject and the eater takes no: kono ryouri wa watashi no kuchi ni au. There is no o.

cards.mean: to have a weakness for, to be crazy about
cards.lit: to have no eyes, that is, to lose all judgement over something

use.how: Xに目がない, about a thing one cannot resist, usually food, drink or a hobby: 甘いものに目がない. Affectionate, often about oneself or family.

near.diff: 大好き is plain 'love'; 目がない stresses being unable to resist it, and always takes に.

cards.cue: Your aunt cannot walk past a bakery without buying a cream puff, however full she is.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は甘[あま]いものに{目[め]がない}。
ctx.en: My father can't resist anything sweet.

ctx.s: 私[わたし]、チーズケーキには{目[め]がなくて}、見[み]るとつい買[か]ってしまう。
ctx.en: I have a real weakness for cheesecake; whenever I see it, I end up buying some.

ctx.s: 「お酒[さけ]、お好[す]きなんですか。」「ええ、日本酒[にほんしゅ]には{目[め]がない}んです。」
ctx.en: "Do you like a drink?" "Yes, I'm crazy about sake."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は昔[むかし]から温泉[おんせん]に{目[め]がない}らしい。
ctx.en: Apparently she has always loved hot springs.

ctx.s: 兄[あに]は新[あたら]しいゲーム機[き]に{目[め]がなく}、発売日[はつばいび]には必[かなら]ず店[みせ]に並[なら]ぶ。
ctx.en: My brother is mad about new game consoles and always queues at the shop on release day.

ctx.s: うちの猫[ねこ]はかつお節[ぶし]に{目[め]がない}。
ctx.en: Our cat goes crazy for bonito flakes.

bad.s: 甘[あま]いものには{目[め]がない}ので、ケーキは食[た]べません。
bad.en: (meant: I'm not interested in sweets, so I don't eat cake)
bad.why: Despite the nai, it means you love it and cannot resist it: the opposite of having no interest.

bad.s: 私[わたし]はお寿司[すし]が{目[め]がない}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm crazy about sushi)
bad.why: The thing one loves takes ni, not ga: watashi wa osushi ni me ga nai.

cards.mean: to be too busy with something to break off
cards.lit: one cannot take one's hands off (what one is doing)

use.how: Predicate about being tied up right now, mostly as an excuse or apology: 今手が離せない. Polite form 手が離せません is common on the phone at work.

near.diff: 目が離せない is that something needs constant watching (a toddler) or is riveting; 手が離せない is that your hands are tied up with a task you cannot stop.
忙しい is being busy in general; 手が離せない says you are in the middle of something and cannot stop it at this moment.

cards.cue: Your phone rings while you are frying tempura in hot oil, so you call out to your flatmate that you can't come to the phone just now.

ctx.s: ごめん、今[いま]{手[て]が離[はな]せない}から、後[あと]で電話[でんわ]するね。
ctx.en: Sorry, I'm in the middle of something; I'll call you back later.

ctx.s: 料理中[りょうりちゅう]で{手[て]が離[はな]せない}から、荷物[にもつ]を受[う]け取[と]ってくれる？
ctx.en: I'm busy cooking and can't stop, so could you take the delivery?

ctx.s: 「田中[たなか]さん、少[すこ]しいいですか。」「すみません、今[いま]ちょっと{手[て]が離[はな]せなくて}。」
ctx.en: "Mr Tanaka, have you got a minute?" "Sorry, I'm a bit tied up right now."

ctx.s: この作業[さぎょう]が終[お]わるまで{手[て]が離[はな]せない}ので、先[さき]に食[た]べていてください。
ctx.en: I can't break off until this job is finished, so please start eating without me.

ctx.s: 担当者[たんとうしゃ]はただいま{手[て]が離[はな]せません}ので、折[お]り返[かえ]しお電話[でんわ]いたします。
ctx.en: The person in charge is busy at the moment, so we will call you back.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は会議[かいぎ]の準備[じゅんび]で{手[て]が離[はな]せない}ようだ。
ctx.en: The manager seems to be tied up preparing for the meeting.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]とは{手[て]が離[はな]せない}ほど仲[なか]がいい。
bad.en: (meant: she and I are inseparable)
bad.why: It means being too busy to stop, not closeness. Inseparable friends are itsumo issho or hanarerarenai naka.

bad.s: 別[わか]れた恋人[こいびと]のことが、まだ{手[て]が離[はな]せない}。
bad.en: (meant: I still can't let go of my ex)
bad.why: It is not the English 'let go'. Not getting over someone is mada wasurerarenai or fukkirenai.

cards.mean: to get hold of, to obtain
cards.lit: to put something into one's hand

use.how: Transitive, with を: チケットを手に入れる. Suggests something hard to come by or wanted for a long time. The intransitive is 手に入る.

near.diff: 手に入る is intransitive (チケットが手に入った, it came to me); 手に入れる is the transitive, the effort of getting it (チケットを手に入れた).

cards.cue: After months of searching online auctions, a collector finally gets the rare first-edition comic he has always wanted.

ctx.s: やっとコンサートのチケットを{手[て]に入[い]れた}。
ctx.en: I finally managed to get tickets for the concert.

ctx.s: その本[ほん]、どこで{手[て]に入[い]れた}の？
ctx.en: Where did you get hold of that book?

ctx.s: 古[ふる]いレコードを{手[て]に入[い]れる}ために、何軒[なんけん]も店[みせ]を回[まわ]った。
ctx.en: I went round shop after shop to find the old record.

ctx.s: 「限定[げんてい]のスニーカー、買[か]えた？」「うん、抽選[ちゅうせん]で{手[て]に入[い]れた}よ。」
ctx.en: "Did you manage to buy the limited-edition trainers?" "Yes, I got a pair through the lottery."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は長年[ながねん]の努力[どりょく]で、夢[ゆめ]だった自分[じぶん]の店[みせ]を{手[て]に入[い]れた}。
ctx.en: Through years of hard work, he finally got the shop of his own he had dreamed of.

ctx.s: 正確[せいかく]な情報[じょうほう]を早[はや]く{手[て]に入[い]れる}のは簡単[かんたん]ではない。
ctx.en: Getting accurate information quickly is not easy.

bad.s: やっとチケットが{手[て]に入[い]れた}。
bad.en: (meant: I finally got the ticket)
bad.why: With ga the intransitive is needed: chiketto ga te ni haitta. Te ni ireru takes o: chiketto o te ni ireta.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]に濡[ぬ]れて、風邪[かぜ]を{手[て]に入[い]れた}。
bad.en: (meant: I got soaked in the rain and caught a cold)
bad.why: It is for obtaining things one wants, not the English 'get' for an illness; catching a cold is kaze o hiku.

cards.mean: to change one's mind
cards.lit: one's intention turns into another

use.how: Intransitive; the person takes の or は: 彼の気が変わる, 私は気が変わった. About a plan or intention changing, often suddenly or on a whim.

near.diff: 考え直す is deliberately reconsidering; 気が変わる is an intention that simply shifts, often with no clear reason.

cards.cue: You had told everyone you would skip the party, but an hour before it started you decided to go after all.

ctx.s: 行[い]くつもりだったけど、{気[き]が変[か]わった}。
ctx.en: I was going to go, but I changed my mind.

ctx.s: {気[き]が変[か]わったら}、いつでも連絡[れんらく]してね。
ctx.en: If you change your mind, get in touch any time.

ctx.s: 赤[あか]いシャツを買[か]うつもりだったが、店[みせ]で{気[き]が変[か]わって}青[あお]にした。
ctx.en: I meant to buy the red shirt, but in the shop I changed my mind and got the blue one.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]に会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めるの？」「うん、もう{気[き]が変[か]わる}ことはないよ。」
ctx.en: "Are you really quitting?" "Yes, I'm not going to change my mind."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]が変[か]わり}やすいので、約束[やくそく]しても当[あ]てにならない。
ctx.en: He changes his mind so easily that you can't count on his promises.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の{気[き]が変[か]わらない}うちに、契約書[けいやくしょ]にサインしてもらおう。
ctx.en: Let's get the boss to sign the contract before he changes his mind.

bad.s: 留学[りゅうがく]して、彼[かれ]は{気[き]が変[か]わって}明[あか]るい人[ひと]になった。
bad.en: (meant: studying abroad changed his personality and he became cheerful)
bad.why: It is a change of intention, not of character. A changed personality is seikaku ga kawatta.

bad.s: その話[はなし]を聞[き]いて、彼[かれ]に対[たい]する{気[き]が変[か]わった}。
bad.en: (meant: after hearing that, my opinion of him changed)
bad.why: It is about a plan or intention, not one's view of a person. Say kare ni taisuru mikata ga kawatta or kimochi ga kawatta.

cards.mean: to be reluctant, not to feel like doing it
cards.lit: one's spirit does not move forward

use.how: Almost always negative, as a predicate about something one is asked or expected to do: 行くのは気が進まない. A soft, polite way to show reluctance.

near.diff: 気が重い is a heavy, gloomy dread of something unpleasant ahead; 気が進まない simply says one does not want to do it.
気が向かない is not being in the mood right now, often for optional things; 気が進まない is reluctance about a specific request or plan.

cards.cue: Your boss asks you to give a speech at a colleague's wedding. You could say yes, but you would really rather not. How do you admit it gently?

ctx.s: 正直[しょうじき]、あの人[ひと]に会[あ]いに行[い]くのは{気[き]が進[すす]まない}。
ctx.en: Honestly, I'm reluctant to go and see that person.

ctx.s: {気[き]が進[すす]まない}なら、無理[むり]に引[ひ]き受[う]けなくてもいいよ。
ctx.en: If you're reluctant, you don't have to force yourself to take it on.

ctx.s: 「お見合[みあ]い、どうするの？」「あまり{気[き]が進[すす]まない}んだよね。」
ctx.en: "So what about the arranged meeting?" "I'm not really keen on it."

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]に頼[たの]まれたが、どうも{気[き]が進[すす]まなかった}。
ctx.en: My senior asked me to do it, but somehow I just didn't want to.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]が進[すす]まない}様子[ようす]で書類[しょるい]にサインした。
ctx.en: He signed the papers with obvious reluctance.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の提案[ていあん]だが、現場[げんば]の多[おお]くは{気[き]が進[すす]まない}ようだ。
ctx.en: It's the president's proposal, but many of the staff on the ground seem reluctant.

bad.s: 最近[さいきん]、勉強[べんきょう]の{気[き]が進[すす]まない}。
bad.en: (meant: my studies aren't making progress lately)
bad.why: It is about not wanting to do something, not about work failing to progress; for that, say benkyou ga susumanai.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の旅行[りょこう]は、とても{気[き]が進[すす]む}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm really looking forward to tomorrow's trip)
bad.why: The phrase lives in the negative; the positive is rare and never means eager excitement. Say tanoshimi da.

cards.mean: to be unable to concentrate, to get distracted
cards.lit: one's attention scatters

use.how: Intransitive, about noise, people or thoughts breaking one's focus: テレビの音で気が散る. Often 気が散って〜できない.

near.diff: 気を抜く is one's own effort or alertness slackening; 気が散る is attention being pulled away by something, against one's will.

cards.cue: You are trying to read for an exam, but your roommate keeps chatting and playing music, and your eyes slide off the page.

ctx.s: テレビがついていると{気[き]が散[ち]る}。
ctx.en: I can't concentrate when the TV is on.

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の工事[こうじ]の音[おと]で{気[き]が散[ち]って}、全然[ぜんぜん]勉強[べんきょう]できない。
ctx.en: The construction noise next door keeps distracting me, and I can't study at all.

ctx.s: 「ごめん、{気[き]が散[ち]る}から今[いま]は話[はな]しかけないで。」
ctx.en: "Sorry, please don't talk to me right now, it breaks my concentration."

ctx.s: スマホが机[つくえ]にあると{気[き]が散[ち]りやすい}ので、別[べつ]の部屋[へや]に置[お]いている。
ctx.en: Having my phone on the desk distracts me easily, so I keep it in another room.

ctx.s: 運転中[うんてんちゅう]に{気[き]が散[ち]る}と、事故[じこ]につながる。
ctx.en: Getting distracted while driving leads to accidents.

ctx.s: 観客[かんきゃく]の声[こえ]に{気[き]が散[ち]った}のか、彼[かれ]は前半[ぜんはん]にミスを重[かさ]ねた。
ctx.en: Perhaps the crowd's noise put him off, because he made mistake after mistake in the first half.

bad.s: 失恋[しつれん]して、心[こころ]が{気[き]が散[ち]って}しまった。
bad.en: (meant: I fell apart after the break-up)
bad.why: It means losing concentration, not emotional collapse; for heartbreak, say ochikomu or kizutsuku.

bad.s: うるさくして、弟[おとうと]の{気[き]を散[ち]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was noisy and distracted my brother)
bad.why: Chiru is intransitive; to distract someone is ki o chirasu: otouto no ki o chirashita.

cards.mean: to be satisfied, to feel one has done enough
cards.lit: one's feelings are settled and done

use.how: Mostly 気が済むまで, 気が済まない or 気が済んだ: about doing or saying enough to let a matter rest. 謝らないと気が済まない.

near.diff: 気が晴れる is gloom lifting, cheering up; 気が済む is feeling enough has been done or said, so one can let the matter go.

cards.cue: Your friend has gone back to check the door lock four times. You sigh and tell them to keep checking until they can finally stop worrying.

ctx.s: {気[き]が済[す]む}まで泣[な]いていいよ。
ctx.en: You can cry for as long as you need to.

ctx.s: 一言[ひとこと]謝[あやま]ってもらわないと{気[き]が済[す]まない}。
ctx.en: I won't be able to let it go until they apologise, even just a word.

ctx.s: 「もう{気[き]が済[す]んだ}？そろそろ帰[かえ]ろうよ。」
ctx.en: "Got it out of your system? Let's head home."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は何[なん]でも自分[じぶん]でやらないと{気[き]が済[す]まない}性格[せいかく]だ。
ctx.en: She's the type who isn't happy unless she does everything herself.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]確認[かくにん]しても{気[き]が済[す]まず}、もう一度[いちど]メールを読[よ]み返[かえ]した。
ctx.en: However many times I checked, I still wasn't at ease, so I read the email over once more.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]を責[せ]めて{気[き]が済[す]む}なら、それでもいいけど。
ctx.en: If blaming them makes you feel you've settled it, fine, but...

bad.s: このレストランの料理[りょうり]に{気[き]が済[す]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I was satisfied with this restaurant's food)
bad.why: It is not satisfaction with food or service (that is manzoku shita); it is about feeling able to let a matter rest.

bad.s: やっと宿題[しゅくだい]が{気[き]が済[す]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: my homework is finally done)
bad.why: Finishing a task is shukudai ga sunda; in this idiom the subject is one's feelings, not the task.

cards.mean: to be short-tempered, quick to lose patience
cards.lit: one's spirit is short

use.how: Describes a person's temperament: 父は気が短い, 気が短い人. A fault; the opposite is 気が長い.

near.diff: 気が強い is being assertive and not backing down; 気が短い is losing patience or temper quickly.

cards.cue: Your uncle honks the moment the light turns green and snaps at the waiter if the food takes a few minutes. What is he like?

ctx.s: うちの父[ちち]は{気[き]が短[みじか]い}。
ctx.en: My dad is short-tempered.

ctx.s: {気[き]が短[みじか]い}人[ひと]は、行列[ぎょうれつ]に並[なら]ぶのが苦手[にがて]だ。
ctx.en: Impatient people hate standing in queues.

ctx.s: 「まだ五分[ごふん]しか待[ま]ってないよ。{気[き]が短[みじか]い}なあ。」
ctx.en: "We've only waited five minutes. You're so impatient."

ctx.s: 若[わか]い頃[ころ]は{気[き]が短[みじか]くて}、よく人[ひと]とけんかした。
ctx.en: When I was young I had a short fuse and often got into fights.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は{気[き]が短[みじか]い}から、報告[ほうこく]は結論[けつろん]から話[はな]したほうがいい。
ctx.en: The manager has no patience, so start your report with the conclusion.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]が短[みじか]い}ところがあるが、根[ね]は優[やさ]しい人[ひと]だ。
ctx.en: He can be quick-tempered, but at heart he's a kind person.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は予定[よてい]が多[おお]くて、{気[き]が短[みじか]い}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm short on time today)
bad.why: It describes a person's temperament, not a lack of time; for that, say jikan ga nai.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]が短[みじか]くて}、仕事[しごと]がとても速[はや]い。
bad.en: (meant: he's quick and efficient at work)
bad.why: It is impatience, a fault, not speed or efficiency; praise would be shigoto ga hayai or tegiwa ga ii.

cards.mean: to be strong-willed and assertive
cards.lit: one's spirit is strong

use.how: Describes a person who stands their ground and won't be pushed around: 姉は気が強い. Can be admiring or mildly critical; the opposite is 気が弱い.

near.diff: 気が短い is losing patience or temper fast; 気が強い is firmness in standing up to people, calm or not.
負けず嫌い is hating to lose; 気が強い is a broader firmness of character in dealing with others.

cards.cue: Your little sister argues back with the older boys, never gives in, and never cries when she is told off. How do you describe her character?

ctx.s: 妹[いもうと]は小[ちい]さい頃[ころ]から{気[き]が強[つよ]い}。
ctx.en: My little sister has been strong-willed since she was small.

ctx.s: {気[き]が強[つよ]い}彼女[かのじょ]は、相手[あいて]が先輩[せんぱい]でもはっきり意見[いけん]を言[い]う。
ctx.en: She's strong-minded and speaks her mind clearly, even to seniors.

ctx.s: 「あの子[こ]、見[み]た目[め]はおとなしいけど、実[じつ]は{気[き]が強[つよ]い}よ。」
ctx.en: "She looks quiet, but actually she's tough as nails."

ctx.s: {気[き]が強[つよ]そうに}見[み]えるけど、本当[ほんとう]は繊細[せんさい]な人[ひと]なんです。
ctx.en: He looks forceful, but he's actually a sensitive person.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]の失礼[しつれい]な態度[たいど]に、{気[き]が強[つよ]い}母[はは]は黙[だま]っていなかった。
ctx.en: My mother, never one to back down, didn't stay quiet about the clerk's rudeness.

ctx.s: 物語[ものがたり]の主人公[しゅじんこう]は{気[き]が強[つよ]く}、誰[だれ]にも負[ま]けない少女[しょうじょ]だ。
ctx.en: The heroine of the story is a strong-willed girl who won't lose to anyone.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は毎日[まいにち]ジムに通[かよ]っていて、{気[き]が強[つよ]い}。
bad.en: (meant: he goes to the gym every day and is physically strong)
bad.why: It describes temperament, not physical strength; for that, say chikara ga tsuyoi.

bad.s: このコーヒーは{気[き]が強[つよ]い}ね。
bad.en: (meant: this coffee is strong)
bad.why: It describes a person's temperament and is never said of food or drink; strong coffee is koi.

cards.mean: to be meek, unable to stand up for oneself
cards.lit: one's spirit is weak

use.how: Describes a timid person who cannot refuse or speak up: 気が弱くて断れない. A mild fault, often said of oneself or with sympathy.

near.diff: 気が小さい stresses timidity and worrying over small things; 気が弱い stresses being unable to stand up for oneself.

cards.cue: Your coworker always takes on extra work because he can't bring himself to say no, even when he is exhausted and it isn't fair.

ctx.s: 私[わたし]は{気[き]が弱[よわ]くて}、頼[たの]まれると断[ことわ]れない。
ctx.en: I'm such a pushover that I can't say no when someone asks me.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]は{気[き]が弱[よわ]い}ので、いつも嫌[いや]な役[やく]を押[お]しつけられている。
ctx.en: My brother is timid, so he always gets stuck with the jobs nobody wants.

ctx.s: 「{気[き]が弱[よわ]い}ところにつけ込[こ]まれないようにね。」
ctx.en: "Don't let people take advantage of how meek you are."

ctx.s: {気[き]が弱[よわ]い}店員[てんいん]は、客[きゃく]の無理[むり]な要求[ようきゅう]にも言[い]い返[かえ]せなかった。
ctx.en: The timid clerk couldn't even answer back to the customer's unreasonable demands.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は優[やさ]しいけれど{気[き]が弱[よわ]く}、上司[じょうし]に意見[いけん]が言[い]えない。
ctx.en: He's kind but meek, and can't give his opinion to his boss.

ctx.s: 昔[むかし]は{気[き]が弱[よわ]かった}が、今[いま]は自分[じぶん]の考[かんが]えをはっきり言[い]える。
ctx.en: I used to be timid, but now I can say clearly what I think.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は数学[すうがく]に{気[き]が弱[よわ]い}。
bad.en: (meant: he's weak at maths)
bad.why: It describes timidity, not weakness in a subject; say suugaku ga nigate da or suugaku ni yowai.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]の地震[じしん]のとき、{気[き]が弱[よわ]かった}。
bad.en: (meant: I was scared during yesterday's earthquake)
bad.why: It is a lasting trait of character, not fear felt in one moment; say kowakatta.

cards.mean: to feel like doing something when the mood strikes
cards.lit: one's spirit turns toward something

use.how: Mostly 気が向いたら, 気が向いたとき or 気が向かない, about optional things like hobbies or invitations: 気が向いたら来てね.

near.diff: 気が進まない is reluctance about a specific thing one is asked to do; 気が向く is acting on a passing whim, with no obligation.

cards.cue: You tell a friend there is no pressure at all: they can drop by your café some time, whenever they happen to be in the mood.

ctx.s: {気[き]が向[む]いたら}、また遊[あそ]びに来[き]てね。
ctx.en: Come round again whenever you feel like it.

ctx.s: 休[やす]みの日[ひ]は、{気[き]が向[む]いた}ときに散歩[さんぽ]に出[で]かける。
ctx.en: On my days off I go for a walk whenever the mood takes me.

ctx.s: 「ピアノ、毎日[まいにち]弾[ひ]いてるの？」「ううん、{気[き]が向[む]いた}ときだけ。」
ctx.en: "Do you play the piano every day?" "No, only when I feel like it."

ctx.s: 雨[あめ]の日[ひ]は{気[き]が向[む]かない}ので、ジョギングを休[やす]む。
ctx.en: On rainy days I'm not in the mood, so I skip my jog.

ctx.s: 兄[あに]は{気[き]が向[む]く}と、夜中[よなか]でも急[きゅう]に料理[りょうり]を始[はじ]める。
ctx.en: When the mood strikes, my brother will suddenly start cooking, even in the middle of the night.

ctx.s: その作家[さっか]は、{気[き]が向[む]いた}ときにしか書[か]かないことで知[し]られている。
ctx.en: That writer is known for writing only when the mood takes him.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しいクラスメートに{気[き]が向[む]いて}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I'm interested in the new classmate)
bad.why: It is about being in the mood to do something, not about being drawn to a person; say ki ni naru.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]、{気[き]が向[む]いたら}この書類[しょるい]を今日中[きょうじゅう]に確認[かくにん]してください。
bad.en: (meant: please check this document by the end of today)
bad.why: It leaves things to someone's whim, so it clashes with a deadline and sounds rude to a boss.

cards.mean: to let one's guard down, to relax one's effort
cards.lit: to take the tension out of one's spirit

use.how: Transitive, a person as subject: 最後まで気を抜くな. Mostly in warnings or explaining a slip (気を抜いた瞬間に); also of resting at home.

near.diff: 手を抜く is deliberately cutting corners on a job; 気を抜く is letting one's alertness or tension drop, often without meaning to.
気が散る is attention pulled away by something outside; 気を抜く is one's own tension or alertness slackening.

cards.cue: Your team leads three to nothing with ten minutes left, and the players start to stroll. The coach shouts at them from the bench.

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]が終[お]わるまで{気[き]を抜[ぬ]かない}でね。
ctx.en: Don't let your guard down until the exam is over.

ctx.s: 「あと十分[じゅっぷん]だ！最後[さいご]まで{気[き]を抜[ぬ]くな}！」
ctx.en: "Ten minutes left! Stay sharp to the very end!"

ctx.s: ちょっと{気[き]を抜[ぬ]いた}瞬間[しゅんかん]に、包丁[ほうちょう]で指[ゆび]を切[き]ってしまった。
ctx.en: The moment I relaxed my attention, I cut my finger with the kitchen knife.

ctx.s: 家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ったときくらい、{気[き]を抜[ぬ]いて}ゆっくりしたい。
ctx.en: At least when I get home, I want to switch off and take it easy.

ctx.s: 山道[やまみち]は、下[くだ]りで{気[き]を抜[ぬ]く}と転[ころ]びやすい。
ctx.en: On mountain trails, if you relax on the way down, it's easy to fall.

ctx.s: 大差[たいさ]でリードしていたチームは後半[こうはん]に{気[き]を抜[ぬ]き}、逆転[ぎゃくてん]を許[ゆる]した。
ctx.en: The team with a big lead eased off in the second half and let their opponents come back to win.

bad.s: 試合[しあい]が終[お]わって、{気[き]が抜[ぬ]いた}。
bad.en: (meant: after the match I felt deflated)
bad.why: Nuku is transitive and needs o; the intransitive is ki ga nuketa, which means feeling deflated.

bad.s: あまりに驚[おどろ]いて、{気[き]を抜[ぬ]いて}しまった。
bad.en: (meant: I was so shocked that I fainted)
bad.why: Fainting is ki o ushinau; this idiom is letting one's attention or effort slacken.

cards.mean: to know a lot of people, to be well connected
cards.lit: one's face is wide

use.how: Describes a person who knows many people: 彼は業界で顔が広い. Usually admiring; the field often comes with で.

near.diff: 顔が利く means one's name gets favours or opens doors somewhere; 顔が広い simply means knowing many people.

cards.cue: You need a good plumber, a lawyer and a venue for a party, and your neighbour seems to know someone for every one of them.

ctx.s: 田中[たなか]さんは本当[ほんとう]に{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}ね。
ctx.en: Tanaka really knows everyone, doesn't he?

ctx.s: {顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}先輩[せんぱい]に頼[たの]んで、いいカメラマンを紹介[しょうかい]してもらった。
ctx.en: I asked a well-connected senior, and they introduced me to a good photographer.

ctx.s: 「翻訳[ほんやく]できる人[ひと]、知[し]らない？」「山田[やまだ]さんに聞[き]いたら？{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}から。」
ctx.en: "Know anyone who can translate?" "Why not ask Yamada? She knows loads of people."

ctx.s: 母[はは]は町内[ちょうない]で{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]く}、道[みち]を歩[ある]けば必[かなら]ず誰[だれ]かに声[こえ]をかけられる。
ctx.en: My mother knows everyone in the neighbourhood; whenever she walks down the street, someone says hello.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は音楽業界[おんがくぎょうかい]で{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}ので、ライブの出演者[しゅつえんしゃ]集[あつ]めを任[まか]された。
ctx.en: He has wide connections in the music business, so he was put in charge of finding acts for the gig.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい営業部長[えいぎょうぶちょう]は、取引先[とりひきさき]にも{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}と評判[ひょうばん]だ。
ctx.en: The new sales manager is said to be well connected among our clients too.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}俳優[はいゆう]で、日本中[にほんじゅう]の人[ひと]が知[し]っている。
bad.en: (meant: he's a famous actor whom everyone in Japan knows)
bad.why: It means he knows many people, not that many people know him; say yuumei na haiyuu.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{顔[かお]が広[ひろ]い}から、どんな失敗[しっぱい]も許[ゆる]してくれる。
bad.en: (meant: he's generous, so he forgives any mistake)
bad.why: Generous tolerance is kokoro ga hiroi; this idiom is only about knowing many people.

cards.mean: (of feelings) to show on one's face
cards.lit: it comes out onto the face

use.how: The subject is a feeling or state: 疲れが顔に出る. Often すぐ顔に出る or 顔に出やすい, about someone who can't hide feelings.

near.diff: 顔に書いてある is a teasing way to say someone's thoughts are obvious; 顔に出る is the plain statement that a feeling shows.

cards.cue: Your friend insists the meeting went fine, but you can see the disappointment at a glance. They can never hide what they feel.

ctx.s: 私[わたし]は気持[きも]ちがすぐ{顔[かお]に出[で]る}タイプだ。
ctx.en: I'm the type whose feelings show on my face straight away.

ctx.s: 疲[つか]れが{顔[かお]に出[で]て}いるよ。今日[きょう]は早[はや]く寝[ね]たら？
ctx.en: You look worn out. Why not go to bed early tonight?

ctx.s: 「嫌[いや]なら嫌[いや]って言[い]えばいいのに。{顔[かお]に出[で]てる}よ。」
ctx.en: "If you don't like it, just say so. It's written all over your face."

ctx.s: 緊張[きんちょう]が{顔[かお]に出[で]ない}ように、面接[めんせつ]の前[まえ]に深呼吸[しんこきゅう]した。
ctx.en: I took a deep breath before the interview so my nerves wouldn't show.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は感情[かんじょう]が{顔[かお]に出[で]にくい}ので、何[なに]を考[かんが]えているのか読[よ]みにくい。
ctx.en: His feelings rarely show on his face, so it's hard to read what he's thinking.

ctx.s: ポーカーでは、考[かんが]えが{顔[かお]に出[で]る}と負[ま]けてしまう。
ctx.en: In poker, if your thoughts show on your face, you lose.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]、有名人[ゆうめいじん]がテレビに{顔[かお]に出[で]た}。
bad.en: (meant: a celebrity appeared on TV yesterday)
bad.why: Appearing on TV is terebi ni deru; this idiom is a feeling showing on someone's face.

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]で私[わたし]は不満[ふまん]を{顔[かお]に出[で]た}。
bad.en: (meant: I let my displeasure show in the meeting)
bad.why: Deru is intransitive: say fuman ga kao ni deta, or with o use the transitive kao ni dashita.

cards.mean: to be unable to keep a secret
cards.lit: one's mouth is light: words float out of it easily

use.how: Describes a person's habit, as a predicate: あの人は口が軽い. A warning or complaint, never praise for being chatty or friendly.

near.diff: 口が滑る is one accidental slip on one occasion; 口が軽い is a person's habit of passing secrets on.
口が堅い is the opposite: someone you can trust with a secret.

cards.cue: You are about to tell a friend some private news, and someone warns you: that friend tells everyone everything. How do they describe the friend?

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{口[くち]が軽[かる]い}から、秘密[ひみつ]は話[はな]さないほうがいいよ。
ctx.en: He can't keep a secret, so you'd better not tell him anything private.

ctx.s: {口[くち]が軽[かる]い}人[ひと]には、大事[だいじ]な相談[そうだん]はできない。
ctx.en: You can't talk important matters over with someone who can't keep things to themselves.

ctx.s: 「誰[だれ]にも言[い]わないでね。」「大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]、私[わたし]そんなに{口[くち]が軽[かる]く}ないよ。」
ctx.en: "Don't tell anyone, okay?" "Don't worry, I'm not someone who blabs."

ctx.s: あの部長[ぶちょう]は{口[くち]が軽[かる]い}ので、人事[じんじ]の話[はなし]がすぐ社内[しゃない]に広[ひろ]まる。
ctx.en: That manager can't keep anything quiet, so news about staff changes spreads around the office at once.

ctx.s: 妹[いもうと]に話[はな]したのが間違[まちが]いだった。あの子[こ]の{口[くち]が軽[かる]い}のを忘[わす]れていた。
ctx.en: Telling my sister was a mistake. I'd forgotten how she can never keep a secret.

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]の{口[くち]が軽[かる]い}せいで、サプライズの計画[けいかく]がいつも本人[ほんにん]にばれてしまう。
ctx.en: Because one of our friends always blabs, our surprise plans keep getting found out by the person they're for.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{口[くち]が軽[かる]い}ので、話[はな]しやすくて楽[たの]しい人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is chatty and easy to talk to, which makes him fun)
bad.why: It is a criticism of someone who leaks secrets, not praise for being talkative or friendly.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]一度[いちど]だけ{口[くち]が軽[かる]くて}、秘密[ひみつ]を言[い]ってしまった。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday, just once, I let a secret slip)
bad.why: It describes a person's habit. A single accidental slip is kuchi ga suberu.

cards.mean: to be good at keeping secrets
cards.lit: one's mouth is firm: it stays shut and nothing gets out

use.how: Describes someone you can trust with confidential matters: 彼女は口が堅い. Usually written 堅い; 固い is also seen.

near.diff: 口が軽い is the opposite: someone who passes secrets on.
頭が固い is rigid, inflexible thinking; 口が堅い is only about not revealing what one has been told.

cards.cue: You need to tell someone about a personal problem and want to be sure it won't go any further. Why do you choose this particular colleague?

ctx.s: 田中[たなか]さんは{口[くち]が堅[かた]い}から、安心[あんしん]して相談[そうだん]できる。
ctx.en: Tanaka never repeats what you tell her, so you can talk things over with her without worrying.

ctx.s: この仕事[しごと]では顧客[こきゃく]の情報[じょうほう]を扱[あつか]うので、{口[くち]が堅[かた]い}人[ひと]が必要[ひつよう]だ。
ctx.en: This job handles customer information, so we need someone who can be trusted to keep quiet.

ctx.s: 「このこと、誰[だれ]かに話[はな]した？」「話[はな]してないよ。僕[ぼく]、{口[くち]は堅[かた]い}ほうだから。」
ctx.en: "Have you told anyone about this?" "No. I'm pretty good at keeping secrets."

ctx.s: 記者[きしゃ]がいくら質問[しつもん]しても、広報[こうほう]の担当者[たんとうしゃ]は{口[くち]が堅[かた]く}、何[なに]も話[はな]さなかった。
ctx.en: However many questions the reporters asked, the press officer gave nothing away.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{口[くち]が堅[かた]い}ので、友達[ともだち]からよく悩[なや]み事[ごと]を打[う]ち明[あ]けられる。
ctx.en: She keeps things to herself, so her friends often confide their worries in her.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]は{口[くち]が堅[かた]くて}、母[はは]への誕生日[たんじょうび]プレゼントが何[なん]なのか、どうしても教[おし]えてくれない。
ctx.en: My little brother won't give anything away; no matter what, he won't tell me what he's getting Mum for her birthday.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は{口[くち]が堅[かた]くて}、一日中[いちにちじゅう]ほとんど話[はな]さない。
bad.en: (meant: my father is a quiet man who hardly talks all day)
bad.why: It is about not revealing secrets, not about being quiet in general. A man of few words is mukuchi.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は{口[くち]が堅[かた]くて}、一度[いちど]決[き]めたことは絶対[ぜったい]に変[か]えない。
bad.en: (meant: my father is stubborn and never changes a decision)
bad.why: Stubbornness is ganko or atama ga katai; this idiom only means keeping secrets.

cards.mean: to offer unwanted opinions on others' affairs
cards.lit: to put one's mouth out into something that is not one's own

use.how: Takes に for the matter meddled in: 人の家のことに口を出す. Often in requests or complaints: 口を出さないで.

near.diff: 手を出す is getting involved in or trying something yourself; 口を出す is commenting on what others are doing.

cards.cue: Your mother-in-law keeps telling you how to raise your children and arrange your kitchen, though nobody asked. What is she doing?

ctx.s: これは私[わたし]の問題[もんだい]だから、{口[くち]を出[だ]さない}で。
ctx.en: This is my problem, so please stay out of it.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は、私[わたし]の服[ふく]の選[えら]び方[かた]にまでいちいち{口[くち]を出[だ]す}。
ctx.en: My mother has something to say about everything, even the clothes I pick.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい部長[ぶちょう]は、現場[げんば]の細[こま]かいやり方[かた]にまで{口[くち]を出[だ]して}くる。
ctx.en: The new manager even interferes in the small details of how we do the work on the floor.

ctx.s: 「お隣[となり]の子育[こそだ]て、ちょっと厳[きび]しすぎない？」「よその家[いえ]のことに{口[くち]を出[だ]す}ものじゃないよ。」
ctx.en: "Aren't the neighbours a bit too strict with their kids?" "How other families do things is none of our business."

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は社長[しゃちょう]を引退[いんたい]した後[あと]も、会社[かいしゃ]の経営[けいえい]に{口[くち]を出[だ]し}続[つづ]けている。
ctx.en: Even after retiring as president, my grandfather keeps interfering in how the company is run.

ctx.s: 息子[むすこ]の進路[しんろ]は本人[ほんにん]が決[き]めることなので、親[おや]は{口[くち]を出[だ]さない}ことにしている。
ctx.en: What our son does after school is his decision, so we, his parents, have decided not to interfere.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]に聞[き]かれたので、授業[じゅぎょう]で{口[くち]を出[だ]して}答[こた]えた。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher asked me, so I answered aloud in class)
bad.why: It means meddling in others' affairs, not speaking aloud. Saying something out loud is koe ni dasu.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しい趣味[しゅみ]として、ゴルフに{口[くち]を出[だ]して}みた。
bad.en: (meant: I tried my hand at golf as a new hobby)
bad.why: Trying something yourself is te o dasu; kuchi o dasu is commenting on other people's business.

cards.mean: to have a sharp tongue, to speak harshly
cards.lit: one's mouth is bad: what comes out of it is rough

use.how: Describes how someone habitually talks; often softened with けど: 口は悪いけど優しい. Used of a person, not of one remark.

near.diff: 口が軽い is leaking secrets; 口が悪い is saying things bluntly or rudely.

cards.cue: Your uncle calls your cooking 'pig food' and your haircut 'a disaster', yet he is the first to help when you're in trouble. How do you describe the way he talks?

ctx.s: 兄[あに]は{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}けど、本当[ほんとう]は優[やさ]しい。
ctx.en: My brother says harsh things, but he's actually kind.

ctx.s: {口[くち]が悪[わる]くて}ごめんね。悪気[わるぎ]はないんだ。
ctx.en: Sorry for being so blunt. I don't mean any harm.

ctx.s: あの監督[かんとく]は{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}ことで有名[ゆうめい]だが、選手[せんしゅ]からの信頼[しんらい]は厚[あつ]い。
ctx.en: That coach is famous for his sharp tongue, but his players trust him completely.

ctx.s: 「お前[まえ]、相変[あいか]わらず{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}な。」「褒[ほ]め言葉[ことば]として受[う]け取[と]っておくよ。」
ctx.en: "You're as rude as ever." "I'll take that as a compliment."

ctx.s: あの人[ひと]は{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}だけだから、言[い]われたことをいちいち気[き]にしなくていいよ。
ctx.en: He's just got a rough way of talking, so don't take everything he says to heart.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}せいで、初対面[しょたいめん]の人[ひと]によく誤解[ごかい]される。
ctx.en: Because she talks so bluntly, people often get the wrong idea about her when they first meet her.

bad.s: 人前[ひとまえ]で話[はな]すのが苦手[にがて]で、私[わたし]は{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}んです。
bad.en: (meant: I'm bad at speaking in front of people)
bad.why: It means talking rudely or harshly, not lacking skill as a speaker. A poor talker is kuchibeta.

bad.s: 秘密[ひみつ]をすぐ人[ひと]に話[はな]すから、彼[かれ]は{口[くち]が悪[わる]い}。
bad.en: (meant: he can't keep a secret, he tells people straight away)
bad.why: Leaking secrets is kuchi ga karui; kuchi ga warui is about harsh words.

cards.mean: to let something slip by accident
cards.lit: one's mouth slips: the words come out before one can stop them

use.how: About one occasion, often with つい or うっかり: つい口が滑った. The transitive 口を滑らせる is also common.

near.diff: 口が軽い is a habit of leaking secrets; 口が滑る is one unintended slip, which can happen to anyone.

cards.cue: In the middle of a chat you accidentally mention your friend's engagement, which was supposed to be secret, and you immediately regret it. What happened?

ctx.s: つい{口[くち]が滑[すべ]って}、秘密[ひみつ]を話[はな]してしまった。
ctx.en: Before I knew it, it slipped out and I'd told the secret.

ctx.s: ごめん、{口[くち]が滑[すべ]った}。今[いま]のは忘[わす]れて。
ctx.en: Sorry, that slipped out. Forget what I just said.

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]で{口[くち]が滑[すべ]って}、前[まえ]の会社[かいしゃ]の不満[ふまん]を言[い]ってしまった。
ctx.en: In the interview I slipped up and complained about my last company.

ctx.s: 「どうして知[し]ってるの？」「妹[いもうと]がうっかり{口[くち]を滑[すべ]らせた}んだよ。」
ctx.en: "How do you know?" "My sister accidentally let it slip."

ctx.s: サプライズのことは、本人[ほんにん]の前[まえ]で{口[くち]が滑[すべ]らない}ように気[き]をつけてね。
ctx.en: Be careful not to let anything slip about the surprise in front of her.

ctx.s: お酒[さけ]が入[はい]って{口[くち]が滑[すべ]り}、彼[かれ]は自分[じぶん]の給料[きゅうりょう]まで話[はな]してしまった。
ctx.en: After a few drinks things started slipping out, and he even ended up telling everyone his salary.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はスピーチの間[あいだ]、{口[くち]が滑[すべ]って}すらすら話[はな]した。
bad.en: (meant: he spoke smoothly and fluently throughout his speech)
bad.why: It means blurting out something one should not have said, not speaking smoothly. Fluent speech is surasura hanasu.

bad.s: わざと{口[くち]が滑[すべ]って}、彼[かれ]の秘密[ひみつ]をみんなに教[おし]えた。
bad.en: (meant: I deliberately told everyone his secret)
bad.why: A slip is by definition an accident, so waza to (on purpose) contradicts it.

cards.mean: (of criticism) to hit home uncomfortably
cards.lit: one's ears hurt: the words are painful to hear

use.how: Said by the person the criticism applies to: 耳が痛い話だ, 耳の痛い意見. It admits the point is fair. Literally it also just means an earache.

near.diff: 耳にたこができる is weariness at hearing the same thing again; 耳が痛い is discomfort because the criticism is true of you.

cards.cue: At a talk on saving money, the speaker describes exactly the impulse buying you do every weekend. How does the talk feel to you?

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]、遅刻[ちこく]が多[おお]いよ。」「{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]い}なあ。」
ctx.en: "You've been late a lot recently." "Ouch, you've got me there."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]の注意[ちゅうい]は{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]い}けど、その通[とお]りだ。
ctx.en: The teacher's warning stings, but it's true.

ctx.s: 甘[あま]い物[もの]好[ず]きの私[わたし]にとって、医者[いしゃ]の話[はなし]は{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]かった}。
ctx.en: As someone with a sweet tooth, I found what the doctor said hit a little too close to home.

ctx.s: 部下[ぶか]からの{耳[みみ]の痛[いた]い}意見[いけん]も、素直[すなお]に聞[き]くようにしている。
ctx.en: I try to listen openly even when my staff tell me things I'd rather not hear.

ctx.s: 運動不足[うんどうぶそく]の方[かた]には{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]い}話[はなし]かもしれませんが、毎日[まいにち]少[すこ]し歩[ある]きましょう。
ctx.en: This may be uncomfortable to hear for those of you who don't exercise, but try to walk a little every day.

ctx.s: 時間[じかん]の使[つか]い方[かた]の講演[こうえん]は、締[し]め切[き]りをよく破[やぶ]る僕[ぼく]には{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]い}内容[ないよう]だった。
ctx.en: The lecture on time management hit home for someone like me who often misses deadlines.

bad.s: 同僚[どうりょう]が上司[じょうし]の悪口[わるぐち]ばかり言[い]うので、{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]い}。
bad.en: (meant: my coworker keeps bad-mouthing the boss, and it's unpleasant to listen to)
bad.why: It is used when the criticism is aimed at you and rings true, not for unpleasant talk about someone else.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]にみんなの前[まえ]で褒[ほ]められて、{耳[みみ]が痛[いた]かった}。
bad.en: (meant: I felt embarrassed when the teacher praised me in front of everyone)
bad.why: It is about criticism that stings, never about praise. Embarrassment at praise is terekusai.

cards.mean: to be sick of hearing the same thing again and again
cards.lit: to get calluses on one's ears from hearing too much (tako here is a callus, not an octopus)

use.how: Mostly in ほど or くらい with 聞く or 言われる: 耳にたこができるほど聞いた. Light, exasperated complaint; often written 耳にタコ.

near.diff: 耳が痛い is criticism that stings because it is true; 耳にたこができる is only tiredness at repetition.

cards.cue: For the hundredth time, your dad starts telling the story of how he met your mum. You groan. How do you say you've heard it plenty already?

ctx.s: その話[はなし]は{耳[みみ]にたこができる}ほど聞[き]いたよ。
ctx.en: I've heard that story so many times I could recite it.

ctx.s: 「宿題[しゅくだい]しなさい」と、毎日[まいにち]母[はは]に{耳[みみ]にたこができる}くらい言[い]われた。
ctx.en: Every day my mother told me to do my homework until I was sick of hearing it.

ctx.s: 「またその話[はなし]？もう{耳[みみ]にたこができる}よ。」
ctx.en: "That story again? I've heard it a million times."

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]の昔[むかし]の自慢話[じまんばなし]は、もう{耳[みみ]にたこができる}ほど聞[き]かされた。
ctx.en: We've been made to listen to the manager's stories about his glory days more times than I can count.

ctx.s: 「安全第一[あんぜんだいいち]」という言葉[ことば]は、新人[しんじん]研修[けんしゅう]で{耳[みみ]にたこができる}ほど繰[く]り返[かえ]された。
ctx.en: "Safety first" was repeated so often in new-staff training that we were all sick of it.

ctx.s: {耳[みみ]にたこができる}ほど「野菜[やさい]も食[た]べなさい」と言[い]っているのに、息子[むすこ]は全然[ぜんぜん]聞[き]かない。
ctx.en: I've told my son to eat his vegetables till I'm blue in the face, but he never listens.

bad.s: 初[はじ]めて聞[き]いた話[はなし]で、{耳[みみ]にたこができる}ほど驚[おどろ]いた。
bad.en: (meant: it was the first time I'd heard it, and I was amazed)
bad.why: It is about having heard something far too many times, not about surprise at something new.

bad.s: 隣[となり]の工事[こうじ]の音[おと]がうるさくて、{耳[みみ]にたこができた}。
bad.en: (meant: the construction noise next door was deafening)
bad.why: It is about the same words or advice repeated, not about loud noise.

cards.mean: to look over, to skim through a document
cards.lit: to pass one's eyes through something written

use.how: Takes に for the written material: 資料に目を通す. Common at work and in polite requests: 目を通していただけますか.

cards.cue: Your boss hands you a twenty-page report before a meeting and asks you to at least run your eyes over it first. What are you asked to do?

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は毎朝[まいあさ]、新聞[しんぶん]に{目[め]を通[とお]す}。
ctx.en: My father looks through the newspaper every morning.

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]の前[まえ]に、この資料[しりょう]に{目[め]を通[とお]して}おいてください。
ctx.en: Please look over these materials before the meeting.

ctx.s: 「契約書[けいやくしょ]、読[よ]んだ？」「ざっと{目[め]を通[とお]した}だけ。」
ctx.en: "Did you read the contract?" "I only skimmed it."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]は、学生[がくせい]のレポートすべてに{目[め]を通[とお]して}からコメントを書[か]いた。
ctx.en: The teacher went through every one of the students' papers before writing her comments.

ctx.s: お忙[いそが]しいところ恐縮[きょうしゅく]ですが、企画書[きかくしょ]に{目[め]を通[とお]して}いただけますか。
ctx.en: I'm sorry to trouble you when you're busy, but could you take a look at the proposal?

ctx.s: メールが多[おお]すぎて、昨日[きのう]は全部[ぜんぶ]には{目[め]を通[とお]せなかった}。
ctx.en: There were too many emails, so yesterday I couldn't get through all of them.

bad.s: 展望台[てんぼうだい]から、町[まち]の景色[けしき]に{目[め]を通[とお]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I gazed at the view of the town from the observation deck)
bad.why: It is used for reading through written material, not for looking at a view or a scene.

bad.s: この資料[しりょう]を{目[め]を通[とお]して}ください。
bad.en: (meant: please look over these materials)
bad.why: The document takes ni, not o: shiryou ni me o toosu. Two o particles in one clause like this is ungrammatical.

cards.mean: to be so busy one's head spins
cards.lit: one's eyes spin: literally, to feel dizzy

use.how: In the busy sense usually 目が回るほど忙しい or 目の回るような忙しさ. It also keeps its literal meaning, to feel dizzy.

near.diff: 猫の手も借りたい stresses wanting any help at all; 目が回る only describes the frantic pace.

cards.cue: In one week you move house, start a new job and host your in-laws. Describe how frantic the week felt.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]どう？」「仕事[しごと]が多[おお]すぎて、{目[め]が回[まわ]り}そうだよ。」
ctx.en: "How are things?" "I've got so much work my head is spinning."

ctx.s: スタッフは十分[じゅうぶん]いたのに、開店[かいてん]初日[しょにち]は{目[め]が回[まわ]る}ほど忙[いそが]しかった。
ctx.en: We had plenty of staff, but even so the opening day was frantic.

ctx.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しと新[あたら]しい仕事[しごと]が重[かさ]なって、{目[め]が回[まわ]る}ような一週間[いっしゅうかん]だった。
ctx.en: Moving house and starting a new job at the same time made it a dizzying week.

ctx.s: 昼時[ひるどき]の店[みせ]は注文[ちゅうもん]が次々[つぎつぎ]に入[はい]り、{目[め]の回[まわ]る}ような忙[いそが]しさだ。
ctx.en: At lunchtime the orders keep pouring into the restaurant, and it's frantic.

ctx.s: 締[し]め切[き]り前[まえ]の編集部[へんしゅうぶ]は、{目[め]が回[まわ]る}ような慌[あわ]ただしさだった。
ctx.en: Before the deadline the editorial office was in a frenzy.

ctx.s: 双子[ふたご]の世話[せわ]に追[お]われて、{目[め]が回[まわ]る}毎日[まいにち]です。
ctx.en: Looking after twins, every day is a whirlwind.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は仕事[しごと]がなくて、{目[め]が回[まわ]る}ほど暇[ひま]だった。
bad.en: (meant: I had no work today and was bored stiff)
bad.why: In this sense it is only about being frantically busy (or literally dizzy), never about having nothing to do.

bad.s: 山[やま]の上[うえ]の美[うつく]しい景色[けしき]に{目[め]が回[まわ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was dazzled by the beautiful view from the mountain)
bad.why: Being captivated by a sight is me o ubawareru; me ga mawaru means dizziness or a frantic pace.

cards.mean: so busy that any help at all would be welcome
cards.lit: to want to borrow even the cat's paws

use.how: Describes one's own busyness, usually with ほど or くらい: 猫の手も借りたいほど忙しい. Not a way to ask a particular person for help.

near.diff: 目が回る only describes a frantic pace; 猫の手も借りたい adds that you would welcome help from anyone.
手が離せない means you can't break off from what you're doing right now; it says nothing about wanting help.

cards.cue: It's harvest time, the farm is short of workers, and the farmer says even the family pet would be useful right now. What expression fits?

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]用紙[ようし]を見[み]た途端[とたん]、覚[おぼ]えたはずの公式[こうしき]が出[で]てこず、{頭[あたま]が真[ま]っ白[しろ]になった}。

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{頭[あたま]が真[ま]っ白[しろ]な}人[ひと]なので、嘘[うそ]をつかない。

cards.mean: to get fired
cards.lit: to become a neck: the image of having one's head cut off, as in kubi o kiru

ctx.en: "What happened with your part-time job?" "I had a fight with the manager and got fired."

cards.r: くびをながくしてまつ
cards.mean: to wait eagerly and impatiently
cards.lit: to wait with one's neck stretched long, craning to see what is coming

use.how: Used for something good one looks forward to over days or months: 発売日を首を長くして待つ. Polite letters use 首を長くしてお待ちしております.

near.t: 居ても立ってもいられない
near.diff: 居ても立ってもいられない is restless agitation right now, often from worry; 首を長くして待つ is happy anticipation over a longer time.

ctx.en: The townspeople had long been eagerly awaiting the completion of the new station.

bad.s: 来週[らいしゅう]の歯医者[はいしゃ]の予約[よやく]が怖[こわ]くて、{首[くび]を長[なが]くして待[ま]って}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I'm dreading next week's dentist appointment)

bad.s: 焦[あせ]らずに、{首[くび]を長[なが]くして待[ま]ちましょう}。
bad.en: (meant: let's wait patiently and calmly)
bad.why: It means impatient eagerness, not calm patience; for waiting patiently say kinaga ni matsu.

cards.mean: to be relieved of a burden of responsibility
cards.lit: the load on one's shoulders comes down

use.how: Said when a duty, role or task one was responsible for is finished or handed over: 発表が終わって肩の荷が下りた. The transitive form is 肩の荷を下ろす.

near.diff: 胸をなで下ろす is relief that a feared outcome did not happen; 肩の荷が下りる is relief at being done with a responsibility.
荷が重い says a responsibility is too heavy for you; 肩の荷が下りる is the relief when it is over.

cards.cue: For a year you were in charge of organising the school reunion. The event went well and you have handed the job to someone else. How do you feel?

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]の役[やく]を後輩[こうはい]に引[ひ]き継[つ]いで、{肩[かた]の荷[に]が下[お]りた}気分[きぶん]だ。
ctx.en: Having handed the club captaincy to a junior, I feel as if a burden has been lifted.

ctx.s: 娘[むすめ]の結婚式[けっこんしき]が終[お]わり、父[ちち]は{肩[かた]の荷[に]が下[お]りた}ような顔[かお]をしていた。
ctx.en: After his daughter's wedding, my father looked like a man relieved of a great burden.

ctx.s: 借金[しゃっきん]を全部[ぜんぶ]返[かえ]し終[お]えて、{肩[かた]の荷[に]が下[お]りる}思[おも]いがした。
ctx.en: When I had paid back all the debt, I felt a heavy load come off my shoulders.

ctx.s: 大会[たいかい]の幹事[かんじ]が終[お]わるまでは、なかなか{肩[かた]の荷[に]が下[お]りない}。

bad.s: マッサージに行[い]ったら、{肩[かた]の荷[に]が下[お]りて}肩[かた]が軽[かる]くなった。
bad.en: (meant: after a massage my stiff shoulders felt lighter)
bad.why: The idiom is about responsibility, not physical stiffness; say kata ga karuku natta or katakori ga toreta.

bad.s: 仕事[しごと]が終[お]わって、やっと{肩[かた]の荷[に]を下[お]りた}。
bad.en: (meant: the work is done and the burden is off me)
bad.why: Oriru is intransitive and takes ga: kata no ni ga orita, or transitively kata no ni o oroshita.

cards.mean: to talk frankly, heart to heart
cards.lit: to split open one's belly and talk, showing what is inside

use.how: Said of two or more people speaking their true feelings openly, often to clear up a problem or build trust: 一度腹を割って話そう.

near.diff: 気が置けない describes a friend you can relax with; 腹を割って話す is the act of an honest, open conversation.
気を許す is letting your guard down with someone; 腹を割って話す is deliberately saying what you really think.

cards.cue: Two colleagues have been quietly resentful of each other for weeks. One suggests going for a drink and putting all their real feelings on the table. What do they propose?

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]、{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]そう}。

ctx.s: 夫婦[ふうふ]で{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]し合[あ]ったら}、誤解[ごかい]が解[と]けた。
ctx.en: When the couple talked it out frankly, the misunderstanding was cleared up.

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]は上司[じょうし]も部下[ぶか]もなしです。{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]しましょう}。」

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]とは、学生時代[がくせいじだい]に{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]せる}仲[なか]になった。

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]は社員[しゃいん]と{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]す}場[ば]を設[もう]けた。
ctx.en: The company president set up a forum where he and the staff could talk frankly.

ctx.s: お互[たが]いに{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]さない}と、この問題[もんだい]は解決[かいけつ]しない。
ctx.en: Unless we both speak honestly, this problem will never be solved.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はいつも{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]す}ので、よく人[ひと]を怒[おこ]らせる。
bad.en: (meant: he is blunt and often offends people)

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]の夜[よる]、日記[にっき]に{腹[はら]を割[わ]って話[はな]した}。
bad.en: (meant: last night I wrote my true feelings in my diary)
bad.why: It needs a person to talk with; you cannot open your heart this way to a diary.

cards.mean: to hold others back, to be a drag on the team
cards.lit: to pull at someone's leg so they cannot move forward

use.how: Xの足を引っ張る: a person who drags a group down, someone who sabotages a rival, or a factor that hurts results (円安が業績の足を引っ張る).

near.diff: 水を差す spoils a mood or a plan at one moment; 足を引っ張る holds back someone's progress or performance.
揚げ足を取る is pouncing on small slips in what someone says; 足を引っ張る is hindering their success.

cards.cue: In a relay race your slow leg cost your team first place, and you apologise to your teammates. What did you do to them?

bad.s: 嫌[いや]がる弟[おとうと]の{足[あし]を引[ひ]っ張[ぱ]って}、パーティーに連[つ]れて行[い]った。
bad.en: (meant: I dragged my reluctant brother along to the party)

cards.mean: to be humble and modest in manner

near.diff: 頭が下がる is the respect you feel for someone's effort; 腰が低い describes a person's humble manner toward others.

cards.mean: (of a task) to be laborious, hard work

ctx.s: 慣[な]れない敬語[けいご]でメールを書[か]くのは、思[おも]ったより{骨[ほね]が折[お]れます}ね。

cards.mean: to cut corners, to do a sloppy job
cards.lit: to pull one's hands out of the work

ctx.en: Even though my opponent was a child, I didn't go easy on him and played all out.

ctx.s: 忙[いそが]しい日[ひ]くらい、夕食[ゆうしょく]の{手[て]を抜[ぬ]いて}もいいと思[おも]う。

bad.en: (meant: I lost concentration for a moment while driving and nearly crashed)

cards.mean: to require a lot of care or effort
cards.lit: it takes up one's hands

near.diff: 手を焼く stresses frustration at someone you cannot manage; 手がかかる just says something needs a lot of care.
骨が折れる says one task is laborious; 手がかかる is care or work that something keeps needing.

ctx.s: この料理[りょうり]は{手[て]がかかる}けど、とてもおいしい。

ctx.s: 「犬[いぬ]と猫[ねこ]、どっちが{手[て]がかからない}?」
ctx.en: "Which needs less looking after, a dog or a cat?"

ctx.s: {手[て]のかかる}子[こ]ほどかわいいと言[い]われる。

ctx.s: 古[ふる]い家[いえ]は修理[しゅうり]に{手[て]がかかる}ので、維持費[いじひ]も高[たか]い。
ctx.en: An old house takes a lot of repair work, so the upkeep is expensive.

ctx.s: この花[はな]は水[みず]やりに{手[て]がかからない}ので、初心者[しょしんしゃ]でも育[そだ]てやすい。
ctx.en: This flower needs little watering or care, so even beginners find it easy to grow.

bad.s: 家[いえ]から駅[えき]まで三十分[さんじっぷん]{手[て]がかかる}。
bad.en: (meant: it takes thirty minutes from my house to the station)

bad.en: (meant: my hands are full with cooking, so I can't answer the phone)
bad.why: Being too busy to stop is te ga hanasenai; te ga kakaru describes what needs care, not your being busy.

cards.mean: to take the trouble to go somewhere in person
cards.lit: to carry one's own feet to a place

use.how: Going somewhere on purpose, often repeatedly or with effort: 何度も現場に足を運ぶ. Polite thanks: 足をお運びいただき, ありがとうございます.

near.diff: 顔を出す is briefly showing up at a gathering; 足を運ぶ stresses the effort of going to a place in person.

cards.cue: Instead of reading online reviews, the writer visited the little mountain inn three times before recommending it. What did she do?

ctx.s: 雨[あめ]の中[なか]、わざわざ{足[あし]を運[はこ]んで}くれてありがとう。
ctx.en: Thank you for taking the trouble to come in the rain.

ctx.s: 「あの美術館[びじゅつかん]、行[い]ったことある?」「うん、もう三回[さんかい]も{足[あし]を運[はこ]んだ}よ。」
ctx.en: "Have you been to that art museum?" "Yes, I've already been there three times."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は契約[けいやく]を取[と]るため、何度[なんど]も客先[きゃくさき]に{足[あし]を運[はこ]んだ}。
ctx.en: To win the contract, he visited the client's office again and again.

ctx.s: ネットで調[しら]べるだけでなく、実際[じっさい]に現地[げんち]へ{足[あし]を運[はこ]んで}みることが大切[たいせつ]だ。
ctx.en: It's important not just to search online but to actually go to the place yourself.

ctx.s: 地元[じもと]の商店街[しょうてんがい]にも、たまには{足[あし]を運[はこ]んで}ください。
ctx.en: Please make the trip to your local shopping street once in a while, too.

ctx.s: 本日[ほんじつ]はお忙[いそが]しい中[なか]、{足[あし]をお運[はこ]び}いただき、誠[まこと]にありがとうございます。
ctx.en: Thank you very much for taking the time to come here today despite your busy schedule.

bad.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの荷物[にもつ]を、トラックで新[あたら]しい家[いえ]に{足[あし]を運[はこ]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I carried the moving boxes to the new house by truck)
bad.why: Here hakobu is about your own feet, so it cannot take luggage as its object; say nimotsu o hakonda.

bad.s: 毎朝[まいあさ]、電車[でんしゃ]で会社[かいしゃ]に{足[あし]を運[はこ]んで}いる。
bad.en: (meant: every morning I commute to the office by train)
bad.why: It implies a special trip made on purpose, not a daily routine; just say kaisha ni kayotte iru.

cards.mean: to get involved in, to try one's hand at
cards.lit: to reach one's hand out toward something

use.how: Xに手を出す: to start doing something new, often risky or outside one's field (株に手を出す). It can also mean to hit someone (先に手を出す).

near.diff: 口を出す is interfering with words in others' business; 手を出す is getting into an activity yourself.
首を突っ込む is poking into matters that are not yours; 手を出す is taking up an activity, often a risky one.

cards.cue: A cautious accountant who never gambled suddenly started buying cryptocurrency after a friend's tip. What did he do with crypto?

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は最近[さいきん]、株[かぶ]に{手[て]を出[だ]した}。
ctx.en: My father recently started dabbling in stocks.

ctx.s: 借金[しゃっきん]してまでギャンブルに{手[て]を出[だ]す}のはやめなさい。
ctx.en: Don't go borrowing money to get into gambling.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は料理[りょうり]、陶芸[とうげい]、ヨガと、色々[いろいろ]な趣味[しゅみ]に{手[て]を出[だ]して}いる。
ctx.en: She has tried her hand at all sorts of hobbies: cooking, pottery, yoga.

ctx.s: 「専門外[せんもんがい]の仕事[しごと]には、安易[あんい]に{手[て]を出[だ]さない}ほうがいい。」
ctx.en: "You shouldn't casually take on work outside your field."

ctx.s: ダイエット中[ちゅう]なのに、つい夜中[よなか]にお菓子[かし]に{手[て]を出[だ]して}しまった。
ctx.en: I'm on a diet, but late at night I couldn't stop myself reaching for the snacks.

ctx.s: その会社[かいしゃ]は不動産[ふどうさん]事業[じぎょう]にまで{手[て]を出[だ]して}失敗[しっぱい]した。

bad.s: 質問[しつもん]がある人[ひと]は{手[て]を出[だ]して}ください。
bad.en: (meant: anyone with a question, please raise your hand)
bad.why: Raising a hand in class is te o ageru; te o dashite sounds like 'hold out your hand'.

cards.mean: to be beyond one's means or ability
cards.lit: the hand does not come out: you cannot even reach for it

use.how: Predicate, often after 高くて or 難しくて: 高くて手が出ない. Said of a price you cannot afford or a problem you cannot even begin.

near.diff: 手に負えない is a person or situation you cannot control; 手が出ない is something you cannot afford or cannot even attempt.

cards.cue: A watch in a shop window costs three months of your salary. How do you say there is no way you could buy it?

ctx.s: このバッグは高[たか]すぎて、とても{手[て]が出[で]ない}。
ctx.en: This bag is far too expensive; there's no way I can buy it.

ctx.s: 都心[としん]のマンションは、私[わたし]たちの給料[きゅうりょう]では{手[て]が出[で]ない}よ。
ctx.en: Flats in the city centre are out of reach on our salaries.

ctx.s: 「新[あたら]しいパソコン、買[か]わないの？」「欲[ほ]しいけど、今[いま]は{手[て]が出[で]ない}んだ。」
ctx.en: "Aren't you buying a new computer?" "I'd like one, but I can't afford it right now."

ctx.s: 英語[えいご]の原書[げんしょ]は難[むずか]しそうで、なかなか{手[て]が出[で]ない}。
ctx.en: Books in the original English look so hard that I can never bring myself to pick one up.

ctx.s: 円安[えんやす]のせいで、輸入品[ゆにゅうひん]にはなかなか{手[て]が出[で]なく}なった。
ctx.en: Because of the weak yen, imported goods have become hard to afford.

ctx.s: 学生[がくせい]には{手[て]が出[で]ない}値段[ねだん]だが、品質[ひんしつ]は確[たし]かだ。
ctx.en: The price is beyond a student's budget, but the quality is genuine.

bad.s: この子[こ]はいたずらばかりで、親[おや]も{手[て]が出[で]ない}。
bad.en: (meant: this child is so naughty even his parents can't handle him)

bad.s: 忙[いそが]しくて、今日[きょう]は電話[でんわ]に{手[て]が出[で]ない}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm too busy to answer the phone today)

cards.mean: to become free, to have one's hands free
cards.lit: the hands become empty

use.how: Said of a person who has finished a task and is free for another: 手が空いたら手伝って. Common in workplace requests.

near.diff: 手が離せない is being too busy to stop what you are doing; 手が空く is the moment you become free.

cards.cue: You need help carrying boxes and ask a coworker to come over once they have finished what they are doing.

ctx.s: {手[て]が空[あ]いたら}、ちょっと手伝[てつだ]ってくれる？
ctx.en: When you're free, could you give me a hand?

ctx.s: 今[いま]、{手[て]が空[あ]いて}いる人[ひと]はいますか。
ctx.en: Is anyone free at the moment?

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]が終[お]わって{手[て]が空[あ]いた}ので、メールの返事[へんじ]を書[か]いた。
ctx.en: The meeting ended and I was free, so I answered my emails.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]の{手[て]が空[あ]く}のを待[ま]って、質問[しつもん]した。
ctx.en: I waited until the shop assistant was free, then asked my question.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもが昼寝[ひるね]をしている間[あいだ]だけ、やっと{手[て]が空[あ]く}。
ctx.en: Only while the baby naps do I finally get a moment free.

ctx.s: 担当者[たんとうしゃ]の{手[て]が空[あ]き}次第[しだい]、折[お]り返[かえ]しお電話[でんわ]いたします。
ctx.en: The person in charge will call you back as soon as they are free.

bad.s: このいす、{手[て]が空[あ]いて}いますか。
bad.en: (meant: is this chair free?)

bad.s: お土産[みやげ]を忘[わす]れて、{手[て]が空[あ]いた}まま友達[ともだち]の家[いえ]に行[い]った。
