cards.mean: to put one's heart into something
cards.lit: to pack one's heart into something

use.how: Mostly as 心を込めて before a verb of making, giving or performing: 心を込めて作る. Said of care and feeling put in for someone.

near.diff: 精を出す is working hard and diligently; 心を込める is putting feeling and care into something made or done for someone.

cards.cue: Your grandmother spent the evening making her grandson's favourite dish by hand, thinking of him all the while. How did she make it?

ctx.s: 母[はは]のために、{心[こころ]を込[こ]めて}ケーキを焼[や]いた。
ctx.en: I baked a cake for my mother with all my heart.

ctx.s: {心[こころ]を込[こ]めて}書[か]いた手紙[てがみ]は、字[じ]が下手[へた]でも伝[つた]わる。
ctx.en: A letter written with feeling gets through even if the handwriting is poor.

ctx.s: 「これ、手作[てづく]りなの？」「うん、一[ひと]つ一[ひと]つ{心[こころ]を込[こ]めて}編[あ]んだんだ。」
ctx.en: "Did you make this yourself?" "Yes, I knitted every one of them with love."

ctx.s: 当店[とうてん]では、スタッフが{心[こころ]を込[こ]めて}おもてなしいたします。
ctx.en: At our shop, our staff will look after you with heartfelt care.

ctx.s: 最後[さいご]の曲[きょく]は、亡[な]くなった祖父[そふ]を思[おも]って{心[こころ]を込[こ]めて}歌[うた]った。

ctx.s: 卒業式[そつぎょうしき]で、校長[こうちょう]は{心[こころ]を込[こ]めた}言葉[ことば]を生徒[せいと]たちに贈[おく]った。

bad.s: 毎日[まいにち]勉強[べんきょう]して、試験[しけん]に{心[こころ]を込[こ]めて}合格[ごうかく]した。
bad.en: (meant: I studied every day and passed the exam through dedication)

bad.en: (meant: my brother is so absorbed in games that he never studies)
bad.why: Being absorbed in something is muchuu ni naru; this idiom is putting feeling into a gift or a task for others.

cards.mean: to lose the will to keep going
cards.lit: one's heart snaps like a stick

use.how: Casual, modern. Predicate, often 心が折れそう or もう心が折れた, after repeated setbacks or a task that feels endless.

near.diff: 弱音を吐く is saying out loud that you cannot cope; 心が折れる is actually losing the will to go on.

cards.mean: to be generous and broad-minded
cards.lit: to have a wide heart

near.diff: 気前がいい is being free with money and gifts; 心が広い is tolerance, forgiving and accepting others.

cards.cue: Your friend waited an hour for you in the rain and just laughed it off. What do you say about your friend?

ctx.s: 私[わたし]の失敗[しっぱい]を笑[わら]って許[ゆる]してくれるなんて、{心[こころ]が広[ひろ]い}ね。

ctx.en: Our department head is generous-hearted and doesn't get angry even at new staff's mistakes.

ctx.en: If I'd been a bit more tolerant, we wouldn't have fought over something so small.

ctx.s: 窓[まど]を割[わ]った近所[きんじょ]の子[こ]を、祖父[そふ]は「子[こ]どものことだから」と許[ゆる]した。{心[こころ]が広[ひろ]い}人[ひと]だ。
ctx.en: My grandfather forgave the neighbour's child who broke our window, saying kids will be kids. He is a big-hearted man.

bad.en: (meant: my new room is spacious and very comfortable)

bad.en: (meant: he is rich and generous, so he always treats everyone)
bad.why: Spending freely on others is kimae ga ii; this idiom means tolerant and forgiving, not open-handed with money.

cards.mean: to take a breather
cards.lit: to take one breath

use.how: Predicate: rest briefly or feel relief once a busy stretch is over, often with やっと or ようやく: やっと一息つける.

near.diff: 手が空く is being free to take on other work; 一息つく is pausing to rest and recover.

cards.cue: After three hours of carrying boxes nonstop, you finally sit down with a cold drink before carrying on.

ctx.en: My work reached a good stopping point, so I had a coffee and took a breather.

ctx.s: ちょっと{一息[ひといき]つこう}か。もう二時間[にじかん]も歩[ある]いているよ。
ctx.en: Shall we take a short break? We've been walking for two hours.

ctx.s: 「引[ひ]っ越[こ]し、終[お]わった？」「うん、やっと{一息[ひといき]つける}よ。」
ctx.en: "Is the move done?" "Yes, at last I can catch my breath."

ctx.s: 山頂[さんちょう]に着[つ]いた登山者[とざんしゃ]たちは、岩[いわ]に腰[こし]を下[お]ろして{一息[ひといき]ついた}。
ctx.en: Reaching the summit, the climbers sat down on a rock and caught their breath.

bad.en: (meant: I saw my test score and sighed in disappointment)

cards.mean: to hide one's true nature behind a meek front
cards.lit: to put on a cat: to look as quiet and tame as a cat

use.how: Predicate, mostly 猫をかぶっている: acting quiet and well-behaved in front of others while being bolder or rougher at heart. Often teasing.

cards.cue: Your loud, bossy little sister turns polite and shy the moment her teacher comes to visit. What is she doing?

ctx.s: 妹[いもうと]は先生[せんせい]の前[まえ]だと{猫[ねこ]をかぶって}いる。
ctx.en: My little sister acts all meek in front of her teacher.

ctx.s: うちの息子[むすこ]、よそでは{猫[ねこ]をかぶって}おとなしいらしい。
ctx.en: Apparently our son plays the good boy and stays quiet when he's away from home.

ctx.s: 「初[はじ]めて会[あ]った時[とき]は静[しず]かな人[ひと]だと思[おも]った。」「あれは{猫[ねこ]をかぶって}たんだよ。」
ctx.en: "When I first met her I thought she was quiet." "She was just putting on an act."

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいクラスでは、最初[さいしょ]の一週間[いっしゅうかん]だけ{猫[ねこ]をかぶって}いた。
ctx.en: In my new class I put on a polite, quiet act for the first week only.

ctx.s: 結婚[けっこん]して三[さん]か月[げつ]、夫[おっと]はもう{猫[ねこ]をかぶる}のをやめたようだ。
ctx.en: Three months into our marriage, my husband seems to have dropped his best behaviour.

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]では{猫[ねこ]をかぶらず}、普段[ふだん]の自分[じぶん]を見[み]せたほうがいい。
ctx.en: In an interview it's better not to put on a front but to show your usual self.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はいつも乱暴[らんぼう]で、みんなの前[まえ]で{猫[ねこ]をかぶって}いる。
bad.en: (meant: he is always rough and shows it openly in front of everyone)
bad.why: It means hiding a bold or rough nature behind a gentle front, not showing that nature openly.

bad.s: ハロウィンで{猫[ねこ]をかぶって}パーティーに行[い]った。
bad.en: (meant: I dressed up as a cat for a Halloween party)
bad.why: It is only figurative, about hiding one's nature; dressing up as a cat is neko no kasou o suru.

cards.mean: to forgive and forget
cards.lit: to let something float away on the water

use.how: Takes a past quarrel or wrong as its object: 過去のことは水に流そう. Said by the wronged side, or asked for: 水に流してください.

near.diff: 水の泡 is effort wasted; 水に流す is choosing to forget a past quarrel or wrong.

cards.cue: Two old friends who fell out years ago meet again and agree to put the old quarrel behind them for good.

ctx.s: 昔[むかし]のことは{水[みず]に流[なが]して}、また仲良[なかよ]くしよう。
ctx.en: Let's put the past behind us and be friends again.

ctx.s: この間[あいだ]の喧嘩[けんか]は、もう{水[みず]に流[なが]した}よ。
ctx.en: I've already forgotten about our fight the other day.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]にごめん。」「わかった。今回[こんかい]だけは{水[みず]に流[なが]す}よ。」
ctx.en: "I'm really sorry." "All right. Just this once, I'll let it go."

ctx.s: あれだけひどいことを言[い]われたら、簡単[かんたん]には{水[みず]に流[なが]せない}。
ctx.en: After being told such cruel things, I can't just forgive and forget.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]と兄[あに]は十年[じゅうねん]ぶりに会[あ]い、わだかまりを{水[みず]に流[なが]した}。
ctx.en: My father and brother met for the first time in ten years and let go of their old bad feeling.

ctx.s: 両社[りょうしゃ]は過去[かこ]の対立[たいりつ]を{水[みず]に流[なが]し}、共同開発[きょうどうかいはつ]に合意[ごうい]した。
ctx.en: The two companies put their past conflict behind them and agreed to joint development.

bad.s: 試合[しあい]に負[ま]けて、一年[いちねん]の努力[どりょく]が{水[みず]に流[なが]れた}。
bad.en: (meant: we lost the match and a year of effort came to nothing)
bad.why: Wasted effort is mizu no awa ni natta; this idiom is about forgiving a past wrong.

bad.s: 人[ひと]の名前[なまえ]をすぐ{水[みず]に流[なが]して}しまう。
bad.en: (meant: I forget people's names right away)
bad.why: Forgetting something by accident is wasureru; this idiom is deliberately letting go of a past quarrel or wrong.

cards.mean: all one's effort come to nothing
cards.lit: a bubble on the water, gone in an instant

use.how: Noun, mostly 〜が水の泡になる or 〜が水の泡だ, with effort, preparation or work as the subject: 努力が水の泡になった.

near.diff: 水に流す is forgiving a past wrong; 水の泡 is effort that has been wasted.

cards.cue: Your laptop dies and three days of unsaved work on a report vanish with it.

ctx.s: パソコンが壊[こわ]れて、三日分[みっかぶん]の作業[さぎょう]が{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}になった。
ctx.en: My computer broke and three days' work went down the drain.

ctx.s: ここでやめたら、今[いま]までの練習[れんしゅう]が{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}だよ。
ctx.en: If you quit now, all your practice so far will be wasted.

ctx.s: 「ダイエット中[ちゅう]なのに、ケーキ食[た]べちゃった。」「一[いっ]か月[げつ]の努力[どりょく]が{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}じゃん。」
ctx.en: "I'm on a diet, but I ate cake." "There goes a month of effort!"

ctx.s: 雨[あめ]で祭[まつ]りが中止[ちゅうし]になり、準備[じゅんび]がすべて{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}となった。
ctx.en: The festival was cancelled because of rain, and all the preparations came to nothing.

ctx.s: 一[ひと]つの不祥事[ふしょうじ]で、長年[ながねん]築[きず]いてきた信頼[しんらい]が{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}になりかねない。
ctx.en: A single scandal could wipe out trust built up over many years.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の一言[ひとこと]で、交渉[こうしょう]チームの苦労[くろう]は{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}と消[き]えた。
ctx.en: With one remark from the company president, all the negotiating team's hard work vanished.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]のせいで、計画[けいかく]が{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}した。
bad.en: (meant: because of the rain, the plan came to nothing)
bad.why: It is a noun and cannot take suru; say mizu no awa ni natta.

bad.s: 全然[ぜんぜん]勉強[べんきょう]しなかったので、テストは{水[みず]の泡[あわ]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: I didn't study at all, so the test went badly)
bad.why: It needs effort that was wasted; with no effort there is nothing to come to nothing. Say tesuto wa hidokatta.

cards.mean: to hold a grudge
cards.lit: to keep something at the root, deep where it stays

use.how: Takes the past slight as its object: 〜を根に持つ, often まだ根に持っている. Said of resentment kept long after the event.

near.diff: 腹が立つ is anger felt in the moment; 根に持つ is resentment kept long afterwards.

cards.cue: A coworker still will not speak to you because you forgot to invite them to lunch two years ago.

ctx.s: あの時[とき]のこと、まだ{根[ね]に持[も]って}るの？
ctx.en: Are you still holding that against me?

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は小[ちい]さなことでもずっと{根[ね]に持[も]つ}タイプだ。
ctx.en: He's the type who holds a grudge even over little things.

ctx.s: 「誕生日[たんじょうび]を忘[わす]れたこと、もう怒[おこ]ってない？」「怒[おこ]ってないけど、ちょっと{根[ね]に持[も]って}る。」
ctx.en: "Are you still angry that I forgot your birthday?" "I'm not angry, but I haven't quite forgotten it."

ctx.s: 注意[ちゅうい]されたことを{根[ね]に持[も]たない}のが、彼女[かのじょ]のいいところだ。
ctx.en: What's good about her is that she doesn't hold it against you when she's told off.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]で反則[はんそく]をされたのを{根[ね]に持[も]って}、彼[かれ]はその選手[せんしゅ]と口[くち]をきかなくなった。
ctx.en: Still bitter about being fouled in the match, he stopped speaking to that player.

ctx.s: 昇進[しょうしん]を逃[のが]したことを{根[ね]に持[も]ち}、彼[かれ]は上司[じょうし]に冷[つめ]たく当[あ]たるようになった。
ctx.en: Resentful at being passed over for promotion, he started treating his boss coldly.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は子[こ]どもの頃[ころ]の夢[ゆめ]を{根[ね]に持[も]って}頑張[がんば]っている。
bad.en: (meant: he works hard, holding on to his childhood dream)
bad.why: It is only for resentment over a past slight; cherishing a dream is yume o mune ni idaku.

bad.s: 父[ちち]はすぐ{根[ね]に持[も]つ}けど、五分[ごふん]で忘[わす]れる。
bad.en: (meant: my father flares up quickly but forgets about it in five minutes)
bad.why: It means lasting resentment, the opposite of anger that passes; a quick temper is sugu katto naru.

cards.mean: to get carried away, to get cocky
cards.lit: to ride the rhythm: choushi is first the pitch and tempo of music

use.how: Used as a verb phrase about someone who, encouraged by praise, luck or a good mood, goes too far: 調子に乗るな. Said to equals, juniors or about oneself.

near.diff: 天狗になる is lasting conceit after success; 調子に乗る is going too far in the moment, often in behaviour rather than attitude.

cards.cue: Your friend won three games in a row, started boasting and raising the stakes, and then lost everything. What happened?

ctx.s: みんなが笑[わら]ったからって、{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]って}ふざけすぎるなよ。
ctx.en: Just because everyone laughed, don't get carried away and fool around too much.

ctx.s: お酒[さけ]が入[はい]ると、父[ちち]はすぐ{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]って}歌[うた]い出[だ]す。
ctx.en: Once he's had a drink, my father gets carried away and starts singing.

ctx.s: 「すみません、ちょっと{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]りすぎ}ました。」
ctx.en: "I'm sorry, I got a bit carried away."

ctx.s: 勝[か]ち続[つづ]けて{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]った}彼[かれ]は、最後[さいご]に大負[おおま]けした。
ctx.en: Carried away by his winning streak, he lost big in the end.

ctx.s: 安[やす]いからと{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]って}買[か]い物[もの]をしたら、カードの請求[せいきゅう]がすごい額[がく]になった。
ctx.en: I got carried away shopping because things were cheap, and my card bill came to a huge amount.

ctx.s: お客[きゃく]さんが来[き]て{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]った}子[こ]どもたちは、部屋中[へやじゅう]を走[はし]り回[まわ]った。
ctx.en: Excited by the visitors, the children got carried away and ran all over the room.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は体[からだ]の{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]って}いるので、たくさん走[はし]れます。
bad.en: (meant: I'm in good shape today, so I can run a lot)
bad.why: Being in good health is choushi ga ii. This idiom means going too far out of overconfidence.

bad.s: お客様[きゃくさま]が{調子[ちょうし]に乗[の]って}、たくさん買[か]ってくださいました。
bad.en: (meant: the customer was in a good mood and kindly bought a lot)
bad.why: It is a criticism, so saying it about a customer you are thanking is insulting and clashes with the honorifics.

cards.mean: to be out of the question, not worth discussing
cards.lit: it does not even become a conversation

use.how: Used as a predicate to dismiss an offer, a plan or a person's performance as too poor to consider: これでは話にならない.

near.diff: 話が違う protests that a promise was broken; 話にならない dismisses something as too poor or absurd to discuss at all.

cards.cue: A buyer offers a tenth of what your used car is worth. You refuse even to negotiate. What do you tell them?

ctx.s: こんな安[やす]い値段[ねだん]じゃ{話[はなし]にならない}よ。
ctx.en: At a price this low, there's nothing to talk about.

ctx.s: 準備[じゅんび]もしないで面接[めんせつ]に行[い]くなんて、{話[はなし]にならない}。
ctx.en: Going to an interview without preparing at all is out of the question.

ctx.s: 「三日[みっか]で全部[ぜんぶ]作[つく]れ？そんなの{話[はなし]になりません}よ。」
ctx.en: "Build the whole thing in three days? That's simply out of the question."

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]は最初[さいしょ]から怒鳴[どな]ってばかりで、まるで{話[はなし]にならなかった}。
ctx.en: He did nothing but shout from the start, so no real discussion was possible.

ctx.s: プロの彼[かれ]と比[くら]べたら、私[わたし]の腕[うで]なんて{話[はなし]にならない}。
ctx.en: Compared with him, a professional, my skill isn't even worth mentioning.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は企画書[きかくしょ]を読[よ]んで、「これでは{話[はなし]にならない}」と突[つ]き返[かえ]した。
ctx.en: The manager read the proposal and handed it back, saying, "This is nowhere near good enough."

bad.s: この映画[えいが]は{話[はなし]にならない}ほど面白[おもしろ]かった。
bad.en: (meant: the film was indescribably good)
bad.why: It is purely negative. For something too good for words, say kotoba ni naranai hodo.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]とは趣味[しゅみ]が違[ちが]うので、{話[はなし]にならない}。
bad.en: (meant: we have different hobbies, so we have nothing to talk about)
bad.why: Having nothing in common to talk about is hanashi ga awanai. This idiom dismisses something as unacceptable.

cards.mean: that is not what was agreed
cards.lit: the story is different (from what I was told)

use.how: A protest when terms change after a promise: 話が違うじゃないか. 話が違ってくる (that changes things) is a separate, neutral use.

near.diff: 話にならない dismisses an offer as absurd; 話が違う complains that what you get differs from what was promised.

cards.cue: Your landlord promised the rent would stay the same, and now announces a rise. How do you protest?

ctx.s: 「えっ、休[やす]みは週[しゅう]に二日[ふつか]って言[い]ったじゃないですか。{話[はなし]が違[ちが]います}よ。」
ctx.en: "What? You said I'd get two days off a week. That's not what we agreed."

ctx.s: 「無料[むりょう]って書[か]いてあったのに、お金[かね]を取[と]るなんて{話[はなし]が違[ちが]う}じゃないか。」
ctx.en: "It said free, and now you're charging me? That's not what you told us."

ctx.s: 手伝[てつだ]うだけと聞[き]いて来[き]たのに、全部[ぜんぶ]任[まか]されるとは{話[はなし]が違[ちが]う}。
ctx.en: I came because I was told I'd just be helping. Being left with the whole job isn't what was agreed.

ctx.s: 旅行会社[りょこうがいしゃ]では海[うみ]の見[み]える部屋[へや]だと言[い]われたのに、{話[はなし]が違[ちが]う}。
ctx.en: The travel agent told us we'd have a sea view room. This isn't what they promised.

ctx.s: 工事[こうじ]が終[お]わってから追加料金[ついかりょうきん]を請求[せいきゅう]され、客[きゃく]は{話[はなし]が違[ちが]う}と怒[おこ]った。
ctx.en: Billed an extra fee after the work was done, the customer angrily said it was not what had been agreed.

ctx.s: 入社[にゅうしゃ]してみたら給料[きゅうりょう]が聞[き]いていたより安[やす]く、{話[はなし]が違[ちが]う}と思[おも]った。
ctx.en: When I joined, the pay was lower than I'd been told, and I felt I'd been misled.

bad.s: テストの計算[けいさん]が{話[はなし]が違[ちが]って}いて、点[てん]が低[ひく]かった。
bad.en: (meant: my calculations in the test were wrong, so my score was low)
bad.why: A wrong answer is machigatte iru. This idiom is about a promise or agreement not being kept.

bad.s: 日本語[にほんご]と英語[えいご]は{話[はなし]が違[ちが]う}。
bad.en: (meant: Japanese and English are spoken differently)
bad.why: Two languages simply differ (chigau). The idiom protests a broken promise, not a difference.

cards.mean: to have plenty in common to talk about
cards.lit: our talk fits together

use.how: Used with と: 彼とは話が合う. Said about people whose shared interests or experiences make conversation easy; the negative 話が合わない is common too.

near.diff: 気が合う is a match of temperament; 話が合う is about shared interests and topics that keep a conversation going.

cards.cue: At a party you meet someone who reads the same manga and supports the same team, and you chat for hours. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]とは好[す]きな音楽[おんがく]が同[おな]じで、{話[はなし]が合[あ]う}。
ctx.en: She and I like the same music, so we always have lots to talk about.

ctx.s: 同[おな]じ年[とし]の子[こ]どもがいるママ友[とも]とは、自然[しぜん]と{話[はなし]が合[あ]う}。
ctx.en: With other mums whose kids are the same age, conversation just flows naturally.

ctx.s: 「新[あたら]しい部署[ぶしょ]の人[ひと]たちとは{話[はなし]が合[あ]い}そう？」
ctx.en: "Do you think you'll have much in common with the people in your new department?"

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]と私[わたし]は釣[つ]りが趣味[しゅみ]なので、年[とし]は離[はな]れていても{話[はなし]が合[あ]う}。
ctx.en: My grandfather and I both love fishing, so despite the age gap we never run out of things to talk about.

ctx.s: 世代[せだい]が違[ちが]うせいか、職場[しょくば]の若[わか]い人[ひと]とはなかなか{話[はなし]が合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: Maybe it's the generation gap, but I rarely find much to talk about with the young people at work.

ctx.s: 初[はじ]めて会[あ]ったのに好[す]きな作家[さっか]が同[おな]じで{話[はなし]が合[あ]い}、三時間[さんじかん]もしゃべっていた。
ctx.en: We'd only just met, but we loved the same author and had so much to talk about that we chatted for three hours.

bad.s: この服[ふく]は私[わたし]に{話[はなし]が合[あ]う}と思[おも]う。
bad.en: (meant: I think these clothes suit me)
bad.why: Clothes suiting someone is niau. This idiom is only about people who enjoy talking together.

bad.s: この二[ふた]つの数字[すうじ]は{話[はなし]が合[あ]わない}。
bad.en: (meant: these two figures don't match)
bad.why: Figures not matching is suuji ga awanai. The hanashi here is talk between people, not data.

cards.mean: to complain that one cannot cope
cards.lit: to spit out weak sounds

use.how: Used as a verb phrase for saying discouraged things like もう無理 when something is hard. Often negative or prohibitive: 弱音を吐かない, 弱音を吐くな.

near.diff: 音を上げる is to give in and admit you cannot go on; 弱音を吐く is voicing discouragement, perhaps while carrying on.

cards.cue: Halfway through a hard training camp, a teammate keeps saying 'I can't do this, I'm not strong enough' but keeps going. What are they doing?

ctx.s: つらくても、彼[かれ]は一度[いちど]も{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]かなかった}。
ctx.en: However hard it got, he never once complained that he couldn't take it.

ctx.s: 「もう無理[むり]」なんて{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]く}のはまだ早[はや]いよ。
ctx.en: It's too early to be saying "I can't do this any more."

ctx.s: 「たまには{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]いて}もいいんだよ。」
ctx.en: "It's all right to admit you're struggling once in a while."

ctx.s: 練習[れんしゅう]が厳[きび]しくて、つい母[はは]に電話[でんわ]で{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]いて}しまった。
ctx.en: Training was so tough that I ended up telling my mother on the phone that I couldn't cope.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は選手[せんしゅ]たちに「試合中[しあいちゅう]に{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]く}な」と言[い]った。
ctx.en: The coach told the players, "No saying you can't do it during the match."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の頃[ころ]は毎晩[まいばん]のように{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]いて}いた彼女[かのじょ]が、今[いま]では立派[りっぱ]なリーダーだ。
ctx.en: She used to say almost every night that she couldn't cope when she was new; now she is a fine leader.

bad.s: 料理[りょうり]がまずかったので、店員[てんいん]に{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]いた}。
bad.en: (meant: the food was bad, so I complained to the waiter)
bad.why: Finding fault with something is monku o iu. This idiom is saying you cannot cope, not complaining about others.

bad.s: 赤[あか]ちゃんが寝[ね]ているので、{弱音[よわね]を吐[は]いて}話[はな]してください。
bad.en: (meant: the baby is asleep, so please speak softly)
bad.why: The weak sounds are words of discouragement, not a quiet voice. Speaking quietly is kogoe de hanasu.

cards.mean: to get one's money's worth
cards.lit: to take back the original outlay, the money first put in

use.how: Used as a verb phrase about using something you paid for until it has been worth the cost: 食べ放題で元を取る. Potential form 元が取れる is very common.

near.diff: 元も子もない means losing everything, gains included; 元を取る means getting back the value of what you paid.

cards.cue: You paid a lot for an all-you-can-eat buffet, so you keep going back for more plates. What are you trying to do?

ctx.s: 食[た]べ放題[ほうだい]なんだから、しっかり{元[もと]を取[と]ろう}。
ctx.en: It's all-you-can-eat, so let's make sure we get our money's worth.

ctx.s: 高[たか]い年間[ねんかん]パスを買[か]ったので、何度[なんど]も行[い]って{元[もと]を取[と]った}。
ctx.en: I'd bought an expensive annual pass, so I went many times and got my money's worth.

ctx.s: 「ジムの会費[かいひ]、ちゃんと{元[もと]を取[と]って}る？」
ctx.en: "Are you actually getting your money's worth out of your gym membership?"

ctx.s: このコーヒーメーカーは高[たか]かったけど、毎日[まいにち]使[つか]えばすぐ{元[もと]が取[と]れる}。
ctx.en: This coffee maker was pricey, but if I use it every day it'll soon pay for itself.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は「せっかく来[き]たんだから{元[もと]を取[と]らなきゃ}」と言[い]って、全部[ぜんぶ]の展示[てんじ]を見[み]て回[まわ]った。
ctx.en: Saying "We've come all this way, we have to get our money's worth," my mother went round every exhibit.

ctx.s: 店[みせ]の改装[かいそう]に大金[たいきん]をかけたが、{元[もと]を取[と]る}までに五年[ごねん]かかった。
ctx.en: We spent a fortune renovating the shop, and it took five years to earn the cost back.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]とけんかしたが、次[つぎ]の日[ひ]には{元[もと]を取[と]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I fought with my friend but we were back to normal the next day)
bad.why: Getting back to how things were is moto ni modoru or nakanaori suru. This idiom is about recovering money spent.

bad.s: 落[お]とした財布[さいふ]を交番[こうばん]で{元[もと]を取[と]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I got my lost wallet back at the police box)
bad.why: Getting a lost thing back is torimodosu. This idiom means getting value equal to what you paid.

cards.mean: to let loose and enjoy one's freedom
cards.lit: to stretch out one's wings, like a bird let out of its cage

use.how: Used as a verb phrase for relaxing freely while a restraint is gone: a boss, parents, rules or daily duties. Often with 思い切り or たまには.

near.diff: 一息つく is a short pause to rest; 羽を伸ばす is enjoying yourself freely because whatever held you back is gone for a while.

cards.cue: Your strict parents are away for a week, and you finally do whatever you like at home. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 親[おや]が旅行中[りょこうちゅう]なので、週末[しゅうまつ]は家[いえ]で{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばした}。
ctx.en: My parents were away on a trip, so I let loose at home over the weekend.

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]が終[お]わったら、温泉[おんせん]で思[おも]い切[き]り{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばし}たい。
ctx.en: When exams are over, I want to go to a hot spring and really let myself go.

ctx.s: 「たまには子[こ]どもを預[あず]けて、{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばして}きたら？」
ctx.en: "Why not leave the kids with someone for once and go enjoy some time to yourself?"

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]が出張[しゅっちょう]でいないので、今日[きょう]は部署[ぶしょ]のみんなが{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばして}いる。
ctx.en: The boss is away on a business trip, so everyone in the department is relaxing today.

ctx.s: 寮[りょう]の厳[きび]しい規則[きそく]から解放[かいほう]され、学生[がくせい]たちは夏休[なつやす]みに{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばした}。
ctx.en: Freed from the strict dormitory rules, the students let loose over the summer holidays.

ctx.s: 久[ひさ]しぶりの一人旅[ひとりたび]で、誰[だれ]にも気[き]を使[つか]わずに{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばす}ことができた。
ctx.en: On my first solo trip in ages, I could enjoy my freedom without having to worry about anyone.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は毎日[まいにち]夜遅[よるおそ]くまで{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばして}働[はたら]いている。
bad.en: (meant: he pushes himself, working late every night)
bad.why: It means relaxing freely, the opposite of overworking. Pushing yourself is muri o suru.

bad.s: その会社[かいしゃ]は海外[かいがい]にも{羽[はね]を伸[の]ばした}。
bad.en: (meant: the company expanded overseas)
bad.why: A business expanding abroad is shinshutsu suru. This idiom is a person relaxing, not growth.

cards.mean: to get goosebumps
cards.lit: bird skin stands up: skin bumpy like a plucked bird's

use.how: Said of cold, fear or disgust: 鳥肌が立つほど怖い. Using it for being thrilled or moved is now very common in speech, but some older speakers consider it a misuse.

near.diff: 冷や汗をかく is fright at a narrow escape or a blunder of one's own; 鳥肌が立つ is skin reacting to cold, horror, disgust or thrill.

cards.cue: Walking alone past an abandoned hospital at night, you hear a door creak and the hair on your arms stands up. What happens to you?

ctx.s: 寒[さむ]さで腕[うで]に{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]って}いる。
ctx.en: I've got goosebumps on my arms from the cold.

ctx.s: 夜[よる]の墓地[ぼち]を一人[ひとり]で歩[ある]いていたら、{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]った}。
ctx.en: Walking alone through the cemetery at night, I got goosebumps.

ctx.s: 黒板[こくばん]を爪[つめ]でひっかく音[おと]を聞[き]くと、{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]つ}。
ctx.en: The sound of nails scratching a blackboard gives me goosebumps.

ctx.s: その事件[じけん]の話[はなし]は、{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]つ}ほど怖[こわ]かった。
ctx.en: The story of that incident was so frightening it gave me goosebumps.

ctx.s: 「あのホラー映画[えいが]、見[み]るたびに{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]つ}んだよね。」
ctx.en: "That horror film gives me goosebumps every time I watch it."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の歌声[うたごえ]があまりにすばらしくて、{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]った}。
ctx.en: Her singing was so amazing it gave me goosebumps.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]つ}ほど暑[あつ]い。
bad.en: (meant: it is so hot today)
bad.why: Goosebumps come from cold, fear or strong feeling, never from heat.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の冗談[じょうだん]がおかしくて、{鳥肌[とりはだ]が立[た]った}。
bad.en: (meant: his joke was so funny I couldn't stop laughing)
bad.why: Laughing hard is oowarai suru or onaka o kakaete warau. Goosebumps are not a reaction to something funny.

cards.mean: to break into a cold sweat
cards.lit: to sweat cold sweat

use.how: Used as a verb phrase about one's own fright at a near miss, a mistake about to come out, or a tight spot: 社長の前で冷や汗をかいた.

near.diff: 手に汗を握る is tense excitement while watching something unfold; 冷や汗をかく is your own fright at a danger or blunder.

cards.cue: In a meeting, you realise you've just called an important client by a rival company's name. How do you react physically?

ctx.s: 自転車[じてんしゃ]で車[くるま]にぶつかりそうになって、{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかいた}よ。
ctx.en: I nearly hit a car on my bike. I broke into a cold sweat.

ctx.s: 発表[はっぴょう]の途中[とちゅう]で資料[しりょう]を忘[わす]れたことに気[き]づき、{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかいた}。
ctx.en: Halfway through my presentation I realised I'd forgotten my notes, and I broke into a cold sweat.

ctx.s: 「社長[しゃちょう]の名前[なまえ]を間違[まちが]えたときは、本当[ほんとう]に{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかき}ました。」
ctx.en: "When I got the president's name wrong, I really broke out in a cold sweat."

ctx.s: 搭乗直前[とうじょうちょくぜん]にパスポートが見当[みあ]たらず、{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかいた}。
ctx.en: Just before boarding I couldn't find my passport, and I broke into a cold sweat.

ctx.s: 面接官[めんせつかん]に答[こた]えられない質問[しつもん]をされ、背中[せなか]に{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかいた}。
ctx.en: The interviewer asked me a question I couldn't answer, and cold sweat ran down my back.

ctx.s: 嘘[うそ]がばれそうになり、彼[かれ]は{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかき}ながら言[い]い訳[わけ]をした。
ctx.en: With his lie about to come out, he made excuses in a cold sweat.

bad.s: サウナに入[はい]って、たくさん{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかいた}。
bad.en: (meant: I sweated a lot in the sauna)
bad.why: Sweating from heat is just ase o kaku. The cold sweat comes from fright or nerves.

bad.s: 冬[ふゆ]は寒[さむ]いので、毎朝[まいあさ]{冷[ひ]や汗[あせ]をかく}。
bad.en: (meant: winter is cold, so I feel chilly every morning)
bad.why: It is not about feeling cold. Feeling chilly is samui or karada ga hieru.

cards.mean: to picture something vividly in one's mind
cards.lit: to float up before one's eyes

use.how: The thing pictured is the subject: 母の顔が目に浮かぶ. Used for remembered scenes and for imagining how someone will react.

near.diff: 目に見えている says a bad outcome is obvious; 目に浮かぶ is a vivid mental picture, remembered or imagined.

cards.cue: Reading your late grandmother's old letter, you suddenly see her standing in her kitchen as clearly as if she were there. What happens?

ctx.s: 合格[ごうかく]を伝[つた]えたときの母[はは]の喜[よろこ]ぶ顔[かお]が{目[め]に浮[う]かぶ}。
ctx.en: I can just picture my mother's happy face when I tell her I passed.

ctx.s: 今[いま]でも、子[こ]どもの頃[ころ]に遊[あそ]んだ川[かわ]が{目[め]に浮[う]かぶ}。
ctx.en: Even now I can see the river where I played as a child.

ctx.s: 「それを聞[き]いたら、部長[ぶちょう]が怒[おこ]る顔[かお]が{目[め]に浮[う]かぶ}よ。」
ctx.en: "I can just picture the boss's angry face on hearing that."

ctx.s: 手紙[てがみ]を読[よ]んでいると、祖母[そぼ]が台所[だいどころ]に立[た]つ姿[すがた]が{目[め]に浮[う]かんだ}。
ctx.en: As I read the letter, I could see my grandmother standing in her kitchen.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の説明[せつめい]は具体的[ぐたいてき]で、その場面[ばめん]がありありと{目[め]に浮[う]かぶ}ようだった。
ctx.en: His description was so concrete that I could picture the scene vividly.

ctx.s: あの厳[きび]しい社長[しゃちょう]が孫[まご]と遊[あそ]ぶ姿[すがた]なんて、ちょっと{目[め]に浮[う]かばない}な。
ctx.en: I can't quite picture that strict company president playing with his grandchildren.

bad.s: 窓[まど]の外[そと]に富士山[ふじさん]が{目[め]に浮[う]かんだ}。
bad.en: (meant: Mount Fuji came into view outside the window)
bad.why: Something actually seen is mieta or me ni haitta. This idiom is only a picture in the mind.

bad.s: 会議中[かいぎちゅう]に、いいアイデアが{目[め]に浮[う]かんだ}。
bad.en: (meant: a good idea came to me during the meeting)
bad.why: Ideas come with atama ni ukabu or omoitsuku. This idiom is for scenes and faces you can picture.

cards.mean: to accept what one is told without question
cards.lit: to swallow something whole, the way a cormorant gulps down a fish without chewing

use.how: Takes information, claims or rumours as its object with を: 噂を鵜呑みにする. Mostly in warnings and criticism: 鵜呑みにしないで.

near.diff: 真に受ける is taking a joke, pleasantry or casual remark as serious; 鵜呑みにする is accepting information or claims without checking them.

cards.cue: Your friend bought an expensive supplement because an advert promised it cures everything, and never checked anything. What did he do with the advert?

ctx.s: 調[しら]べもせずにネットの情報[じょうほう]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}はいけない。
ctx.en: You mustn't believe what you read online without checking it.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は広告[こうこく]の言葉[ことば]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}、高[たか]いサプリを買[か]ってしまった。
ctx.en: He believed the advert without question and ended up buying expensive supplements.

ctx.s: 「専門家[せんもんか]がそう言[い]ってたよ。」「でも、それを{鵜呑[うの]みにする}のは危[あぶ]ないと思[おも]うな。」
ctx.en: "An expert said so." "Still, I think it's risky to just take that at face value."

ctx.s: 噂[うわさ]を{鵜呑[うの]みにした}社員[しゃいん]たちは、事実[じじつ]を確[たし]かめようともしなかった。
ctx.en: The staff who swallowed the rumour didn't even try to check the facts.

ctx.s: 教科書[きょうかしょ]の説明[せつめい]も{鵜呑[うの]みにせず}、自分[じぶん]で確[たし]かめなさい。
ctx.en: Don't accept even the textbook's explanation blindly; check it for yourself.

ctx.s: 調査結果[ちょうさけっか]を{鵜呑[うの]みにする}前[まえ]に、誰[だれ]が調[しら]べたのかを確認[かくにん]しよう。
ctx.en: Before accepting the survey results as they are, let's check who carried out the survey.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]に教[おし]わった方法[ほうほう]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}、成績[せいせき]が上[あ]がりました。
bad.en: (meant: I followed my teacher's method faithfully and my grades went up)
bad.why: It always implies foolishly accepting without checking, so it cannot praise following good advice.

bad.s: 周[まわ]りに反対[はんたい]されても、彼[かれ]は自分[じぶん]の夢[ゆめ]を{鵜呑[うの]みにして}頑張[がんば]った。
bad.en: (meant: he kept believing in his dream despite opposition)
bad.why: It is about uncritically accepting what others tell you, not about faith or conviction in your own goals.

cards.mean: to take at face value what was not meant seriously
cards.lit: to receive words as truth (ma), as if they had been meant in earnest

use.how: Takes a joke, pleasantry, flattery or offhand remark as object with を; very often in 真に受けないで. The speaker implies the words were not meant seriously.

near.diff: 鵜呑みにする is accepting information or claims without checking; 真に受ける is taking a joke or polite remark as if it were meant seriously.

cards.cue: A neighbour said "Drop by anytime!" just to be polite, and you actually turned up at their door on Sunday. What did you do with the remark?

ctx.s: 冗談[じょうだん]だよ。{真[ま]に受[う]けない}で。
ctx.en: I'm only joking. Don't take it seriously.

ctx.s: 「今度[こんど]遊[あそ]びに来[き]てね」という社交辞令[しゃこうじれい]を{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、本当[ほんとう]に行[い]ってしまった。
ctx.en: I took "come and visit sometime" literally, though it was only politeness, and actually went.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]は「天才[てんさい]だね」と言[い]われたのを{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、すっかりその気[き]になっている。
ctx.en: My little brother believed it when someone called him a genius, and now he's completely full of himself.

ctx.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]、明日[あした]は休[やす]んでいいって言[い]ってたよね？」「まさか、あれを{真[ま]に受[う]けた}の？」
ctx.en: "The manager said we could take tomorrow off, right?" "Don't tell me you took that seriously."

ctx.s: 酔[よ]った勢[いきお]いでした約束[やくそく]なんて、{真[ま]に受[う]ける}人[ひと]はいないよ。
ctx.en: Nobody takes a promise made while drunk seriously.

ctx.s: エイプリルフールの記事[きじ]を{真[ま]に受[う]けた}読者[どくしゃ]から、問[と]い合[あ]わせが相次[あいつ]いだ。
ctx.en: Readers who believed the April Fools' article sent in one enquiry after another.

bad.s: 医者[いしゃ]の説明[せつめい]を{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、毎日[まいにち]薬[くすり]を飲[の]んでいる。
bad.en: (meant: I followed the doctor's advice and take my medicine every day)
bad.why: It implies the words were not meant seriously; for serious advice you simply believe or follow it.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は仕事[しごと]を{真[ま]に受[う]けて}、毎晩[まいばん]遅[おそ]くまで働[はたら]いている。
bad.en: (meant: he takes his job seriously and works late every night)
bad.why: Its object is something someone said, not a task; taking one's work seriously is a different expression.

cards.mean: to accept someone's kind offer gratefully
cards.lit: to lean on someone's kind words, the way a child leans on an indulgent parent

use.how: Said politely to the person who made the offer, usually after being urged: では、お言葉に甘えて. Common in speech and business email.

cards.cue: Your host insists you leave the washing-up and go and rest. You decline once, they insist again, and you accept. What do you say?

ctx.s: 「どうぞ座[すわ]ってください。」「では、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}。」
ctx.en: "Please, have a seat." "Well then, thank you, I will."

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]はもう帰[かえ]っていいよ。」「すみません、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}お先[さき]に失礼[しつれい]します。」
ctx.en: "You can go home now." "Thank you, then I'll take you up on that and head off."

ctx.s: 「遠慮[えんりょ]しないで、たくさん食[た]べてね。」「ありがとうございます。{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えさせて}いただきます。」
ctx.en: "Don't hold back, eat as much as you like." "Thank you, I'll gladly accept."

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]が駅[えき]まで車[くるま]で送[おく]ると言[い]ってくれたので、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]える}ことにした。
ctx.en: My senior colleague offered to drive me to the station, so I decided to accept.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]か断[ことわ]ったが、おばあさんが譲[ゆず]らないので、最後[さいご]は{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えた}。
ctx.en: I said no several times, but the old lady wouldn't take no for an answer, so in the end I accepted her kindness.

ctx.s: 締[し]め切[き]りを延[の]ばしていただけるとのこと、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}来週[らいしゅう]提出[ていしゅつ]いたします。
ctx.en: Since you kindly offered to extend the deadline, I will gratefully take you up on it and submit next week.

bad.s: 店員[てんいん]に{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}、お水[みず]をくださいと頼[たの]んだ。
bad.en: (meant: I politely asked the waiter for some water)
bad.why: It accepts an offer someone else has made; it cannot introduce a request of your own.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]に褒[ほ]められて、{お言葉[ことば]に甘[あま]えて}とてもうれしかった。
bad.en: (meant: my teacher praised me and I was delighted)
bad.why: It is about accepting an offer of help or a favour, not about enjoying a compliment.

cards.mean: to be a good judge of people or things
cards.lit: to have eyes that see: eyes that can tell what is good from what is not

use.how: Predicate about a person, often with what is judged: 人を見る目がある. The negative 見る目がない criticises poor judgment.

near.diff: 甘いものに目がない means being crazy about something; only 見る目がない, the negative of this idiom, means poor judgment.

cards.cue: Every person your manager has ever hired has turned out to be excellent. What can you say about her?

ctx.s: この絵[え]を選[えら]ぶなんて、君[きみ]は{見[み]る目[め]がある}ね。
ctx.en: You picked this painting? You've got a good eye.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は人[ひと]を{見[み]る目[め]がある}から、彼女[かのじょ]が採用[さいよう]した人[ひと]はみんな優秀[ゆうしゅう]だ。
ctx.en: She's a good judge of people, so everyone she hires turns out to be excellent.

ctx.s: 部下[ぶか]を{見[み]る目[め]がない}上司[じょうし]の下[もと]では、優秀[ゆうしゅう]な人[ひと]ほど辞[や]めていく。
ctx.en: Under a boss who can't judge his staff, the best people are the first to leave.

ctx.s: あんな人[ひと]と付[つ]き合[あ]うなんて、私[わたし]は人[ひと]を{見[み]る目[め]がなかった}。
ctx.en: Going out with someone like that... I was a poor judge of character.

ctx.s: 骨董品[こっとうひん]の世界[せかい]では、本物[ほんもの]を{見[み]る目[め]がある}かどうかがすべてだ。
ctx.en: In the antiques trade, everything depends on whether you can tell the genuine article.

ctx.s: 無名[むめい]だった頃[ころ]の彼[かれ]を見[み]つけたスカウトは、さすがに{見[み]る目[め]があった}。
ctx.en: The scout who discovered him back when he was unknown certainly knew talent when he saw it.

bad.s: 祖父[そふ]は八十歳[はちじゅっさい]だが、まだ{見[み]る目[め]がある}ので眼鏡[めがね]はいらない。
bad.en: (meant: my grandfather is eighty but his eyesight is still good)
bad.why: It is about judgment and taste, not about eyesight.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は甘[あま]いものに{見[み]る目[め]がある}ので、毎日[まいにち]ケーキを食[た]べている。
bad.en: (meant: he loves sweets, so he eats cake every day)
bad.why: Loving something is the different idiom me ga nai; this one praises good judgment.

cards.mean: to encourage someone to take the plunge
cards.lit: to push someone gently on the back so they take the step forward

use.how: Object is a person hesitating over a step they want to take: 友達の背中を押す. Often てくれた, or passive 背中を押された. A word or event can also be the subject.

near.diff: 一肌脱ぐ is stepping in to do real work to help someone; 背中を押す is giving the encouragement that lets them act for themselves.

cards.cue: You were unsure about applying to study abroad until a teacher told you to go for it, and so you did. What did the teacher do for you?

ctx.s: 迷[まよ]っていた私[わたし]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}くれたのは、母[はは]の一言[ひとこと]だった。
ctx.en: What gave me the push I needed when I was hesitating was something my mother said.

ctx.s: 「転職[てんしょく]、まだ迷[まよ]ってるの？」「うん、誰[だれ]かに{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}ほしいんだ。」
ctx.en: "Still unsure about changing jobs?" "Yeah, I want someone to give me a push."

ctx.s: 留学[りゅうがく]するか悩[なや]んでいる友達[ともだち]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}あげたい。
ctx.en: I want to encourage my friend, who can't decide whether to study abroad.

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]が夢[ゆめ]を叶[かな]えたのを見[み]て、{背中[せなか]を押[お]された}気[き]がした。
ctx.en: Seeing my senior make her dream come true felt like a push to go for mine.

ctx.s: この本[ほん]は、新[あたら]しいことを始[はじ]めたい人[ひと]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}くれる。
ctx.en: This book gives encouragement to people who want to start something new.

ctx.s: 低金利[ていきんり]が、家[いえ]の購入[こうにゅう]を考[かんが]える人[ひと]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}いる。
ctx.en: Low interest rates are encouraging people who are thinking of buying a home.

bad.s: 母[はは]は毎朝[まいあさ]、宿題[しゅくだい]をしなさいと私[わたし]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]す}。
bad.en: (meant: my mother nags me every morning to do my homework)
bad.why: It is encouragement toward a step the person wants to take, not nagging about chores.

bad.s: 上司[じょうし]は嫌[いや]がる部下[ぶか]の{背中[せなか]を押[お]して}、無理[むり]やり契約[けいやく]させた。
bad.en: (meant: the boss forced his unwilling subordinate to sign)
bad.why: It is supportive encouragement of someone's own wish, never pressure that forces a person against their will.

cards.mean: to psych oneself up
cards.lit: to put fighting spirit into oneself, as with a shout before a bout

use.how: Of oneself before an effort: 気合を入れていこう. As 気合を入れて + verb, doing something with extra energy; or someone rallies others: 選手に気合を入れる.

near.diff: 本腰を入れる is getting seriously committed to a task over time; 気合を入れる is summoning energy for the effort right in front of you.
気を引き締める is becoming alert and careful so as not to slip up; 気合を入れる is firing up energy and spirit.

cards.cue: Just before the final, the captain slaps his own cheeks and shouts to fire himself up. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 明日[あした]は決勝[けっしょう]だ。大[おお]きな声[こえ]を出[だ]して、{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}いこう！
ctx.en: The final is tomorrow. Let's shout it out and get fired up!

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は両手[りょうて]で頬[ほお]を叩[たた]いて{気合[きあい]を入[い]れた}。
ctx.en: He slapped his cheeks with both hands to psych himself up.

ctx.s: 「その服[ふく]、すごいね。」「今日[きょう]はデートだから、ちょっと{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}きたんだ。」
ctx.en: "Wow, look at that outfit." "I've got a date today, so I made a bit of an effort."

ctx.s: 「よし、やるぞ！」と{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}、大掃除[おおそうじ]に取[と]りかかった。
ctx.en: Saying "Right, let's do this!", I psyched myself up and got stuck into the big clean.

ctx.s: 朝[あさ]は苦手[にがて]なので、濃[こ]いコーヒーで{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}から仕事[しごと]を始[はじ]める。
ctx.en: I'm not a morning person, so I fire myself up with strong coffee before starting work.

ctx.s: 負[ま]けている選手[せんしゅ]たちに、監督[かんとく]が大声[おおごえ]で{気合[きあい]を入[い]れた}。
ctx.en: The coach roared at his losing players to fire them up.

bad.s: 疲[つか]れたので、ソファに寝転[ねころ]んで{気合[きあい]を入[い]れた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was tired, so I lay on the sofa to recharge)
bad.why: It means summoning energy and fighting spirit for an effort, not resting or relaxing.

bad.s: 道[みち]が凍[こお]っているから、{気合[きあい]を入[い]れて}ゆっくり歩[ある]こう。
bad.en: (meant: the road is icy, so let's walk slowly and carefully)
bad.why: It is about energy and drive; being careful and cautious is ki o tsukeru, not this.

cards.mean: to feel that one's effort is getting results
cards.lit: to feel a response come back into one's hand, as when a fish takes the line

use.how: Said by the person who made the effort, about an exam, interview, project or attempt: 試験は手応えがあった. 手応えがない means no sign of results.

near.diff: 軌道に乗る says a project is actually running smoothly; 手応えがある is the felt sense that one's effort is working.

cards.cue: Walking out of a job interview, you feel your answers landed and it went well. How do you describe the interview to a friend?

ctx.s: 今日[きょう]の試験[しけん]は{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
ctx.en: I feel today's exam went well.

ctx.s: 「面接[めんせつ]どうだった？」「うん、けっこう{手応[てごた]えがあった}よ。」
ctx.en: "How was the interview?" "Yeah, I think it went pretty well."

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい教[おし]え方[かた]を試[ため]してみたら、生徒[せいと]たちの目[め]が輝[かがや]き、{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
ctx.en: When I tried a new way of teaching, the students' eyes lit up and I felt it was working.

ctx.s: 説明会[せつめいかい]は質問[しつもん]もたくさん出[で]て、{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
ctx.en: Lots of questions came up at the information session, so I felt it really worked.

ctx.s: いくら練習[れんしゅう]しても{手応[てごた]えがない}ので、やり方[かた]を変[か]えてみた。
ctx.en: However much I practised I wasn't getting anywhere, so I tried changing my approach.

ctx.s: 営業[えいぎょう]を始[はじ]めて半年[はんとし]、ようやく{手応[てごた]えがある}と感[かん]じられるようになった。
ctx.en: Six months into the sales job, I'm finally starting to feel my efforts are paying off.

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たって、{手応[てごた]えがあった}。
bad.en: (meant: I won the lottery and felt lucky)
bad.why: It is the felt sense that one's own effort is working; a lucky win involves no effort that could pay off.

bad.s: このステーキは肉[にく]が厚[あつ]くて、{手応[てごた]えがある}ね。
bad.en: (meant: this steak is thick and nicely chewy)
bad.why: Chewiness is hagotae; this idiom is about feeling that an effort is producing results.

cards.mean: to flatter, to butter someone up
cards.lit: to grind sesame seeds in a mortar

use.how: The person flattered takes に: 上司にごまをする. Criticises insincere flattery for gain; said of oneself it is joking. Noun: ごますり.

near.diff: 顔色をうかがう is anxiously watching someone's mood; ごまをする is actively flattering them to gain something.

cards.cue: A coworker laughs at all the boss's jokes and praises his taste in ties, hoping for a promotion. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はいつも部長[ぶちょう]に{ごまをすって}いる。
ctx.en: He's always buttering up the department head.

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]は優[やさ]しいね。何[なに]か欲[ほ]しいの？」「ばれた？ちょっと{ごまをすって}みたんだ。」
ctx.en: "You're being sweet today. Want something?" "Busted. I was trying a little flattery."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]に{ごまをすっても}、成績[せいせき]は上[あ]がらないよ。
ctx.en: Sucking up to the teacher won't raise your grades.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はお小遣[こづか]いを増[ふ]やしてもらおうと、父[ちち]に{ごまをすり}始[はじ]めた。
ctx.en: Hoping for a bigger allowance, my little brother started sweet-talking our father.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の前[まえ]でだけ{ごまをする}人[ひと]は、同僚[どうりょう]に信用[しんよう]されない。
ctx.en: People who only flatter when the president is around don't earn their colleagues' trust.

ctx.s: 実力[じつりょく]で認[みと]められたいから、{ごまをする}ようなことはしたくない。
ctx.en: I want to be recognised for my ability, so I don't want to resort to flattery.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]の誕生日[たんじょうび]に、心[こころ]から{ごまをすった}。
bad.en: (meant: I sincerely complimented my friend on her birthday)
bad.why: It always means insincere flattery for one's own gain, never sincere praise.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は上司[じょうし]を{ごまをすって}出世[しゅっせ]した。
bad.en: (meant: he flattered his boss and got promoted)
bad.why: The person flattered takes ni, not o; the o in the idiom already belongs to goma.

cards.mean: to grit one's teeth and endure
cards.lit: to clench one's teeth tightly together

use.how: Mostly as 歯を食いしばって + verb (耐える, 頑張る, 続ける): enduring pain, hardship or frustration and carrying on.

near.diff: 歯が立たない means being no match for an opponent or problem; 歯を食いしばる means enduring hardship and carrying on.

cards.cue: In the last kilometre of a marathon, every step hurts, but you clamp your jaw and refuse to stop. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 痛[いた]かったが、{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}我慢[がまん]した。
ctx.en: It hurt, but I gritted my teeth and bore it.

ctx.s: 「もう走[はし]れない。」「あと少[すこ]しだ、{歯[は]を食[く]いしばれ}！」
ctx.en: "I can't run any more." "Just a bit further, grit your teeth!"

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の頃[ころ]は失敗[しっぱい]ばかりだったが、{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}続[つづ]けてきた。
ctx.en: As a newcomer I failed constantly, but I gritted my teeth and kept at it.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]が亡[な]くなった後[あと]、母[はは]は{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}三人[さんにん]の子[こ]どもを育[そだ]てた。
ctx.en: After my father died, my mother struggled on and raised three children.

ctx.s: 悔[くや]しさに{歯[は]を食[く]いしばる}選手[せんしゅ]の姿[すがた]が、テレビに映[うつ]っていた。
ctx.en: The television showed the player clenching his teeth in frustration.

ctx.s: 苦[くる]しいときこそ{歯[は]を食[く]いしばる}ことが大切[たいせつ]だと、祖父[そふ]はよく言[い]っていた。
ctx.en: My grandfather often said that it is when times are hard that you must grit your teeth and endure.

bad.s: 硬[かた]いおせんべいを{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}食[た]べた。
bad.en: (meant: I crunched my way through a hard rice cracker)
bad.why: It means clenching the teeth to endure, not biting or chewing food.

bad.s: 旅行[りょこう]が楽[たの]しかったので、最後[さいご]まで{歯[は]を食[く]いしばって}楽[たの]しんだ。
bad.en: (meant: the trip was fun, so I enjoyed it to the very end)
bad.why: It is only for enduring pain, hardship or frustration, never for enjoying something.

cards.mean: to hit a wall, to run into an obstacle
cards.lit: to walk straight into a wall that blocks the way ahead

use.how: Said of a person or project whose progress stops at an obstacle: 研究が壁にぶつかる. The obstacle can be named: 敬語という壁にぶつかる.

near.diff: 歯が立たない says a particular opponent or problem is beyond you; 壁にぶつかる says progress on a longer path has come to a halt.

cards.cue: After a year of steady progress on the piano, you suddenly can't improve however much you practise. What has happened?

ctx.s: 誰[だれ]でも一度[いちど]は{壁[かべ]にぶつかる}ものだよ。
ctx.en: Everyone hits a wall at some point.

ctx.s: 日本語[にほんご]の勉強[べんきょう]で、敬語[けいご]という{壁[かべ]にぶつかった}。
ctx.en: In my Japanese studies, I ran into the wall of honorific language.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]、仕事[しごと]どう？」「正直[しょうじき]、ちょっと{壁[かべ]にぶつかって}るんだ。」
ctx.en: "How's work lately?" "Honestly, I've kind of hit a wall."

ctx.s: {壁[かべ]にぶつかった}ときこそ、基本[きほん]に戻[もど]るべきだ。
ctx.en: When you hit a wall, that's exactly when you should go back to basics.

ctx.s: 研究[けんきゅう]は資金不足[しきんぶそく]という{壁[かべ]にぶつかり}、中断[ちゅうだん]された。
ctx.en: The research ran into a lack of funding and was put on hold.

ctx.s: 上達[じょうたつ]が止[と]まったと感[かん]じたら、それは{壁[かべ]にぶつかって}いる証拠[しょうこ]かもしれない。
ctx.en: If you feel you've stopped improving, it may be a sign that you've hit a wall.

bad.s: 母[はは]と意見[いけん]が合[あ]わず、夕食[ゆうしょく]の時[とき]に{壁[かべ]にぶつかった}。
bad.en: (meant: my mother and I disagreed and clashed over dinner)
bad.why: It is about progress being blocked by an obstacle, not about quarrelling with a person.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は努力[どりょく]を続[つづ]けて、ついに{壁[かべ]にぶつかった}。
bad.en: (meant: he kept working hard and finally reached his goal)
bad.why: It means getting stuck, not succeeding: even after hard work it describes a setback, never reaching the goal.

cards.mean: to backfire
cards.lit: the reverse side of the die comes up: the opposite of the face you were hoping for

use.how: Subject is a choice, plan or move that was meant to help: 〜したのが裏目に出た. It turned out to do the opposite of its aim.

near.diff: 水の泡 is effort that comes to nothing; 裏目に出る is a move that produces the opposite of what it aimed at.
墓穴を掘る stresses that one ruined oneself by one's own act, often by talking; 裏目に出る is any well-meant move that backfires.

cards.cue: A shop cut its prices to win customers, but buyers decided the goods must be cheap junk and sales fell. What happened to the plan?

ctx.s: 良[よ]かれと思[おも]って言[い]ったことが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]た}。
ctx.en: Something I said with the best intentions had the opposite effect.

ctx.s: 近道[ちかみち]をしようとしたのが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]て}、かえって遅[おそ]くなった。
ctx.en: Trying to take a shortcut backfired and I ended up even later.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]の選手[せんしゅ]交代[こうたい]が{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]て}、チームは逆転[ぎゃくてん]負[ま]けした。
ctx.en: The manager's substitution backfired, and the team lost after leading.

ctx.s: 「慎重[しんちょう]すぎたのが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]た}かな」「うん、もう少[すこ]し早[はや]く決[き]めればよかったね」
ctx.en: "Maybe being so cautious backfired." "Yeah, we should have decided a bit sooner."

ctx.s: 今日[きょう]はやることなすこと{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]る}。
ctx.en: Today everything I try just backfires.

ctx.s: 円安[えんやす]を見越[みこ]した投資[とうし]は、急[きゅう]な円高[えんだか]で{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]た}。
ctx.en: The investment made in expectation of a weaker yen backfired when the yen suddenly strengthened.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]が{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]て}、試合[しあい]が中止[ちゅうし]になった。
bad.en: (meant: the rain caused the match to be cancelled)
bad.why: It is said of a choice or plan that brought the opposite of its aim, not of weather or plain bad luck.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]のアドバイスが{裏目[うらめ]に出[で]て}、試験[しけん]に合格[ごうかく]できた。
bad.en: (meant: thanks to his advice I passed the exam)
bad.why: It always means a move turned out badly; a good outcome can never be said to backfire.

cards.mean: to want something desperately
cards.lit: a hand reaches out of one's throat to grab the thing one craves

use.how: Almost always 喉から手が出るほど欲しい, about a specific thing, person or chance one craves: 喉から手が出るほど欲しい人材.

near.diff: 目がない is a lasting weakness for a kind of thing (甘い物に目がない); 喉から手が出る is craving one particular thing right now.

cards.cue: A collector spots, in a shop window, the rare stamp he has been hunting for twenty years, at a price he cannot quite afford. How much does he want it?

ctx.s: あのゲーム機[き]が{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しい。
ctx.en: I want that game console so badly I can taste it.

ctx.s: 今[いま]、{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しいものってある？
ctx.en: Is there anything you're dying to have right now?

ctx.s: どの会社[かいしゃ]にとっても、経験[けいけん]のあるエンジニアは{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しい人材[じんざい]だ。
ctx.en: For every company, experienced engineers are exactly the people they are desperate to hire.

ctx.s: 「そのチケット、余[あま]ってるなら譲[ゆず]ってくれない？{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しかったんだ」
ctx.en: "If you've got a spare ticket, could you let me have it? I've been dying to get one."

ctx.s: 終了[しゅうりょう]間際[まぎわ]、{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しかった一点[いってん]がついに入[はい]った。
ctx.en: Just before the final whistle, the goal they had been desperate for finally went in.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]が{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど欲[ほ]しがっていたのは、お金[かね]ではなく自由[じゆう]な時間[じかん]だった。
ctx.en: What he craved more than anything was not money but time of his own.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は甘[あま]いものには{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}。
bad.en: (meant: I have a weakness for sweets)
bad.why: It describes craving one particular thing, usually 'want it so much that...'; a standing fondness for sweets is me ga nai.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]の日[ひ]は、{喉[のど]から手[て]が出[で]る}ほど学校[がっこう]に行[い]きたくない。
bad.en: (meant: on rainy days I desperately don't want to go to school)
bad.why: It pictures grabbing at something one craves; it cannot express a strong wish to avoid something.

cards.mean: (of food) to be absolutely delicious
cards.lit: the food is so good that one's cheeks fall off

use.how: Said by the eater about food: ほっぺたが落ちそう！ or ほっぺたが落ちるほどおいしい. Warm, a little playful.

near.diff: 口に合う is a modest 'suits your taste' (お口に合うといいのですが); ほっぺたが落ちる is an enthusiastic 'it's heavenly'.

cards.cue: You take the first bite of your grandmother's homemade dessert and it is so good you close your eyes. What do you exclaim?

ctx.s: このケーキ、{ほっぺたが落[お]ちそう}！
ctx.en: This cake is heavenly!

ctx.s: おばあちゃんの作[つく]るおはぎは、{ほっぺたが落[お]ちる}ほどおいしい。
ctx.en: The rice cakes Grandma makes are out of this world.

ctx.s: 「この焼[や]き肉[にく]、どう？」「{ほっぺたが落[お]ちそう}だよ！」
ctx.en: "How's the barbecue?" "Unbelievably good!"

ctx.s: 旅館[りょかん]で出[で]た新鮮[しんせん]な刺身[さしみ]は、まさに{ほっぺたが落[お]ちる}味[あじ]だった。
ctx.en: The fresh sashimi served at the inn tasted absolutely divine.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもたちは{ほっぺたが落[お]ちそうな}顔[かお]でアイスを食[た]べていた。
ctx.en: The children were eating their ice cream with looks of pure bliss.

ctx.s: 北海道[ほっかいどう]で、{ほっぺたが落[お]ちる}ほどおいしいものを食[た]べたことある？
ctx.en: Have you ever eaten anything out of this world in Hokkaido?

bad.s: この映画[えいが]は{ほっぺたが落[お]ちる}ほど面白[おもしろ]い。
bad.en: (meant: this film is incredibly entertaining)
bad.why: It praises only the taste of food, never a film, a book or an experience.

bad.s: 外[そと]が寒[さむ]くて、{ほっぺたが落[お]ちそう}だ。
bad.en: (meant: it's so cold my cheeks are numb)
bad.why: Despite the image, it never describes the cheeks themselves; it only means food is delicious.

cards.mean: to refuse to listen to anyone
cards.lit: to have no ears for listening

use.how: Said of someone who brushes off advice, warnings or objections: 誰の意見にも聞く耳を持たない. Almost always in the negative.

near.diff: 頭が固い is rigid thinking as a trait; 聞く耳を持たない is shutting out what people are telling one about a matter.
耳を傾ける is the opposite: listening attentively to what someone says.

cards.cue: You have warned your uncle again and again that his new investment looks like a scam, but he waves away every word before you finish. How would you describe him?

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は一度[いちど]決[き]めたら、誰[だれ]の意見[いけん]にも{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]たない}。
ctx.en: Once my father has decided, he won't hear anyone's opinion.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]注意[ちゅうい]しても、弟[おとうと]は{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]たなかった}。
ctx.en: However many times I warned him, my little brother wouldn't listen.

ctx.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]に相談[そうだん]してみたら？」「無駄[むだ]だよ。{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]ってくれない}んだから」
ctx.en: "Why not talk to the manager?" "No point. He just won't listen."

ctx.s: 怒[おこ]っているときの彼女[かのじょ]は{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]たない}から、落[お]ち着[つ]くまで待[ま]とう。
ctx.en: When she's angry she won't listen to a word, so let's wait until she calms down.

ctx.s: 市[し]は住民[じゅうみん]の反対[はんたい]に{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]たず}、計画[けいかく]を進[すす]めた。
ctx.en: Turning a deaf ear to the residents' objections, the city pushed ahead with the plan.

ctx.s: どうしてあの人[ひと]は、医者[いしゃ]の忠告[ちゅうこく]に{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]とうとしない}のだろう。
ctx.en: Why won't he even try to listen to his doctor's advice?

bad.s: 祖父[そふ]は年[とし]のせいで{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]たない}。
bad.en: (meant: my grandfather is hard of hearing because of his age)
bad.why: It is a refusal to listen, an attitude, not deafness; being hard of hearing is mimi ga tooi.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]の話[はなし]に{聞[き]く耳[みみ]を持[も]って}、ノートを取[と]った。
bad.en: (meant: I listened carefully to the teacher and took notes)
bad.why: Its rare positive form means being willing to hear people out, not listening closely to a lesson; for that use mimi o katamukeru.

cards.mean: to add one remark too many and spoil things
cards.lit: one word too many

use.how: Predicate about a person or a remark: 彼はいつも一言多い, その一言が多い. The extra remark is tactless and spoils what came before.

near.diff: 口が悪い is harsh, rude speech in general; 一言多い is a tactless extra remark tacked on, often after something nice.
口が滑る is letting slip what should stay secret; 一言多い is saying something needless that annoys.

cards.cue: Your friend says, 'Nice cooking, for once.' The compliment would have been fine if he had stopped after the first two words. What is his problem?

ctx.s: 君[きみ]はいつも{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]い}んだよ。
ctx.en: You always have to say one thing too many.

ctx.s: 「料理[りょうり]上手[じょうず]だね。見[み]た目[め]によらず」「その{一言[ひとこと]が多[おお]い}の！」
ctx.en: "You're a good cook. Not that you look it." "You didn't need to add that!"

ctx.s: せっかく褒[ほ]めたのに「でも」と付[つ]け足[た]してしまい、また{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]かった}と反省[はんせい]した。
ctx.en: I paid a compliment, then tacked on a 'but', and kicked myself for saying one word too many again.

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]に謝[あやま]ったのはよかったが、最後[さいご]に言[い]い訳[わけ]をしたのは{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]かった}。
ctx.en: Apologising to the boss was fine, but the excuse at the end was one remark too many.

ctx.s: 「ねえ、私[わたし]って{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]い}かな？」
ctx.en: "Hey, do you think I tend to say one thing too many?"

ctx.s: 夫[おっと]の{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]い}癖[くせ]のせいで、せっかくの雰囲気[ふんいき]が台無[だいな]しになった。
ctx.en: My husband's habit of adding one remark too many ruined what had been a lovely mood.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は会議[かいぎ]でいつも{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]く}発言[はつげん]する。
bad.en: (meant: he always speaks a lot in meetings)
bad.why: It is not about talking a lot; it means adding one tactless remark that spoils things.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{一言[ひとこと]多[おお]い}人[ひと]で、いつもみんなを褒[ほ]めてくれる。
bad.en: (meant: she is generous with kind words)
bad.why: It is always a criticism; the extra word is one that annoys or hurts, never a kind one.

cards.mean: to find fault with something
cards.lit: to stick a flaw onto something

use.how: 〜にけちをつける: grudging, petty fault-finding aimed at something others made, did or decided: 人の料理にけちをつける.

near.diff: 揚げ足を取る pounces on slips in someone's words; けちをつける finds petty fault with a thing, plan or result.

cards.cue: A coworker sneers at every proposal anyone brings to the meeting, always digging up some petty flaw, even in the choice of font. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 人[ひと]の料理[りょうり]に{けちをつける}なら、自分[じぶん]で作[つく]って。
ctx.en: If you're going to pick at other people's cooking, make it yourself.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は何[なに]にでも{けちをつけたがる}。
ctx.en: He has to find fault with absolutely everything.

ctx.s: 「この絵[え]、色[いろ]が地味[じみ]じゃない？」「せっかくのプレゼントに{けちをつけない}でよ」
ctx.en: "Isn't this painting a bit drab?" "Don't pick holes in a present someone gave you!"

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい企画[きかく]に{けちをつけられて}、やる気[き]をなくした。
ctx.en: They nitpicked my new project idea and I lost all my motivation.

ctx.s: 審判[しんぱん]の判定[はんてい]にいちいち{けちをつける}選手[せんしゅ]は、ファンにも嫌[きら]われる。
ctx.en: Players who quibble with every one of the referee's calls end up disliked even by fans.

ctx.s: 完成[かんせい]してから{けちをつける}くらいなら、どうして最初[さいしょ]に言[い]わなかったの？
ctx.en: If you were going to find fault once it was finished, why didn't you say so at the start?

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はお金[かね]に{けちをつける}人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he is stingy with money)
bad.why: The word kechi alone means stingy, but the whole idiom means finding fault, not being tight-fisted.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]が作文[さくぶん]の間違[まちが]いに丁寧[ていねい]に{けちをつけて}くれた。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher kindly pointed out the mistakes in my essay)
bad.why: It is grudging, petty criticism, never kindly help; helpful correction is shiteki suru or naosu.

cards.mean: to put on a front to look better off than one is
cards.lit: to puff up one's mie, the way one looks in other people's eyes

use.how: Said of someone (often oneself) spending, claiming or acting beyond reality to impress: 見栄を張って高い店でおごる. Mild criticism.

near.diff: 猫をかぶる hides one's real character behind a meek act; 見栄を張る makes oneself look richer or more capable than one is.
鯖を読む fudges a number such as one's age; 見栄を張る is any show of status or ability one does not really have.

cards.cue: To impress old classmates, a man rents a luxury car for the school reunion and lets everyone think it is his. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 無理[むり]して{見栄[みえ]を張[は]らなくて}もいいよ。
ctx.en: You don't have to strain yourself trying to impress anyone.

ctx.s: 英語[えいご]が話[はな]せると{見栄[みえ]を張[は]った}せいで、通訳[つうやく]を頼[たの]まれてしまった。
ctx.en: Because I showed off and claimed I could speak English, I got asked to interpret.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]は給料[きゅうりょう]、そんなに高[たか]くないんでしょ？」「ばれた？ちょっと{見栄[みえ]を張[は]った}んだ」
ctx.en: "Your salary isn't really that high, is it?" "Caught me. I was putting on a bit of a show."

ctx.s: 同窓会[どうそうかい]のために、{見栄[みえ]を張[は]って}姉[あね]のブランドバッグを借[か]りた。
ctx.en: For the reunion, I borrowed my sister's designer bag to look more successful than I am.

ctx.s: {見栄[みえ]を張[は]って}ローンで高級車[こうきゅうしゃ]を買[か]った彼[かれ]は、毎月[まいつき]の支払[しはら]いに苦[くる]しんでいる。
ctx.en: Having bought a luxury car on credit to keep up appearances, he now struggles with the monthly payments.

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]の前[まえ]で、つい{見栄[みえ]を張[は]って}しまうことはありませんか？
ctx.en: Don't you sometimes catch yourself showing off in front of your friends?

bad.s: 息子[むすこ]が合格[ごうかく]して、母[はは]は{見栄[みえ]を張[は]った}。
bad.en: (meant: when her son passed, the mother felt proud)
bad.why: It means putting on a false front, not feeling pride; being proud of one's child is hana ga takai.

bad.s: 面接[めんせつ]なので、清潔[せいけつ]な服[ふく]を着[き]て{見栄[みえ]を張[は]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I wore clean, neat clothes for the interview)
bad.why: Dressing properly is not showing off; the idiom implies pretending to be richer or better than one is.

cards.t: 穴があったら入りたい
cards.r: あながあったらはいりたい
cards.mean: so embarrassed one wants to disappear
cards.lit: if there were a hole, I would crawl into it

use.how: About one's own embarrassment after a blunder: 穴があったら入りたい気分だ, 〜くらい恥ずかしい, or said on its own.

near.diff: 合わせる顔がない is being too ashamed to face someone one has let down; 穴があったら入りたい is wanting to vanish after a blunder.
肩身が狭い is a lasting feeling of being looked down on in a group; 穴があったら入りたい is a burst of embarrassment.

cards.cue: After your speech you notice the price tag has been hanging from your new jacket the whole time, in full view of the audience. How do you feel?

ctx.s: みんなの前[まえ]で転[ころ]んで、{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたい}気分[きぶん]だった。
ctx.en: I tripped in front of everyone and wanted the ground to swallow me up.

ctx.s: 取引先[とりひきさき]の名前[なまえ]を呼[よ]び間違[まちが]えて、{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたい}くらい恥[は]ずかしかった。
ctx.en: I called the client by the wrong name and was so embarrassed I wanted to disappear.

ctx.s: 「昨日[きのう]の会議[かいぎ]、社長[しゃちょう]の前[まえ]で寝[ね]てたよ」「うそ…{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたい}」
ctx.en: "You fell asleep in front of the president at yesterday's meeting." "No way... I want to crawl into a hole."

ctx.s: 若[わか]いころに書[か]いた詩[し]を読[よ]み返[かえ]すと、{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたく}なる。
ctx.en: Whenever I reread the poems I wrote when I was young, I want to curl up and hide.

ctx.s: 自信[じしん]満々[まんまん]で答[こた]えたのに全然[ぜんぜん]違[ちが]っていて、{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたかった}。
ctx.en: I answered with total confidence and was completely wrong; I wished I could vanish.

ctx.s: 皆様[みなさま]の前[まえ]でこのような失敗[しっぱい]をしてしまい、{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたい}思[おも]いです。
ctx.en: Having made such a blunder in front of you all, I wish I could disappear.

bad.s: 地震[じしん]が怖[こわ]くて、{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたい}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm so scared of the earthquake I want to hide)
bad.why: It is about embarrassment over one's own blunder, not fear or wanting shelter.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{穴[あな]があったら入[はい]りたい}性格[せいかく]で、人前[ひとまえ]で話[はな]せない。
bad.en: (meant: he's painfully shy and can't speak in public)
bad.why: It is a passing feeling after a particular blunder, not a shy personality; a shy person is hazukashigariya.

cards.mean: a piece of cake, very easy
cards.lit: before breakfast: so easy it could be done before one has even eaten

use.how: Predicate about a task, often with a confident or boastful air: こんなの朝飯前だ, 〜なんて朝飯前さ. Casual; avoid it with customers or superiors.

near.diff: お安い御用 is a warm 'happy to' in reply to a favour; 朝飯前 describes a task as easy for someone, often boastfully.

cards.cue: A friend who is a professional programmer is asked whether fixing a typo on a website is hard. He just shrugs. How does he describe the job?

ctx.s: こんな計算[けいさん]、{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}だよ。
ctx.en: A sum like this is a piece of cake.

ctx.s: プロの料理人[りょうりにん]にとって、卵焼[たまごや]きくらい{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}だ。
ctx.en: For a professional cook, an omelette is child's play.

ctx.s: 「この問題[もんだい]、難[むずか]しくない？」「僕[ぼく]には{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}だね」
ctx.en: "Isn't this problem hard?" "For me it's a breeze."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は三[さん]か国語[こくご]を話[はな]すので、簡単[かんたん]な通訳[つうやく]なんて{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}だ。
ctx.en: She speaks three languages, so a bit of simple interpreting is nothing to her.

ctx.s: 山登[やまのぼ]りに慣[な]れた祖父[そふ]には、この程度[ていど]の坂[さか]は{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}らしい。
ctx.en: For my grandfather, a seasoned climber, a slope like this is apparently a walk in the park.

ctx.s: 簡単[かんたん]そうに見[み]えて、実[じつ]は{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}とはいかない仕事[しごと]もある。
ctx.en: Some jobs look easy but turn out to be anything but a piece of cake.

bad.s: 締[し]め切[き]りが{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}なので、急[いそ]いでいる。
bad.en: (meant: the deadline is imminent, so I'm in a hurry)
bad.why: It means a task is very easy; it says nothing about a deadline or time running short.

bad.s: お客様[きゃくさま]、配送[はいそう]日[び]の変更[へんこう]ですね。{朝飯前[あさめしまえ]}です！
bad.en: (meant, to a customer: changing the delivery date is no trouble at all)
bad.why: Boasting that a task is easy sounds cocky and casual to a customer; a clerk says kashikomarimashita.

cards.mean: no trouble at all, happy to do it
cards.lit: a cheap errand: 'cheap' in the sense that it costs one hardly any effort

use.how: A friendly reply accepting a favour: お安い御用だ / です / さ. Said to friends, family, neighbours; with customers or bosses use かしこまりました.

near.diff: 朝飯前 says a task is easy for one, often boastfully; お安い御用 is a warm yes to someone's request.

cards.cue: A neighbour apologetically asks whether you could water her plants while she is away for the weekend, and you are glad to help. What do you reply?

ctx.s: 「ちょっと手伝[てつだ]ってくれる？」「{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だよ」
ctx.en: "Could you give me a hand?" "Sure, no problem."

ctx.s: 荷物[にもつ]を預[あず]かるくらい、{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}さ。
ctx.en: Looking after your bags? That's no trouble at all.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]にいいの？忙[いそが]しいんじゃない？」「これくらい{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だって」
ctx.en: "Are you sure? Aren't you busy?" "Something this small? Happy to do it."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]に電球[でんきゅう]の交換[こうかん]を頼[たの]まれ、「{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}」と笑[わら]って引[ひ]き受[う]けた。
ctx.en: When my grandmother asked me to change a light bulb, I laughed and said, "No trouble at all."

ctx.s: 写真[しゃしん]を頼[たの]まれた男性[だんせい]は「{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}ですよ」とカメラを受[う]け取[と]った。
ctx.en: Asked to take a photo, the man said, "Happy to," and took the camera.

ctx.s: 「遠慮[えんりょ]しないで。駅[えき]まで送[おく]るよ。{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だ」と叔父[おじ]は車[くるま]の鍵[かぎ]を取[と]った。
ctx.en: "Don't be shy. I'll drive you to the station. Happy to do it," said my uncle, picking up his car keys.

bad.s: この問題[もんだい]は{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}なので、すぐに解[と]けた。
bad.en: (meant: this problem was easy, so I solved it right away)
bad.why: It is a reply agreeing to a favour, not a description of an easy task; for that say asameshimae or kantan.

bad.s: このかばんはセールで{お安[やす]い御用[ごよう]}だった。
bad.en: (meant: this bag was cheap in the sale)
bad.why: Here yasui means 'easy to grant' and has nothing to do with price; for a bargain say yasukatta.

cards.mean: to play it safe, to take precautions
cards.lit: to take the serious view: to treat a small risk as if it mattered

use.how: Mostly 大事を取って + an act of holding back (休む, 欠場する, 中止する), when the risk is small but one is careful anyway.

near.diff: 気を配る is attentive care for people or details; 大事を取る is one cautious decision, usually to rest or cancel, just in case.

cards.cue: Your knee twinged on a jog. It feels fine now, but you sit out tomorrow's match just in case. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 熱[ねつ]は下[さ]がったけど、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}今日[きょう]は休[やす]みます。
ctx.en: My fever has gone down, but I'll stay home today to be on the safe side.

ctx.s: 選手[せんしゅ]は軽[かる]いけがだったが、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}試合[しあい]を欠場[けつじょう]した。
ctx.en: The player's injury was minor, but he sat out the match as a precaution.

ctx.s: 足[あし]はまだ痛[いた]む?{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}明日[あした]の練習[れんしゅう]は休[やす]んだら?
ctx.en: Does your leg still hurt? Why not skip tomorrow's practice, just to be safe?

ctx.s: 台風[たいふう]が近[ちか]づいているので、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}イベントを中止[ちゅうし]することにした。
ctx.en: With a typhoon approaching, we decided to cancel the event as a precaution.

ctx.s: 医者[いしゃ]の勧[すす]めで、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}もう一日[いちにち]入院[にゅういん]することになった。
ctx.en: On the doctor's advice, I'm staying in hospital one more day to be safe.

ctx.s: 道[みち]が凍[こお]っていたので、{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}車[くるま]で出[で]かけるのはやめた。
ctx.en: The roads were icy, so I played it safe and didn't take the car out.

bad.s: 祖母[そぼ]の手紙[てがみ]を{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I keep my grandmother's letters carefully)
bad.why: Keeping something safe needs a different phrase; this idiom means holding back, usually resting or cancelling, as a precaution.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]で{大事[だいじ]を取[と]って}満点[まんてん]を取[と]った。
bad.en: (meant: I did what mattered and got full marks)
bad.why: It does not mean achieving something important; it means being cautious, usually by resting or cancelling.

cards.mean: to look the other way at something one should act on
cards.lit: a pretence of not seeing what one has seen

use.how: A noun, mostly in 見て見ぬふりをする or 見て見ぬふりはできない; said of ignoring wrongdoing or someone's trouble that one has noticed.

near.diff: 知らんぷり is any pretending not to know or notice; 見て見ぬふり stresses that one saw a problem and chose not to act.

cards.cue: Everyone in the office knows the manager pads his expense claims, but nobody says a word. What are they doing?

ctx.s: いじめを{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をするのは、いじめているのと同[おな]じだ。
ctx.en: Looking the other way at bullying is the same as doing the bullying.

ctx.s: 電車[でんしゃ]で困[こま]っているお年寄[としよ]りがいたのに、みんな{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をしていた。
ctx.en: An elderly person on the train needed help, but everyone pretended not to notice.

ctx.s: 「会社[かいしゃ]の不正[ふせい]に気[き]づいたら、どうする?」「{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}はできないよ。」
ctx.en: "What would you do if you found fraud at your company?" "I couldn't just look the other way."

ctx.s: ごみを捨[す]てる人[ひと]を見[み]ても、つい{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をしてしまう。
ctx.en: Even when I see someone dumping litter, I end up looking the other way.

ctx.s: 問題[もんだい]を{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}してきた結果[けっか]、事態[じたい]はさらに悪化[あっか]した。
ctx.en: Because the problem had been ignored for so long, the situation got even worse.

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の家[いえ]から毎晩[まいばん]怒鳴[どな]り声[ごえ]が聞[き]こえるのに、{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}でいいのだろうか。
ctx.en: I hear shouting from next door every night. Is it right to just turn a blind eye?

bad.s: 眠[ねむ]かったので、映画[えいが]を{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}をして寝[ね]ていた。
bad.en: (meant: I was sleepy, so I pretended to watch the film and dozed)
bad.why: It means pretending not to have seen something, not pretending to watch.

bad.s: 暗[くら]くて看板[かんばん]が{見[み]て見[み]ぬふり}だった。
bad.en: (meant: it was too dark to see the sign)
bad.why: It is a deliberate choice to ignore what one saw, never a failure to see.

cards.mean: to be deeply moved, to feel a lump in one's throat
cards.lit: one's chest grows hot

use.how: Xに胸が熱くなる, or Xを見て/聞いて胸が熱くなる: being moved by someone's kindness, effort or a reunion.

near.diff: 胸が痛む is pain from sympathy or guilt; 胸が熱くなる is a warm surge of being moved.

cards.cue: At the farewell party your old coach thanks the team and his voice breaks. You feel a warm surge rise inside you. How do you describe it?

ctx.s: 母[はは]からの手紙[てがみ]を読[よ]んで、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
ctx.en: Reading my mother's letter, I was deeply moved.

ctx.s: 最後[さいご]まで諦[あきら]めずに走[はし]る選手[せんしゅ]の姿[すがた]に、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
ctx.en: Seeing the runner keep going to the very end moved me deeply.

ctx.s: 「あの映画[えいが]、どうだった?」「ラストシーンで{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}よ。」
ctx.en: "How was that film?" "The last scene really got to me."

ctx.s: 卒業式[そつぎょうしき]で生徒[せいと]たちの歌[うた]を聞[き]いていると、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなる}。
ctx.en: Listening to the students sing at graduation, I feel a lump in my throat.

ctx.s: 被災地[ひさいち]に全国[ぜんこく]から届[とど]いた励[はげ]ましの声[こえ]に、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなる}思[おも]いがした。
ctx.en: I was moved by the words of encouragement sent to the disaster area from all over the country.

ctx.s: 十年[じゅうねん]ぶりに恩師[おんし]と再会[さいかい]したとき、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなって}言葉[ことば]が出[で]なかった。
ctx.en: Meeting my old teacher again after ten years, I was so moved I couldn't speak.

bad.s: 失礼[しつれい]なことを言[い]われて、{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: someone was rude to me and I got angry)
bad.why: It is the warm feeling of being moved, never anger; anger needs a different idiom altogether.

bad.s: みんなの前[まえ]で転[ころ]んで、恥[は]ずかしくて{胸[むね]が熱[あつ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: I fell over in front of everyone and blushed)
bad.why: Embarrassment makes your face hot, not your chest; a hot chest means being moved, never being embarrassed.

cards.mean: (of words or manner) to grate on one, to offend
cards.lit: to brush against one's feelings

use.how: Xが気に障る, with a remark, tone or habit as subject; 気に障ったらごめん softens one's own words. A mild irritation, not rage.

near.diff: 腹が立つ is the anger itself, said of oneself; 気に障る names the remark or manner that rubs one the wrong way.

cards.cue: You told a friend her new haircut was 'bold', and now she has gone quiet. You apologise in case your remark upset her.

ctx.s: 悪気[わるぎ]はないのだろうが、彼[かれ]の言[い]い方[かた]は少[すこ]し{気[き]に障[さわ]る}。
ctx.en: He probably means no harm, but the way he talks grates on me a little.

ctx.s: {気[き]に障[さわ]ったら}ごめんね。そんなつもりじゃなかったんだ。
ctx.en: Sorry if that upset you. I didn't mean it that way.

ctx.s: 何[なに]か{気[き]に障[さわ]る}ことでも言[い]いましたか。
ctx.en: Did I say something to offend you?

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の人[ひと]がペンをカチカチ鳴[な]らす音[おと]が、どうも{気[き]に障[さわ]る}。
ctx.en: The clicking of my neighbour's pen really gets on my nerves.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は部下[ぶか]の何気[なにげ]ない一言[ひとこと]が{気[き]に障[さわ]った}らしく、急[きゅう]に黙[だま]り込[こ]んだ。
ctx.en: A casual remark from a junior seemed to rub the manager the wrong way, and he suddenly went silent.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]の{気[き]に障[さわ]らない}ように、言葉[ことば]を選[えら]んで話[はな]す。
ctx.en: I choose my words so as not to offend the other person.

bad.s: 泥棒[どろぼう]に家[いえ]を荒[あ]らされて、{気[き]に障[さわ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was furious when burglars wrecked my house)
bad.why: It is a mild irritation at words or manner, far too light for a serious harm like a burglary.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は彼[かれ]の態度[たいど]を{気[き]に障[さわ]る}。
bad.en: (meant: his attitude annoys me)
bad.why: It takes no object: the annoying remark or attitude must be the subject, marked with ga, not with o.

cards.mean: to feel awkward or diffident about doing something
cards.lit: one's spirit draws back

use.how: Mostly Vのは気が引ける: reluctance because the act would impose on others, seem presumptuous or unfair. 何度も頼むのは気が引ける.

near.diff: 気が重い is dread of an unpleasant task; 気が引ける is feeling that doing something would be imposing or presumptuous.

cards.cue: Your neighbour has already driven you to the station three times this month. You need a lift again, but asking makes you uneasy.

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]にまたお金[かね]を借[か]りるのは{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}。
ctx.en: I feel bad borrowing money from my friend again.

ctx.s: みんなが残業[ざんぎょう]しているのに、一人[ひとり]だけ先[さき]に帰[かえ]るのは{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}なあ。
ctx.en: Everyone's working late. I feel awkward being the only one to go home early.

ctx.s: 「手伝[てつだ]ってもらってばかりで、{気[き]が引[ひ]けます}。」「気[き]にしないでください。」
ctx.en: "I feel bad, you're always helping me." "Don't worry about it."

ctx.s: こんなに高[たか]いお土産[みやげ]をもらうのは、なんだか{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}。
ctx.en: I feel a bit uncomfortable accepting such an expensive gift.

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]の作品[さくひん]を自分[じぶん]で褒[ほ]めるのは{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}が、今回[こんかい]はよくできたと思[おも]う。
ctx.en: It feels awkward to praise my own work, but I think this one turned out well.

ctx.s: 忙[いそが]しそうな先生[せんせい]に質問[しつもん]するのは{気[き]が引[ひ]けた}が、思[おも]い切[き]って研究室[けんきゅうしつ]を訪[たず]ねた。
ctx.en: I hesitated to bother my busy professor with questions, but I plucked up the courage and went to her office.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}ように、花[はな]を贈[おく]った。
bad.en: (meant: I sent her flowers to catch her interest)
bad.why: Catching someone's interest is the transitive ki o hiku; this idiom is one's own reluctance to impose.

bad.s: 高[たか]い所[ところ]は危[あぶ]ないから{気[き]が引[ひ]ける}。
bad.en: (meant: high places are dangerous, so they scare me)
bad.why: It is social reluctance from feeling presumptuous, not physical fear of danger.

cards.mean: to jump the gun, to get ahead of oneself
cards.lit: one's mind is quick: it runs ahead of events

use.how: Mostly light teasing about a person who plans or celebrates too soon: 気が早いね. Also 気の早い + noun.

near.diff: 気が短い is a short temper or impatience with waiting; 気が早い is acting or planning before the time has come.

cards.cue: Your friend has an interview next week and is already choosing furniture for a flat in the new city. What do you tease him with?

ctx.s: まだ十月[じゅうがつ]なのに、もう年賀状[ねんがじょう]を書[か]いているの?{気[き]が早[はや]い}ね。
ctx.en: It's only October and you're already writing New Year cards? You're getting ahead of yourself.

ctx.s: 合格[ごうかく]発表[はっぴょう]の前[まえ]にお祝[いわ]いだなんて、{気[き]が早[はや]すぎる}よ。
ctx.en: Celebrating before the results are out? That's jumping the gun.

ctx.s: 「結婚式[けっこんしき]はどこでする?」「{気[き]が早[はや]い}なあ、まだ付[つ]き合[あ]って一[いっ]か月[げつ]だよ。」
ctx.en: "Where will you have the wedding?" "Slow down, we've only been dating a month."

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は{気[き]が早[はや]くて}、孫[まご]が生[う]まれる前[まえ]からランドセルを買[か]ってきた。
ctx.en: My father got ahead of himself and bought a school satchel before his grandchild was even born.

ctx.s: {気[き]の早[はや]い}桜[さくら]が、もう咲[さ]き始[はじ]めている。
ctx.en: Some eager cherry trees have already started to bloom.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]はまだ前半[ぜんはん]なのに、勝[か]ったつもりで騒[さわ]ぐのは{気[き]が早[はや]い}。
ctx.en: It's still the first half; cheering as if we'd won is premature.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]が早[はや]い}から、難[むずか]しい問題[もんだい]もすぐに解[と]ける。
bad.en: (meant: he's quick-witted, so he solves hard problems fast)
bad.why: It means getting ahead of oneself, not being quick-witted; it is never praise for a sharp mind.

bad.s: 弟[おとうと]は{気[き]が早[はや]く}走[はし]って、一位[いちい]になった。
bad.en: (meant: my brother ran fast and came first)
bad.why: It describes a premature mindset, not physical speed, and cannot be used as an adverb of running.

cards.mean: to pay careful attention to every detail
cards.lit: to hand out one's attention all around

use.how: Nに気を配る: steady attention to people's needs or to many details (health, safety, guests). 周りに気を配る.

near.diff: 気をつける is being careful to avoid a danger or mistake; 気を配る is attention spread over people or many details.
気を遣う is taking pains over others' feelings, often at a cost to oneself; 気を配る is watchful attention spread over many people or details.

cards.cue: Before the festival opens, the organiser keeps checking the exits, the lighting, the first-aid tent and the queues all at once. What is she doing?

ctx.s: 母[はは]は台所[だいどころ]の隅々[すみずみ]まで{気[き]を配[くば]って}、いつも清潔[せいけつ]にしている。
ctx.en: My mother keeps an eye on every corner of the kitchen and always keeps it clean.

ctx.s: 幹事[かんじ]は会場[かいじょう]の手配[てはい]から料理[りょうり]、席順[せきじゅん]まで{気[き]を配[くば]った}。
ctx.en: The organiser saw to every detail, from booking the venue to the food and the seating plan.

ctx.s: 「接客[せっきゃく]で大切[たいせつ]なことは?」「お客様[きゃくさま]一人一人[ひとりひとり]に{気[き]を配[くば]る}ことです。」
ctx.en: "What matters most in customer service?" "Paying attention to every single customer."

ctx.s: このレストランは、器[うつわ]や照明[しょうめい]にまで{気[き]が配[くば]られて}いる。
ctx.en: At this restaurant, attention has been paid even to the tableware and lighting.

ctx.s: 司会[しかい]の彼女[かのじょ]は、会場[かいじょう]全体[ぜんたい]の様子[ようす]に{気[き]を配[くば]り}ながら進行[しんこう]した。
ctx.en: As MC, she kept an eye on the whole room as she ran the event.

ctx.s: 工事現場[こうじげんば]では、周囲[しゅうい]の安全[あんぜん]に十分[じゅうぶん]{気[き]を配[くば]る}必要[ひつよう]がある。
ctx.en: On a construction site, you must pay close attention to the safety of everything around you.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の結果[けっか]に{気[き]を配[くば]って}、眠[ねむ]れなかった。
bad.en: (meant: I was so worried about my exam results I couldn't sleep)
bad.why: It is active attentiveness to people or details, not anxiety; it cannot describe lying awake worrying.

bad.s: 危[あぶ]ない!車[くるま]に{気[き]を配[くば]って}!
bad.en: (meant: Look out! Watch out for the car!)
bad.why: A shouted warning to avoid danger is ki o tsukete; this idiom is ongoing, considerate attention.

cards.mean: to trust someone and let one's guard down with them
cards.lit: to loosen one's guard of mind

use.how: (人)に気を許す. Often in warnings or negatives: 簡単に気を許すな, 気を許せない相手.

near.diff: 気が置けない describes a friend one is fully at ease with; 気を許す is the act of lowering one's guard, often with a warning not to.

cards.cue: A friendly stranger on a trip offers to mind your bag. Your friend warns you not to relax around people so quickly. What does she tell you not to do?

ctx.s: 猫[ねこ]がやっと私[わたし]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]して}、膝[ひざ]に乗[の]ってきた。
ctx.en: The cat finally trusted me enough to climb onto my lap.

ctx.s: 優[やさ]しそうに見[み]えるけど、簡単[かんたん]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]しちゃ}だめだよ。
ctx.en: He seems kind, but don't let your guard down too easily.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は誰[だれ]にも{気[き]を許[ゆる]さない}性格[せいかく]で、本音[ほんね]を話[はな]さない。
ctx.en: He never lets his guard down with anyone and doesn't say what he really thinks.

ctx.s: ライバル会社[がいしゃ]の担当者[たんとうしゃ]とは、どんなに親[した]しくなっても{気[き]を許[ゆる]せない}。
ctx.en: However friendly I get with the rival firm's rep, I can never fully trust him.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]の友人[ゆうじん]だからこそ、{気[き]を許[ゆる]して}悩[なや]みを打[う]ち明[あ]けられた。
ctx.en: Because she was a friend of many years, I trusted her and told her my worries.

ctx.s: 「この人[ひと]なら大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]」と{気[き]を許[ゆる]した}相手[あいて]に、お金[かね]をだまし取[と]られた。
ctx.en: I was swindled out of money by someone I had trusted, thinking he was safe.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]が謝[あやま]ったので、遅刻[ちこく]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]した}。
bad.en: (meant: he apologised, so I forgave his lateness)
bad.why: Forgiving a fault is the plain verb yurusu alone; with ki it means lowering one's guard toward a person.

bad.s: 母[はは]が旅行[りょこう]に{気[き]を許[ゆる]して}くれた。
bad.en: (meant: my mother let me go on the trip)
bad.why: Giving permission is the plain verb alone; this idiom is about trust and is directed at a person, not an activity.

cards.mean: (of a friend) close enough to be completely at ease with
cards.lit: one cannot feel any reserve toward them: there is no distance to keep

use.how: Mostly 気の置けない + 友人/仲間/相手. Often misread, even by natives, as 'untrustworthy'; it means the opposite.

near.diff: 気を許す is lowering one's guard toward someone, often cautioned against; 気が置けない describes a friend with whom no guard is needed.
気が合う is getting on well, sharing tastes; 気が置けない is needing no reserve or politeness with someone.
