cards.cue: For your birthday you invite only your oldest friends, the ones you never have to mind your manners with. How do you describe them?

ctx.s: 週末[しゅうまつ]は{気[き]の置[お]けない}友達[ともだち]と、遠慮[えんりょ]なく飲[の]みに行[い]く。
ctx.en: At the weekend I'm going drinking with friends I don't have to stand on ceremony with.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]とは学生時代[がくせいじだい]からの付[つ]き合[あ]いで、気[き]を遣[つか]う必要[ひつよう]もない{気[き]の置[お]けない}仲[なか]だ。
ctx.en: I've known him since our student days; we're so close there's no need to be polite with each other.

ctx.s: 「今日[きょう]は誰[だれ]が来[く]るの?」「{気[き]の置[お]けない}仲間[なかま]だけだから、気楽[きらく]においでよ。」
ctx.en: "Who's coming today?" "Just close friends, so come along and relax."

ctx.s: {気[き]の置[お]けない}相手[あいて]だからこそ、本音[ほんね]で相談[そうだん]できる。
ctx.en: Because we're so close, I can talk to her honestly about anything.

ctx.s: 結婚式[けっこんしき]の二次会[にじかい]には、{気[き]の置[お]けない}友人[ゆうじん]だけを招[まね]いた。
ctx.en: For the wedding after-party, we invited only our closest friends.

ctx.s: 転勤先[てんきんさき]で、遠慮[えんりょ]なく愚痴[ぐち]を言[い]い合[あ]える{気[き]の置[お]けない}同僚[どうりょう]ができた。
ctx.en: After my transfer I found a colleague I can moan to freely, with no need for politeness.

bad.s: 何[なに]を考[かんが]えているかわからない人[ひと]なので、{気[き]が置[お]けない}。
bad.en: (meant: I can never tell what he's thinking, so I can't relax around him)
bad.why: A common misreading: it means one can relax completely with someone, never that one must stay on guard.

bad.s: 子[こ]どもが一人[ひとり]で留守番[るすばん]しているので、{気[き]が置[お]けない}。
bad.en: (meant: my child is home alone, so I can't stop worrying)
bad.why: It describes a close, easy relationship, never unease or worry about a situation.

cards.mean: to pull oneself together after a setback
cards.lit: to take hold of one's spirits again

use.how: Mostly 気を取り直して + the next action, after a disappointment or failure: 落ち込んだが、気を取り直して…

near.diff: 気を引き締める is tightening one's focus before a challenge; 気を取り直す is recovering one's spirits after a setback.

cards.cue: Your cake collapsed in the oven an hour before the party. You sigh, wipe your hands and start a new batch. What did you do?

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]に落[お]ちたけど、{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}また頑張[がんば]ろう。
ctx.en: I failed the exam, but I'll pick myself up and try again.

ctx.s: 「振[ふ]られちゃったよ。」「つらいね。でも{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}、何[なに]か食[た]べに行[い]こう。」
ctx.en: "I got dumped." "That's rough. But chin up, let's go and get something to eat."

ctx.s: 雨[あめ]で遠足[えんそく]が中止[ちゅうし]になった子[こ]どもたちは、{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}教室[きょうしつ]でゲームを始[はじ]めた。
ctx.en: When the trip was rained off, the children cheered up and started playing games in the classroom.

ctx.s: 先制点[せんせいてん]を許[ゆる]したが、選手[せんしゅ]たちはすぐに{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]し}、反撃[はんげき]に出[で]た。
ctx.en: They conceded the first goal, but the players quickly regrouped and went on the attack.

ctx.s: 企画[きかく]は却下[きゃっか]されたが、彼女[かのじょ]は{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}新[あたら]しい案[あん]を考[かんが]え始[はじ]めた。
ctx.en: Her proposal was rejected, but she pulled herself together and started on a new plan.

ctx.s: 道[みち]に迷[まよ]って一時間[いちじかん]も無駄[むだ]にした。{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}、地図[ちず]を見直[みなお]そう。
ctx.en: We got lost and wasted a whole hour. Let's shake it off and check the map again.

bad.s: 一週間[いっしゅうかん]寝込[ねこ]んだが、やっと風邪[かぜ]から{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]した}。
bad.en: (meant: after a week in bed I finally got over my cold)
bad.why: It is recovering one's spirits after a disappointment, not recovering from an illness.

bad.s: 行[い]くと言[い]っていたが、{気[き]を取[と]り直[なお]して}行[い]かないことにした。
bad.en: (meant: I'd said I'd go, but changed my mind and didn't)
bad.why: It does not mean changing one's mind; it means regaining heart to carry on with the same thing.

cards.mean: to brace oneself and stay focused
cards.lit: to pull one's spirit tight, like tightening a loose belt or rope

use.how: Said before a challenge or after a success, to guard against carelessness: 気を引き締めて頑張ります. Intransitive form: 気が引き締まる.

near.diff: 気を取り直す is recovering your spirits after a setback; 気を引き締める is tightening your focus so you don't slip, often when things are going well.

cards.cue: Your team has just won the semifinal. The coach reminds everyone that the final is tomorrow and nobody may get complacent.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]の前[まえ]に、もう一度[いちど]{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めた}。
ctx.en: Before the match, I braced myself once more.

ctx.s: 「勝[か]ったからといって油断[ゆだん]せず、{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めて}いこう。」
ctx.en: "Just because we won doesn't mean we can relax. Let's stay focused."

ctx.s: 年末[ねんまつ]は事故[じこ]が増[ふ]えます。{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めて}安全運転[あんぜんうんてん]を心[こころ]がけましょう。
ctx.en: Accidents rise at the end of the year. Stay alert and make a point of driving safely.

ctx.s: 「ここからが本番[ほんばん]だ。」監督[かんとく]の一言[ひとこと]で、チーム全員[ぜんいん]が{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めた}。
ctx.en: "This is where it really starts." At the coach's words, the whole team pulled themselves together.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいプロジェクトが始[はじ]まり、社員[しゃいん]一同[いちどう]{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めて}取[と]り組[く]んでいます。
ctx.en: A new project has begun, and all of our staff are tackling it with renewed focus.

ctx.s: 合格[ごうかく]はまだ通過点[つうかてん]だ。入学後[にゅうがくご]も{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めて}勉強[べんきょう]を続[つづ]けたい。
ctx.en: Passing the exam is only a milestone. Even after I start school, I want to stay focused and keep studying.

bad.s: 仕事[しごと]で疲[つか]れたので、温泉[おんせん]で{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]めた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was tired from work, so I relaxed at a hot spring)
bad.why: It is the opposite of relaxing: it means tightening your focus. To say you unwound, use nonbiri shita or kutsuroida.

bad.s: 先輩[せんぱい]にまたお願[ねが]いするのは{気[き]を引[ひ]き締[し]める}。
bad.en: (meant: I feel awkward asking my senior for another favour)
bad.why: Feeling awkward or diffident about asking is ki ga hikeru. This idiom is a deliberate act of bracing yourself.

cards.mean: to have a hard time dealing with someone
cards.lit: to burn one's hands: something is too hot to handle comfortably

use.how: Xに手を焼く: you struggle with a troublesome person or problem (a child, a customer, pests) but are still dealing with it. Passive 手を焼かされる is common.

near.diff: 手に負えない means it is beyond you altogether; 手を焼く means it is a struggle but you are still coping with it.

cards.cue: Every evening your toddler refuses vegetables, throws food and runs from the table. You are worn out, but you keep trying.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]のいたずらには{手[て]を焼[や]いて}いる。
ctx.en: My little brother's pranks give me a hard time.

ctx.s: 二歳[にさい]の娘[むすめ]がご飯[はん]を食[た]べてくれず、毎日[まいにち]{手[て]を焼[や]いて}います。
ctx.en: My two-year-old daughter won't eat, and I struggle with her every day.

ctx.s: 「あのお客[きゃく]さんには、みんな{手[て]を焼[や]いてる}んだよ。」
ctx.en: "Everyone has trouble with that customer, you know."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の頃[ころ]は、扱[あつか]いにくい上司[じょうし]にずいぶん{手[て]を焼[や]かされた}。
ctx.en: When I was new, a difficult boss gave me a really hard time.

ctx.s: 毎年[まいとし]夏[なつ]になると、庭[にわ]の雑草[ざっそう]に{手[て]を焼[や]く}。
ctx.en: Every summer, the weeds in the garden are a real headache.

ctx.s: その町[まち]では、ごみをあさるカラスに住民[じゅうみん]が{手[て]を焼[や]いて}いる。
ctx.en: In that town, residents are struggling with crows that rummage through the rubbish.

bad.s: 料理中[りょうりちゅう]にフライパンに触[さわ]って、{手[て]を焼[や]いた}。
bad.en: (meant: I touched the frying pan while cooking and burned my hand)
bad.why: The idiom is never a literal burn. For an injury, say te o yakedo shita.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]の引[ひ]っ越[こ]しで{手[て]を焼[や]いて}あげた。
bad.en: (meant: I helped my friend move house)
bad.why: It means struggling with something troublesome, not helping. To help, say te o kashita or tetsudatta.

cards.mean: to take measures, to act in time
cards.lit: to make a move: te here is a step or means, as in a game, played against a problem

use.how: Xに手を打つ or 早めに手を打つ: take action against a problem before it worsens. It can also mean to settle on terms (この値段で手を打とう).

near.diff: 手を尽くす is trying every possible means; 手を打つ is taking a step against a problem, usually in time.

cards.cue: Sales have fallen for three months running. The manager says something must be done now, before it gets any worse.

ctx.s: 問題[もんだい]が大[おお]きくなる前[まえ]に{手[て]を打[う]とう}。
ctx.en: Let's do something before the problem gets bigger.

ctx.s: 「このままだと赤字[あかじ]だ。何[なに]か{手[て]を打[う]たない}と。」
ctx.en: "At this rate we'll be in the red. We have to do something."

ctx.s: 雨漏[あまも]りに早[はや]めに{手[て]を打[う]って}おいたので、被害[ひがい]は少[すく]なかった。
ctx.en: I dealt with the roof leak early, so there wasn't much damage.

ctx.s: 「もう{手[て]を打[う]って}ありますから、ご心配[しんぱい]なく。」
ctx.en: "Steps have already been taken, so please don't worry."

ctx.s: 店長[てんちょう]は客[きゃく]が減[へ]り始[はじ]めたとき、すぐに{手[て]を打[う]った}。
ctx.en: When customers started dropping off, the store manager took action right away.

ctx.s: 若手[わかて]の退職[たいしょく]が続[つづ]いているのに、会社[かいしゃ]はまだ何[なん]の{手[て]も打[う]って}いない。
ctx.en: Young staff keep quitting, yet the company still hasn't done anything about it.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しい趣味[しゅみ]として、ギターに{手[て]を打[う]って}みた。
bad.en: (meant: I tried my hand at guitar as a new hobby)
bad.why: It means taking measures against a problem. To try your hand at something new, say te o dashite mita.

bad.s: 会社[かいしゃ]はその問題[もんだい]を{手[て]を打[う]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the company dealt with the problem)
bad.why: The problem cannot take o, since te already does. Mark the problem with ni (mondai ni te o utta).

cards.mean: to pull out of a deal or project
cards.lit: to draw one's hand back from something one was holding

use.how: Xから手を引く: withdraw from a business, project or affair you were involved in. Literally, 子どもの手を引く also means to lead a child by the hand.

near.diff: 足を洗う is quitting a disreputable job or way of life for good; 手を引く is withdrawing from any project or affair.
手を抜く is doing a job carelessly; 手を引く is stopping your involvement altogether.

cards.cue: After two years of losses, a company announces it will stop investing in a joint venture and leave it to its partner.

ctx.s: スポンサーが{手[て]を引[ひ]いた}ため、その大会[たいかい]は中止[ちゅうし]になった。

cards.mean: to be more than one can handle
cards.lit: it cannot be carried in one's hands: too much to take on

cards.mean: to be on the edge of one's seat
cards.lit: to clench one's fists until they are wet with sweat

near.diff: 息をのむ is a sudden gasp at a striking sight, beautiful or shocking; 手に汗を握る is sustained suspense over how something will turn out.

cards.mean: to suddenly change one's attitude completely
cards.lit: to flip one's hand over, palm up to palm down, in an instant

bad.en: (meant: it rained, so I changed my plans)

cards.mean: to save someone's face, to let them keep their pride
cards.lit: to keep someone's face standing upright, so that it is not knocked down

bad.en: (meant: I got angry when my brother teased me)

cards.mean: to bring shame on someone
cards.lit: to smear mud on someone's face

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]で名前[なまえ]を読[よ]み間違[まちが]えて、ちょっと{顔[かお]に泥[どろ]を塗[ぬ]った}。

cards.mean: to watch someone's mood before acting

ctx.en: "Stop worrying about how people will react and say what you think."

ctx.en: As a child, I lived always keeping an anxious eye on my father's moods.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]は客[きゃく]の{顔色[かおいろ]をうかがいつつ}、新商品[しんしょうひん]を勧[すす]めた。

cards.mean: to be too ashamed to face someone

ctx.en: We lost the big match because of my mistake, and I couldn't face anyone on the team.

ctx.s: 家[いえ]を飛[と]び出[だ]して十年[じゅうねん]、今[いま]さら家族[かぞく]に{合[あ]わせる顔[かお]がない}と思[おも]っていた。

cards.mean: (of behaviour) too bad to be overlooked

ctx.en: "Should we say something to those kids?" "Yes, this really is too much to let pass."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の態度[たいど]が{目[め]に余[あま]る}ので、部長[ぶちょう]はついに彼[かれ]を呼[よ]び出[だ]した。
ctx.en: The new recruit's attitude was so bad that the manager finally called him in.

ctx.s: 観光客[かんこうきゃく]のマナー違反[いはん]が{目[め]に余[あま]る}として、市[し]は罰金[ばっきん]を導入[どうにゅう]した。
ctx.en: Saying tourists' bad manners had become intolerable, the city introduced fines.

cards.r: めからうろこがおちる
cards.mean: to have one's eyes suddenly opened to the truth
cards.lit: scales fall from one's eyes

story.text: In the New Testament, Saul, who persecuted the early Christians, is struck blind by a light from heaven on the road to Damascus. Three days later a disciple named Ananias lays his hands on him, something like scales falls from his eyes, he can see again, and he is baptised. The phrase came into Japanese through Bible translation; in Japanese it is now said of any sudden realisation.
story.source: New Testament, Acts of the Apostles 9:18

use.how: Predicate, often 目から鱗が落ちた or 目から鱗が落ちる思いだ; also shortened to 目から鱗. Said of advice or an idea that suddenly makes something clear.

cards.cue: A tutor shows you a simple trick that makes a grammar point you'd struggled with for years suddenly obvious.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]の説明[せつめい]を聞[き]いて、{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちた}。
ctx.en: When I heard the teacher's explanation, it all suddenly made sense.

ctx.s: この記事[きじ]を読[よ]めば、きっと{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちる}はずだ。
ctx.en: Read this article and I'm sure it'll be an eye-opener for you.

ctx.s: 「この方法[ほうほう]、試[ため]してみた？」「うん、{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちた}よ。もっと早[はや]く知[し]りたかった。」
ctx.en: "Have you tried this method?" "Yes, it was a revelation. I wish I'd known sooner."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]の料理[りょうり]のコツは、どれも{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちる}ようなものばかりだった。
ctx.en: My grandmother's cooking tips were all real eye-openers.

ctx.s: 部下[ぶか]の何気[なにげ]ない一言[ひとこと]に、{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちる}思[おも]いだった。
ctx.en: A casual remark from my junior opened my eyes.

ctx.s: 海外[かいがい]で暮[く]らし、日本[にほん]の常識[じょうしき]が世界[せかい]の常識[じょうしき]ではないと知[し]って、{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちた}。
ctx.en: Living abroad, I learned that what is common sense in Japan is not common sense everywhere, and my eyes were opened.

bad.s: 悲[かな]しい映画[えいが]を見[み]て、{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちた}。
bad.en: (meant: I cried at a sad film)
bad.why: It means a sudden insight, nothing to do with tears; for crying say namida ga deta.

bad.s: 突然[とつぜん]の大[おお]きな音[おと]に、{目[め]から鱗[うろこ]が落[お]ちた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was startled by a sudden loud noise)
bad.why: It is a sudden understanding, not surprise or fright; for a scare say bikkuri shita.

cards.mean: to have a bitter experience, to learn the hard way
cards.lit: to meet a painful 'eye': me here means an experience, as in hidoi me

use.how: Predicate, often as a warning: 甘く見ると痛い目に遭うよ. Said of suffering a bad consequence, usually of carelessness, that teaches a lesson.

near.diff: 裏目に出る is a plan or action backfiring; 痛い目に遭う is the person suffering a painful experience.

cards.cue: Your friend lends money to anyone who asks without a second thought. You warn him that one day this will cost him dearly.

ctx.s: 甘[あま]く見[み]ていると、{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]う}よ。
ctx.en: If you take it lightly, you'll get burned.

ctx.s: 昔[むかし]、ネットのうまい話[はなし]を信[しん]じて{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]った}ことがある。
ctx.en: I once believed a too-good-to-be-true deal online and paid for it.

ctx.s: 「また株[かぶ]を買[か]うの？」「前[まえ]に{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]った}から、今度[こんど]は慎重[しんちょう]にやるよ。」
ctx.en: "You're buying shares again?" "I got burned last time, so I'll be careful this time."

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]わない}と、あの人[ひと]はわからないだろう。
ctx.en: He won't understand until he learns it the hard way.

ctx.s: 準備[じゅんび]なしで冬山[ふゆやま]に登[のぼ]り、{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]う}登山者[とざんしゃ]は少[すく]なくない。
ctx.en: Quite a few climbers go up winter mountains unprepared and pay a heavy price.

ctx.s: 保証人[ほしょうにん]になって{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]った}父[ちち]は、「簡単[かんたん]に判子[はんこ]を押[お]すな」とよく言[い]う。
ctx.en: My father, who got burned after acting as a guarantor, often says, "Never put your seal on anything lightly."

bad.s: 目[め]にゴミが入[はい]って、{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: some dust got in my eye and it hurt)
bad.why: Here me means an experience, not the eye; for a sore eye say me ga itakatta.

bad.s: 旅行[りょこう]で素晴[すば]らしい人[ひと]たちと出会[であ]い、{痛[いた]い目[め]に遭[あ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I had an unforgettable experience meeting wonderful people on the trip)
bad.why: It is always an unpleasant, painful experience, never a memorable good one.

cards.mean: to listen attentively to
cards.lit: to tilt one's ear toward something

use.how: Verb with に: 意見に耳を傾ける. Said of deliberately and seriously listening to opinions, someone's words, or music; leans to writing and careful speech.

near.diff: 聞く耳を持たない is refusing to listen at all; 耳を傾ける is listening carefully and openly.

cards.cue: A new mayor holds town meetings, lets every resident speak, and takes notes on each complaint.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもの話[はなし]にもっと{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]けて}ください。
ctx.en: Please listen more carefully to what your children say.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい市長[しちょう]は、市民[しみん]の声[こえ]によく{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]ける}人[ひと]だ。
ctx.en: The new mayor is someone who really listens to the citizens.

ctx.s: 「どうして彼[かれ]は人気[にんき]があるの？」「相手[あいて]の話[はなし]に真剣[しんけん]に{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]ける}からだよ。」
ctx.en: "Why is he so popular?" "Because he really listens to what people tell him."

ctx.s: 観客[かんきゃく]は息[いき]をひそめて、ピアノの音[おと]に{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]けた}。
ctx.en: The audience held their breath and listened intently to the piano.

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]は若[わか]い社員[しゃいん]の意見[いけん]にも{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]ける}べきだ。
ctx.en: The company should listen to the opinions of its young employees too.

ctx.s: 反対派[はんたいは]の主張[しゅちょう]に{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]けず}、計画[けいかく]は強引[ごういん]に進[すす]められた。
ctx.en: Without listening to the opponents' arguments, the plan was forced through.

bad.s: 駅[えき]で偶然[ぐうぜん]、友達[ともだち]の噂[うわさ]に{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]けた}。
bad.en: (meant: at the station I happened to overhear a rumour about my friend)
bad.why: It is deliberate, attentive listening; hearing something by chance is mimi ni suru or komimi ni hasamu.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は先生[せんせい]の話[はなし]を{耳[みみ]を傾[かたむ]けた}。
bad.en: (meant: I listened carefully to the teacher)
bad.why: The thing listened to takes ni, not o: sensei no hanashi ni mimi o katamuketa.

cards.mean: to be unable to believe one's ears
cards.lit: to doubt one's own ears

use.how: Predicate, usually past: 耳を疑った; also before a noun: 耳を疑うようなニュース. Said of hearing news or words so unexpected you cannot believe them, good or bad.

near.t: 開いた口が塞がらない
near.diff: 開いた口が塞がらない is being dumbfounded by someone's outrageous behaviour; 耳を疑う is disbelief at something heard, good or bad.

cards.cue: On the phone you are told you have won first prize in a contest you had forgotten entering. You can't believe what you just heard.

ctx.s: 合格[ごうかく]の知[し]らせを聞[き]いて、思[おも]わず{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]った}。
ctx.en: When I heard I had passed, I couldn't believe my ears.

ctx.s: 「来月[らいげつ]で会社[かいしゃ]がなくなるって本当[ほんとう]？」「僕[ぼく]も最初[さいしょ]は{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]った}よ。」
ctx.en: "Is it true the company is closing next month?" "I couldn't believe my ears at first either."

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の口[くち]から出[で]た言葉[ことば]に、全員[ぜんいん]が{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]った}。
ctx.en: No one could believe their ears at what came out of the president's mouth.

ctx.s: あの温厚[おんこう]な先輩[せんぱい]が怒鳴[どな]ったなんて、{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]う}話[はなし]だ。
ctx.en: That our gentle senior actually shouted at someone is hard to believe.

ctx.s: {耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]う}ようなニュースが、朝[あさ]から次々[つぎつぎ]と流[なが]れてきた。
ctx.en: Unbelievable news kept coming in from the morning on.

ctx.s: 受話器[じゅわき]の向[む]こうで「一等[いっとう]です」と言[い]われ、彼女[かのじょ]は{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]った}。
ctx.en: When the voice on the phone said "You've won first prize," she couldn't believe her ears.

bad.s: 雪[ゆき]の中[なか]に桜[さくら]が咲[さ]いているのを見[み]て、{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I couldn't believe my eyes when I saw cherry blossoms in the snow)
bad.why: For something seen, say me o utagau (doubt one's eyes); this idiom is only for something heard.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の話[はなし]は嘘[うそ]っぽいので、ずっと{耳[みみ]を疑[うたが]って}いる。
bad.en: (meant: his story sounds like a lie, so I've been doubting it)
bad.why: It is momentary shock at surprising news, not suspicion of a claim; for distrust say utagatte iru.

cards.mean: to cut into a conversation
cards.lit: to slip one's mouth in between others' words

use.how: Verb, often with に: 話に口を挟む; often in warnings (口を挟まないで) or the polite cushion 口を挟むようですが. Said of breaking into a conversation already going on.

near.diff: 口を出す is meddling with opinions in matters that are not yours; 口を挟む is cutting into a conversation while others are speaking.

cards.cue: Two colleagues are explaining a plan to the boss, and a third keeps cutting in before they can finish a sentence.

ctx.s: 人[ひと]が話[はな]している時[とき]に{口[くち]を挟[はさ]まないで}。
ctx.en: Don't butt in when someone is talking.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は私[わたし]たちの話[はなし]に、ときどき冗談[じょうだん]で{口[くち]を挟[はさ]む}。
ctx.en: My grandmother sometimes chips into our conversations with a joke.

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]の会話[かいわ]があまりに速[はや]くて、{口[くち]を挟[はさ]む}すきがなかった。
ctx.en: The two of them talked so fast that I couldn't get a word in.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]と母[はは]が言[い]い合[あ]っていて、私[わたし]は{口[くち]を挟[はさ]めなかった}。
ctx.en: My parents were arguing, and I couldn't cut in.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]が話[はな]し終[お]わらないうちに、新人[しんじん]が「でも」と{口[くち]を挟[はさ]んだ}。
ctx.en: Before the manager had finished speaking, the new recruit cut in with "But..."

ctx.s: 「すみません、{口[くち]を挟[はさ]む}ようですが、その数字[すうじ]は去年[きょねん]のものです。」
ctx.en: "Sorry to interrupt, but those figures are last year's."

bad.s: 電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]って、勉強[べんきょう]に{口[くち]を挟[はさ]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: the phone rang and interrupted my studying)
bad.why: Only a person cutting into a conversation with words; for something interrupting an activity say jama ga haitta.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は無口[むくち]なので、会議[かいぎ]ではいつも{口[くち]を挟[はさ]んで}いる。
bad.en: (meant: he's quiet, so he always keeps his mouth shut in meetings)
bad.why: Hasamu here is to put in, not to clamp shut: it means speaking up uninvited; for staying quiet say damatte iru.

cards.mean: to say the same thing in unison
cards.lit: to line up mouths so they say the same

use.how: Almost always 口を揃えて + a verb of saying: 口を揃えて言う. Said of several people speaking in chorus or all giving the same opinion.

near.diff: 口裏を合わせる is secretly agreeing on a story in advance, usually to deceive; 口を揃える is simply many people saying the same thing.

cards.cue: You ask five former students what their old teacher was like, and every one of them gives the same answer: strict but kind.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもたちは{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}「いただきます」と言[い]った。
ctx.en: The children said "itadakimasu" all together.

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]はみんな{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}、あの店[みせ]のラーメンがおいしいと言[い]う。
ctx.en: All my friends say with one voice that the ramen at that place is good.

ctx.s: 「新[あたら]しい課長[かちょう]、どんな人[ひと]？」「みんな{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}優[やさ]しいって言[い]ってるよ。」
ctx.en: "What's the new section chief like?" "Everyone says the same: he's kind."

ctx.s: 専門家[せんもんか]は{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}、早[はや]めの対策[たいさく]が必要[ひつよう]だと指摘[してき]する。
ctx.en: Experts are unanimous that early measures are needed.

ctx.s: 近所[きんじょ]の人[ひと]たちは{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}「真面目[まじめ]な青年[せいねん]だった」と話[はな]した。
ctx.en: The neighbours all said the same thing: "He was a serious young man."

ctx.s: 家族[かぞく]全員[ぜんいん]に{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}反対[はんたい]され、留学[りゅうがく]をあきらめた。
ctx.en: My whole family was against it with one voice, so I gave up on studying abroad.

bad.s: 犯人[はんにん]たちは捕[つか]まる前[まえ]に、こっそり{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}おいた。
bad.en: (meant: before they were caught, the culprits had secretly agreed on their story)
bad.why: Secretly agreeing on a story beforehand is kuchiura o awaseru; this idiom is the act of saying the same thing.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は一人[ひとり]で{口[くち]を揃[そろ]えて}はっきり話[はな]した。
bad.en: (meant: he spoke clearly on his own)
bad.why: It needs several people saying the same thing; one person cannot do it alone.

cards.t: 開いた口が塞がらない
cards.r: あいたくちがふさがらない
cards.mean: to be dumbfounded by someone's absurdity
cards.lit: the mouth that fell open will not close

use.how: Predicate, often after あきれて: あきれて開いた口が塞がらない. Said of someone's outrageous or shameless behaviour, never of a pleasant surprise.

near.diff: 耳を疑う is disbelief at something heard, good or bad; 開いた口が塞がらない is exasperation at someone's outrageous conduct.

cards.cue: A coworker who did none of the work on a project presents it to the boss as entirely his own. You are speechless at his nerve.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の言[い]い訳[わけ]には、{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらない}。
ctx.en: His excuse leaves me speechless.

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]のミスを人[ひと]のせいにするなんて、あきれて{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらない}よ。
ctx.en: Blaming others for his own mistake? I'm lost for words.

ctx.s: 「隣[となり]の人[ひと]、また夜中[よなか]に騒[さわ]いでたの？」「そう。注意[ちゅうい]したら逆[ぎゃく]に怒[おこ]られて、{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらなかった}。」
ctx.en: "Were the neighbours making noise in the night again?" "Yes. When I complained, they got angry at me. I was speechless."

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]も練習[れんしゅう]に来[こ]なかった人[ひと]が試合[しあい]に出[で]たいと言[い]い出[だ]し、{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらなかった}。
ctx.en: Someone who never came to a single practice announced he wanted to play in the match; we were dumbfounded.

ctx.s: 客[きゃく]の無茶[むちゃ]な要求[ようきゅう]に、店員[てんいん]たちは{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらない}様子[ようす]だった。
ctx.en: The staff looked stunned by the customer's outrageous demands.

ctx.s: 水[みず]一本[いっぽん]に千円[せんえん]も取[と]るなんて、{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらない}と思[おも]いませんか。
ctx.en: Charging a thousand yen for a bottle of water: don't you think that's outrageous?

bad.s: 富士山[ふじさん]の美[うつく]しさに、{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらなかった}。
bad.en: (meant: I was awestruck by the beauty of Mt Fuji)
bad.why: It expresses exasperation at absurd behaviour; for awe say iki o nonda or mitoreta.

bad.s: 合格[ごうかく]の知[し]らせがうれしくて、{開[あ]いた口[くち]が塞[ふさ]がらなかった}。
bad.en: (meant: I was so happy about passing I was speechless)
bad.why: It is never used for happy surprise; it is disgust at someone's nerve. Say ureshikute kotoba ga denakatta.

cards.mean: to get one's stories straight beforehand
cards.lit: to make what lies behind each person's words line up

use.how: Verb, often 口裏を合わせて + verb: 口裏を合わせてごまかす. Said of people agreeing in advance what they will say, usually to hide the truth.

near.diff: 口を揃える is many people saying the same thing, often sincerely; 口裏を合わせる is prearranging a story, usually to deceive.

cards.cue: Two brothers broke a vase. Before their mother comes home, they agree that both will say the cat knocked it over.

ctx.s: 兄弟[きょうだい]で{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせて}、猫[ねこ]が花瓶[かびん]を割[わ]ったことにした。
ctx.en: The brothers got their story straight and claimed the cat had broken the vase.

ctx.s: 「先生[せんせい]に聞[き]かれたら、図書館[としょかん]にいたって言[い]ってね」「わかった、{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせて}おくよ。」
ctx.en: "If the teacher asks, say we were in the library." "OK, I'll back up your story."

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]の話[はなし]が細[こま]かいところまで同[おな]じなのは、{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせた}からだろう。
ctx.en: Their stories match down to the details; they must have agreed on them beforehand.

ctx.s: 社員[しゃいん]たちは{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせ}、ミスを隠[かく]そうとした。
ctx.en: The employees got their stories straight and tried to cover up the mistake.

ctx.s: 警察[けいさつ]は、容疑者[ようぎしゃ]たちが事前[じぜん]に{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせて}いた疑[うたが]いがあるとみている。
ctx.en: The police suspect that the suspects had coordinated their statements in advance.

ctx.s: もしかして、みんなで{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせて}る？話[はなし]ができすぎだよ。
ctx.en: Have you all agreed on this story? It's a bit too neat.

bad.s: みんなで{口裏[くちうら]を合[あ]わせて}、「誕生日[たんじょうび]おめでとう」と言[い]った。
bad.en: (meant: we all said "happy birthday" together)
bad.why: Saying something together is kuchi o soroeru; this idiom is secretly agreeing on a story beforehand.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]とは{口裏[くちうら]が合[あ]って}、いつも楽[たの]しく話[はな]せる。
bad.en: (meant: he and I get on well and always have fun talking)
bad.why: Getting on in conversation is hanashi ga au; this idiom is a deliberate, usually dishonest, prearranged story.

cards.mean: to feel too indebted to stand up to someone
cards.lit: cannot raise one's head (in front of that person)

use.how: Xには頭が上がらない: you owe X so much (or X has such a hold on you) that you can't argue back. Always about a particular person; often said humorously of a spouse.

near.diff: 頭が下がる is admiring someone's effort; 頭が上がらない is being unable to stand up to someone because you owe them.
合わせる顔がない is shame after letting someone down; 頭が上がらない is lasting indebtedness for what they did for you.

cards.cue: Your older sister paid your rent for a year when you were broke, so now you never say no when she asks for a favour.

ctx.s: 母[はは]には今[いま]でも{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がらない}。
ctx.en: Even now I can never stand up to my mother.

ctx.s: 大学[だいがく]の学費[がくひ]を出[だ]してくれた兄[あに]には、{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がらない}。
ctx.en: I owe my brother, who paid my university fees, far too much to ever argue with him.

ctx.s: 「うちの部長[ぶちょう]、奥[おく]さんには{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がらない}らしいよ。」
ctx.en: "Apparently our department head can't say a word against his wife."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の頃[ころ]に何度[なんど]も助[たす]けてもらったので、田中[たなか]さんには{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がらない}んです。
ctx.en: Tanaka helped me out so many times when I was new that I could never refuse them anything.

ctx.s: 留守[るす]の間[あいだ]ずっと猫[ねこ]の世話[せわ]をしてもらって、お隣[となり]さんには{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がりません}。
ctx.en: The neighbours looked after our cat the whole time we were away; we're forever in their debt.

ctx.s: 借金[しゃっきん]を肩代[かたが]わりしてもらって以来[いらい]、彼[かれ]は叔父[おじ]に{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がらなくなった}。
ctx.en: Ever since his uncle took over his debts, he hasn't been able to stand up to him.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]に落[お]ちて、{頭[あたま]が上[あ]がらない}。
bad.en: (meant: I failed the exam and feel too low to lift my head)

bad.s: 泣[な]いている子[こ]どもの{胸[むね]をなで下[お]ろして}あげた。
bad.en: (meant: I soothed the crying child)
bad.why: It is only about your own relief, never soothing someone else. To comfort a child, say senaka o sasutte ageta.

cards.mean: to make up one's mind and accept whatever comes
cards.lit: to bind one's belly tight: the belly (hara) is where Japanese places one's resolve

use.how: Said when facing a risky or unavoidable outcome: 腹をくくって〜する, もう腹をくくるしかない. It means accepting the consequences, not merely deciding.

near.diff: 腹を決める is simply deciding firmly; 腹をくくる adds being ready to take whatever consequences follow.
高をくくる means to underestimate something; it shares くくる but is the opposite of bracing oneself.

cards.cue: The operation is risky, but without it she will not recover. After a sleepless night she tells her family she will go ahead, come what may. What has she done?

ctx.s: もう逃[に]げられない。{腹[はら]をくくろう}。
ctx.en: There's no way out now. Let's brace ourselves and face it.

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めて独立[どくりつ]すると{腹[はら]をくくった}。
ctx.en: I made up my mind to quit the company and go independent, whatever happens.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]に一人[ひとり]で留学[りゅうがく]するの？」「うん、もう{腹[はら]をくくった}から」
ctx.en: "Are you really going to study abroad on your own?" "Yes, I've made up my mind and I'm ready for it."

ctx.s: 失敗[しっぱい]したら責任[せきにん]を取[と]る。そう{腹[はら]をくくって}社長[しゃちょう]に提案[ていあん]した。
ctx.en: If it failed, I would take responsibility. With that resolve, I put the proposal to the president.

ctx.s: 手術[しゅじゅつ]を受[う]けるかどうか迷[まよ]っていた父[ちち]も、ようやく{腹[はら]をくくった}ようだ。
ctx.en: My father, who had been unsure whether to have the operation, seems to have finally steeled himself.

ctx.s: ここまで来[き]たら、{腹[はら]をくくって}最後[さいご]までやるしかない。
ctx.en: Now that we've come this far, we just have to accept it and see it through.

bad.s: 弟[おとうと]にケーキを食[た]べられて、{腹[はら]をくくった}。
bad.en: (meant: my brother ate my cake and I got angry)
bad.why: Getting angry is hara ga tatsu; hara wo kukuru is bracing oneself to face a hard outcome.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の試験[しけん]を前[まえ]に、{腹[はら]がくくった}。
bad.en: (meant: I steeled myself before tomorrow's exam)
bad.why: Kukuru is transitive: one binds one's own belly, so the particle is always wo, never ga.

cards.mean: to quit a bad way of life
cards.lit: to wash one's feet: to wash off the dirt of the places one has been walking

use.how: 〜から足を洗う: to leave crime, gambling or a disreputable trade for good. Also said half-jokingly of quitting a gruelling line of work.

near.diff: 手を引く is pulling out of one deal or project; 足を洗う is leaving a whole way of life, usually one seen as bad.

cards.cue: A former pickpocket now runs a bakery and has not stolen anything in ten years. What has he done with his old life?

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は悪[わる]い仲間[なかま]から{足[あし]を洗[あら]った}。
ctx.en: He broke away from his bad crowd for good.

ctx.s: ギャンブルからはもう{足[あし]を洗[あら]った}と父[ちち]は言[い]う。
ctx.en: My father says he has given up gambling for good.

ctx.s: 「昔[むかし]は万引[まんび]きばかりしてたって本当[ほんとう]？」「中学生[ちゅうがくせい]の頃[ころ]ね。もうとっくに{足[あし]を洗[あら]った}よ」
ctx.en: "Is it true you used to shoplift all the time?" "Back in middle school. I gave that up long ago."

ctx.s: 元[もと]暴走族[ぼうそうぞく]の彼[かれ]は、{足[あし]を洗[あら]って}今[いま]は整備士[せいびし]として働[はたら]いている。
ctx.en: A former biker-gang member, he went straight and now works as a mechanic.

ctx.s: 詐欺[さぎ]グループから{足[あし]を洗[あら]う}のは簡単[かんたん]ではない。
ctx.en: Getting out of a fraud ring is not easy.

ctx.s: 激務[げきむ]の広告[こうこく]業界[ぎょうかい]から{足[あし]を洗[あら]って}、田舎[いなか]でカフェを開[ひら]いた。
ctx.en: I got out of the gruelling advertising business for good and opened a café in the countryside.

bad.s: 長年[ながねん]続[つづ]けたボランティア活動[かつどう]から{足[あし]を洗[あら]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I retired from the volunteer work I had done for years)
bad.why: It implies the life left behind was shameful or something to escape; said of volunteer work it sounds like an insult to it. Say yameta or intai shita.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は悪[わる]い仕事[しごと]を{足[あし]を洗[あら]った}。
bad.en: (meant: he quit his shady work)
bad.why: What you leave is marked with kara (warui shigoto kara ashi wo arau); the wo already belongs to ashi.

cards.mean: to take advantage of someone's weak position
cards.lit: to look at someone's feet, to judge how tired and stuck they are

story.text: In the Edo period travellers went on foot along the highways and could hire a palanquin or a packhorse for the next stretch. The bearers and horse drivers, it is said, looked at a traveller's feet: someone footsore and worn out could not afford to refuse, so they asked a higher fare.

use.how: Of a seller or negotiator who exploits another's need: 足元を見て高く売る. Very often passive: 足元を見られる, to be taken advantage of.

near.diff: 弱みにつけ込む is exploiting any weakness; 足元を見る is typically pushing price or terms when the other side has no choice.

cards.cue: Your car broke down in the mountains, and the only tow-truck driver around quotes five times the normal price because he knows you have no other option. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 台風[たいふう]の日[ひ]に{足元[あしもと]を見[み]られて}、傘[かさ]を千円[せんえん]で買[か]わされた。
ctx.en: On the day of the typhoon they took advantage of me and I had to pay a thousand yen for an umbrella.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]に{足元[あしもと]を見[み]られない}よう、急[いそ]いでいることは隠[かく]しておこう。
ctx.en: Let's hide the fact that we're in a hurry, so they can't take advantage of us.

ctx.s: あの業者[ぎょうしゃ]は客[きゃく]の{足元[あしもと]を見[み]て}、修理[しゅうり]代[だい]を吊[つ]り上[あ]げる。
ctx.en: That contractor sizes up its customers' predicament and jacks up the repair bill.

ctx.s: 「向[む]こうは期限[きげん]が迫[せま]ってるのを知[し]ってるからね」「完全[かんぜん]に{足元[あしもと]を見[み]られてる}な」
ctx.en: "They know our deadline is close." "They're totally exploiting our position."

ctx.s: 資金[しきん]不足[ぶそく]の会社[かいしゃ]は銀行[ぎんこう]に{足元[あしもと]を見[み]られ}、厳[きび]しい条件[じょうけん]を飲[の]まされた。
ctx.en: The cash-strapped company was taken advantage of by the bank and forced to accept harsh terms.

ctx.s: 人[ひと]の{足元[あしもと]を見[み]る}ような商売[しょうばい]は長続[ながつづ]きしない。
ctx.en: A business that preys on people's predicaments won't last.

bad.s: 困[こま]っている友達[ともだち]の{足元[あしもと]を見[み]て}、お金[かね]を貸[か]してあげた。
bad.en: (meant: seeing my friend was in trouble, I lent them money)
bad.why: It means exploiting someone's predicament, never noticing it in order to help.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は人[ひと]の{足元[あしもと]を見[み]る}のが上手[じょうず]で、みんなに信頼[しんらい]されている。
bad.en: (meant: she is good at understanding people's circumstances, so everyone trusts her)
bad.why: It is always criticism: someone who does it is grasping, not perceptive or trustworthy.

cards.mean: to hesitate, to have second thoughts
cards.lit: to tread the second step: one foot goes forward, then the next only marks time on the spot

use.how: 〜に二の足を踏む, 〜することに二の足を踏む, 値段を見て二の足を踏む: holding back from a decision or purchase out of worry about cost or risk.

near.diff: 気が進まない is not wanting to do it; 二の足を踏む is wanting to but holding back over cost or risk.

cards.cue: You have wanted a new camera for months, but when you see the final price at the till you put it back and walk away to think again. What did you do?

ctx.s: 値段[ねだん]を見[み]て、つい{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]んで}しまった。
ctx.en: When I saw the price, I couldn't help having second thoughts.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい仕事[しごと]に興味[きょうみ]はあるが、転勤[てんきん]があると聞[き]いて{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]んで}いる。
ctx.en: I'm interested in the new job, but hearing it involves relocation makes me hesitate.

ctx.s: 「あのマンション、買[か]うの？」「欲[ほ]しいんだけど、ローンを考[かんが]えると{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]んじゃって}」
ctx.en: "Are you buying that flat?" "I'd love to, but when I think about the loan I keep holding back."

ctx.s: 初期[しょき]費用[ひよう]が高[たか]いため、導入[どうにゅう]に{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]む}企業[きぎょう]も多[おお]い。
ctx.en: Because of the high start-up costs, many companies hesitate to adopt it.

ctx.s: 留学[りゅうがく]したい気持[きも]ちはあったが、治安[ちあん]が心配[しんぱい]で{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]んだ}。
ctx.en: I did want to study abroad, but worries about safety made me hold back.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]失敗[しっぱい]した人[ひと]ほど、再[ふたた]び挑戦[ちょうせん]することに{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]み}がちだ。
ctx.en: The people who have failed once are the ones who tend to hesitate to try again.

bad.s: 名前[なまえ]を聞[き]かれて、一瞬[いっしゅん]{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: when asked my name, I paused for a second before answering)
bad.why: It is holding back from a step or decision one is weighing, not a momentary pause in speech.

bad.s: 階段[かいだん]で{二[に]の足[あし]を踏[ふ]んで}転[ころ]んでしまった。
bad.en: (meant: I missed my footing on the stairs and fell)
bad.why: It is never about real stepping; it only describes hesitating over a decision.

cards.mean: to nitpick someone's words
cards.lit: to grab a raised leg: catching the leg an opponent lifts, as in grappling, and tipping them over

use.how: 人の揚げ足を取る, 揚げ足を取られる, or the noun 揚げ足取り. Criticises seizing on a slip or a turn of phrase to score points.

near.diff: けちをつける is finding fault with anything; 揚げ足を取る seizes on a slip or wording in what someone said.

cards.cue: In a meeting you say 'about a hundred people came', and a colleague cuts in: 'Ninety-seven, actually. Can we trust anything you say?' What is he doing?

ctx.s: 人[ひと]の{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]る}のはやめなさい。
ctx.en: Stop picking on every little thing people say.

ctx.s: ちょっと言[い]い間違[まちが]えただけなのに、{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]られた}。

ctx.s: 「今[いま]、『絶対[ぜったい]』って言[い]ったよね？」「そうやって{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]らないで}よ」
ctx.en: "You just said 'definitely', didn't you?" "Don't pounce on every word like that."

ctx.s: ネットでは、有名人[ゆうめいじん]の発言[はつげん]の{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]る}書[か]き込[こ]みが絶[た]えない。
ctx.en: Online there is no end of posts nitpicking what celebrities say.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は議論[ぎろん]に負[ま]けそうになると、相手[あいて]の{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]り}始[はじ]める。

ctx.s: {揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]られない}よう、記者[きしゃ]会見[かいけん]では言葉[ことば]を慎重[しんちょう]に選[えら]んだ。
ctx.en: So as not to give anyone a slip to pounce on, she chose her words carefully at the press conference.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]は私[わたし]の作文[さくぶん]の{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]って}、丁寧[ていねい]に直[なお]してくれた。
bad.en: (meant: my teacher went through my essay and corrected it carefully)

bad.s: 夫[おっと]は私[わたし]の料理[りょうり]に{揚[あ]げ足[あし]を取[と]って}ばかりいる。
bad.en: (meant: my husband keeps finding fault with my cooking)
bad.why: It targets slips in what someone says; complaining about food or things is kechi wo tsukeru.

cards.r: あしもとにもおよばない
cards.mean: to be nowhere near as good as
cards.lit: cannot even reach someone's feet: so far below them that one does not come up to their feet

use.how: AはBの足元にも及ばない: A is far below B in skill or quality. Often said modestly of oneself next to someone admired. Only used in the negative.

near.diff: 歯が立たない is failing when you take someone or something on; 足元にも及ばない is a standing comparison of level.
右に出る者はいない praises the person at the top; 足元にも及ばない stresses how far below them the other is.

cards.cue: A keen amateur cook eats at a famous chef's restaurant and says his own cooking is not remotely in the same league. How does he put it?

ctx.en: When it comes to English, I'm nowhere near my brother.

ctx.s: 「絵[え]、上手[じょうず]だね」「いえいえ、先生[せんせい]の{足元[あしもと]にも及[およ]びません}」

ctx.s: この安[やす]いコピー品[ひん]は、品質[ひんしつ]では本物[ほんもの]の{足元[あしもと]にも及[およ]ばない}。

cards.mean: to get down to something in earnest
cards.lit: to put one's real hips into it: to settle one's hips firmly, the stance for serious work

near.diff: 気合を入れる is psyching oneself up for an effort; 本腰を入れる is committing seriously to a task over time.

cards.cue: With six months left before the entrance exam, a student who has studied on and off deletes his games and draws up a daily study plan. What is he doing?

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]は海外[かいがい]市場[しじょう]の開拓[かいたく]に{本腰[ほんごし]を入[い]れ}始[はじ]めた。

cards.mean: to be no match for
cards.lit: the teeth won't go in: something too hard to bite into

use.how: 〜には歯が立たない: said by or of the side that cannot cope with an opponent, a problem or a text: 相手が強すぎて歯が立たない.

cards.cue: A club tennis player faces a former national champion and loses every game without once coming close. How would she describe the match?

ctx.en: "How was that university's entrance exam?" "The maths was completely beyond me."

ctx.s: 最新[さいしん]の将棋[しょうぎ]ソフトには、トップ棋士[きし]でも{歯[は]が立[た]たない}と言[い]われる。
ctx.en: It is said that even top professional shogi players are no match for the latest shogi software.

bad.en: (meant: this hard problem was beyond me)

cards.mean: to be pressed by a looming deadline

near.diff: 一刻を争う is every moment mattering in an emergency; 尻に火がつく is being driven to act because things were left too late.

ctx.en: "You still haven't done your summer homework?" "No, I can't get going until the deadline is breathing down my neck."

cards.mean: to fudge numbers, especially one's age

cards.mean: a premonition

bad.en: (meant: I had a feeling I would get full marks)
bad.why: It is a hunch that foretells a real event, almost always a bad one such as an accident or a death; a hopeful guess about oneself is just a feeling, not a premonition.

cards.mean: to throw cold water on a plan or a good mood
cards.lit: to pour water into something, cooling what was hot and rising

use.how: 〜に水を差す: the object is a mood, plan, talk or relationship (盛り上がり, 話, 仲). Said of a remark or event that spoils it; often 水を差すようで悪いけど.

near.diff: 口を挟む is cutting into other people's conversation; 水を差す is dampening an enthusiasm, a plan or a good mood.
けちをつける is finding fault with something; 水を差す is spoiling the momentum or mood, even with a fair point.

ctx.en: The lovely atmosphere was spoiled.

bad.en: (meant: I sang a song at the birthday party and livened things up)

cards.mean: to make a bad situation worse
cards.lit: to pour oil onto a fire

cards.mean: completely groundless

near.diff: 濡れ衣を着せる is pinning a false accusation on a person; 根も葉もない describes any rumour or claim with no basis at all.

cards.mean: to acknowledge someone's superiority
cards.lit: to place one stone first, as the weaker player does in the game of Go

story.text: In the board game Go, when two players of unequal strength meet, the weaker one places one or more stones on the board before play begins, as a handicap. Laying down that first stone is an admission that the opponent is the stronger player. From this, the phrase came to mean recognising someone as better than oneself and treating them with respect.

足元にも及ばない says one is nowhere near their level; 一目置く is respect, without saying how far behind one is.

ctx.en: She's someone people in the company hold in high regard.

cards.mean: to become natural and at home in a role
cards.lit: to suit the boards: to look at home on the wooden floor of the stage

story.text: In Japanese theatre, kabuki included, the word for 'the boards' means the stage. When an actor's performance had, through long experience, come to fit the stage naturally, he was said to have settled onto the boards. The phrase then spread to anyone who has grown comfortably into a job, a role or a way of behaving.
story.source: Japanese theatre usage, where 板 means the stage

use.how: Subject is a role, manner or look that takes time to grow into: 店長ぶりが板についてきた / スーツ姿が板につく. Usually with てきた or た.

near.diff: 様になる is simply looking right, possibly at once; 板につく stresses an ease that came with time in the role.

ctx.en: A year into motherhood, she now holds her baby with ease.

ctx.en: My polite Japanese, so stiff at first, has gradually become natural.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の司会[しかい]はまだ{板[いた]についていない}が、一生懸命[いっしょうけんめい]さは伝[つた]わってくる。
ctx.en: He isn't quite at ease as host yet, but his effort comes through.

ctx.s: 舞台[ぶたい]に立[た]って十年[じゅうねん]、彼女[かのじょ]の演技[えんぎ]はすっかり{板[いた]についた}。

near.diff: 折り紙付き describes something whose quality is already certified; 太鼓判を押す is a person's act of guaranteeing it.

ctx.s: 「どこも悪[わる]くない」と医者[いしゃ]に{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]された}。
ctx.en: The doctor assured me there was nothing wrong with me at all.

ctx.s: この店[みせ]のラーメンは、グルメな友達[ともだち]も{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]す}おいしさだ。
ctx.en: The ramen here is so good that even my foodie friend vouches for it.

ctx.s: 「この中古車[ちゅうこしゃ]、本当[ほんとう]に大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]？」「整備士[せいびし]の私[わたし]が{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]します}よ」
ctx.en: "Is this used car really all right?" "I'm a mechanic, and I guarantee it."

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]が{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]す}だけあって、その新人[しんじん]はすぐにレギュラーになった。
ctx.en: As you'd expect with the manager vouching for him, the rookie soon became a regular.

ctx.s: 専門家[せんもんか]が品質[ひんしつ]に{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]した}新製品[しんせいひん]が、来月[らいげつ]発売[はつばい]される。
ctx.en: A new product whose quality experts have vouched for goes on sale next month.

bad.s: 明日[あした]は晴[は]れると{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]す}けど、自信[じしん]はない。
bad.en: (meant: I'll say it will be sunny tomorrow, but I'm not sure)
bad.why: It is a firm guarantee from someone confident; pairing it with not being sure contradicts it.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は私[わたし]の企画[きかく]に{太鼓判[たいこばん]を押[お]して}、全部[ぜんぶ]やり直[なお]させた。
bad.en: (meant: the manager rejected my proposal and made me redo all of it)
bad.why: It only ever means vouching for quality; it cannot mean condemning or rejecting something.

cards.mean: to be singled out and chosen
cards.lit: a white-feathered arrow comes to stand in someone's roof

story.text: As the expression is traditionally explained, a god who demanded a young girl as a sacrifice would mark the house it had chosen by shooting an arrow fletched with white feathers into its roof, and that family had to give up their daughter. Being picked out by the arrow was once a calamity; today the phrase is mostly used of being chosen from among many for an important role.
story.source: Japanese folk belief about human sacrifice (人身御供) demanded by a god

use.how: 〜に白羽の矢が立つ: the chosen person or place takes に; the choosers can say 〜に白羽の矢を立てる. Said of being deliberately picked from many for a role.

cards.cue: Out of two hundred staff, the board needs someone to head the risky new overseas branch, and after weeks of debate they pick a quiet section chief.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいリーダーとして、彼[かれ]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]った}。
ctx.en: He was the one chosen as the new leader.

ctx.s: 「どうして私[わたし]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]った}んですか」
ctx.en: "Why was I the one who got picked?"

ctx.s: 友人[ゆうじん]の結婚式[けっこんしき]でスピーチをする役[やく]として、僕[ぼく]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]った}。
ctx.en: I was the one picked to give the speech at my friend's wedding.

ctx.s: 主役[しゅやく]として{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]った}のは、まだ無名[むめい]の新人[しんじん]だった。
ctx.en: The one singled out for the lead role was a still-unknown newcomer.

ctx.s: 大会[たいかい]の開催地[かいさいち]として、この小[ちい]さな町[まち]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]った}。
ctx.en: This small town was the one chosen to host the tournament.

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]は再建[さいけん]を任[まか]せる人物[じんぶつ]として、外部[がいぶ]の経営者[けいえいしゃ]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]を立[た]てた}。
ctx.en: The company singled out an outside executive as the person to entrust with its turnaround.

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじを買[か]ったら、私[わたし]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]って}一等[いっとう]が当[あ]たった。
bad.en: (meant: I bought a lottery ticket and won first prize)
bad.why: It means being deliberately picked by people for a role, not winning something by chance.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]に{白羽[しらは]の矢[や]が立[た]って}、来月[らいげつ]から海外[かいがい]へ遊[あそ]びに行[い]く。
bad.en: (meant: he is lucky enough to be going abroad on holiday next month)
bad.why: It is about being chosen by others for a role or task, not about having a lucky chance for oneself.

cards.mean: to ignore one's own faults while criticising others
cards.lit: to put something up on the shelf, out of sight

use.how: Almost always 自分のことは棚に上げて, followed by criticising someone else. Said critically of another person, or wryly of oneself.

near.diff: 見て見ぬふり is pretending not to see someone else's wrongdoing; 棚に上げる is ignoring one's own fault while blaming others.

cards.cue: Your boss, who turns up late to every single meeting, gives the team a long lecture about punctuality.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は自分[じぶん]のことは{棚[たな]に上[あ]げて}、人[ひと]の悪口[わるくち]ばかり言[い]う。
ctx.en: He ignores his own faults and does nothing but badmouth others.

ctx.s: 「遅刻[ちこく]が多[おお]いのは誰[だれ]？自分[じぶん]のこと{棚[たな]に上[あ]げない}でよ」
ctx.en: "Who's the one who's always late? Don't act as if that isn't you."

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]の部屋[へや]の散[ち]らかりようは{棚[たな]に上[あ]げて}、母[はは]は僕[ぼく]に片付[かたづ]けろと言[い]う。
ctx.en: Mum tells me to tidy up, conveniently forgetting how messy her own room is.

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]のことは{棚[たな]に上[あ]げて}言[い]うけど、もう少[すこ]し早[はや]く寝[ね]たほうがいいよ。
ctx.en: I know I'm one to talk, but you should go to bed a bit earlier.

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]の失敗[しっぱい]を{棚[たな]に上[あ]げて}部下[ぶか]を責[せ]める上司[じょうし]は、信頼[しんらい]されない。
ctx.en: A boss who blames his staff while ignoring his own mistakes will never be trusted.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は自[みずか]らの不正[ふせい]を{棚[たな]に上[あ]げ}、記事[きじ]で他社[たしゃ]を厳[きび]しく批判[ひはん]した。
ctx.en: Ignoring his own misconduct, he harshly criticised other companies in his article.

bad.s: 自分[じぶん]の手柄[てがら]は{棚[たな]に上[あ]げて}、チームのみんなを褒[ほ]めた。
bad.en: (meant: he modestly set aside his own credit and praised the team)
bad.why: It means ignoring one's own faults in order to criticise others; it is never modesty and never leads to praise.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の失敗[しっぱい]は{棚[たな]に上[あ]げて}、許[ゆる]してあげよう。
bad.en: (meant: let's overlook his mistake and forgive him)
bad.why: It is about one's own faults, not forgiving someone else's; letting another person's mistake go calls for a different idiom.

cards.mean: to give up on something as hopeless
cards.lit: to throw down the spoon: the spoon a doctor used to measure out and mix medicine

story.text: In traditional Japanese medicine the doctor measured out and blended medicine with a spoon (saji). A doctor who judged a patient beyond cure would throw the spoon aside and stop preparing medicine. From this, the phrase came to mean giving up on anyone or anything as beyond help.
story.source: Traditional Japanese medical practice; the standard dictionary explanation

use.how: Said of someone who was trying to cure, fix or teach and stops: 医者もさじを投げた. The hopeless case can take に: あの子には先生もさじを投げた.

near.diff: 手を引く is withdrawing from an involvement for any reason; さじを投げる is giving up because you judge the case hopeless.
手に負えない says something is beyond your power to handle; さじを投げる is the act of giving up on it.

cards.cue: Three repairmen have tried to fix an old washing machine; the last one shakes his head, packs his tools and says nothing more can be done. What did he do?

ctx.s: このパソコンは古[ふる]すぎて、修理屋[しゅうりや]さんも{さじを投[な]げた}。
ctx.en: This computer is so old that even the repair shop gave up on it.

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]教[おし]えても覚[おぼ]えないので、先生[せんせい]もとうとう{さじを投[な]げて}しまった。
ctx.en: He never remembered no matter how many times he was taught, so in the end even the teacher gave up on him.

ctx.s: 「このバグ、もう無理[むり]だよ」「ここで{さじを投[な]げたら}終[お]わりだよ。もう少[すこ]し調[しら]べよう」
ctx.en: "This bug is impossible." "If we give up on it now, that's the end. Let's look into it a bit more."

ctx.s: どの医者[いしゃ]も{さじを投[な]げた}病気[びょうき]が、新[あたら]しい薬[くすり]で治[なお]った。
ctx.en: An illness that every doctor had given up on was cured with a new drug.

ctx.s: 専門家[せんもんか]が{さじを投[な]げる}ほど、この古文書[こもんじょ]の文字[もじ]は読[よ]みにくい。
ctx.en: The writing in this old document is so hard to read that even experts give up on it.

ctx.s: 親[おや]にも{さじを投[な]げられた}弟[おとうと]だったが、今[いま]では立派[りっぱ]な社会人[しゃかいじん]だ。
ctx.en: My younger brother was someone even our parents had given up on, but now he is a fine, responsible adult.

bad.s: 将来[しょうらい]の夢[ゆめ]に{さじを投[な]げて}、会社員[かいしゃいん]になった。
bad.en: (meant: I gave up my dream and became an office worker)
bad.why: It is giving up on curing or fixing a case judged hopeless, not abandoning one's own dream or goal; for that, use the plain verb for giving up.

bad.s: 疲[つか]れたので、今日[きょう]の練習[れんしゅう]は{さじを投[な]げた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was tired, so I skipped today's practice)
bad.why: It means abandoning something as hopeless after trying hard to fix it, not skipping a task because one is tired.

cards.mean: to remain unconvinced
cards.lit: it does not drop into the gut: what you were told never settles inside you

use.how: Mostly in the negative, about an explanation, decision or event that seems off: どうも腑に落ちない, 腑に落ちない点がある. The speaker understood it but is not convinced.

near.diff: 首をかしげる is tilting the head, the visible sign of doubt; 腑に落ちない is the inner feeling that something does not add up.
耳を疑う is disbelief on hearing shocking news; 腑に落ちない is a quieter, lingering sense that an explanation does not fit.

cards.cue: The courier says your parcel was handed over at the door, but you were home all day and nobody rang. Their answer leaves you uneasy. How do you feel about it?

ctx.s: 説明[せつめい]を聞[き]いても、どうも{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}。
ctx.en: Even after hearing the explanation, something just doesn't sit right with me.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]が急[きゅう]に会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めた理由[りゆう]が、今[いま]でも{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}。
ctx.en: I still can't accept the reason he gave for suddenly quitting the company.

ctx.s: 「何[なに]か{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}ことでもあるの？」「うん、話[はなし]がうますぎる気[き]がして」
ctx.en: "Is there something that doesn't add up for you?" "Yeah, it sounds too good to be true."

ctx.s: 鍵[かぎ]は閉[し]めたはずなのに開[あ]いていた。{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}話[はなし]だ。
ctx.en: I'm sure I locked it, yet it was open. Something about it doesn't add up.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は頷[うなず]きはしたが、まだ{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}様子[ようす]だった。
ctx.en: The department head did nod, but still looked unconvinced.

ctx.s: この判定[はんてい]には{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}点[てん]が多[おお]い、と専門家[せんもんか]は指摘[してき]した。
ctx.en: Experts pointed out that there is a lot in this decision that is hard to accept.

bad.s: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べすぎて、お腹[なか]が{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちない}。
bad.en: (meant: I ate too much lunch and my stomach feels heavy)
bad.why: The gut is only an image here; the phrase means not being convinced, never a physical feeling in the stomach.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]の声[こえ]が小[ちい]さくて、{腑[ふ]に落[お]ちなかった}。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher spoke so quietly that I couldn't follow)
bad.why: It is about not accepting something you did hear and understand, not about failing to hear or follow it.

cards.mean: to make no progress, to get nowhere
cards.lit: the fence will not open: rachi is the fence around a horse-riding ground

use.how: Said of talks, inquiries or dealings that are stuck: このままでは埒が明かない. Often the reason for changing approach: 電話では埒が明かないので直接行った.

near.diff: 話にならない dismisses the other side's position as absurd; 埒が明かない says the matter is stuck and getting nowhere.
手を焼く is struggling to cope with a difficult person or problem; 埒が明かない is that the process itself makes no headway.

cards.cue: You have emailed customer support five times and every reply just asks you to wait, so you decide to go to their office in person. Why?

ctx.s: このまま話[はな]し合[あ]っても{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}よ。
ctx.en: If we just keep talking like this, we'll get nowhere.

ctx.s: 電話[でんわ]では{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}ので、直接[ちょくせつ]会[あ]いに行[い]った。
ctx.en: We were getting nowhere on the phone, so I went to see them in person.

ctx.s: 「担当者[たんとうしゃ]じゃ{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}な。上[うえ]の人[ひと]を呼[よ]んでもらおう」
ctx.en: "We're getting nowhere with the person in charge. Let's ask them to call someone higher up."

ctx.s: 一人[ひとり]で悩[なや]んでいても{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}から、誰[だれ]かに相談[そうだん]してみたら？
ctx.en: Worrying about it on your own won't get you anywhere, so why not talk it over with someone?

ctx.s: メールのやり取[と]りでは{埒[らち]が明[あ]かず}、結局[けっきょく]会議[かいぎ]を開[ひら]くことになった。
ctx.en: Going back and forth by email got us nowhere, so in the end we decided to hold a meeting.

ctx.s: 二社[にしゃ]の契約[けいやく]交渉[こうしょう]は、何[なん]か月[げつ]も{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}まま続[つづ]いている。
ctx.en: Contract negotiations between the two companies have dragged on for months without getting anywhere.

bad.s: そんな{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}ことを言[い]うなんて失礼[しつれい]だ。
bad.en: (meant: it's rude to say such outrageous things)
bad.why: It means a matter is getting nowhere, not that behaviour is outrageous; the learner is mixing it up with furachi (outrageous, unruly).

bad.s: 鍵[かぎ]が壊[こわ]れて、ドアの{埒[らち]が明[あ]かない}。
bad.en: (meant: the lock is broken and the door won't open)
bad.why: The opening fence is only the image; the phrase is about stalled talks or dealings, never a real door that won't open.

cards.mean: to speed something up, to spur it on
cards.lit: to apply the spurs: digging the spurs into a horse to make it go faster

use.how: XがYに拍車をかける: a factor speeds up a trend or effort already under way, often a bad trend (物価高に拍車をかける). Intransitive form: 〜に拍車がかかる.

near.diff: 火に油を注ぐ inflames anger or a conflict; 拍車をかける speeds up any trend or process that is already moving.
背中を押す gives a person the push to make a decision; 拍車をかける speeds up a trend or process, not a person.

cards.cue: Prices were already creeping up; then a poor harvest sent them climbing much faster. What did the harvest do to the rise in prices?

ctx.s: テレビで紹介[しょうかい]されたことが、店[みせ]の人気[にんき]に{拍車[はくしゃ]をかけた}。
ctx.en: Being featured on TV gave the shop's popularity a further boost.

ctx.s: 優勝[ゆうしょう]を目指[めざ]して、選手[せんしゅ]たちは練習[れんしゅう]に{拍車[はくしゃ]をかけた}。
ctx.en: Aiming for the championship, the players stepped up their training.

ctx.s: 「値上[ねあ]げが客離[きゃくばな]れに{拍車[はくしゃ]をかけた}みたい」「やっぱり高[たか]すぎたんだね」
ctx.en: "It seems the price rise sped up the loss of customers." "So it really was too expensive."

ctx.s: 円安[えんやす]が物価[ぶっか]の上昇[じょうしょう]に{拍車[はくしゃ]をかけて}いる。
ctx.en: The weak yen is accelerating the rise in prices.

ctx.s: スマホの普及[ふきゅう]で、若者[わかもの]の本[ほん]離[ばな]れに{拍車[はくしゃ]がかかった}。
ctx.en: The spread of smartphones has sped up young people's drift away from books.

ctx.s: 町[まち]の高齢化[こうれいか]に{拍車[はくしゃ]をかける}ように、若[わか]い世代[せだい]が次々[つぎつぎ]と出[で]ていった。
ctx.en: As if to hasten the town's ageing, the young generation left one after another.

bad.s: 円安[えんやす]が物価[ぶっか]の上昇[じょうしょう]を{拍車[はくしゃ]をかけた}。
bad.en: (meant: the weak yen sped up the rise in prices)
bad.why: The spur already takes o, so the trend being sped up must be marked with ni, not a second o.

bad.s: 遅刻[ちこく]しそうだったので、自転車[じてんしゃ]に{拍車[はくしゃ]をかけた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was about to be late, so I pedalled faster)
bad.why: It is figurative, for trends and efforts, not for physically going faster; on a bike you simply raise your speed.

cards.mean: to play a part in bringing something about
cards.lit: to take on one role: kau, to buy, here means taking a part on of one's own accord

use.how: 〜に一役買う: a person or thing plays a helpful part in some result or cause: 町おこしに一役買う. Often 一役買っている.

near.diff: 一肌脱ぐ is stepping in to help a particular person out of goodwill; 一役買う is contributing a part to a result or cause, and a thing can be its subject.

cards.cue: A café started selling cakes made with the town's strawberries, and tourists began to visit the town again. What did the café do for the town's revival?

ctx.s: この祭[まつ]りは、町[まち]の活性化[かっせいか]に{一役[ひとやく]買[か]って}いる。
ctx.en: This festival is doing its part to revitalise the town.

ctx.s: 「今回[こんかい]の成功[せいこう]には、君[きみ]のアイデアも{一役[ひとやく]買[か]った}よ」
ctx.en: "Your idea played its part in this success too."

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は退職[たいしょく]後[ご]、子[こ]どもたちの見守[みまも]り活動[かつどう]に{一役[ひとやく]買[か]って}いる。
ctx.en: Since retiring, my grandfather has been doing his part in a neighbourhood scheme that keeps an eye on local children.

ctx.s: 地元[じもと]の高校生[こうこうせい]が、観光[かんこう]ポスターの制作[せいさく]に{一役[ひとやく]買[か]った}。
ctx.en: Local high-school students played a part in making the tourism posters.

ctx.s: 定期的[ていきてき]な運動[うんどう]は、ストレスの解消[かいしょう]にも{一役[ひとやく]買[か]う}と言[い]われる。
ctx.en: Regular exercise is said to help in relieving stress, too.

ctx.s: 海岸[かいがん]の清掃[せいそう]に{一役[ひとやく]買[か]おう}と、多[おお]くの住民[じゅうみん]が集[あつ]まった。
ctx.en: Many residents gathered to do their bit for the beach clean-up.

bad.s: 君[きみ]のアイデアが成功[せいこう]を{一役[ひとやく]買[か]った}。
bad.en: (meant: your idea played a part in the success)
bad.why: The result one contributes to is marked with ni, not o; with o it reads as if the success itself were bought.

bad.s: 学芸会[がくげいかい]の劇[げき]で、私[わたし]は王様[おうさま]として{一役[ひとやく]買[か]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I played the king in the school play)
bad.why: It means contributing to an outcome, not literally acting a part on stage; for that, say you performed the king's role.

cards.mean: to make sense, to be logical
cards.lit: the line runs straight through: a thread of reasoning that holds from start to end

use.how: Said of an argument, explanation or demand: 筋が通っている, 筋の通った説明. Of a person, 筋の通った人 acts on consistent principles. 筋が通らない can also mean unfair or improper.

near.diff: 的を射る says a remark hits the key point; 筋が通る says reasoning is consistent from start to end.
腑に落ちない is the listener's feeling of not being convinced; 筋が通る judges the reasoning itself as consistent.

cards.cue: The new rule seems strict, but each step of the manager's reasoning follows from the last and you cannot find a hole in it. What do you say about her reasoning?

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の説明[せつめい]は{筋[すじ]が通[とお]って}いる。
ctx.en: His explanation makes sense.

ctx.s: 言[い]っていることに{筋[すじ]が通[とお]って}いないから、誰[だれ]も納得[なっとく]しない。
ctx.en: What he says doesn't hang together, so nobody is convinced.

ctx.s: 「それは{筋[すじ]が通[とお]らない}よ。約束[やくそく]したのは君[きみ]でしょう」
ctx.en: "That's not right. You were the one who made the promise."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は頑固[がんこ]だったが、{筋[すじ]の通[とお]った}人[ひと]だった。
ctx.en: My grandmother was stubborn, but she was a woman of principle.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]の要求[ようきゅう]は厳[きび]しいが、{筋[すじ]は通[とお]って}いる。
ctx.en: The other side's demands are tough, but they are reasonable.

ctx.s: この推理[すいり]小説[しょうせつ]は、犯人[はんにん]の動機[どうき]にも{筋[すじ]が通[とお]って}いて面白[おもしろ]い。
ctx.en: This mystery novel is good: even the culprit's motive makes sense.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{筋[すじ]が通[とお]って}いて、とてもきれいだ。
bad.en: (meant: she has fine features and is very pretty)
bad.why: Only hanasuji ga tooru describes a straight, well-shaped nose; on its own this phrase is about logic or principle, never looks.

bad.s: 電車[でんしゃ]が時間[じかん]どおりに来[き]て、{筋[すじ]が通[とお]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the train came on time and everything went to plan)
bad.why: It judges reasoning or conduct as consistent, not events going smoothly or going to plan.

cards.mean: to hit the mark, to be to the point
cards.lit: to shoot an arrow into the target

use.how: Mostly 的を射た〜 or 的を射ている, of a remark, question, criticism or summary that hits the key point. 的を得る is also heard but often criticised as a mistake; use 射る.

near.diff: 筋が通る says reasoning is consistent from start to end; 的を射る says a remark goes straight to the heart of the matter.
耳が痛い is how the hearer feels when criticism hits home; 的を射る judges the remark itself as on target.

cards.cue: In a long, wandering meeting, a new employee asks one short question that goes straight to the real problem everyone had been circling. How would you describe the question?

ctx.s: それは{的[まと]を射[い]た}質問[しつもん]ですね。
ctx.en: That's a question that really hits the mark.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]の指摘[してき]はいつも{的[まと]を射[い]て}いる。
ctx.en: The teacher's comments are always spot on.

ctx.s: 「彼[かれ]の意見[いけん]、{的[まと]を射[い]て}たね」「うん、まさにそこが問題[もんだい]なんだよ」
ctx.en: "His opinion was right on the mark, wasn't it?" "Yeah, that's exactly where the problem lies."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の{的[まと]を射[い]た}一言[ひとこと]で、長[なが]い会議[かいぎ]が一気[いっき]にまとまった。
ctx.en: One spot-on remark from the new hire brought the long meeting together at once.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の批判[ひはん]は一言[ひとこと]だけだったが、{的[まと]を射[い]て}いたので誰[だれ]も反論[はんろん]できなかった。
ctx.en: Her criticism was just one remark, but it was so on target that nobody could argue back.

ctx.s: 解説者[かいせつしゃ]の{的[まと]を射[い]た}説明[せつめい]のおかげで、試合[しあい]の流[なが]れがよく分[わ]かった。
ctx.en: Thanks to the commentator's to-the-point explanation, I could follow how the match unfolded.

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじで{的[まと]を射[い]て}、百万円[ひゃくまんえん]当[あ]たった。
bad.en: (meant: I hit the jackpot and won a million yen in the lottery)
bad.why: It praises a remark or judgment for hitting the point, not luck; a lottery ticket simply wins (ataru).

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は料理[りょうり]が{的[まと]を射[い]て}いる。
bad.en: (meant: he is a skilled cook)
bad.why: It describes remarks, questions and judgments that are on point, never a person's skill at something.

cards.mean: to step up and help out wholeheartedly
cards.lit: to bare one's shoulder: slipping an arm out of the kimono sleeve to set to hard work

use.how: Of stepping in to help someone else with real effort: 友人のために一肌脱ぐ. Common as an offer, 一肌脱ごう, or a request, 一肌脱いでくれないか.

near.diff: 手を貸す is any help, even a small hand; 一肌脱ぐ is taking real trouble on yourself for someone's sake.
一役買う is contributing a part to a result or cause; 一肌脱ぐ is coming to the rescue of a particular person out of goodwill.

cards.cue: An old friend's small bakery is about to close, and you, a web designer, offer to build their online shop for free over your weekends. What are you doing?

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]が困[こま]っているなら、{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]ごう}。
ctx.en: If my friend is in trouble, I'll do what I can to help.

ctx.s: 「引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの人手[ひとで]が足[た]りないんだ」「よし、僕[ぼく]が{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]ぐ}よ」
ctx.en: "We're short of hands for the move." "Right, I'll pitch in."

ctx.s: 後輩[こうはい]のために{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]いで}、取引先[とりひきさき]を紹介[しょうかい]してあげた。
ctx.en: I went out of my way for my junior colleague and introduced them to some of our clients.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]、ここは一[ひと]つ{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]いで}いただけませんか。
ctx.en: Boss, could you possibly step in and help us out this time?

ctx.s: 地元[じもと]の商店街[しょうてんがい]を救[すく]おうと、有名[ゆうめい]な料理人[りょうりにん]が{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]いだ}。
ctx.en: A famous chef stepped in to help save the local shopping street.

ctx.s: いつもお世話[せわ]になっている先輩[せんぱい]の頼[たの]みとあっては、{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]がない}わけにはいかない。
ctx.en: When it's a request from a senior colleague who has always looked after me, I can't refuse to help.

bad.s: 暑[あつ]いので、上着[うわぎ]を{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]いだ}。
bad.en: (meant: it was hot, so I took off my jacket)
bad.why: It is only figurative, for helping someone; taking off clothes is just the plain verb nugu.

bad.s: 自分[じぶん]の昇進[しょうしん]のために{一肌[ひとはだ]脱[ぬ]いだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I worked hard to get myself promoted)
bad.why: It means putting oneself out to help another person, never working hard for one's own benefit.

cards.mean: to dig one's own grave
cards.lit: to dig the grave pit: preparing one's own grave with one's own hands

use.how: Of someone whose own words or acts bring about their own downfall, often by saying too much: 余計なことを言って墓穴を掘った. Also 自ら墓穴を掘る.

near.diff: 裏目に出る is any well-meant move that backfires; 墓穴を掘る stresses that one ruined oneself by one's own act, often by talking.
口が滑る is letting something slip by accident; 墓穴を掘る is the self-inflicted damage, however it was caused.

cards.cue: Asked only whether he had finished his homework, a boy added, "and I definitely didn't play games all night," which made his mother check. What did he do?

ctx.s: 言[い]い訳[わけ]をしすぎて、かえって{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]った}。
ctx.en: I made too many excuses and only dug myself in deeper.

ctx.s: 「それ以上[いじょう]しゃべると{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]る}よ」と友達[ともだち]に止[と]められた。
ctx.en: My friend stopped me: "Say any more and you'll dig your own grave."

ctx.s: 知[し]ったかぶりで難[むずか]しい質問[しつもん]に答[こた]えようとして、{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]った}。
ctx.en: I pretended to know and tried to answer a hard question, and only made things worse for myself.

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]は、警察[けいさつ]しか知[し]らないはずの事実[じじつ]を口[くち]にして{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]った}。
ctx.en: The culprit dug their own grave by mentioning a fact only the police could have known.

ctx.s: 完璧[かんぺき]な計画[けいかく]のつもりが、自分[じぶん]で{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]る}結果[けっか]になった。
ctx.en: What I thought was a perfect plan ended up being my own undoing.

ctx.s: 「行[い]ってないよ。あの店[みせ]、料理[りょうり]はまずかったけど」「…今[いま]、{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]った}ね」
ctx.en: "I didn't go. The food at that place was awful, though." "...You just gave yourself away."

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の嘘[うそ]をばらして、彼[かれ]の{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I exposed his lie and ruined him)
bad.why: It is always one's own downfall, brought on by oneself; you cannot dig someone else's grave with it.

bad.s: 台風[たいふう]で電車[でんしゃ]が止[と]まって、{墓穴[ぼけつ]を掘[ほ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the typhoon stopped the trains and I was in trouble)
bad.why: The trouble must come from one's own words or actions, not from bad luck or outside events.

cards.mean: too late to do anything about it
cards.lit: after the festival: turning up when the festival is over and nothing is left to see

use.how: A predicate noun, usually 〜ても後の祭りだ or 気づいた時には後の祭りだった: regret when it is too late to change anything.

near.diff: 水の泡 is effort that came to nothing; 後の祭り is realising too late that the chance to act has passed.
元も子もない is losing even what you started with; 後の祭り is that it is now too late to act.

cards.cue: You realise the concert tickets went on sale last week and have all sold out. Complaining now will change nothing. How would you sum it up?

ctx.s: 今[いま]さら謝[あやま]っても{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}だ。
ctx.en: It's too late to apologise now.

ctx.s: 気[き]づいた時[とき]には、もう{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}だった。
ctx.en: By the time I noticed, it was already too late.

ctx.s: 「バックアップを取[と]っておけばよかった」「消[き]えてからじゃ{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}だよ」
ctx.en: "I should have made a backup." "Once it's deleted, it's too late for that."

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]が終[お]わってから答[こた]えを思[おも]い出[だ]しても{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}だ。
ctx.en: Remembering the answer after the exam is over does you no good.

ctx.s: {後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}にならないよう、保険[ほけん]の内容[ないよう]は今[いま]のうちに確認[かくにん]しておこう。
ctx.en: So that it isn't too late when it matters, let's check what the insurance covers now.

ctx.s: 契約書[けいやくしょ]にサインした後[あと]で条件[じょうけん]の悪[わる]さに気[き]づいたが、{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}だった。
ctx.en: I noticed how bad the terms were only after signing the contract, but by then it was too late.

bad.s: パーティーの後[あと]で、みんなで{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}を楽[たの]しんだ。
bad.en: (meant: after the party we all enjoyed an after-party)
bad.why: It is never a real celebration; it means a regret that something can no longer be done.

bad.s: 締[し]め切[き]りは来週[らいしゅう]だから、まだ{後[あと]の祭[まつ]り}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the deadline is next week, so there's still time)
bad.why: It means it is already too late, so it cannot describe a case where there is still time to act.

cards.mean: to lose everything, gains and all
cards.lit: neither the principal nor the interest is left: moto is the capital, ko the interest it breeds

use.how: Usually after a condition: 〜したら／〜しては元も子もない. Warns that overdoing something would wipe out both what one has and what one hoped to gain.

near.diff: 水の泡 is effort that has come to nothing; 元も子もない warns that going too far would lose even what one started with.

cards.cue: Your friend plans to skip sleep for a week to finish a project. You warn that if they collapse, the project and their health both go. What do you say?

ctx.s: 無理[むり]して体[からだ]を壊[こわ]したら{元[もと]も子[こ]もない}よ。
ctx.en: If you push yourself and ruin your health, you lose everything.

ctx.s: 節約[せつやく]しすぎて病気[びょうき]になっては{元[もと]も子[こ]もない}。
ctx.en: Saving so hard that you fall ill defeats the whole purpose.

ctx.s: 「もっと値上[ねあ]げしようか」「お客[きゃく]さんが来[こ]なくなったら{元[もと]も子[こ]もない}でしょう」
ctx.en: "Shall we raise prices again?" "If customers stop coming, we'll lose everything."

ctx.s: 急[いそ]いで仕上[しあ]げても、ミスだらけでは{元[もと]も子[こ]もない}。
ctx.en: Finishing fast is no use if the work is full of mistakes.

ctx.s: 欲張[よくば]って儲[もう]けを全部[ぜんぶ]つぎ込[こ]んだ結果[けっか]、{元[もと]も子[こ]もなくなった}。
ctx.en: Out of greed he poured all his profits back in, and ended up losing everything.

ctx.s: 規制[きせい]を厳[きび]しくしすぎて、産業[さんぎょう]そのものが衰[おとろ]えては{元[もと]も子[こ]もない}。
ctx.en: If regulation is made so strict that the industry itself declines, the whole point is lost.

bad.s: 電車[でんしゃ]で財布[さいふ]を落[お]として、{元[もと]も子[こ]もない}。
bad.en: (meant: I dropped my wallet on the train and lost everything)
bad.why: It is said when overreaching wipes out a gain and its basis; a plain accidental loss is not described this way.

bad.s: これは{元[もと]も子[こ]もある}安全[あんぜん]な計画[けいかく]だ。
bad.en: (meant: this is a safe plan that keeps everything)
bad.why: The expression exists only in the negative; there is no positive form "moto mo ko mo aru".

cards.mean: a world of difference
cards.lit: the gap between the clouds in the sky and the mud on the ground

use.how: A noun phrase: AとBでは雲泥の差がある／雲泥の差だ. Stresses a huge gap in quality or level between two things being compared.

near.diff: 足元にも及ばない says one side is far below the other, often oneself; 雲泥の差 simply names the huge gap between two things.

cards.cue: You compare the cramped, dark flat you rented as a student with the bright new one you live in now. How do you describe the gap?

ctx.s: 前[まえ]のパソコンとは、速[はや]さが{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}だ。
ctx.en: The speed is worlds apart from my old computer.

ctx.s: プロと素人[しろうと]では、技術[ぎじゅつ]に{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}がある。
ctx.en: There is a world of difference in skill between a professional and an amateur.

ctx.s: 「新[あたら]しい部屋[へや]はどう？」「前[まえ]と比[くら]べたら{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}だよ」
ctx.en: "How's the new place?" "Compared with the old one, it's a world apart."

ctx.s: 準備[じゅんび]をした人[ひと]としなかった人[ひと]では、結果[けっか]に{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}が出[で]た。
ctx.en: Between those who prepared and those who didn't, the results were worlds apart.

ctx.s: 同[おな]じ材料[ざいりょう]でも、作[つく]る人[ひと]の腕[うで]で味[あじ]に{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}がつく。
ctx.en: Even with the same ingredients, the cook's skill makes a world of difference to the taste.

ctx.s: 十年前[じゅうねんまえ]と比[くら]べると、地方[ちほう]の交通[こうつう]の便[べん]は{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}である。
ctx.en: Compared with ten years ago, transport links in the regions are worlds apart.

bad.s: 二人[ふたり]の身長[しんちょう]は一[いっ]センチしか違[ちが]わず、{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the two differ in height by only a centimetre)
bad.why: It means an enormous gap; it cannot describe a tiny difference.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はテストで私[わたし]を{雲泥[うんでい]の差[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: he beat me by a mile in the test)
bad.why: It is a noun phrase used with ga aru or da; it cannot be turned into a verb with suru.

cards.mean: to get on track and run smoothly
cards.lit: to get onto the track: a train on its rails or a satellite settling into orbit

near.diff: 調子に乗る is a person getting carried away and cocky; 軌道に乗る is an undertaking settling into steady progress.
