ctx.en: Until the business got going, I worked without a day off.

ctx.s: 「新事業[しんじぎょう]はいかがですか」「おかげさまで、ようやく{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]りました}」
ctx.en: "How is the new venture?" "Thank you, it's finally up and running."

ctx.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]して半年[はんとし]、新[あたら]しい生活[せいかつ]がようやく{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]った}。
ctx.en: Six months after the move, my new life has finally settled into a routine.

ctx.s: まずはこのプロジェクトを{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]せる}ことが先決[せんけつ]だ。
ctx.en: The first priority is to get this project on track.

ctx.s: 復興計画[ふっこうけいかく]が{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]る}には、なお数年[すうねん]かかる見通[みとお]しだ。
ctx.en: It is expected to take several more years for the reconstruction plan to get properly under way.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は褒[ほ]められて{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]り}、自慢[じまん]ばかりしている。
bad.en: (meant: he got carried away after being praised and keeps boasting)
bad.why: Getting cocky is choshi ni noru; this idiom is about a project running smoothly, not a person's mood.

bad.s: 電車[でんしゃ]に遅[おく]れそうだったので、急[いそ]いで{軌道[きどう]に乗[の]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was about to miss the train, so I hurried and got on)
bad.why: It is figurative, about undertakings settling down; boarding a train is simply densha ni noru.

cards.mean: to warn someone in advance
cards.lit: to drive in a nail: fixing something firmly so that it cannot shift later

use.how: The person warned takes に: 〜に〜ないように釘を刺す. A firm warning beforehand so that they will not do something one fears they might.

near.diff: 念を押す just confirms a point to avoid a mix-up; 釘を刺す warns someone off something one suspects they will do.

cards.cue: Your brother always spreads your secrets. Before telling him your news, you warn him sharply not to breathe a word of it. What did you do?

ctx.s: 母[はは]に「今度[こんど]は無駄遣[むだづか]いしないでね」と{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]された}。
ctx.en: My mother warned me: "Don't waste your money this time."

ctx.s: 「このことは誰[だれ]にも言[い]わないでよ」と、口[くち]の軽[かる]い友達[ともだち]に{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]して}おいた。
ctx.en: I warned my loose-lipped friend beforehand: "Don't tell anyone about this."

ctx.s: 「また飲[の]みすぎないでよ」「わかってるって。そんなに{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]さなくても}いいよ」
ctx.en: "Don't drink too much again." "I know. You don't have to warn me like that."

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は遅刻[ちこく]の多[おお]い彼[かれ]に、明日[あした]は遅[おく]れるなと{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
ctx.en: The manager warned him, since he is often late, not to be late tomorrow.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は試合前[しあいまえ]、選手[せんしゅ]たちに油断[ゆだん]するなと{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
ctx.en: Before the match, the coach warned the players not to get complacent.

ctx.s: 大家[おおや]さんは入居者[にゅうきょしゃ]に、夜中[よなか]に騒[さわ]がないようにと{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
ctx.en: The landlord warned the tenants not to make noise late at night.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]は合格[ごうかく]した生徒[せいと]に「おめでとう」と{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher told the student who passed "congratulations")
bad.why: It is a warning against doing something; congratulations or praise is never a warning.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は部下[ぶか]を{釘[くぎ]を刺[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the manager warned his subordinate)
bad.why: The person warned takes ni, not o: buka ni kugi o sasu. Two o-objects in a row is ungrammatical.

cards.mean: to stress a point again to make sure it is understood
cards.lit: to press one's thought home: nen is a concern held in mind, pressed firmly onto the listener

use.how: With a quotation or clause: 「〜ね」と念を押す, 〜に念を押す. Repeating or confirming a point, such as a time or a promise, so that there is no mistake.

near.diff: 釘を刺す is a pre-emptive warning against bad behaviour; 念を押す is neutral checking that something is understood or agreed.

cards.cue: Before hanging up, you repeat to the courier once more that the parcel must arrive by ten tomorrow, just to be sure. What did you do?

ctx.s: 「明日[あした]は八時[はちじ]集合[しゅうごう]だよ」と{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
ctx.en: "We meet at eight tomorrow, remember," I reminded them.

ctx.s: 出[で]かける前[まえ]に、妻[つま]に「鍵[かぎ]、閉[し]めたよね？」と{念[ねん]を押[お]された}。
ctx.en: Before we went out, my wife made sure: "You locked the door, right?"

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]に大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]？」と、彼[かれ]は何度[なんど]も{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
ctx.en: "Are you really sure it's all right?" he asked again and again.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]は「返品[へんぴん]はできませんが、よろしいですか」と{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
ctx.en: The clerk checked once more: "Returns aren't possible. Is that all right?"

ctx.s: 「締[し]め切[き]りは金曜日[きんようび]で間違[まちが]いないですね」と{念[ねん]を押[お]す}と、担当者[たんとうしゃ]はうなずいた。
ctx.en: When I double-checked, "The deadline is definitely Friday, isn't it?", the person in charge nodded.

ctx.s: 契約[けいやく]の前[まえ]に、条件[じょうけん]に変更[へんこう]がないか{念[ねん]を押[お]して}おいた。
ctx.en: Before signing, I made sure once more that the terms had not changed.

bad.s: エレベーターのボタンを{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I pressed the lift button)
bad.why: Pressing a button is botan o osu; this idiom is only about confirming a point with someone.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の結果[けっか]が心配[しんぱい]で、一晩中[ひとばんじゅう]{念[ねん]を押[お]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I was so anxious about my results that I worried all night)
bad.why: It is said to someone to confirm a point; it does not mean to fret or worry alone.

cards.mean: not worth the trouble or cost
cards.lit: does not square with its share: what comes back does not match what is put in

use.how: Predicate about a job, deal or effort: この仕事は割に合わない. Says the reward is too small for the effort, risk or cost involved.

cards.cue: A part-time job means long night shifts and heavy lifting, yet pays barely above the minimum. How do you sum it up?

ctx.s: こんなに大変[たいへん]なのに時給[じきゅう]がこれでは、{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: It's this hard and pays only this much an hour? It isn't worth it.

ctx.s: 往復[おうふく]三時間[さんじかん]かけて安[やす]いスーパーに行[い]くのは、{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}よ。
ctx.en: Spending three hours there and back to go to a cheap supermarket isn't worth it.

ctx.s: 「その依頼[いらい]、受[う]けるの？」「手間[てま]ばかりかかって{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}から、断[ことわ]るよ」
ctx.en: "Are you taking that job?" "It's all hassle and doesn't pay, so I'm turning it down."

ctx.s: 危険[きけん]な仕事[しごと]なのに給料[きゅうりょう]が安[やす]く、{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}と辞[や]める人[ひと]が多[おお]い。
ctx.en: The work is dangerous but the pay is low, so many people quit, saying it isn't worth it.

ctx.s: 罰金[ばっきん]の額[がく]を考[かんが]えれば、駐車違反[ちゅうしゃいはん]は{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: Given the size of the fine, parking illegally just doesn't pay.

ctx.s: 小[ちい]さな農家[のうか]にとって、この作物[さくもつ]を育[そだ]てるのは{割[わり]に合[あ]わなく}なっている。
ctx.en: For small farmers, growing this crop is no longer worth the cost.

bad.s: この服[ふく]は、サイズが{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}。
bad.en: (meant: these clothes don't fit me)
bad.why: It weighs reward against effort or cost; clothes that do not fit are simply saizu ga awanai.

bad.s: 思[おも]ったより{割[わり]に合[あ]わない}点数[てんすう]が取[と]れて、とても嬉[うれ]しかった。
bad.en: (meant: I got a better score than I deserved and was delighted)
bad.why: It only says the return falls short of the effort; it never describes a pleasing surprise.

cards.mean: to pay out of one's own pocket
cards.lit: to cut one's own belly: the cost comes out of oneself, not out of someone else's purse

use.how: Said when one pays a cost that a company, school or someone else might have been expected to cover: 自腹を切って買う. Also 自腹で払う.

cards.cue: The company refuses to buy the software the team needs, so the team leader pays for it personally. What did the leader do?

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]の飲[の]み会[かい]なのに、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]る}ことになった。
ctx.en: It was a company party, yet I ended up paying my own way.

ctx.s: 経費[けいひ]で落[お]ちないので、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}本[ほん]を買[か]った。
ctx.en: It couldn't go on expenses, so I bought the books with my own money.

ctx.s: 「その参考書[さんこうしょ]、学校[がっこう]が買[か]ってくれたの？」「ううん、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]った}よ」
ctx.en: "Did the school buy you that study guide?" "No, I paid for it myself."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]は{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}、生徒[せいと]たちにお菓子[かし]を配[くば]った。
ctx.en: The teacher bought sweets for the pupils out of their own pocket.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]が{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}、チーム全員[ぜんいん]に夕食[ゆうしょく]をごちそうしてくれた。
ctx.en: The department head treated the whole team to dinner out of their own pocket.

ctx.s: 授業[じゅぎょう]で使[つか]う教材[きょうざい]を、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}用意[ようい]する教員[きょういん]も少[すく]なくない。
ctx.en: Quite a few teachers pay out of their own pockets for the materials they use in class.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]におごってもらって、{自腹[じばら]を切[き]った}。
bad.en: (meant: my friend treated me, so I didn't pay)
bad.why: It means paying with your own money; when someone else pays for you, you have not paid out of your own pocket.

bad.s: ミスの責任[せきにん]を取[と]って、彼[かれ]は{自腹[じばら]を切[き]って}会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めた。
bad.en: (meant: he took responsibility for the mistake and resigned)
bad.why: It is only about paying with one's own money; taking the blame and resigning is sekinin o toru, not this phrase.

cards.mean: ominous, an unlucky thing to say
cards.lit: not even a matter of omens: so ill-starred it should not be said at all

story.text: Engi began as a Buddhist term, the rendering of the Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda: the teaching that all things arise in dependence on causes and conditions. In Japan the word came to mean the founding story of a temple or shrine, and later a sign of what is to come. Engi ga ii is a good omen; engi de mo nai rejects a remark as so ill-omened it should not be spoken.
story.source: Buddhist term 縁起 (Sanskrit pratītyasamutpāda, dependent origination)

use.how: A retort to talk of death, failure or disaster, as if saying it could make it happen: 縁起でもないこと言わないで. Also as a predicate: 〜なんて縁起でもない.

cards.cue: On the morning of a long road trip, a friend starts joking about what would happen if you crashed. You tell them to stop tempting fate.

ctx.s: {縁起[えんぎ]でもない}ことを言[い]わないで。
ctx.en: Don't say such ominous things.

ctx.s: 「試験[しけん]に落[お]ちたらどうしよう」「{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}。大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だよ」
ctx.en: "What if I fail the exam?" "Don't tempt fate. You'll be fine."

ctx.s: 出発[しゅっぱつ]の朝[あさ]に事故[じこ]の話[はなし]なんて、{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}。
ctx.en: Talking about accidents on the morning we set off? That's asking for bad luck.

ctx.s: 「もしものときのために遺言[ゆいごん]を書[か]いておこうかな」「やめてよ、{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}」
ctx.en: "Maybe I should write a will, just in case." "Stop it, don't even say that."

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は、お見舞[みま]いに鉢植[はちう]えを持[も]っていくのは{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}と言[い]った。
ctx.en: My grandmother said taking a potted plant to someone in hospital is bad luck.

ctx.s: 受験生[じゅけんせい]の前[まえ]では、「落[お]ちる」のような{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}言葉[ことば]は使[つか]わないようにしている。
ctx.en: In front of students facing entrance exams, I avoid ill-omened words like "fall".

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たるなんて、{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}！
bad.en: (meant: winning the lottery, what luck!)
bad.why: It rebukes ill-omened talk; good fortune is engi ga ii, never this phrase.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]、その企画[きかく]は{縁起[えんぎ]でもない}と思[おも]います。
bad.en: (meant: sir, I think that plan is a bad idea)
bad.why: It is about words that seem to invite bad luck, not a judgement that a plan is unwise, and it is too blunt for a superior.

cards.r: きゅうしにいっしょうをえる
cards.mean: to have a narrow escape from death
cards.lit: out of nine chances of death, to get the one chance of life

use.how: Predicate, usually past, about a person who survived an accident, disaster or illness that should have killed them: 事故で九死に一生を得た.

near.diff: 危機一髪 names the hair's-breadth moment of danger itself; 九死に一生を得る says someone came through a deadly situation alive.

cards.cue: A climber was buried by an avalanche and dug out alive after a full day under the snow. How do the news reports describe the survival?

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は若[わか]いころ、交通事故[こうつうじこ]で{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: When he was young, my father barely survived a car accident.

ctx.s: 雪崩[なだれ]に巻[ま]き込[こ]まれた登山者[とざんしゃ]が、{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: A climber caught in an avalanche narrowly escaped death.

ctx.s: 「あの船[ふね]の事故[じこ]で助[たす]かったの？」「うん、まさに{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}よ」
ctx.en: "You survived that boat accident?" "Yes, I really did cheat death."

ctx.s: 心臓[しんぞう]が止[と]まったが、居合[いあ]わせた医師[いし]のおかげで{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: His heart stopped, but thanks to a doctor who happened to be there, he survived against the odds.

ctx.s: {九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}経験[けいけん]から、彼[かれ]は命[いのち]の大切[たいせつ]さを語[かた]り続[つづ]けている。
ctx.en: Having escaped death by a whisker, he keeps speaking about how precious life is.

ctx.s: 漁船[ぎょせん]は嵐[あらし]で転覆[てんぷく]したが、乗組員[のりくみいん]は全員[ぜんいん]{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
ctx.en: The fishing boat capsized in the storm, but the whole crew narrowly escaped with their lives.

bad.s: 消防士[しょうぼうし]が子[こ]どもを{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]た}。
bad.en: (meant: the firefighter saved the child)
bad.why: The subject is the person who survived, and the phrase takes no other object; a rescuer saving someone is tasukeru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{九死[きゅうし]に一生[いっしょう]を得[え]て}、そのまま亡[な]くなった。
bad.en: (meant: he very nearly survived but died)
bad.why: It means one did survive; it cannot be followed by the person's death.

cards.mean: every moment counts
cards.lit: to fight over a single moment: ikkoku, literally one koku of time, here means an instant

use.how: Predicate or modifier about an emergency: 事態は一刻を争う, 一刻を争う状況. Says delay would cause real harm, so there is no time to lose.

cards.cue: A man has collapsed on the station platform and is not breathing. You tell the staff the ambulance cannot wait a single minute.

ctx.s: 患者[かんじゃ]の容体[ようだい]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}。
ctx.en: The patient's condition is critical; there's no time to lose.

ctx.s: {一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}状況[じょうきょう]なので、すぐに救急車[きゅうきゅうしゃ]を呼[よ]んでください。
ctx.en: Every second counts, so please call an ambulance right away.

ctx.s: 「明日[あした]まで待[ま]てない？」「だめだ、これは{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}問題[もんだい]なんだ」
ctx.en: "Can't it wait until tomorrow?" "No, this is a matter where every moment counts."

ctx.s: 地震[じしん]の後[あと]、がれきの下[した]の人[ひと]を助[たす]け出[だ]すのは{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}作業[さぎょう]だった。
ctx.en: After the earthquake, getting people out from under the rubble was a race against time.

ctx.s: システムの不具合[ふぐあい]で顧客[こきゃく]データが消[き]えかけており、対応[たいおう]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}。
ctx.en: A system fault is about to wipe customer data, so the response cannot wait a moment.

ctx.s: 被災地[ひさいち]への支援[しえん]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]う}と、専門家[せんもんか]は訴[うった]えた。
ctx.en: Experts urged that aid to the disaster area is needed without a moment's delay.

bad.s: 二人[ふたり]は優勝[ゆうしょう]をかけて{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the two fought it out for the title)
bad.why: Here arasou does not mean competing with a rival; the phrase says a matter is so urgent no time can be lost.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{一刻[いっこく]を争[あらそ]って}考[かんが]えてから、ゆっくり答[こた]えた。
bad.en: (meant: he thought for a moment and then answered slowly)
bad.why: It does not mean "for a moment"; it describes an emergency where any delay does harm.

cards.mean: to be caught between two sides
cards.lit: to end up pinched between two boards

use.how: Usually AとBの板挟みになる or 二人の間で板挟みになる: said of someone squeezed between two people or groups whose demands clash.

near.diff: 進退きわまる is being stuck with no way forward or back; 板挟みになる is being pulled by two parties whose wishes conflict.

cards.cue: Your boss wants the project done a month early; your team says that is impossible and wants you to tell the boss. You are stuck in the middle.

ctx.en: I'm caught between my mother and my wife, and I really don't know what to do.

ctx.s: 中間[ちゅうかん]管理職[かんりしょく]は、上司[じょうし]と部下[ぶか]の{板挟[いたばさ]みになり}やすい。
ctx.en: Middle managers easily get caught between their bosses and their staff.

ctx.s: 「どっちの味方[みかた]なの？」と聞[き]かれて、二人[ふたり]の友達[ともだち]の間[あいだ]で{板挟[いたばさ]みになった}。
ctx.en: Asked "Whose side are you on?", I found myself caught between my two friends.

ctx.s: 「店長[てんちょう]、大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]ですか」「本社[ほんしゃ]とお客[きゃく]さんの{板挟[いたばさ]みになって}、もう限界[げんかい]だよ」
ctx.en: "Are you all right, manager?" "I'm stuck between head office and the customers, and I've had about all I can take."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は会社[かいしゃ]と労働[ろうどう]組合[くみあい]の{板挟[いたばさ]みになり}、眠[ねむ]れない日[ひ]が続[つづ]いた。
ctx.en: Caught between the company and the union, he went through night after sleepless night.

ctx.s: 親[おや]の希望[きぼう]と自分[じぶん]の夢[ゆめ]の{板挟[いたばさ]みになった}とき、あなたならどうしますか。
ctx.en: If you were caught between your parents' wishes and your own dream, what would you do?

bad.s: ケーキとアイスのどちらにしようか、{板挟[いたばさ]みになって}迷[まよ]った。
bad.en: (meant: I couldn't decide between cake and ice cream)

bad.en: (meant: I'm under pressure from deadlines)
bad.why: There must be two opposing sides pulling at you; pressure from one source such as a deadline is owareru.

cards.mean: to cause friction
cards.lit: corners stick up: something sharp-edged juts out and grates on the people around it

use.how: Subject is a way of speaking or acting: そう言うと角が立つ. Often in 角が立たないように, about avoiding needless offence to people one deals with.

near.diff: 波風が立つ is trouble stirring in a group or family; 角が立つ is the harsh edge of a particular remark or way of doing something.

cards.cue: You want to decline a neighbour's invitation, but just saying 'I don't want to' would sour things. How would that blunt refusal come across?

ctx.s: そんな言[い]い方[かた]をしたら{角[かど]が立[た]つ}よ。
ctx.en: If you put it like that, you'll rub people the wrong way.

ctx.s: {角[かど]が立[た]たない}ように、やんわりと断[ことわ]った。
ctx.en: I turned it down gently so as not to cause any bad feeling.

ctx.s: 「はっきり言[い]ったほうがいいかな」「でも、それだと{角[かど]が立[た]つ}んじゃない？」
ctx.en: "Should I just say it straight?" "But wouldn't that cause friction?"

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]で上司[じょうし]の間違[まちが]いを指摘[してき]すると{角[かど]が立[た]つ}ので、後[あと]で個別[こべつ]に伝[つた]えた。
ctx.en: Pointing out my boss's mistake in the meeting would have caused friction, so I mentioned it privately afterwards.

ctx.s: メールだと冷[つめ]たく読[よ]めて{角[かど]が立[た]つ}こともあるから、電話[でんわ]で話[はな]そう。
ctx.en: In an email it can read as cold and come across badly, so let's talk on the phone.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{角[かど]が立[た]たない}言葉[ことば]を選[えら]ぶのが本当[ほんとう]にうまい。
ctx.en: She's really good at choosing words that don't ruffle anyone.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は朝[あさ]から{角[かど]が立[た]って}いて、誰[だれ]とも話[はな]さない。
bad.en: (meant: my father has been in a bad mood since morning)
bad.why: It describes a remark or action that grates on others, not a person's mood; for a bad mood say kigen ga warui.

bad.en: (meant: the minister's remark caused a nationwide controversy)
bad.why: It is about friction between people who deal with each other; a public uproar over a statement is butsugi o kamosu.

cards.mean: to underestimate, to take lightly
cards.lit: to tie up the total: to settle in advance on how much something will amount to

use.how: Usually 〜と高をくくる or 高をくくっていたら…: assuming something will be easy or harmless, and usually being proved wrong.

near.diff: 甘く見る takes a direct object (相手を甘く見る); 高をくくる is usually a と-clause assumption that something will turn out to be no big deal.

ctx.en: I assumed it would be easy, and then I couldn't do it at all.

ctx.en: Thinking it was just a cold, I didn't bother going to the doctor.

ctx.en: Taking it for granted that it wouldn't rain was my mistake.

ctx.s: 「締[し]め切[き]りまでまだ一週間[いっしゅうかん]あるし」「そうやって{高[たか]をくくって}ると、また徹夜[てつや]になるよ」
ctx.en: "There's still a week until the deadline." "If you take it that lightly, you'll be up all night again."

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]は格下[かくした]だと{高[たか]をくくった}チームは、前半[ぜんはん]だけで三点[さんてん]を奪[うば]われた。
ctx.en: Sure its opponents were weaker, the team gave up three goals in the first half alone.

ctx.s: どうせ誰[だれ]も気[き]づかないと{高[たか]をくくる}のは危険[きけん]だ。
ctx.en: It's dangerous to assume that nobody will notice anyway.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]を{高[たか]をくくって}、宿題[しゅくだい]を出[だ]さなかった。
bad.en: (meant: I underestimated the teacher and didn't hand in my homework)
bad.why: It does not take a person as its object; say sensei o amaku mite, or put the assumption in a to-clause.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は謙虚[けんきょ]で、いつも自分[じぶん]の成果[せいか]を{高[たか]をくくって}話[はな]す。
bad.en: (meant: he's modest and always plays down his achievements)
bad.why: It is a careless assumption that something will be easy, not modestly downplaying oneself.

cards.r: みぎにでるものはいない
cards.mean: no one is better at it
cards.lit: there is no one who comes out on his right

story.text: In Han-dynasty China the right was ranked above the left, so a place on someone's right was a higher place. To say that no one 'comes out on his right' meant that no one ranks above him. The same custom gave the word sasen, 'moving to the left', for a demotion, a word Japanese still uses.
story.source: Classical Chinese 無出其右 and the Han-dynasty custom of ranking right above left

use.how: Usually 〜にかけては Xの右に出る者はいない: high praise that no one surpasses a person in one particular skill or field.

near.diff: 一目置く is the respectful attitude others take toward someone abler; 右に出る者はいない flatly states that no one is better.

cards.cue: Whenever a computer breaks in your office, everyone goes to the same colleague, who always fixes it faster than anyone else could.

ctx.s: 料理[りょうり]にかけては、母[はは]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}。
ctx.en: When it comes to cooking, nobody beats my mother.

ctx.s: この町[まち]で寿司[すし]を握[にぎ]らせたら、あの職人[しょくにん]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}。
ctx.en: Nobody in this town makes sushi better than that chef.

ctx.s: 「パソコンのことは誰[だれ]に聞[き]けばいい？」「田中[たなか]さんだね。社内[しゃない]で彼[かれ]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}よ」
ctx.en: "Who should I ask about computers?" "Tanaka. Nobody in the company knows more than him."

ctx.s: 交渉[こうしょう]のうまさでは、彼女[かのじょ]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいなかった}。
ctx.en: No one could match her skill at negotiating.

ctx.s: 短距離走[たんきょりそう]では、今[いま]のところ彼[かれ]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}と言[い]われている。
ctx.en: In sprinting, he is said to have no equal at the moment.

ctx.s: 書道[しょどう]の世界[せかい]において、氏[し]の{右[みぎ]に出[で]る者[もの]はいない}。
ctx.en: In the world of calligraphy, no one surpasses him.

cards.mean: to give a vague answer to dodge the issue
cards.lit: to make the tea cloudy

near.diff: 言葉を濁す is simply not saying something clearly; お茶を濁す is getting through the moment with a vague or makeshift stand-in.

ctx.s: 政府[せいふ]の答弁[とうべん]は、具体的[ぐたいてき]な数字[すうじ]を示[しめ]さずに{お茶[ちゃ]を濁[にご]す}ものだった。
ctx.en: The government's answer gave no concrete figures and simply skirted the issue.

bad.en: (meant: I said clearly 'I'm not going' and turned it down)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の冗談[じょうだん]が会議[かいぎ]の雰囲気[ふんいき]を{お茶[ちゃ]を濁[にご]した}。
bad.en: (meant: his joke spoiled the mood of the meeting)
bad.why: It is about dodging a question or task yourself, and it takes no second object; spoiling a mood is mizu o sasu.

cards.mean: to see one's way to finishing
cards.lit: the mark one is aiming at stands up: the goal comes into view

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい部品[ぶひん]が届[とど]いたので、修理[しゅうり]の{めどが立[た]った}と連絡[れんらく]があった。

bad.en: (meant: I've written and handed in the report, so it's finished)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の顔[かお]を見[み]て、怒[おこ]っている{めどが立[た]った}。
bad.en: (meant: from his face I could tell he was angry)
bad.why: It is about seeing a path to getting something done, not reading someone's feelings; that is sasshi ga tsuku.

cards.mean: to cause controversy
cards.lit: to brew public argument, the way sake is slowly brewed

near.diff: 波紋を呼ぶ is a statement or event sending out ripples of reaction; 物議を醸す stresses that it sets off argument and criticism.

cards.cue: A minister makes an offhand remark about pensioners, and for a week the papers, TV and social media argue over whether it was acceptable.

ctx.s: 大臣[だいじん]の発言[はつげん]が{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]して}いる。

ctx.en: With its graphic scenes, the film caused controversy even before its release.

ctx.s: 「あのコマーシャル、ネットで炎上[えんじょう]してるね」「うん、かなり{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]して}るみたい」

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はあえて{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]す}ような作品[さくひん]を発表[はっぴょう]し続[つづ]けている。
ctx.en: He keeps deliberately putting out work that is bound to cause controversy.

bad.s: 新商品[しんしょうひん]が大人気[だいにんき]で、{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the new product was a huge hit and caused a sensation)

bad.s: 昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]をどこで食[た]べるか、友達[ともだち]と{物議[ぶつぎ]を醸[かも]して}喧嘩[けんか]になった。
bad.en: (meant: my friend and I argued over where to have lunch)
bad.why: It is public controversy set off by a statement or act, not a private argument between two people.

cards.mean: to compete fiercely
cards.lit: to grind away the shinogi, the raised ridge along a sword blade, as two swords clash again and again

use.how: AとBがしのぎを削る / 〜でしのぎを削る: rivals of similar strength competing hard for the same prize, market or title.

near.diff: 火花を散らす is a sharp, heated clash at one moment; しのぎを削る is a sustained, close contest between rivals.

cards.cue: Three convenience-store chains keep opening shops on the same street and launching rival lunch boxes every month, each trying to win the same customers.

cards.mean: to become conceited after success
cards.lit: to turn into a tengu, the long-nosed mountain spirit of folklore, with one's nose held high

use.how: Xは天狗になっている / 天狗になるな: said of someone who has grown full of themselves after praise or success.

cards.r: かんにんぶくろのおがきれる

cards.r: ひとすじなわではいかない

cards.mean: to be too heavy a responsibility

cards.t: 居ても立ってもいられない

cards.mean: to falsely accuse someone
cards.lit: to make someone wear wet clothes: to dress them in a guilt that is not theirs

use.how: Xに(Yの)濡れ衣を着せる; most often passive: 万引きの濡れ衣を着せられる. Always a false accusation; clearing it is 濡れ衣を晴らす.

bad.en: (meant: he really stole it, so the police charged him)

cards.mean: to be momentarily tempted into wrongdoing
cards.lit: a demon comes over you: an evil spirit slips into your mind for a moment

use.how: Usually past, as an explanation or excuse for one lapse: 魔が差した, つい魔が差して. Ranges from a midnight snack to a real offence.

near.diff: 出来心 is a noun for the sudden bad impulse itself (出来心で盗んだ); 魔が差す is the verb phrase for being seized by it.

cards.cue: A normally honest cashier explains why, that one time, she slipped a banknote from the till into her pocket.

ctx.en: I'm on a diet, but temptation got the better of me and I ate ramen in the middle of the night.

ctx.en: Anyone can have a moment of weakness. Don't judge a person by one mistake.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は三年間[さんねんかん]、計画的[けいかくてき]に会社[かいしゃ]のお金[かね]を盗[ぬす]み続[つづ]けた。{魔[ま]が差[さ]した}のだ。
bad.en: (meant: he systematically stole for three years; he was simply wicked)
bad.why: It is a single momentary impulse, not deliberate wrongdoing planned and repeated over years.

bad.s: 出[で]かけたら急[きゅう]に雨[あめ]が降[ふ]ってきて、{魔[ま]が差[さ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I went out and bad luck struck when it suddenly rained)
bad.why: It is a wrong impulse inside your own mind, not misfortune that happens to you from outside.

cards.mean: to rack one's brains
cards.lit: to wring out your wisdom: squeeze your mind like a cloth for the last drop of ideas

use.how: Verb phrase, often with みんなで: thinking hard to find a way through a specific problem, especially under limits of money, time or space.

near.diff: 頭を抱える is being at a loss, stuck with a problem; 知恵を絞る is actively working hard to find a solution.

cards.cue: Your club has almost no budget, so everyone sits down together to come up with clever ways to hold the festival anyway.

ctx.en: The budget is small, so we'll just have to think creatively.

ctx.s: 「どうすればお客[きゃく]さんが増[ふ]えるか、一緒[いっしょ]に{知恵[ちえ]を絞[しぼ]ろう}。」

ctx.s: いくら{知恵[ちえ]を絞[しぼ]って}も、いいアイデアが浮[う]かばなかった。
ctx.en: No matter how hard I racked my brains, no good idea came to me.

ctx.s: 狭[せま]い部屋[へや]を広[ひろ]く使[つか]うために、{知恵[ちえ]を絞[しぼ]った}収納術[しゅうのうじゅつ]を紹介[しょうかい]します。
ctx.en: Here are some ingenious storage ideas for making the most of a small room.

bad.en: (meant: I worked hard to memorise a hundred English words)

bad.s: 困[こま]っている後輩[こうはい]に{知恵[ちえ]を絞[しぼ]って}あげた。
bad.en: (meant: I gave my struggling junior some advice)
bad.why: Lending someone your ideas is chie o kasu. Chie o shiboru is your own hard thinking, not something you give to another person.

cards.mean: conversation becomes lively
cards.lit: flowers bloom on the conversation: the talk opens up and blossoms

use.how: Often with a topic before it: 思い出話に花が咲く, 昔話に花が咲く. Narrates a pleasant, lively chat among people, usually in the past tense.

near.diff: 話が弾む says a conversation flows easily; 話に花が咲く pictures a topic, often shared memories, blossoming into a long happy chat.
話が合う says two people have common ground to talk about; 話に花が咲く describes a particular chat turning lively.

cards.cue: At a class reunion, old friends start reminiscing about school days and keep talking happily for hours.

ctx.s: 久[ひさ]しぶりに会[あ]った友[とも]だちと、{話[はなし]に花[はな]が咲[さ]いた}。

ctx.s: 同窓会[どうそうかい]では、学生時代[がくせいじだい]の思[おも]い出[で]{話[ばなし]に花[はな]が咲[さ]いた}。

ctx.en: We were supposed to plan the trip, but we got so carried away talking about food that nothing got decided.

bad.en: (meant: the principal gave a long speech on his own for an hour)
bad.why: It needs people chatting together. One person talking at an audience is not a conversation blooming.

cards.mean: to chime in to show one is listening
cards.lit: to strike the answering hammer blow

story.text: In a Japanese forge, the master smith and an assistant strike the hot metal in turn, the assistant's hammer answering the master's in a steady rhythm. That answering stroke was called aizuchi, the 'matching hammer'. The word came to mean the short replies a listener puts in to keep a speaker going.

use.how: Xに相槌を打つ: short listening signals (うん, へえ, なるほど) while someone talks. 適当に相槌を打つ means only pretending to listen.

bad.en: (meant: I cut in on the manager to voice my objection)

cards.mean: things are taking an ominous turn

ctx.en: With dark clouds gathering over the economy, many companies are cutting back on hiring.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]が急[きゅう]に黙[だま]り込[こ]んだのを見[み]て、会議[かいぎ]の{雲行[くもゆ]きが怪[あや]しい}と感[かん]じた。

cards.mean: starting before everything is ready
cards.lit: a departure after giving up on the rest: the train pulls out without waiting for everyone

story.text: The phrase began as railway language: when departure time came or a train was full, it pulled out even though not everyone waiting had got on, giving up on (mikiri) the rest. From there it came to mean pushing ahead with a decision or a project before discussion or preparation is complete.

use.how: Noun (見切り発車で始める, 見切り発車だ) or verb 見切り発車する. Mostly criticises a plan begun before preparation or agreement was complete.

near.diff: 見切りをつける is giving up on someone or something as hopeless; 見切り発車 is starting something before it is ready.

ctx.en: "You're starting to build it before the specs are even settled? That's jumping the gun."

ctx.en: The app, rushed out without enough testing, was full of bugs.

bad.en: (meant: the train left on schedule)

bad.en: (meant: I gave up on my dream of being a singer and took an office job)
bad.why: Giving up on something is mikiri o tsukeru. Mikiri hassha is starting something too early.

cards.mean: to feel deflated once the tension is gone
cards.lit: the ki goes out of you, the way the fizz goes out of an opened drink (a beer gone flat is also said to have lost its ki)

use.how: Predicate with the person as subject, after a strain ends: 試験が終わって気が抜けた. It happens to you; 気が抜けない means you cannot relax your guard.

near.diff: 気を抜く is letting your guard down, a lapse you are blamed for; 気が抜ける is the limp, empty feeling that comes by itself once the pressure is off.
拍子抜け is the letdown when something turns out easier or smaller than you braced for; 気が抜ける is the slump after a real strain is over.

ctx.s: 定年[ていねん]退職[たいしょく]した父[ちち]は、{気[き]が抜[ぬ]けた}ように一日中[いちにちじゅう]テレビを見[み]ている。
ctx.en: Since retiring, my father sits in front of the TV all day as if the life has gone out of him.

ctx.s: 受験[じゅけん]が終[お]わって{気[き]が抜[ぬ]けた}のか、弟[おとうと]は春休[はるやす]みの間[あいだ]ずっと寝[ね]てばかりいる。
ctx.en: Maybe it's the slump after his entrance exams, but my little brother has done nothing but sleep all spring break.

cards.mean: to be left blank and stunned with surprise

cards.mean: to blush scarlet with embarrassment

cards.mean: to try every possible means

ctx.s: 管理会社[かんりがいしゃ]の{腰[こし]が重[おも]く}、エレベーターの修理[しゅうり]がいつまでも始[はじ]まらない。
ctx.en: The management company drags its feet, and the lift repairs never seem to start.

ctx.s: {腰[こし]の重[おも]い}彼[かれ]が自分[じぶん]から旅行[りょこう]に行[い]こうと言[い]い出[だ]したので、驚[おどろ]いた。
ctx.en: I was surprised when he, of all people, suggested a trip himself; he usually never wants to do anything.

ctx.s: 年[とし]を取[と]るにつれて、新[あたら]しいことを始[はじ]めるのに{腰[こし]が重[おも]くなった}。
ctx.en: As I've got older, I've become slow to start anything new.

bad.s: あの店員[てんいん]さんはとても{腰[こし]が重[おも]くて}、丁寧[ていねい]に対応[たいおう]してくれた。
bad.en: (meant: that shop assistant was very humble and dealt with me politely)
bad.why: Humble and polite is koshi ga hikui. Koshi ga omoi criticises someone for being slow to act.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{腰[こし]が重[おも]い}ので、軽率[けいそつ]な判断[はんだん]をしない頼[たの]もしいリーダーだ。
bad.en: (meant: he is steady and careful, a reliable leader who never decides rashly)
bad.why: It criticises sluggishness, not praises prudence. For careful judgment say shinchou da.

cards.mean: to try to seem older or more capable than one is
cards.lit: to stretch up on tiptoe to look taller

use.how: Predicate, often 背伸びする without を, or 背伸びした before a noun. About acting more grown-up or advanced than one is; gently critical, or positive when aiming a little higher.

near.diff: 見栄を張る is putting on a front to look richer or better off; 背伸びをする is reaching beyond one's age or level, often out of eagerness to grow up.

cards.cue: Your thirteen-year-old daughter insists on wearing heels and reading her father's economics books, though she understands little of them. You smile about it.

ctx.en: My daughter is in junior high and, wanting to seem grown-up, only wants to wear adult-looking clothes.

ctx.s: 「無理[むり]に{背伸[せの]びしなくて}いいよ。今[いま]の君[きみ]のままで十分[じゅうぶん]だ。」
ctx.en: "You don't have to pretend to be more than you are. You're fine just as you are."

ctx.s: 初[はじ]めてのデートで{背伸[せの]びをして}、飲[の]めもしないブラックコーヒーを注文[ちゅうもん]した。
ctx.en: On our first date I tried to look grown-up and ordered black coffee, which I can't even drink.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]なのに{背伸[せの]びをして}、難[むずか]しい仕事[しごと]を一人[ひとり]で引[ひ]き受[う]けてしまった。
ctx.en: I was only a newcomer, but I overreached and took on a difficult job all by myself.

ctx.en: I decided to aim a little high and apply to a top university.

ctx.s: 十代[じゅうだい]の頃[ころ]の日記[にっき]は、{背伸[せの]びした}難[むずか]しい言葉[ことば]ばかりで恥[は]ずかしい。
ctx.en: My teenage diary is embarrassing, full of big words I used to sound grown-up.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は毎日[まいにち]牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]を飲[の]んで、{背伸[せの]びをした}。
bad.en: (meant: he drank milk every day and grew taller)
bad.why: Growing taller is se ga nobiru. Senobi o suru is stretching up on tiptoe, or trying to seem more than one is.

bad.s: 五十代[ごじゅうだい]の父[ちち]が{背伸[せの]びをして}、若者[わかもの]の流行語[りゅうこうご]を使[つか]っている。
bad.en: (meant: my fifty-something father is trying to act young with teen slang)
bad.why: Senobi reaches upward, to seem older or more advanced. Trying to look younger is wakazukuri.

cards.mean: to gasp in awe or shock
cards.lit: to swallow one's breath: the sharp intake of air at a sudden sight

use.how: Reaction to something seen or heard that is stunning, shocking or tense: 景色に息を呑んだ. Often before a noun: 息を呑むほど美しい, 息を呑む接戦.

near.diff: 目を見張る is being impressed by how remarkable something is, such as progress or skill; 息を呑む is a sudden gasp at beauty, shock or suspense.
息が詰まる is feeling stifled by a tense or oppressive atmosphere over time; 息を呑む is a momentary gasp.

cards.cue: You round a bend on a mountain road and the whole valley lies below you under fresh snow. For a second you can't breathe.

ctx.s: 山頂[さんちょう]から見[み]た朝日[あさひ]の美[うつく]しさに、思[おも]わず{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
ctx.en: The sunrise seen from the summit was so beautiful that I caught my breath without meaning to.

ctx.s: 事故[じこ]の映像[えいぞう]が流[なが]れると、会場[かいじょう]の全員[ぜんいん]が{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
ctx.en: When the footage of the accident was shown, everyone in the hall gasped.

ctx.s: 「最後[さいご]のシーン、{息[いき]を呑[の]む}ほどきれいだったね。」
ctx.en: "That last scene was breathtakingly beautiful, wasn't it?"

ctx.s: ドアを開[あ]けた瞬間[しゅんかん]、彼女[かのじょ]は荒[あ]らされた部屋[へや]を見[み]て{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
ctx.en: The moment she opened the door, she saw the ransacked room and gasped.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]は最後[さいご]まで{息[いき]を呑[の]む}接戦[せっせん]が続[つづ]いた。
ctx.en: The match stayed a breathtakingly close contest right to the end.

ctx.s: 観客[かんきゃく]は{息[いき]を呑[の]んで}綱渡[つなわた]りを見守[みまも]った。
ctx.en: The audience watched the tightrope walk with bated breath.

bad.s: ジョギングのあと、ベンチに座[すわ]って{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: after jogging I sat on a bench and got my breath back)
bad.why: It is a gasp at something striking, not recovering after exercise. Getting your breath back is iki o totonoeru or hitoiki tsuku.

bad.s: 怒[おこ]られるのが怖[こわ]くて、言[い]いたいことを{息[いき]を呑[の]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I was afraid of being told off, so I swallowed what I wanted to say)
bad.why: Holding back your words is kotoba o nomikomu. Iki o nomu takes no other object and is a gasp, not self-restraint.

cards.mean: win or lose, staking everything on a gamble
cards.lit: 'one or eight': a gambler's all-or-nothing call on how things will fall

use.how: Adverb before a risky move (一か八かやってみる, 一か八か勝負に出る) or before a noun: 一か八かの賭け. Said when success is a toss-up and there is no safer option.

near.diff: 思い切って just means boldly taking the plunge; 一か八か stresses that it could fail completely and the result is down to luck.

cards.cue: Two minutes left, a goal down, the coach pulls the goalkeeper and sends everyone forward. It will either work or they lose by more.

ctx.s: もう時間[じかん]がない。{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}やってみよう。
ctx.en: There's no time left. Let's just go for it and see.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は貯金[ちょきん]を全部[ぜんぶ]使[つか]って、{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}の勝負[しょうぶ]に出[で]た。
ctx.en: He put all his savings in and staked everything on one throw.

ctx.s: 「間[ま]に合[あ]わないかもしれないけど、{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}走[はし]ってみる！」
ctx.en: "I might not make it, but I'm going to run for it anyway!"

ctx.s: 残[のこ]り数秒[すうびょう]、彼[かれ]は{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}遠[とお]くからシュートを放[はな]った。
ctx.en: With seconds left, he took a do-or-die shot from long range.

ctx.s: 第一志望[だいいちしぼう]の大学[だいがく]しか受[う]けないなんて、{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}の賭[か]けだよ。
ctx.en: Applying only to your first-choice university is an all-or-nothing gamble.

ctx.s: {一[いち]か八[ばち]か}告白[こくはく]してみたら、なんと付[つ]き合[あ]えることになった。
ctx.en: I took a chance and confessed my feelings, and to my amazement we ended up going out.

bad.s: 毎朝[まいあさ]{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}の時間[じかん]に起[お]きている。
bad.en: (meant: I get up at seven or eight every morning)
bad.why: It is not 'one number or another'; it is a fixed phrase for an all-or-nothing gamble. 'Around seven or eight' is shichiji ka hachiji goro.

bad.s: 絶対[ぜったい]に失敗[しっぱい]しない計画[けいかく]だから、{一[いち]か八[ばち]か}やってみよう。
bad.en: (meant: the plan can't fail, so let's go ahead)
bad.why: Ichi ka bachi ka means the outcome is a toss-up, so it contradicts a plan that is sure to work.

cards.mean: taking one's anger out on innocent people
cards.lit: striking out in all eight directions: hitting whoever happens to be near

use.how: Noun, usually 〜に八つ当たりする or それは八つ当たりだ: venting anger caused by one thing on a person or object that had nothing to do with it.

near.diff: 逆恨み is resenting someone who did you no wrong, often the very person who helped or warned you; 八つ当たり is venting anger from elsewhere on whoever is nearby.

cards.cue: Your boss told you off at work, and as soon as you get home you snap at your little brother for leaving his shoes in the hall.

ctx.s: 試合[しあい]に負[ま]けたからって、弟[おとうと]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}しないで。
ctx.en: Just because you lost the match, don't take it out on your little brother.

ctx.s: 「ごめん、さっきのはただの{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}だった。」
ctx.en: "Sorry, I was only taking it out on you back there."

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]に叱[しか]られた父[ちち]は、帰[かえ]ってくるなり家族[かぞく]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}した。
ctx.en: After being scolded by his boss, my father came home and immediately took it out on the family.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は物[もの]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}して、ドアを思[おも]い切[き]り閉[し]めた。
ctx.en: He took it out on things and slammed the door as hard as he could.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}する客[きゃく]を見[み]ると、嫌[いや]な気分[きぶん]になる。
ctx.en: Seeing customers take their bad mood out on shop staff makes me feel awful.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は「私[わたし]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}されても困[こま]るよ」とため息[いき]をついた。
ctx.en: My mother sighed, "Don't take it out on me, it isn't my fault."

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は約束[やくそく]を破[やぶ]った友達[ともだち]に{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}した。
bad.en: (meant: he got angry at the friend who broke the promise)

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじで{八[や]つ当[あ]たり}して、大金[たいきん]を手[て]に入[い]れた。
bad.en: (meant: I hit the jackpot in the lottery and won a fortune)

cards.mean: knowing full well
cards.lit: knowing it a hundred times over

use.how: Predicate, usually 〜は百も承知だ or 〜を百も承知で: stresses that one is fully aware of a risk or objection, often before going ahead anyway.

near.diff: 承知の上 plainly says something was done knowingly; 百も承知 is more emphatic and often impatient: I know that perfectly well.

cards.cue: Your friend warns you again that the hike is long and steep. You've done it twice and cut them off: yes, I'm perfectly aware.

ctx.s: 危[あぶ]ないことは{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}だ。それでも行[い]きたい。
ctx.en: I know perfectly well it's dangerous. I still want to go.

ctx.s: 「言[い]われなくても{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "You don't need to tell me. I know that full well."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は反対[はんたい]されるのを{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}で、会議[かいぎ]で意見[いけん]を述[の]べた。
ctx.en: Knowing full well he would be opposed, he gave his opinion at the meeting.

ctx.s: 甘[あま]い物[もの]が体[からだ]に悪[わる]いのは{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}なのに、つい食[た]べてしまう。
ctx.en: I know perfectly well that sweets are bad for me, but I end up eating them anyway.

ctx.s: 無理[むり]なお願[ねが]いなのは{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}ですが、もう一度[いちど]ご検討[けんとう]いただけませんか。
ctx.en: I am fully aware this is a difficult request, but could you possibly reconsider?

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は批判[ひはん]が出[で]るのを{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}の上[うえ]で、若手[わかて]を起用[きよう]した。
ctx.en: Fully aware that he would be criticised, the manager picked the young players.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]、明日[あした]の集合時間[しゅうごうじかん]、{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}しました。
bad.en: (meant: Understood, sir, about tomorrow's meeting time)
bad.why: It is not a polite acknowledgement like shouchi shimashita and never takes shimashita. It means 'I know that perfectly well' and sounds impatient.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は本[ほん]をたくさん読[よ]むので、何[なん]でも{百[ひゃく]も承知[しょうち]}な人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he reads a lot, so he is very knowledgeable)
bad.why: It is about being fully aware of one particular fact, not about knowing a lot. A well-informed person is monoshiri.

cards.mean: to stubbornly refuse to give in
cards.lit: to hold one's pride stretched taut, refusing to let it bend

use.how: Predicate about a person who will not back down, apologise or accept help out of pride: 意地を張らないで謝りなよ. Often 意地を張って〜しない.

near.diff: 意地になる is getting fixated on doing something to prove a point; 意地を張る is refusing to concede, apologise or accept help.

cards.cue: Your sister is obviously lost but won't look at the map you offer, because she insisted earlier that she knew the way.

ctx.s: {意地[いじ]を張[は]らないで}、早[はや]く謝[あやま]りなよ。
ctx.en: Stop being stubborn and just apologise.

ctx.s: 本当[ほんとう]は寂[さび]しいのに、彼[かれ]は{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}「一人[ひとり]で平気[へいき]だ」と言[い]った。
ctx.en: He was actually lonely, but out of pride he insisted he was fine on his own.

ctx.s: 「いつまで{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}るの？もう仲直[なかなお]りしたら？」
ctx.en: "How long are you going to keep this up? Why not make up already?"

ctx.s: 道[みち]に迷[まよ]ったのに、父[ちち]は{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}誰[だれ]にも道[みち]を聞[き]かなかった。
ctx.en: We were lost, but my father stubbornly refused to ask anyone for directions.

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]とも{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}、一週間[いっしゅうかん]も口[くち]をきかなかった。
ctx.en: Neither of them would give in, and they didn't speak for a whole week.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもが{意地[いじ]を張[は]る}のは、自分[じぶん]の気持[きも]ちを分[わ]かってほしいからだ。
ctx.en: When children dig their heels in, it is because they want their feelings understood.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は夢[ゆめ]のために、毎日[まいにち]{意地[いじ]を張[は]って}練習[れんしゅう]している。
bad.en: (meant: he perseveres with practice every day for his dream)
bad.why: It criticises proud refusal to give in, not admirable perseverance. For that say nebarizuyoku or ganbatte iru.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{意地[いじ]を張[は]る}人[ひと]で、よく他人[たにん]の悪口[わるくち]を言[い]う。
bad.en: (meant: she is a mean person who often badmouths others)
bad.why: Mean or spiteful is iji ga warui or ijiwaru. Iji o haru is being stubborn, not being nasty to others.

cards.mean: to feel gloomy and depressed
cards.lit: one's spirit sinks inward and down

use.how: Predicate about one's mood being dragged down by weather, news, a dreary place or a long situation: 雨が続いて気が滅入る. Also 気が滅入るような話.

near.diff: 気が重い is dread about something you have to do; 気が滅入る is a general gloom brought on by your surroundings or circumstances.

cards.cue: It has rained for ten days, the flat is dim all day and every news story is bad. You tell a friend how it is making you feel.

ctx.s: 雨[あめ]の日[ひ]が続[つづ]くと{気[き]が滅入[めい]る}。
ctx.en: When the rain goes on day after day, I start to feel down.

ctx.s: 暗[くら]いニュースばかりで、見[み]ているだけで{気[き]が滅入[めい]って}くる。
ctx.en: It's nothing but grim news; just watching it gets me down.

ctx.s: 「窓[まど]のない部屋[へや]で一日中[いちにちじゅう]働[はたら]いていると、{気[き]が滅入[めい]って}くるよ。」
ctx.en: "Working all day in a room with no windows really starts to get you down."

ctx.s: 散[ち]らかった部屋[へや]を見[み]ると{気[き]が滅入[めい]る}ので、週末[しゅうまつ]に片付[かたづ]けた。
ctx.en: Looking at my messy room was getting me down, so I tidied it at the weekend.

ctx.s: 入院[にゅういん]が長[なが]くなり、祖母[そぼ]はすっかり{気[き]が滅入[めい]って}いるようだ。
ctx.en: Her stay in hospital has dragged on, and my grandmother seems thoroughly low.

ctx.s: 冬[ふゆ]は四時[よじ]過[す]ぎに暗[くら]くなるので、どうしても{気[き]が滅入[めい]る}。
ctx.en: In winter it gets dark just after four, so I can't help feeling gloomy.

bad.s: 宝[たから]くじが当[あ]たって、{気[き]が滅入[めい]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I won the lottery and was over the moon)
bad.why: It means the opposite: feeling gloomy and low. For delight say ooyorokobi shita.

bad.s: テレビの音[おと]で{気[き]が滅入[めい]って}、勉強[べんきょう]に集中[しゅうちゅう]できない。
bad.en: (meant: the TV noise distracts me so I can't concentrate on studying)
bad.why: Being distracted is ki ga chiru. Ki ga meiru is a gloomy mood, not a loss of focus.

cards.mean: for one's attention to slacken without meaning to
cards.lit: one's mind goes slack, like a string that has loosened

use.how: Predicate about attention or discipline relaxing, often after success, near the end or once used to something: 慣れて気が緩む. Usually explains a mistake or warns against one.

near.diff: 気が抜ける is feeling deflated and flat once tension is gone; 気が緩む is attention slackening, which tends to cause mistakes.
気を抜く is choosing to relax or ease off; 気が緩む happens to you without your meaning it.

cards.cue: Leading easily in the last lap, a runner eases off, stops looking back, and is overtaken metres from the line.

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]が終[お]わって{気[き]が緩[ゆる]んだ}のか、帰[かえ]りの電車[でんしゃ]に傘[かさ]を忘[わす]れた。
ctx.en: Maybe I got careless once the exams were over: I left my umbrella on the train home.

ctx.s: 運転[うんてん]に慣[な]れて{気[き]が緩[ゆる]む}と、事故[じこ]を起[お]こしやすい。
ctx.en: When you get used to driving and stop paying close attention, accidents become more likely.

ctx.s: 「入社[にゅうしゃ]して三[さん]か月[げつ]くらいが、一番[いちばん]{気[き]が緩[ゆる]み}やすいからね。」
ctx.en: "About three months into a job is when people most easily get careless, you know."

ctx.s: 休[やす]み明[あ]けで{気[き]が緩[ゆる]んで}いたのか、計算[けいさん]ミスが多[おお]かった。
ctx.en: Maybe my mind was still on holiday; I made a lot of calculation mistakes.

ctx.s: 大差[たいさ]でリードして知[し]らないうちに{気[き]が緩[ゆる]んだ}のか、終盤[しゅうばん]に三点[さんてん]を失[うしな]った。
ctx.en: With a big lead, perhaps their focus slipped without their noticing, because they gave up three goals near the end.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は「勝[か]って{気[き]が緩[ゆる]む}のが一番[いちばん]怖[こわ]い」と選手[せんしゅ]に話[はな]した。
ctx.en: The coach told the players, "What I fear most is that winning makes you careless."

bad.s: マッサージを受[う]けて、肩[かた]の{気[き]が緩[ゆる]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: after the massage my shoulder muscles loosened up)
bad.why: Ki is the mind, not the body. Stiff shoulders loosening is kata no kori ga hogureta.

bad.s: 母[はは]は{気[き]が緩[ゆる]い}人[ひと]で、何[なん]でも許[ゆる]してくれる。
bad.en: (meant: my mother is lenient and lets me do anything)
bad.why: The idiom is the verb yurumu for a lapse in attention, not a character trait. A lenient person is amai or kandai.

cards.mean: to feel overwhelmed by the sheer scale of something
cards.lit: one's mind drifts far away, as when one is about to faint

use.how: Predicate or before a noun (気が遠くなるような時間, 量, 作業) about staggering numbers, time, distance or effort. Literally it also means to start to faint.

near.diff: 途方に暮れる is not knowing what to do next; 気が遠くなる is being staggered by how vast or long something is.

cards.cue: You learn that copying one old scroll by hand took a monk forty years, and you try to imagine all those days.

ctx.s: 本[ほん]を千冊[せんさつ]読[よ]むなんて、聞[き]いただけで{気[き]が遠[とお]くなる}。
ctx.en: Read a thousand books? Just hearing it makes my head spin.

ctx.s: 宇宙[うちゅう]の広[ひろ]さを考[かんが]えると{気[き]が遠[とお]くなる}。
ctx.en: Thinking about the size of the universe makes my mind reel.

ctx.s: 「この量[りょう]を全部[ぜんぶ]手書[てが]きで写[うつ]すの？{気[き]が遠[とお]くなる}ね。」
ctx.en: "We have to copy all of this out by hand? That's mind-boggling."

ctx.s: あの星[ほし]の光[ひかり]は何万年[なんまんねん]も前[まえ]のものだと知[し]って、{気[き]が遠[とお]くなった}。
ctx.en: When I learned that the light from that star left it tens of thousands of years ago, my mind boggled.

ctx.s: 職人[しょくにん]は{気[き]が遠[とお]くなる}ような時間[じかん]をかけて、一枚[いちまい]の布[ぬの]を織[お]り上[あ]げる。
ctx.en: The artisan spends a staggering amount of time weaving a single piece of cloth.

ctx.s: ローンを返[かえ]し終[お]わるまで三十五年[さんじゅうごねん]と聞[き]いて、{気[き]が遠[とお]くなる}思[おも]いがした。
ctx.en: When I heard it would take thirty-five years to pay off the loan, I felt dizzy at the thought.

bad.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]して、実家[じっか]から{気[き]が遠[とお]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: after moving, I live further from my parents' home)
bad.why: It is not about physical distance; it is the dizzy feeling at a vast scale. Say jikka kara tooku natta.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]とは最近[さいきん]{気[き]が遠[とお]くなって}、あまり話[はな]さない。
bad.en: (meant: we've drifted apart lately and hardly talk)
bad.why: Drifting apart is soen ni naru. Ki ga tooku naru is being staggered by scale, or nearly fainting.

cards.mean: to feel a twinge of guilt
cards.lit: one's own mind finds fault: the heart reproaches itself

use.how: Predicate about one's own slight guilt over a small wrong: 嘘をついたのが気がとがめる. Often 〜のは気がとがめる or 〜て気がとがめる.

near.diff: 気が引ける is hesitating because something feels awkward or presumptuous; 気がとがめる is guilt because you feel you have done something a little wrong.

cards.cue: You called in sick to go to a concert, and the next morning a colleague kindly asks whether you're feeling better.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どものおやつをこっそり食[た]べてしまい、{気[き]がとがめた}。
ctx.en: I secretly ate the children's snacks and felt a bit guilty.

ctx.s: 仮病[けびょう]で休[やす]んだのに同僚[どうりょう]に心配[しんぱい]されて、{気[き]がとがめた}。
ctx.en: I'd faked being sick, so when my colleague was worried about me I felt guilty.

ctx.s: 「拾[ひろ]ったお金[かね]、使[つか]っちゃったの？{気[き]がとがめない}？」
ctx.en: "You spent the money you found? Doesn't your conscience bother you?"

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]の誘[さそ]いを嘘[うそ]の理由[りゆう]で断[ことわ]ってしまい、少[すこ]し{気[き]がとがめて}いる。
ctx.en: I turned down my friend's invitation with a made-up excuse, and it's nagging at me a little.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]がとがめた}のか、次[つぎ]の日[ひ]に自分[じぶん]から謝[あやま]りに来[き]た。
ctx.en: Perhaps his conscience pricked him, because the next day he came to apologise of his own accord.

ctx.s: 母[はは]の誕生日[たんじょうび]を忘[わす]れていたのが{気[き]がとがめて}、花[はな]を買[か]って帰[かえ]った。
ctx.en: Feeling guilty that I'd forgotten my mother's birthday, I bought flowers on the way home.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]に財布[さいふ]を盗[ぬす]まれて、{気[き]がとがめた}。
bad.en: (meant: a friend stole my wallet and I was hurt and angry)
bad.why: It is guilt about your own small wrong, never resentment at what someone else did. Say hara ga tatta or kizutsuita.

bad.s: 部下[ぶか]のミスに{気[き]がとがめて}、厳[きび]しく注意[ちゅうい]した。
bad.en: (meant: I found fault with my subordinate's mistake and scolded them)
bad.why: Togameru alone can mean to reproach someone, but ki ga togameru is always your own conscience pricking you.

cards.mean: to be unable to fathom why anyone would do that
cards.lit: their mind cannot be known

use.how: Usually 〜する人の気が知れない or Xの気が知れない: says another person's choice is beyond understanding, with clear disapproval.

near.diff: 首をかしげる is being puzzled or doubtful about something; 気が知れない bluntly rejects another person's choice as incomprehensible.

cards.cue: Your neighbour drives an hour every weekend to queue overnight for limited-edition trainers, then never wears them. You say what you think of it.

ctx.s: こんなに寒[さむ]い日[ひ]に海[うみ]で泳[およ]ぐ人[ひと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
ctx.en: I can't understand people who swim in the sea on a day this cold.

ctx.s: 「三時間[さんじかん]も並[なら]んでラーメンを食[た]べるの？{気[き]が知[し]れない}な。」
ctx.en: "Queue for three hours for a bowl of ramen? I don't get it."

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]の前日[ぜんじつ]に徹夜[てつや]でゲームをするなんて、弟[おとうと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
ctx.en: Gaming all night the day before an exam? I can't fathom what my brother is thinking.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は「道[みち]にごみを捨[す]てる人[ひと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}」といつも怒[おこ]っている。
ctx.en: My grandfather is always grumbling, "I'll never understand people who drop litter in the street."

ctx.s: お金[かね]を払[はら]ってまで怖[こわ]い思[おも]いをしに行[い]く人[ひと]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
ctx.en: I can't see why anyone would pay money just to be scared.

ctx.s: あんな条件[じょうけん]で契約[けいやく]にサインした社長[しゃちょう]の{気[き]が知[し]れない}と、社員[しゃいん]たちはあきれた。
ctx.en: The staff were appalled; they couldn't fathom why the president had signed a contract on those terms.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の天気[てんき]はまだ{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
bad.en: (meant: tomorrow's weather is still unknown)
bad.why: It is about another person's baffling choice, not about facts that are unknown. Say mada wakaranai.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しい先生[せんせい]は来[き]たばかりで、まだ{気[き]が知[し]れない}。
bad.en: (meant: the new teacher has only just arrived, so we don't know what they're like)
bad.why: It is not 'not yet known'; it condemns someone's choice as incomprehensible. Say donna hito ka mada wakaranai.

cards.mean: to find someone or something not to one's liking
cards.lit: one's ki will not eat it: something one's spirit refuses to swallow

use.how: Predicate with が: あいつの態度が気に食わない. A blunt, rough way to voice dislike of a person, attitude or way of doing things. Used almost only in the negative.

near.diff: 気に障る is being offended by a particular remark or act; 気に食わない is a standing dislike, often of a whole person or manner, and sounds blunter.

cards.cue: You can't say exactly why, but the new guy's smug manner just rubs you the wrong way, and you grumble about him to a friend.

ctx.s: あの人[ひと]のことは、どうも{気[き]に食[く]わない}。
ctx.en: I just don't like that person, somehow.

ctx.s: 「何[なに]がそんなに{気[き]に食[く]わない}の？」
ctx.en: "What is it you dislike so much?"

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい上司[じょうし]は、部下[ぶか]の意見[いけん]が{気[き]に食[く]わない}とすぐ怒[おこ]る。
ctx.en: The new boss gets angry straight away when he doesn't like what his staff say.

ctx.s: 理由[りゆう]はないけど、あいつの態度[たいど]が{気[き]に食[く]わなくて}、つい冷[つめ]たくしてしまった。
ctx.en: There's no real reason, but I didn't like his attitude, so I ended up being cold to him.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は、孫[まご]の派手[はで]な髪[かみ]の色[いろ]が{気[き]に食[く]わない}らしい。
ctx.en: Grandpa apparently doesn't approve of his grandson's loud hair colour.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は、{気[き]に食[く]わない}相手[あいて]とは口[くち]もきかない。
ctx.en: He won't even speak to people he doesn't like.

bad.s: お腹[なか]がいっぱいで、もう{気[き]に食[く]わない}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm full and can't eat any more)
bad.why: Kuu here has nothing to do with eating food; the phrase only expresses dislike of someone or something.

bad.s: 「お客様[きゃくさま]、どのデザインが{気[き]に食[く]わない}でしょうか。」
bad.en: (meant: Sir, which design is not to your liking?)
bad.why: It is rough and hostile in tone. To a customer, say o-ki ni mesanai.

cards.mean: to keep someone in one's thoughts with concern
cards.lit: to hang someone on one's ki: to keep them hooked in one's mind

use.how: Takes を, usually 〜のことを気にかける or 気にかけてくれる. Said of caring concern for another person's welfare or a matter one keeps watch over.

near.diff: 気にする is worrying or being bothered, often about oneself (人の目を気にする); 気にかける is warm, ongoing concern for someone else.
気を配る is being attentive to everyone's needs in a situation; 気にかける is keeping a particular person or matter in mind over time.

cards.cue: Your old teacher still emails now and then to ask how you're getting on since you moved abroad. You tell a friend how kind that is.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]はいつも私[わたし]のことを{気[き]にかけて}くれる。
ctx.en: My teacher always looks out for me.

ctx.s: 「あの子[こ]、最近[さいきん]元気[げんき]がないから、少[すこ]し{気[き]にかけて}あげてね。」
ctx.en: "That kid has been down lately, so keep an eye on him for me, would you?"

ctx.s: 一人暮[ひとりぐ]らしの祖母[そぼ]を{気[き]にかけて}、毎週[まいしゅう]電話[でんわ]している。
ctx.en: I worry about my grandmother living alone, so I phone her every week.

ctx.s: 入社[にゅうしゃ]したばかりの頃[ころ]、先輩[せんぱい]たちが何[なに]かと{気[き]にかけて}くれた。
ctx.en: When I had just joined the company, the senior staff looked out for me in all sorts of ways.

ctx.s: {気[き]にかけて}いただき、ありがとうございます。おかげさまで元気[げんき]になりました。
ctx.en: Thank you for your concern. I'm well again now, thanks to you.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は、試合[しあい]に出[で]られない選手[せんしゅ]のことも{気[き]にかけて}いた。
ctx.en: The coach also kept the players who couldn't get a game in his thoughts.

bad.s: 書類[しょるい]の間違[まちが]いに{気[き]にかけた}。
bad.en: (meant: I noticed a mistake in the document)
bad.why: Noticing something is kizuku. Ki ni kakeru is ongoing concern for someone or something, and it takes o, not ni.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{気[き]にかけて}ドアを閉[し]めた。
bad.en: (meant: he closed the door carefully)
bad.why: It does not mean 'carefully'. For doing something with care, say ki o tsukete or sotto.

cards.mean: to take one's mind off a worry
cards.lit: to blur one's ki: to mix the mind up with something else so the worry gets lost in it

use.how: Often 〜で気を紛らわす or 気を紛らわすために: doing something on purpose to stop thinking about worry, pain, boredom or sadness.

near.diff: 気が晴れる means the gloom actually lifts; 気を紛らわす is a deliberate diversion, and the worry is still there underneath.
気が散る is having one's attention scattered against one's will; 気を紛らわす is choosing a distraction to escape a worry.

cards.cue: Waiting all evening for a phone call about your father's surgery, you put on a film just so you won't keep thinking about it.

ctx.s: 不安[ふあん]な夜[よる]は、音楽[おんがく]を聴[き]いて{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわす}。
ctx.en: On anxious nights I listen to music to take my mind off things.

ctx.s: 結果[けっか]を待[ま]つ間[あいだ]、{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわそう}と部屋[へや]の掃除[そうじ]を始[はじ]めた。
ctx.en: While waiting for the results, I started cleaning my room to keep my mind off them.

ctx.s: 「{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわす}のに、映画[えいが]でも見[み]に行[い]かない？」
ctx.en: "Why don't we go and see a film or something, to take your mind off it?"

ctx.s: 失恋[しつれん]した彼女[かのじょ]は、仕事[しごと]に打[う]ち込[こ]んで{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわして}いた。
ctx.en: After her heartbreak, she threw herself into work to keep from dwelling on it.

ctx.s: 歯医者[はいしゃ]の待合室[まちあいしつ]で、子供[こども]は絵本[えほん]で{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわして}いた。
ctx.en: In the dentist's waiting room, the child kept her mind off it with a picture book.

ctx.s: 痛[いた]みから{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわす}ため、看護師[かんごし]さんが話[はな]しかけてくれた。
ctx.en: The nurse chatted to me to take my mind off the pain.

bad.s: 隣[となり]の工事[こうじ]の音[おと]がうるさくて、勉強中[べんきょうちゅう]に{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわして}しまう。
bad.en: (meant: the building work next door is so noisy that I get distracted while studying)
bad.why: Unwanted distraction is ki ga chiru. Ki o magirawasu is choosing a diversion to escape something unpleasant.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]に合格[ごうかく]して、うれしくて{気[き]を紛[まぎ]らわした}。
bad.en: (meant: I passed the exam and celebrated because I was so happy)
bad.why: It is a way of escaping worry, pain or sadness, not of expressing joy.

cards.mean: to fret anxiously over an outcome
cards.lit: to knead one's ki: the mind squeezed and kneaded over and over by worry

use.how: Verb phrase with を; the worry is often given as 〜かと気を揉む, and 気を揉ませる is to cause others worry. Said of waiting anxiously for news or for how something will turn out.

near.diff: 気が気でない is stronger: so anxious one can think of nothing else; 気を揉む is fretting, which can go on quietly for days.
気にする is minding or being bothered by something; 気を揉む is anxious fretting over an outcome that is still unknown.

cards.cue: For days your mother has been quietly worrying whether your brother's job interview went well, asking you again and again if he has heard.

ctx.s: 娘[むすめ]の進路[しんろ]がなかなか決[き]まらず、母[はは]はずっと{気[き]を揉[も]んで}いる。
ctx.en: My daughter still hasn't decided what to do after school, and my mother has been fretting about it all along.

ctx.s: 雨[あめ]で運動会[うんどうかい]が中止[ちゅうし]にならないかと{気[き]を揉[も]む}。
ctx.en: I'm fretting over whether the sports day will be called off for rain.

ctx.s: 「そんなに{気[き]を揉[も]まなくても}、きっと大丈夫[だいじょうぶ]だよ。」
ctx.en: "You don't need to worry yourself like that. I'm sure it'll be fine."

ctx.s: 契約[けいやく]がまとまるかどうか、担当者[たんとうしゃ]は一週間[いっしゅうかん]{気[き]を揉[も]み}続[つづ]けた。
ctx.en: For a whole week, the person in charge fretted over whether the contract would go through.

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]の結果[けっか]が来[こ]ないので、毎日[まいにち]{気[き]を揉[も]んで}ばかりいる。
ctx.en: The interview result hasn't come, so I spend every day doing nothing but worrying.

ctx.s: 連絡[れんらく]もせずに帰[かえ]りが遅[おそ]くなり、家族[かぞく]に{気[き]を揉[も]ませて}しまった。
ctx.en: I came home late without letting anyone know and left my family worrying.

bad.s: 肩[かた]が凝[こ]ったので、{気[き]を揉[も]んで}もらった。
bad.en: (meant: my shoulders were stiff, so I had them massaged)
bad.why: Momu here is only figurative. Ki o momu means fretting; for a massage say kata o monde moratta.

bad.s: 明日[あした]の旅行[りょこう]が楽[たの]しみで、{気[き]を揉[も]んで}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I'm excited about tomorrow's trip)
bad.why: It is anxiety about an uncertain outcome, never happy anticipation. Say wakuwaku shite iru.

cards.mean: to be put in a good mood by praise or success
cards.lit: to make one's ki good: something lifts one's spirits

use.how: Usually past, with the cause in に or a て-clause: 褒められて気をよくした. Often leads on to what the pleased person then did, sometimes with a hint of irony.

near.diff: 気が晴れる is gloom or worry clearing away; 気をよくする is being pleased and encouraged by a specific compliment or success.

cards.cue: A salesperson tells you a jacket looks great on you, and, feeling flattered, you end up buying two.

ctx.s: 料理[りょうり]を褒[ほ]められて{気[き]をよくした}父[ちち]は、また作[つく]ると言[い]った。
ctx.en: Pleased at having his cooking praised, my father said he'd make it again.

ctx.s: 初戦[しょせん]の勝利[しょうり]に{気[き]をよくした}チームは、次[つぎ]の試合[しあい]も勢[いきお]いよく戦[たたか]った。
ctx.en: Buoyed by their first win, the team played the next match with great energy too.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]に「お似合[にあ]いです」と言[い]われて{気[き]をよくし}、つい二着[にちゃく]も買[か]ってしまった。
ctx.en: Flattered when the shop assistant said it suited me, I ended up buying two.

ctx.s: 「あのお客[きゃく]さん、少[すこ]し値引[ねび]きしたら{気[き]をよくして}、常連[じょうれん]になってくれたよ。」
ctx.en: "That customer was so pleased when I gave him a small discount that he became a regular."

ctx.s: 前年[ぜんねん]の売[う]り上[あ]げに{気[き]をよくして}、社長[しゃちょう]は今年[ことし]の目標[もくひょう]を高[たか]くした。
ctx.en: Encouraged by last year's sales, the president set a higher target for this year.

ctx.s: 株[かぶ]で少[すこ]し儲[もう]けて{気[き]をよくした}彼[かれ]は、さらに大金[たいきん]をつぎ込[こ]んだ。
ctx.en: Pleased with a small profit on shares, he poured in a lot more money.

bad.s: 「お客様[きゃくさま]、どうぞ{気[き]をよくして}お過[す]ごしください。」
bad.en: (meant: please enjoy your stay)
bad.why: It is not a wish or request to be cheerful; it describes someone pleased by a particular cause.

bad.s: 「雪[ゆき]だから、運転[うんてん]には{気[き]をよくして}ね。」
bad.en: (meant: it's snowing, so drive carefully)
bad.why: Being careful is ki o tsukeru. Ki o yoku suru is being pleased by praise or success.

cards.mean: to keep a sharp watch for wrongdoing
cards.lit: to make one's eyes glint: eyes kept sharp and bright, watching

use.how: Usually 〜に目を光らせる or 〜がないか目を光らせる, often in ている. Said of guards, police, teachers or parents watching for misconduct.

near.diff: 目が離せない is not being able to look away, because something might happen or is gripping; 目を光らせる is deliberate surveillance for wrongdoing.

cards.cue: During the exam the invigilator walks slowly between the desks, watching for anyone trying to cheat.

ctx.s: 店[みせ]の入[い]り口[ぐち]では、警備員[けいびいん]が{目[め]を光[ひか]らせて}いる。
ctx.en: A security guard keeps a close watch at the shop entrance.

ctx.s: 試験中[しけんちゅう]、先生[せんせい]はカンニングがないか{目[め]を光[ひか]らせて}いた。
ctx.en: During the exam the teacher was watching closely for any cheating.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]この辺[へん]で空[あ]き巣[す]が多[おお]いから、みんなで{目[め]を光[ひか]らせよう}。」
ctx.en: "There have been a lot of burglaries round here lately, so let's all keep our eyes peeled."

ctx.s: 税務署[ぜいむしょ]は、ネットで稼[かせ]ぐ人[ひと]の申告[しんこく]漏[も]れに{目[め]を光[ひか]らせて}いる。
ctx.en: The tax office is keeping a sharp eye out for people who earn online and fail to declare it.

ctx.s: 親[おや]が{目[め]を光[ひか]らせて}いるので、弟[おとうと]は夜中[よなか]にゲームができない。
ctx.en: Our parents keep such a close watch that my little brother can't play games at night.

ctx.s: 大会[たいかい]の期間中[きかんちゅう]は、運営側[うんえいがわ]がチケットの不正[ふせい]な転売[てんばい]に{目[め]を光[ひか]らせる}。
ctx.en: During the tournament, the organisers watch closely for illegal ticket resale.

bad.s: 好[す]きな人[ひと]に会[あ]えて、彼女[かのじょ]は{目[め]を光[ひか]らせた}。
bad.en: (meant: her eyes sparkled with joy at seeing the person she liked)
bad.why: Eyes shining with joy is me o kagayakaseru. Me o hikaraseru is a watchful, suspicious look.

bad.s: 「明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]の資料[しりょう]に{目[め]を光[ひか]らせて}おいてください。」
bad.en: (meant: please look over the materials for tomorrow's meeting)
bad.why: Looking something over is me o toosu. Me o hikaraseru is keeping watch for wrongdoing.

cards.t: 目に入れても痛くない
cards.r: めにいれてもいたくない
cards.mean: to dote on a child or grandchild
cards.lit: it would not hurt even if you put them in your eye: so dear that even that would cause no pain

use.how: Usually before ほどかわいい or as a noun modifier: 目に入れても痛くない孫. Said of a parent's or grandparent's doting love for a small child, with affectionate exaggeration.

near.diff: 目がない is having a weakness for something, usually food or a hobby; 目に入れても痛くない is doting love for a child.

cards.cue: Your stern grandfather melts completely whenever his first grandchild toddles into the room, and gives her anything she asks for.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]にとって、初孫[ういまご]は{目[め]に入[い]れても痛[いた]くない}存在[そんざい]だ。
ctx.en: To my grandfather, his first grandchild is the apple of his eye.

cards.mean: to be captivated by the sight of something

cards.mean: to witness something with one's own eyes

cards.mean: to get worked up over trivial faults

cards.mean: to be struck by how remarkable something is

目を奪われる is being so captivated, often by beauty, that you cannot look away; 目を見張る is astonished admiration.

bad.en: (meant: thank you for the offer, but we must politely decline the project)
bad.why: It is dismissive and sounds arrogant to the other side. A polite refusal is konkai wa miokurasete itadakimasu.

cards.mean: to pout in discontent
cards.lit: to make one's mouth pointed: to push the lips out

use.how: Describes the face someone makes when sulky or dissatisfied, often with a complaint: 「えー」と口を尖らせた. Common in narration about children.

cards.cue: You tell your seven-year-old that the trip to the park is cancelled because of rain. Describe the face they make as they whine.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はおやつを取[と]られて{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせた}。
ctx.en: My little brother pouted when his snack was taken.

ctx.s: 「えー、もう帰[かえ]るの？」と娘[むすめ]は{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせた}。
ctx.en: "What, we're going home already?" my daughter pouted.

ctx.s: 宿題[しゅくだい]をしなさいと言[い]われると、息子[むすこ]はすぐ{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせる}。
ctx.en: Whenever he's told to do his homework, my son immediately pouts.

ctx.s: 「そんなに{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせない}で、理由[りゆう]を話[はな]してごらん。」
ctx.en: "Don't pout like that. Tell me why."

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]だけ掃除[そうじ]当番[とうばん]が多[おお]いと、彼女[かのじょ]は{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせて}文句[もんく]を言[い]った。
ctx.en: Pouting, she complained that she alone had been given extra cleaning duty.

ctx.s: 判定[はんてい]に納得[なっとく]できない選手[せんしゅ]は、{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせながら}ベンチに戻[もど]った。
ctx.en: Unhappy with the call, the player walked back to the bench with a pout.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は激怒[げきど]して、{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせながら}机[つくえ]を叩[たた]いた。
bad.en: (meant: my father flew into a rage and pounded the desk)
bad.why: It is a sulky, rather childish look of discontent, not violent rage. For rage, say gekido shite or kao o makka ni shite.

bad.s: 誕生日[たんじょうび]のプレゼントをもらって、妹[いもうと]はうれしそうに{口[くち]を尖[とが]らせた}。
bad.en: (meant: my sister beamed with delight at her birthday present)
bad.why: It is a face of discontent or complaint, so it cannot show delight. For a happy face, say niko niko shita or kao o kagayakaseta.

cards.mean: to give the same warning over and over
cards.lit: to make one's mouth go sour from saying the same thing so often

use.how: Almost always 口を酸っぱくして言う / 注意する: repeated advice or warnings given for the listener's good. Also 口が酸っぱくなるほど言った.

near.diff: 耳にたこができる is the listener's side: sick of hearing it. 口を酸っぱくする is the speaker's side: warning again and again.

cards.cue: For years your grandfather kept telling you never to borrow money. Now, in debt, you remember how often he said it.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は毎晩[まいばん]{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}「早[はや]く寝[ね]なさい」と言[い]っていた。
ctx.en: Every night my mother would tell me over and over to go to bed early.

ctx.s: 「{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}言[い]ってるでしょう。出[で]かけるときは鍵[かぎ]をかけなさいって。」
ctx.en: "How many times have I told you? Lock the door when you go out."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]が{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}注意[ちゅうい]したのに、また宿題[しゅくだい]を忘[わす]れた生徒[せいと]がいる。
ctx.en: Even though the teacher warned them again and again, some students forgot their homework again.

ctx.s: コーチは選手[せんしゅ]たちに、準備[じゅんび]運動[うんどう]の大切[たいせつ]さを{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}説[と]いた。
ctx.en: The coach kept stressing to the players how important it is to warm up.

ctx.s: 情報[じょうほう]の持[も]ち出[だ]しについては、上司[じょうし]から{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}言[い]われている。
ctx.en: Our manager has warned us time and again about taking company data out of the office.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]が{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}言[い]っていた「借金[しゃっきん]はするな」という言葉[ことば]を、今[いま]になって思[おも]い出[だ]す。
ctx.en: Only now do I remember my grandfather's words, repeated so often: never borrow money.

bad.s: 「昨日[きのう]一度[いちど]だけ、{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}注意[ちゅうい]しました。」
bad.en: (meant: I warned him firmly once, yesterday)
bad.why: The phrase means saying it many times, so it contradicts ichido dake. For one firm warning, say tsuyoku chuui shimashita.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は同僚[どうりょう]に嫉妬[しっと]して、{口[くち]を酸[す]っぱくして}悪口[わるぐち]を言[い]った。
bad.en: (meant: jealous of a colleague, he spoke about them bitterly)
bad.why: It is for well-meant advice or warnings repeated for the listener's good, not bitter or spiteful talk.

cards.mean: to be taken in by someone's smooth talk
cards.lit: to ride on someone's mouth-cart: to be carried along by their glib talk

use.how: Aの口車に乗る, very often passive 口車に乗せられる: said of oneself or others who were talked into something by a smooth talker.

near.diff: 口がうまい describes the talker as smooth-tongued; 口車に乗る describes the person who falls for that talk.

cards.cue: A salesman's patter persuades your aunt to buy a pricey water purifier she doesn't need. Later she admits she fell for his talk.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]って}、いらない物[もの]まで買[か]ってしまった。
ctx.en: I fell for the shop assistant's sales talk and ended up buying things I didn't even need.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]る}なよ。うまい話[はなし]には裏[うら]があるから。」
ctx.en: "Don't fall for his smooth talk. When something sounds too good, there's a catch."

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]せられて}、飲[の]み会[かい]の幹事[かんじ]を引[ひ]き受[う]けてしまった。
ctx.en: My friends sweet-talked me into organising the party.

ctx.s: 「また営業[えいぎょう]の人[ひと]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]った}の？」
ctx.en: "Did you get talked into it by a salesperson again?"

ctx.s: 高[たか]い利回[りまわ]りをうたう業者[ぎょうしゃ]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]り}、老後[ろうご]の資金[しきん]を失[うしな]った人[ひと]もいる。
ctx.en: Some people were taken in by firms promising high returns and lost their retirement savings.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は用心深[ようじんぶか]く、電話[でんわ]の詐欺師[さぎし]の{口車[くちぐるま]には乗[の]らなかった}。
ctx.en: My grandmother is cautious and didn't fall for the phone scammer's patter.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]って}、勉強[べんきょう]が好[す]きになった。
bad.en: (meant: my teacher's encouraging words made me like studying)
bad.why: Kuchiguruma is always glib, manipulative talk, so this accuses the teacher of tricking you. Say sensei no kotoba ni hagemasarete.

bad.s: 「雨[あめ]だったので、駅[えき]まで友達[ともだち]の{口車[くちぐるま]に乗[の]った}。」
bad.en: (meant: it was raining, so I got a lift to the station in my friend's car)
bad.why: Kuchiguruma is not a car. For getting a lift, say tomodachi no kuruma ni nosete moratta.

cards.mean: to be the first to speak or act
cards.lit: to light the kuchibi, the small priming flame that sets off a gun or a charge

use.how: The subject is whoever starts a discussion, criticism or chain of events: 私が口火を切った, 値下げ競争の口火を切る.

cards.cue: At a tense meeting no one wants to speak first. Finally you raise your hand and say what everyone is thinking, and the discussion begins.

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]で誰[だれ]も話[はな]さないので、私[わたし]が{口火[くちび]を切[き]った}。
ctx.en: Nobody was speaking at the meeting, so I got the ball rolling.

ctx.s: 「じゃあ、僕[ぼく]から{口火[くちび]を切[き]ります}ね。」
ctx.en: "Well then, I'll start us off."

ctx.s: 誰[だれ]が{口火[くちび]を切[き]る}か、皆[みな]が互[たが]いの顔[かお]をうかがっていた。
ctx.en: Everyone was glancing at each other, waiting to see who would speak first.

ctx.s: 討論会[とうろんかい]は、反対派[はんたいは]の代表[だいひょう]が{口火[くちび]を切[き]る}形[かたち]で始[はじ]まった。
ctx.en: The debate opened with the opposition's representative speaking first.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]が{口火[くちび]を切[き]る}と、ほかの社員[しゃいん]も次々[つぎつぎ]に不満[ふまん]を口[くち]にし始[はじ]めた。
ctx.en: Once she spoke up, the other employees began voicing their complaints one after another.

ctx.s: 今回[こんかい]の値下[ねさ]げ競争[きょうそう]の{口火[くちび]を切[き]った}のは、大手[おおて]スーパーだった。
ctx.en: It was a major supermarket chain that started this latest price war.

bad.s: 「時間[じかん]になったので、ここで話[はな]し合[あ]いの{口火[くちび]を切[き]ります}。」
bad.en: (meant: time is up, so I'll cut the discussion off here)
bad.why: Kiru here means lighting the fuse, so the phrase starts things. To end a discussion, say koko de uchikirimasu.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は怒[おこ]って、友達[ともだち]に{口火[くちび]を切[き]った}。
bad.en: (meant: he got angry and lashed out at his friend)
bad.why: It is not 'spitting fire' at someone. It means being the first to begin, and it takes no target marked with ni.

cards.mean: not nearly as good as one boasted
cards.lit: not even as much as one's mouth: the deeds fall short of the words

use.how: A mocking verdict on someone who talked big and then failed: 口ほどにもないやつだ, 口ほどにもなかった. Rude if said to someone's face.

near.diff: 見かけ倒し is falling short of how something looks; 口ほどにもない is falling short of what someone boasted.

cards.cue: Your cousin bragged all week that he was unbeatable at chess, then lost to your ten-year-old sister in five minutes. What do you say?

ctx.s: 「強[つよ]いって自慢[じまん]してたのに、{口[くち]ほどにもない}な。」
ctx.en: "You kept bragging about how strong you were, but you're nothing special."

ctx.s: 「料理[りょうり]が得意[とくい]だって言[い]ってたけど、{口[くち]ほどにもなかった}ね。」
ctx.en: "You said you were a great cook, but it wasn't all that, was it?"

ctx.s: ゲームでは無敵[むてき]だと豪語[ごうご]していた兄[あに]は、妹[いもうと]にあっさり負[ま]けた。{口[くち]ほどにもない}とはこのことだ。
ctx.en: My brother, who boasted he was unbeatable at the game, lost easily to our little sister. All talk, if ever I saw it.

ctx.s: 試合前[しあいまえ]にさんざん挑発[ちょうはつ]してきた相手[あいて]は、まったく{口[くち]ほどにもなかった}。
ctx.en: The opponent who taunted us so much before the match was nowhere near as good as his talk.

ctx.s: 大口[おおぐち]をたたいていた新人[しんじん]は、初[はじ]めての営業[えいぎょう]で一件[いっけん]も契約[けいやく]が取[と]れず、{口[くち]ほどにもなかった}。
ctx.en: The new hire who talked so big didn't land a single contract on his first sales round; he was all talk.

ctx.s: {口[くち]ほどにもない}と言[い]われたくないので、本番[ほんばん]まで必死[ひっし]に練習[れんしゅう]した。
ctx.en: I didn't want people to say I was all talk, so I practised like mad until the day of the performance.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は何[なに]も自慢[じまん]しない人[ひと]だが、実力[じつりょく]は{口[くち]ほどにもない}。
bad.en: (meant: he never boasts, and his skills are poor)
bad.why: The phrase needs earlier boasting to fall short of. For someone who never boasts, just say jitsuryoku wa amari nai.

bad.s: 「下手[へた]だって言[い]ってたのに、ピアノ上手[じょうず]だね。{口[くち]ほどにもない}よ。」
bad.en: (meant: you said you were bad, but you play the piano well)
bad.why: It only means worse than claimed, and it is a put-down. For better than claimed, say omotta yori jouzu da ne.

cards.mean: to be vain about something and flaunt it
cards.lit: to hang something on one's nose, where the nose, as in many idioms, stands for pride

use.how: Xを鼻にかける, where X is an advantage: looks, money, a degree, a famous parent. Criticises someone else; people rarely say it of themselves.

near.diff: 鼻が高い is feeling proud, often with good reason (of a child, of one's work); 鼻にかける is flaunting an advantage in a way others dislike.

cards.cue: A classmate from a rich family keeps mentioning his father's company and his imported car, and talks down to everyone. Describe him.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は頭[あたま]がいいことを{鼻[はな]にかけて}いる。
ctx.en: He's full of himself about being clever.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]、東大出[とうだいで]を{鼻[はな]にかける}から苦手[にがて]なんだ。」
ctx.en: "That guy is always flaunting his Tokyo University degree, so I can't stand him."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は少[すこ]し英語[えいご]が話[はな]せるのを{鼻[はな]にかけて}、いつも人[ひと]の発音[はつおん]を直[なお]す。
ctx.en: He can speak a bit of English and shows off about it, always correcting other people's pronunciation.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の息子[むすこ]であることを{鼻[はな]にかけた}態度[たいど]に、社員[しゃいん]はうんざりしていた。
ctx.en: The staff were fed up with the way he flaunted being the president's son.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は若[わか]い頃[ころ]、有名[ゆうめい]な歌手[かしゅ]だったが、それを少[すこ]しも{鼻[はな]にかけなかった}。
ctx.en: My grandmother was a famous singer when she was young, but she never once made anything of it.

ctx.s: 「経験[けいけん]を{鼻[はな]にかけて}後輩[こうはい]を見下[みくだ]すのはやめてください。」
ctx.en: "Please stop lording your experience over the junior staff."

bad.s: 息子[むすこ]が大学[だいがく]に合格[ごうかく]して、私[わたし]は{鼻[はな]にかけて}います。
bad.en: (meant: my son got into university and I am very proud)
bad.why: Hana ni kakeru criticises showing off and needs an object. For honest pride in your child, say hana ga takai.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は風邪[かぜ]で{鼻[はな]にかけた}声[こえ]をしている。
bad.en: (meant: she has a nasal voice because of her cold)
bad.why: A nasal voice is hana ni kakatta koe, with intransitive kakaru. Hana ni kakeru is only about flaunting an advantage.

cards.mean: (of affectation) to become tiresome and off-putting
cards.lit: to stick in the nose, like a smell that will not go away

use.how: The subject is someone's manner, way of talking or attitude: 彼の自慢話が鼻につく. Said of what grates more with repetition; also of a cloying smell.

near.diff: 鼻にかける describes the show-off's own behaviour; 鼻につく is the onlooker's irritation at it: 彼が学歴を鼻にかけるのが鼻につく.

cards.cue: Your new coworker is pleasant enough, but the way she keeps dropping the names of famous people she knows is starting to grate on you.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の自慢話[じまんばなし]が{鼻[はな]につく}。
ctx.en: His bragging gets on my nerves.

ctx.s: 「あの店員[てんいん]、丁寧[ていねい]すぎて逆[ぎゃく]に{鼻[はな]につかない}？」
ctx.en: "Doesn't that shop assistant's over-politeness actually rub you the wrong way?"

ctx.s: 最初[さいしょ]は面白[おもしろ]かったが、同[おな]じ冗談[じょうだん]を何度[なんど]も聞[き]くうちに{鼻[はな]につく}ようになった。
ctx.en: It was funny at first, but after hearing the same joke again and again it started to grate.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]のきざな話[はな]し方[かた]が、どうも{鼻[はな]について}仕方[しかた]がない。
ctx.en: Her affected way of talking really gets on my nerves.

ctx.s: この小説[しょうせつ]は文章[ぶんしょう]はうまいが、作者[さくしゃ]の教養[きょうよう]を見[み]せつける書[か]き方[かた]が{鼻[はな]につく}。
ctx.en: The novel is well written, but the way the author shows off his learning is off-putting.

ctx.s: 香水[こうすい]をつけすぎると、甘[あま]い香[かお]りがかえって{鼻[はな]につく}。
ctx.en: If you put on too much perfume, the sweet scent becomes cloying instead.

bad.s: 焼[や]きたてのパンのいい匂[にお]いが{鼻[はな]について}、幸[しあわ]せな気分[きぶん]になった。
bad.en: (meant: the lovely smell of fresh bread reached me and made me happy)
