bad.s: 突然[とつぜん]殴[なぐ]られて、{鼻[はな]についた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was suddenly hit and got angry)
bad.why: Hana ni tsuku is a slow irritation at someone's manner, and that manner is its subject. For sudden anger, say hara ga tatsu or atama ni kuru.

cards.mean: to outdo someone who looked down on one
cards.lit: to lay open someone's nose; the nose stands for the pride you catch off guard

use.how: 相手の鼻を明かす, often as 鼻を明かしてやる (I'll show them). Said of beating a rival, or someone who underestimated you, by surprise.

near.diff: 見返す is proving people who looked down on you wrong by succeeding over time; 鼻を明かす is getting the better of them, usually in one surprising stroke.

cards.cue: Your older brother always says you'll never beat him at chess. Tonight, after months of secret practice, you checkmate him in twenty moves.

ctx.s: いつか兄[あに]の{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かして}やりたい。
ctx.en: Someday I want to get one over on my big brother.

ctx.s: 「無理[むり]だと笑[わら]った連中[れんちゅう]の{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かして}やろうぜ。」
ctx.en: "Let's show the guys who laughed and said we couldn't do it."

ctx.s: 弱小[じゃくしょう]チームが優勝候補[ゆうしょうこうほ]を破[やぶ]り、評論家[ひょうろんか]たちの{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かした}。
ctx.en: The underdogs beat the favourites and made the pundits look foolish.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は誰[だれ]にも言[い]わずに勉強[べんきょう]を続[つづ]け、合格[ごうかく]してみんなの{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かした}。
ctx.en: He kept studying without telling anyone, passed, and proved everyone wrong.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の企画[きかく]が採用[さいよう]され、ベテランたちは{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かされた}形[かたち]になった。
ctx.en: The rookie's proposal was accepted, and the veterans were effectively shown up.

ctx.s: 「どうやってライバル社[しゃ]の{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かす}か、それが問題[もんだい]だ。」
ctx.en: "How do we get the better of our rival company? That's the question."

bad.s: お世話[せわ]になった先生[せんせい]の{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かして}、感謝[かんしゃ]の気持[きも]ちを伝[つた]えた。
bad.en: (meant: I impressed the teacher who had helped me, to show my gratitude)
bad.why: Hana wo akasu is getting the better of a rival or someone who underestimated you, not a respectful way to impress someone you owe.

bad.s: 試合[しあい]でライバルに{鼻[はな]を明[あ]かした}。
bad.en: (meant: my rival got the better of me in the match)
bad.why: The winner is the subject and the loser's nose the object: raibaru no hana wo akashita. Being outdone yourself is raibaru ni hana wo akasareta.

cards.mean: levelling off, having hit a ceiling
cards.lit: head-hitting: something rising until it bumps its head on the ceiling

use.how: A noun: 頭打ちになる, 頭打ちだ, 頭打ちの状態. Said of figures, growth, prices, pay or a record that has stopped rising.

near.diff: 伸び悩む is growth that is slow and disappointing; 頭打ち says it has reached a limit and stopped rising altogether.

cards.cue: Sales of your app doubled every year until last spring; since then, month after month, the number has stayed exactly where it is.

ctx.s: 最近[さいきん]、売[う]り上[あ]げが{頭打[あたまう]ち}だ。
ctx.en: Sales have levelled off lately.

ctx.s: 「給料[きゅうりょう]はもう{頭打[あたまう]ち}だから、転職[てんしょく]を考[かんが]えている。」
ctx.en: "My salary has hit its ceiling, so I'm thinking of changing jobs."

ctx.s: 練習量[れんしゅうりょう]を増[ふ]やしても、記録[きろく]は{頭打[あたまう]ち}になってしまった。
ctx.en: Even with more training, my times have stopped improving.

ctx.s: 「成績[せいせき]が{頭打[あたまう]ち}なのは、勉強[べんきょう]の仕方[しかた]に問題[もんだい]があるからかもしれないよ。」
ctx.en: "Maybe your grades have stalled because there's something wrong with the way you study."

ctx.s: スマートフォンの国内市場[こくないしじょう]は、{頭打[あたまう]ち}の状態[じょうたい]が続[つづ]いている。
ctx.en: The domestic smartphone market has stayed flat for some time.

ctx.s: 人口[じんこう]が減[へ]る中[なか]、国内[こくない]の旅行者数[りょこうしゃすう]もいずれ{頭打[あたまう]ち}になるとの見方[みかた]がある。
ctx.en: With the population shrinking, some expect the number of domestic travellers to plateau eventually.

bad.s: ドアに{頭打[あたまう]ち}して、すごく痛[いた]かった。
bad.en: (meant: I hit my head on the door and it really hurt)
bad.why: Atamauchi is only figurative, for figures that stop rising. Bumping your head is atama wo butsukeru.

bad.s: 不景気[ふけいき]で、売[う]り上[あ]げが一気[いっき]に半分[はんぶん]まで{頭打[あたまう]ち}になった。
bad.en: (meant: in the recession, sales suddenly halved)
bad.why: Atamauchi means rising figures stop at a ceiling, not that they fall. For a drop, say ochikonda or hangen shita.

cards.mean: to show one's talent and rise above others
cards.lit: to show the top of one's head above the crowd

story.text: The phrase goes back to the epitaph the Tang writer Han Yu composed for his friend Liu Zongyuan. Han Yu wrote that Liu, though still young, passed the imperial examination and 'stood out sharply, showing the top of his head', so that people said the Liu family had produced a fine son.

use.how: Xが頭角を現す, often with めきめき(と) or 次第に. Said of a person, or a team, rising out of a group of peers: 新人がめきめき頭角を現した.

near.diff: 肩を並べる is reaching the level of those at the top; 頭角を現す is the moment of standing out from one's peers on the way up.

cards.cue: A quiet junior engineer who joined two years ago has started producing the best designs in the department, and the managers are beginning to notice her.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は高校時代[こうこうじだい]から{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]して}いた。
ctx.en: He was already standing out in high school.

ctx.s: 「あの若手[わかて]、最近[さいきん]{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]して}きたね。」
ctx.en: "That young guy has really started to shine lately, hasn't he?"

ctx.s: 入社[にゅうしゃ]三年目[さんねんめ]で、彼女[かのじょ]はめきめきと{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]した}。
ctx.en: In her third year at the company, she quickly made her mark.

ctx.s: 無名[むめい]の新人作家[しんじんさっか]が、デビュー作[さく]で一気[いっき]に{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]した}。
ctx.en: An unknown new writer made a name for herself at a stroke with her debut.

ctx.s: この棋士[きし]は十代[じゅうだい]で{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]し}、二十歳[はたち]でタイトルを取[と]った。
ctx.en: This shogi player made his mark in his teens and won a title at twenty.

ctx.s: どの分野[ぶんや]でも、{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]す}人[ひと]は人一倍[ひといちばい]努力[どりょく]している。
ctx.en: In any field, the people who rise above the rest work harder than anyone else.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は怒[おこ]ると{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]す}ので怖[こわ]い。
bad.en: (meant: my father is scary because he shows his horns when he gets angry)
bad.why: The kaku here is not a demon's horn. Tokaku wo arawasu praises rising talent; for showing a fierce side, say honsho wo arawasu.

bad.s: 雲[くも]が晴[は]れて、富士山[ふじさん]が{頭角[とうかく]を現[あらわ]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the clouds cleared and the peak of Mount Fuji appeared)
bad.why: It is said of people whose ability stands out, not of things coming into view. Say Fujisan ga sugata wo arawashita.

cards.mean: flatly, without hearing the other side out
cards.lit: from over someone's head, pressing down on them from above

use.how: Adverb before verbs of scolding or rejecting: 頭ごなしに叱る, 否定する, 決めつける. Usually of a parent, teacher or boss towards someone below them.

near.diff: 頭から (頭から疑う) is 'from the outset, without question'; 頭ごなしに adds the overbearing, top-down manner of someone scolding or overruling.

cards.cue: Your teenager tries to explain why they came home late, but before they can finish a sentence you start shouting. Later you regret the way you scolded.

ctx.s: 父[ちち]はいつも{頭[あたま]ごなしに}怒[おこ]る。
ctx.en: My father always yells at us without listening.

ctx.s: 「話[はなし]も聞[き]かずに{頭[あたま]ごなしに}否定[ひてい]しないでよ。」
ctx.en: "Don't just shoot it down without even hearing me out."

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]は、僕[ぼく]が犯人[はんにん]だと{頭[あたま]ごなしに}決[き]めつけた。
ctx.en: The teacher decided I was the culprit without listening to my side.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもを{頭[あたま]ごなしに}叱[しか]ると、本当[ほんとう]の理由[りゆう]を話[はな]してくれなくなる。
ctx.en: If you scold children without hearing them out, they stop telling you the real reason.

ctx.s: 部下[ぶか]の意見[いけん]を{頭[あたま]ごなしに}退[しりぞ]ける上司[じょうし]は、信頼[しんらい]されない。
ctx.en: A boss who dismisses their staff's views out of hand will not be trusted.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいアイデアを{頭[あたま]ごなしに}批判[ひはん]するのではなく、まず試[ため]してみよう。
ctx.en: Rather than flatly criticising new ideas, let's try them out first.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]は僕[ぼく]の作文[さくぶん]を{頭[あたま]ごなしに}褒[ほ]めてくれた。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher praised my essay wholeheartedly)

bad.s: 間違[まちが]いが多[おお]かったので、教科書[きょうかしょ]を{頭[あたま]ごなしに}読[よ]み直[なお]した。
bad.en: (meant: I'd made a lot of mistakes, so I reread the textbook from the beginning)
bad.why: 'From the beginning' is saisho kara or atama kara. Atamagonashi ni is about the manner of scolding or dismissing a person.

cards.mean: looking unconcerned as if nothing happened
cards.lit: a cool face: no sweat and no flush, as if nothing were going on

use.how: 涼しい顔をする, 涼しい顔で〜. Mostly of someone unbothered when they should be worried or are to blame; also of doing something hard with ease.

near.diff: 知らん顔 is pretending not to know or ignoring someone; 涼しい顔 is looking calm and untroubled, whether from nerve or from ease.

cards.cue: Your colleague missed the deadline that made the whole team work all weekend, and on Monday he strolls in sipping coffee, completely unbothered.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は遅刻[ちこく]しても{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}をしている。
ctx.en: Even when he's late, he looks completely unbothered.

ctx.s: 「みんなが困[こま]ってるのに、よく{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}でいられるね。」
ctx.en: "Everyone's in trouble, and you can just stand there looking like nothing's wrong?"

ctx.s: 自分[じぶん]のミスなのに、彼女[かのじょ]は{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}で人[ひと]のせいにした。
ctx.en: It was her own mistake, yet she calmly blamed someone else.

ctx.s: マラソンを走[はし]り終[お]えた彼[かれ]は、{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}で「まだ走[はし]れる」と言[い]った。
ctx.en: Having just finished the marathon, he said, without a hint of strain, "I could keep going."

ctx.s: 記者[きしゃ]に厳[きび]しく質問[しつもん]されても、監督[かんとく]は{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}を崩[くず]さなかった。
ctx.en: Even under tough questioning from reporters, the manager kept his unruffled look.

ctx.s: みんなが悩[なや]んだ難問[なんもん]を、その少年[しょうねん]は{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}で解[と]いてしまった。
ctx.en: The problem everyone had struggled with, the boy solved without breaking a sweat.

bad.s: 冷[つめ]たいシャワーを浴[あ]びて、{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}になった。
bad.en: (meant: I took a cold shower and my face felt cool)
bad.why: The phrase is about looking unconcerned, not physical coolness. Say sappari shita or suzushiku natta.

bad.s: 心配[しんぱい]していた検査[けんさ]の結果[けっか]が良[よ]くて、母[はは]は{涼[すず]しい顔[かお]}になった。
bad.en: (meant: the test result she had worried about was fine, and my mother looked relieved)
bad.why: Relief after worry is hotto shita kao. Suzushii kao is looking untroubled while there is still something to be troubled about.

cards.mean: to be drowning in debt
cards.lit: one's neck will not turn: so weighed down one cannot even turn one's head

use.how: Predicate, typically 借金で首が回らない. Said of a person, household or business swamped by debts or payments, not of being busy.

near.diff: 手が回らない is being too busy to attend to something; 首が回らない is being weighed down by debts.

cards.cue: Your friend took out loans for a car, a flat and a restaurant that failed, and now can't keep up with the repayments on any of them.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は借金[しゃっきん]で{首[くび]が回[まわ]らない}。
ctx.en: He's up to his neck in debt.

ctx.s: 「カードを使[つか]いすぎて、今月[こんげつ]は{首[くび]が回[まわ]らない}よ。」
ctx.en: "I went overboard on my card, and this month I'm drowning in bills."

ctx.s: 店[みせ]は赤字[あかじ]続[つづ]きで、とうとう{首[くび]が回[まわ]らなく}なった。
ctx.en: After losing money month after month, the shop was finally swamped with debt.

ctx.s: ギャンブルで{首[くび]が回[まわ]らなく}なる前[まえ]に、やめたほうがいい。
ctx.en: You'd better quit gambling before you're buried in debt.

ctx.s: 住宅[じゅうたく]ローンと教育費[きょういくひ]で、我[わ]が家[や]は{首[くび]が回[まわ]らない}状態[じょうたい]だ。
ctx.en: Between the mortgage and the school fees, our household can barely keep its head above water.

ctx.s: 事業[じぎょう]に失敗[しっぱい]して{首[くび]が回[まわ]らなかった}頃[ころ]、助[たす]けてくれたのは古[ふる]い友人[ゆうじん]だった。
ctx.en: When my business failed and I was drowning in debt, it was an old friend who helped me out.

bad.s: 仕事[しごと]が忙[いそが]しくて、掃除[そうじ]まで{首[くび]が回[まわ]らない}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm so busy at work that I can't get round to cleaning)
bad.why: Being too busy to deal with something is te ga mawaranai. Kubi ga mawaranai is about debt.

bad.s: 「僕[ぼく]、昨日[きのう]会社[かいしゃ]で{首[くび]が回[まわ]らなかった}んだ。」
bad.en: (meant: I got fired at work yesterday)
bad.why: Being fired is kubi ni naru. Kubi ga mawaranai is about being swamped by debts, not about losing a job.

cards.mean: to rank alongside, to be on a par with
cards.lit: to stand or walk shoulder to shoulder

use.how: AがBと肩を並べる: A reaches the level of B, usually someone or something strong. Also literal: 肩を並べて歩く, to walk side by side.

near.diff: 頭角を現す is standing out from one's peers; 肩を並べる is reaching the same level as a particular strong rival or leader.

cards.cue: Ten years ago your town's tiny sake brewery was unknown; now its sake wins the same prizes as the country's most famous makers.

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]は{肩[かた]を並[なら]べて}駅[えき]まで歩[ある]いた。
ctx.en: The two of them walked side by side to the station.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の腕前[うでまえ]は、もうプロと{肩[かた]を並[なら]べる}ほどだ。
ctx.en: His skill is now on a par with the professionals.

ctx.s: 「いつか先輩[せんぱい]と{肩[かた]を並[なら]べて}仕事[しごと]ができるようになりたいです。」
ctx.en: "Someday I want to be good enough to work alongside you as an equal."

ctx.s: 町[まち]の小[ちい]さな工場[こうじょう]が、今[いま]では大企業[だいきぎょう]と{肩[かた]を並[なら]べる}存在[そんざい]になった。
ctx.en: A small local factory has now become a match for the big corporations.

ctx.s: この大学[だいがく]は、研究[けんきゅう]の分野[ぶんや]で世界[せかい]の名門校[めいもんこう]と{肩[かた]を並[なら]べて}いる。
ctx.en: In research, this university ranks alongside the world's elite schools.

ctx.s: 日本[にほん]の選手[せんしゅ]が世界[せかい]の強豪[きょうごう]と{肩[かた]を並[なら]べる}日[ひ]は来[く]るだろうか。
ctx.en: Will the day come when Japanese players stand level with the world's best?

bad.s: 決勝[けっしょう]でライバルと{肩[かた]を並[なら]べ}、大差[たいさ]で勝[か]った。
bad.en: (meant: in the final I beat my rival by a wide margin)
bad.why: Kata wo naraberu means being equal, so it cannot describe winning by a wide margin. Say raibaru wo yabutta.

bad.s: 兄弟喧嘩[きょうだいげんか]になると、母[はは]はいつも弟[おとうと]と{肩[かた]を並[なら]べる}。
bad.en: (meant: whenever we brothers fight, Mum always takes my younger brother's side)
bad.why: Taking someone's side is kata wo motsu. Kata wo naraberu is about equal rank or walking side by side.

cards.mean: to relax and stop trying so hard
cards.lit: to let the tension go out of one's shoulders

use.how: Often as advice: 肩の力を抜いて (relax, don't try so hard). Said of someone stiff with nerves or over-effort; 肩の力が抜ける is the intransitive.

near.diff: 気を抜く is letting your attention slip, usually a fault; 肩の力を抜く is a good thing: dropping needless tension while still doing the work.

cards.cue: Before her first big presentation, your colleague has rewritten her slides five times and is pale with nerves. You give her some advice.

ctx.en: "It doesn't have to be perfect. Ease up a bit."

ctx.s: 本番[ほんばん]で{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いたら}、かえっていい演奏[えんそう]ができた。

ctx.en: With bringing up children, it's best to relax and enjoy it.

ctx.s: 一人暮[ひとりぐ]らしを始[はじ]めた頃[ころ]は頑張[がんば]りすぎていたが、最近[さいきん]は{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]ける}ようになった。

bad.en: (meant: he lost the match and his shoulders slumped in disappointment)

bad.s: 面倒[めんどう]だったので、宿題[しゅくだい]は{肩[かた]の力[ちから]を抜[ぬ]いて}適当[てきとう]に済[す]ませた。
bad.en: (meant: it was a chore, so I cut corners and did my homework any old way)
bad.why: Doing sloppy work on purpose is te wo nuku. Kata no chikara wo nuku means dropping needless tension, not doing less.

cards.mean: to feel heartache for someone's suffering
cards.lit: one's chest aches: sorrow or pity felt as a pain in the chest

use.how: Intransitive predicate for the feeler: ニュースを見て胸が痛んだ, often after と or を見ると. Also before a noun: 胸が痛む話. Said of others' suffering, or of regret for hurting someone.

near.diff: 胸が熱くなる is being moved by something good or touching; 胸が痛む is pain at suffering or sad news.

ctx.s: 仕事[しごと]で疲[つか]れた母[はは]が無理[むり]に笑[わら]っているのを見[み]ると、{胸[むね]が痛[いた]む}。
ctx.en: It hurts to see my mother, worn out from work, forcing herself to smile.

ctx.s: 戦争[せんそう]で苦[くる]しむ人々[ひとびと]のことを思[おも]うと、{胸[むね]の痛[いた]む}思[おも]いがする。
ctx.en: When I think of the people suffering in the war, I feel real anguish.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]は「社員[しゃいん]を減[へ]らすのは{胸[むね]が痛[いた]む}決断[けつだん]だった」と語[かた]った。
ctx.en: The president said that cutting staff had been a painful decision.

bad.en: (meant: I was so happy at the news that I passed that I was overcome)
bad.why: It is pain at something sad. For joy or being moved, say mune ga ippai ni natta or mune ga atsuku natta.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]のつらい話[はなし]が私[わたし]の{胸[むね]を痛[いた]んだ}。
bad.en: (meant: his sad story pained me)

cards.mean: (of a story or act) to touch the heart
cards.lit: to strike the chest: a sincere word or deed hits you where your feelings are

use.how: The subject is the thing that moves: 彼のスピーチが人々の胸を打った. The person moved uses the passive: 手紙に胸を打たれた. Also before a noun: 胸を打つ物語.

near.diff: 胸が熱くなる describes the feeling welling up in you; 胸を打つ describes the story, words or act that causes it.

cards.cue: An injured runner limps to the finish line long after everyone else, and the crowd falls silent, deeply moved. Describe what her effort did.

ctx.en: Her speech moved a great many people.

ctx.s: 「この映画[えいが]、最後[さいご]の場面[ばめん]が{胸[むね]を打[う]つ}んだよ。」
ctx.en: "The last scene of this film really gets to you."

ctx.s: 怪我[けが]を抱[かか]えながら最後[さいご]まで走[はし]った選手[せんしゅ]の姿[すがた]は、観客[かんきゃく]の{胸[むね]を打[う]った}。
ctx.en: The sight of the athlete running to the end despite her injury moved the spectators.

ctx.s: 飾[かざ]らない言葉[ことば]だからこそ、{胸[むね]を打[う]つ}ものがある。
ctx.en: It is precisely because the words are plain that there is something moving about them.

ctx.s: 家族[かぞく]の再生[さいせい]を描[えが]いたこの小説[しょうせつ]は、世代[せだい]を超[こ]えて読者[どくしゃ]の{胸[むね]を打[う]って}きた。

bad.en: (meant: I was moved by that film)
bad.why: The thing that moves you is the subject. With yourself as subject, use the passive: sono eiga ni mune wo utareta.

bad.en: (meant: his joke was so funny I loved it)

cards.mean: to thrill with anticipation
cards.lit: one's chest dances: the heart jumps with excitement

use.how: Predicate for the feeler, often after と思うと, or before a noun: 胸が躍る展開. Always pleasant excitement about something new or coming. Transitive form: 胸を躍らせる.

near.diff: 胸をなで下ろす is relief after a worry is gone; 胸が躍る is excitement about something good still ahead.

cards.cue: It's the night before your first trip abroad, and you're too excited to sleep, imagining everything you'll see.

ctx.s: 明日[あした]から初[はじ]めての海外[かいがい]旅行[りょこう]だと思[おも]うと、{胸[むね]が躍[おど]る}。
ctx.en: When I think that my first trip abroad starts tomorrow, my heart leaps.

ctx.s: 好[す]きな作家[さっか]の新作[しんさく]が出[で]ると聞[き]いて、{胸[むね]が躍[おど]った}。
ctx.en: I was thrilled to hear that my favourite author has a new book coming out.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい生活[せいかつ]が始[はじ]まる春[はる]は、いつも{胸[むね]が躍[おど]る}季節[きせつ]だ。
ctx.en: Spring, when new lives begin, is always an exciting season.

ctx.s: 「次[つぎ]はどんな冒険[ぼうけん]が待[ま]っているんだろう」と、少年[しょうねん]は{胸[むね]を躍[おど]らせた}。
ctx.en: "I wonder what adventure is waiting next," the boy thought, his heart racing with excitement.

ctx.s: {胸[むね]が躍[おど]る}ような展開[てんかい]の連続[れんぞく]で、一気[いっき]に読[よ]んでしまった。
ctx.en: It was one thrilling twist after another, and I read it in one sitting.

ctx.s: 初[はじ]めての舞台[ぶたい]を前[まえ]に、不安[ふあん]よりも{胸[むね]の躍[おど]る}思[おも]いのほうが強[つよ]かった。
ctx.en: Before my first time on stage, excitement was stronger than nerves.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]に落[お]ちるかもしれないと思[おも]うと、{胸[むね]が躍[おど]る}。
bad.en: (meant: my heart pounds with anxiety when I think I might fail)
bad.why: It is only happy excitement. For a heart pounding with worry, say mune ga dokidoki suru or fuan ni naru.

bad.s: 仕事[しごと]が無事[ぶじ]に終[お]わって、{胸[むね]が躍[おど]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was relieved the job ended without trouble)
bad.why: Relief after a worry is hotto shita or mune wo nadeoroshita. Mune ga odoru looks forward to something exciting.

cards.mean: to sound out someone's real intentions
cards.lit: to feel around in someone's belly, where the real thoughts are kept

use.how: Transitive: 相手の腹を探る, usually by indirect questions or small talk. Noun: 腹の探り合い. Passive 痛くもない腹を探られる is being suspected for nothing.

near.diff: 腹を割って話す is talking openly and honestly; 腹を探る is quietly trying to find out what the other person really thinks.

cards.cue: Over lunch, a rival company's manager keeps asking casual questions, trying to find out whether your firm plans to bid on the same contract.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は世間話[せけんばなし]をしながら、こちらの{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]って}いるようだった。
ctx.en: While making small talk, he seemed to be trying to work out what we were really after.

ctx.s: 「急[きゅう]に食事[しょくじ]に誘[さそ]うなんて、もしかして私[わたし]の{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]ろう}としてる？」
ctx.en: "Inviting me to dinner out of nowhere... are you trying to find out what I'm thinking?"

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]の前[まえ]に、先方[せんぽう]の{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]って}おく必要[ひつよう]がある。
ctx.en: Before the meeting, we need to sound out what the other side really wants.

ctx.s: 両社[りょうしゃ]の交渉[こうしょう]は、{腹[はら]の探[さぐ]り合[あ]い}が続[つづ]いて少[すこ]しも進[すす]まなかった。
ctx.en: The talks between the two companies went nowhere, with each side just trying to read the other.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は遠回[とおまわ]しな質問[しつもん]をして、私[わたし]の{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]ろう}とした。
ctx.en: My mother asked roundabout questions, trying to find out what I was really thinking.

ctx.s: 何[なに]もしていないのに痛[いた]くもない{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]られて}、本当[ほんとう]に不愉快[ふゆかい]だ。
ctx.en: I haven't done anything, yet I'm being treated with suspicion. It's really unpleasant.

bad.s: 体調[たいちょう]が悪[わる]いので、医者[いしゃ]に{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]って}もらった。
bad.en: (meant: I felt ill, so I had the doctor examine my stomach)
bad.why: The idiom is only about hidden intentions. For a medical check, say onaka wo mite moratta.

bad.s: 「部長[ぶちょう]、私[わたし]の{腹[はら]を探[さぐ]って}ください。本音[ほんね]を話[はな]します。」
bad.en: (meant: please hear me out, I'll tell you what I really think)
bad.why: Probing is covert and done to someone, not invited. To offer an honest talk, say hara wo watte hanashimashou.

cards.r: はらわたがにえくりかえる
cards.mean: to seethe with rage inside
cards.lit: one's guts boil and churn over: anger so strong it seems to cook the insides

use.how: Predicate for the angry person, often as 腸が煮えくり返る思い/ような怒り. For deep fury at an injustice, often held in rather than shown.

near.diff: 頭に来る is everyday, sudden anger, often at small things; 腸が煮えくり返る is far stronger, seething fury at a real wrong.

cards.cue: Your boss presents your project as his own work at the board meeting. You smile politely, but inside you are furious.

ctx.s: 十年[じゅうねん]も信[しん]じてきた親友[しんゆう]に裏切[うらぎ]られたと知[し]り、{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]った}。
ctx.en: When I learned that the friend I had trusted for ten years had betrayed me, I was seething.

ctx.s: 「あいつのせいで店[みせ]を失[うしな]ったんだ。今[いま]思[おも]い出[だ]しても{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]る}よ。」
ctx.en: "I lost my shop because of him. Even now, thinking about it makes my blood boil."

ctx.s: 手柄[てがら]を上司[じょうし]に横取[よこど]りされ、{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]る}思[おも]いだった。
ctx.en: My boss stole the credit for my work, and I was boiling with rage.

ctx.s: 顔[かお]では笑[わら]っていたが、内心[ないしん]は{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]って}いた。
ctx.en: He was smiling on the outside, but inside he was seething.

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]に反省[はんせい]の様子[ようす]がないと聞[き]き、遺族[いぞく]は{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]る}ような怒[いか]りを感[かん]じた。
ctx.en: Hearing that the culprit showed no remorse, the victim's family felt a burning rage.

ctx.s: 動物[どうぶつ]を虐待[ぎゃくたい]する動画[どうが]を見[み]て、{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]る}ほどの怒[いか]りを覚[おぼ]えた。
ctx.en: Watching a video of someone abusing an animal, I felt a rage that made my insides boil.

bad.s: 夕食[ゆうしょく]を食[た]べ過[す]ぎて、{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I ate too much at dinner and my stomach was churning)
bad.why: It describes rage, not digestion. For an upset stomach, say onaka no choushi ga warui or i ga mukamuka suru.

bad.s: ちょっと{腸[はらわた]が煮[に]えくり返[かえ]った}けど、すぐに忘[わす]れた。
bad.en: (meant: I was a bit annoyed but soon forgot about it)
bad.why: It means intense, lasting fury, so 'a bit' and 'soon forgot' contradict it. For mild irritation, say chotto iratto shita.

cards.mean: to branch out into new areas of business
cards.lit: to spread one's hands wider: to reach out over a bigger range of things

use.how: Takes に for the new field: 不動産にも手を広げる. Said of companies, shops or professionals; 手を広げすぎる warns of overreaching.

near.diff: 手を出す is trying one new thing, often rashly; 手を広げる is widening the range of an existing business or activity.

cards.cue: A bakery that did well now also runs a café and a catering service, and is planning a cooking school.

ctx.s: 業績[ぎょうせき]が好調[こうちょう]なうちに、海外[かいがい]にも{手[て]を広[ひろ]げる}べきだ。
ctx.en: While business is going well, we should expand overseas as well.

ctx.s: 「{手[て]を広[ひろ]げ}すぎると、本業[ほんぎょう]がおろそかになるよ。」
ctx.en: "If you spread yourself too thin, your core business will suffer."

ctx.s: パン屋[や]として始[はじ]めた店[みせ]が、今[いま]ではカフェ経営[けいえい]にも{手[て]を広[ひろ]げた}。
ctx.en: The shop started as a bakery and has now expanded into running a café as well.

ctx.s: 翻訳[ほんやく]だけでなく、通訳[つうやく]の仕事[しごと]にも{手[て]を広[ひろ]げる}つもりです。
ctx.en: I'm planning to branch out from translation into interpreting work too.

ctx.s: 次々[つぎつぎ]と新[あたら]しい分野[ぶんや]に{手[て]を広[ひろ]げた}結果[けっか]、資金[しきん]繰[ぐ]りが苦[くる]しくなった。
ctx.en: Having moved into one new field after another, the company ran into cash-flow trouble.

ctx.s: 地方[ちほう]の小[ちい]さな酒蔵[さかぐら]が、ネット販売[はんばい]に{手[て]を広[ひろ]げて}全国[ぜんこく]に客[きゃく]を増[ふ]やした。
ctx.en: A small country sake brewery branched out into online sales and won customers all over Japan.

bad.s: 困[こま]っている同僚[どうりょう]に{手[て]を広[ひろ]げた}。
bad.en: (meant: I gave my struggling colleague a hand)
bad.why: Helping someone is te wo kasu or te wo sashinoberu. Te wo hirogeru is about expanding into new fields.

bad.s: 店[みせ]を改装[かいそう]して、売[う]り場[ば]の{手[て]を広[ひろ]げた}。
bad.en: (meant: we renovated and enlarged the sales floor)
bad.why: For physical space, say uriba wo hirogeta. The idiom is about the range of activities, not floor area.

cards.mean: to get mixed up in wrongdoing
cards.lit: to dye one's hands: to dip them into something that leaves a mark

use.how: Takes に for the wrongdoing: 犯罪に手を染める, 不正に手を染める. Marks the start of the involvement; in modern use almost always about crime or dishonesty.

near.diff: 足を洗う is quitting a bad way of life; 手を染める is getting into wrongdoing in the first place.
手を出す is getting into anything, good or bad, often on a whim; 手を染める is only for crime or dishonesty and stresses the moral stain.

cards.cue: A respected accountant, drowning in debt, starts secretly moving company money into his own account.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は借金[しゃっきん]に追[お]われ、ついに犯罪[はんざい]に{手[て]を染[そ]めた}。
ctx.en: Hounded by debt, he finally turned to crime.

ctx.s: 「お金[かね]のためでも、不正[ふせい]に{手[て]を染[そ]める}ことだけはするな。」
ctx.en: "Even for money, never get involved in anything dishonest."

ctx.s: 真面目[まじめ]だった社員[しゃいん]が、なぜ横領[おうりょう]に{手[て]を染[そ]めた}のか。
ctx.en: Why did such a conscientious employee get into embezzlement?

ctx.s: 若[わか]い頃[ころ]に悪事[あくじ]に{手[て]を染[そ]めた}男[おとこ]が、今[いま]は若者[わかもの]の更生[こうせい]を支[ささ]えている。
ctx.en: A man who did wrong in his youth now helps young people get back on track.

ctx.s: 楽[らく]に稼[かせ]げるという誘[さそ]いに乗[の]って、詐欺[さぎ]に{手[て]を染[そ]めて}しまう若者[わかもの]もいる。
ctx.en: Some young people take the bait of easy money and end up involved in fraud.

ctx.s: 「一度[いちど]でも違法[いほう]な取引[とりひき]に{手[て]を染[そ]めたら}、抜[ぬ]け出[だ]すのは難[むずか]しいですか。」
ctx.en: "If you get involved in illegal deals even once, is it hard to get out?"

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は地域[ちいき]のボランティア活動[かつどう]に{手[て]を染[そ]めて}いる。
bad.en: (meant: she is involved in local volunteering)
bad.why: Today it implies wrongdoing, so this sounds like an accusation. For good work, say tazusawatte iru or torikunde iru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は犯罪[はんざい]から{手[て]を染[そ]めて}、真面目[まじめ]に働[はたら]き始[はじ]めた。
bad.en: (meant: he quit crime and started working honestly)
bad.why: Quitting is ashi wo arau (hanzai kara ashi wo arau). Te wo someru is the opposite, starting, and takes ni, not kara.

cards.mean: to break off a shady connection
cards.lit: to cut the hands apart: to sever the grip that joins you to someone

use.how: Takes と for the person or group: 悪い仲間と手を切る. A deliberate break with people or a group you should not be linked to, often with きっぱり.

near.diff: 手を引く is pulling out of a project or deal; 手を切る is cutting ties with people or a group.
足を洗う is quitting a way of life; 手を切る is severing the link with particular people.

cards.cue: Your younger brother keeps getting into trouble because of the gang he hangs around with. You tell him to stop seeing them for good.

ctx.s: 「あんな連中[れんちゅう]とは、早[はや]く{手[て]を切[き]った}ほうがいい。」

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]は問題[もんだい]のある取引先[とりひきさき]と{手[て]を切[き]る}ことを決[き]めた。
ctx.en: The company decided to sever its ties with the problematic supplier.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は悪[わる]い仲間[なかま]ときっぱり{手[て]を切[き]り}、地元[じもと]に戻[もど]った。
ctx.en: He made a clean break with his bad friends and went back to his hometown.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]にあの男[おとこ]と{手[て]を切[き]る}気[き]があるの？」
ctx.en: "Do you really mean to have nothing more to do with that man?"

ctx.en: Having paid off the debt, I was finally able to break free of the loan sharks.

ctx.en: A company that cannot cut its ties with organised crime will lose people's trust sooner or later.

bad.s: 仲[なか]のいい友達[ともだち]が引[ひ]っ越[こ]して、{手[て]を切[き]って}しまった。
bad.en: (meant: my close friend moved away and we lost touch)

bad.en: (meant: we pulled out of the new project because the budget ran short)
bad.why: Withdrawing from a project or deal is te wo hiku. Te wo kiru takes to and a person or group.

cards.mean: to pull strings behind the scenes
cards.lit: to send one's hands around: to reach the result by a back way, out of sight

use.how: Often with 裏で or ～に手を回す for the people approached; 手を回してもらう for a favour. Covert arrangement for a result; can be helpful or shady.

near.diff: 根回し is informally sounding people out before a decision so it goes through smoothly; 手を回す is quietly using connections or influence to bring about a result.

cards.cue: A complaint about the factory never made the papers, and staff suspect someone quietly asked a contact at the newspaper.

ctx.s: 「誰[だれ]かが裏[うら]で{手[て]を回[まわ]した}に違[ちが]いない。」
ctx.en: "Someone must have been pulling strings behind the scenes."

ctx.s: 「チケット、どうやって取[と]ったの？」「知[し]り合[あ]いにちょっと{手[て]を回[まわ]して}もらったんだ。」

ctx.en: My father had a word with a doctor he knows, so I was admitted to hospital right away.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は上層部[じょうそうぶ]に{手[て]を回[まわ]して}、ライバルの企画[きかく]をつぶした。
ctx.en: He worked on the top brass behind the scenes and killed his rival's proposal.

ctx.s: 不祥事[ふしょうじ]が表[おもて]に出[で]ないよう、会社[かいしゃ]はあらゆる方面[ほうめん]に{手[て]を回[まわ]した}。
ctx.en: The company pulled strings everywhere to keep the scandal from coming out.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]が採用[さいよう]されたのは、親[おや]が{手[て]を回[まわ]した}からだという噂[うわさ]だ。

bad.en: (meant: the doctor tried every possible treatment to save the patient)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は会議[かいぎ]の場[ば]で堂々[どうどう]と{手[て]を回[まわ]して}、自分[じぶん]の案[あん]を説明[せつめい]した。
bad.en: (meant: he openly explained his proposal at the meeting)

cards.mean: as clearly as if one held it in one's hand
cards.lit: as if taking it into one's hand: so clear you could almost pick it up and look at it

use.how: Adverb before a verb of perceiving: 手に取るように分かる, 見える, 聞こえる, 伝わる. Said of others' feelings, a situation or a distant scene.

near.diff: 目に浮かぶ is picturing something in your imagination; 手に取るように says something is perceived or understood very clearly.

ctx.s: 壁[かべ]が薄[うす]くて、隣[となり]の部屋[へや]の会話[かいわ]が{手[て]に取[と]るように}聞[き]こえる。
ctx.en: The walls are thin, so I can hear every word of the conversation next door.

ctx.en: "I can read your thoughts like an open book."

ctx.s: 山頂[さんちょう]からは、町[まち]の様子[ようす]が{手[て]に取[と]るように}見[み]えた。
ctx.en: From the summit, we could see the town as clearly as if it were right in front of us.

ctx.s: この本[ほん]を読[よ]むと、江戸[えど]時代[じだい]の人々[ひとびと]の暮[く]らしが{手[て]に取[と]るように}分[わ]かる。
ctx.en: Reading this book, you can see the everyday life of people in the Edo period with great clarity.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]には、相手[あいて]チームの作戦[さくせん]が{手[て]に取[と]るように}読[よ]めていた。
ctx.en: The coach could read the other team's tactics perfectly.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]の古[ふる]い手紙[てがみ]から、当時[とうじ]の不安[ふあん]な気持[きも]ちが{手[て]に取[と]るように}伝[つた]わってくる。
ctx.en: From my grandmother's old letters, her anxiety at the time comes through vividly.

bad.en: (meant: pick this book up and give it a read)
bad.why: Picking something up is te ni totte (te ni totte yonde mite). Te ni toru you ni means 'with great clarity'.

bad.en: (meant: it will certainly be sunny tomorrow)
bad.why: It is not 'certainly'. It only modifies verbs of seeing, hearing or understanding: wakaru, mieru, kikoeru.

cards.mean: to be too preoccupied to get on with anything
cards.lit: it won't stick to the hands: the task keeps slipping out of your grip

use.how: Predicate with the neglected task as subject: 仕事が手につかない. The cause is a worry or excitement on one's mind, usually given in a 〜て clause.

near.diff: 手が離せない means you are too busy with one task to stop; 手につかない means your mind is elsewhere so you cannot do the task at all.

cards.cue: You are waiting for a call about your job interview and keep staring at the same page of your homework. How is your studying going?

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]の結果[けっか]が気[き]になって、勉強[べんきょう]が{手[て]につかない}。
ctx.en: I'm so anxious about my exam results that I can't concentrate on studying.

ctx.en: Every time I remembered my trip starts tomorrow, I couldn't keep my mind on work.

ctx.en: "You haven't got anywhere with it." "I've been waiting for her reply and couldn't settle to anything."

ctx.s: 兄[あに]の手術[しゅじゅつ]が終[お]わるまで、母[はは]は家事[かじ]が{手[て]につかない}様子[ようす]だった。
ctx.en: Until my brother's operation was over, Mum seemed unable to get on with the housework.

ctx.s: 合格[ごうかく]発表[はっぴょう]の前[まえ]の日[ひ]は、誰[だれ]でも何[なに]も{手[て]につかない}ものだ。
ctx.en: On the day before the results are announced, nobody can settle to anything.

ctx.s: 地震[じしん]のニュースが気[き]になって、仕事[しごと]が{手[て]につかない}社員[しゃいん]も多[おお]かった。
ctx.en: Many employees were so worried by the earthquake news that they couldn't focus on their work.

bad.en: (meant: I'm so busy I can't even answer the phone)
bad.why: It is about a distracted mind, not a full schedule. For being too busy to break off, say te ga hanasenai.

bad.en: (meant: he has great focus and always gets absorbed in his work)

story.text: In bugaku, the dance repertoire of Japanese court music, the dance Ama is followed by a piece called Ni-no-mai, 'the second dance'. In it two masked dancers, an old man with a laughing face and an old woman with a swollen one, try to copy the Ama dance and get it comically wrong. From this, performing the second dance came to mean imitating someone else and failing in the same way.

ctx.s: 夫[おっと]が{重[おも]い腰[こし]を上[あ]げる}のを待[ま]っていたら、いつまでも庭[にわ]の手入[てい]れができない。
ctx.en: If I wait for my husband to get round to it, the garden will never get done.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は毎朝[まいあさ]五時[ごじ]に{重[おも]い腰[こし]を上[あ]げて}、ジョギングしている。
bad.en: (meant: he gets up at five every morning and goes jogging)
bad.why: It marks one action finally taken after long delay, not a diligent daily habit.

bad.s: すぐに行動[こうどう]する彼[かれ]は、いつも{重[おも]い腰[こし]を上[あ]げる}のが早[はや]い。
bad.en: (meant: he acts at once and is always quick off the mark)
bad.why: The image presupposes reluctance. For someone quick to act say koshi ga karui or futtowaaku ga karui.

cards.mean: to interrupt someone mid-story and spoil it
cards.lit: to break the waist of a story: snap it in the middle so it can no longer stand up

use.how: Verb phrase with a person (or an interruption) as subject: 人の話の腰を折る. Common as an apology before cutting in: 話の腰を折って悪いけど.

near.diff: 口を挟む is simply cutting into a conversation; 話の腰を折る stresses that the interruption broke the flow of someone's story or explanation.
水を差す dampens a mood or a plan; 話の腰を折る breaks off what someone is in the middle of saying.

cards.cue: Your friend is just reaching the funny part of her travel story when your brother asks what's for dinner, and she loses the thread.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はいつも人[ひと]の{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]る}。
ctx.en: My little brother always cuts in on people's stories.

ctx.s: 「{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]って}ごめん、それっていつの話[はなし]？」
ctx.en: "Sorry to interrupt, but when was this?"

ctx.s: 面白[おもしろ]いところだったのに、電話[でんわ]が鳴[な]って{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]られた}。
ctx.en: It was just getting to the good part when the phone rang and broke off the story.

ctx.s: せっかく盛[も]り上[あ]がってきたところなのに、{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]らない}でよ。
ctx.en: It was just getting good, so don't break off my story!

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]が冗談[じょうだん]で{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]った}せいで、彼女[かのじょ]は何[なに]を言[い]おうとしていたか忘[わす]れてしまった。
ctx.en: Because he cut in with a joke, she forgot what she had been about to say.

ctx.s: 相手[あいて]の{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]らず}、最後[さいご]まで聞[き]くのが聞[き]き上手[じょうず]のこつだ。
ctx.en: The secret of being a good listener is to hear people out without breaking in.

bad.s: 資金[しきん]不足[ぶそく]で、工場[こうじょう]の建設[けんせつ]工事[こうじ]が{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]られた}。
bad.en: (meant: a lack of funds halted the factory construction)
bad.why: It is about breaking off someone's talk in mid-flow, not halting a project. For work stopped partway, say chūdan sareta or tonza shita.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は{話[はなし]の腰[こし]を折[お]って}、先生[せんせい]の説明[せつめい]を静[しず]かに聞[き]いた。
bad.en: (meant: I sat attentively and listened quietly to the teacher)
bad.why: It does not mean bowing or listening respectfully; it means interrupting, the opposite of listening quietly.

cards.mean: to feel a chill of horror
cards.lit: one's spine goes cold: the shiver that runs down the back at something frightening

use.how: Predicate about the speaker's reaction to something eerie or to a danger just realised: 考えただけで背筋が寒くなる. Often 背筋が寒くなるような話.

near.diff: 鳥肌が立つ can also come from cold, disgust or being deeply moved; 背筋が寒くなる is only a chill of fear or horror.
冷や汗をかく is the nervous sweat of a tight spot you are in; 背筋が寒くなる is the chill of dread, often on realising what could have happened.

cards.cue: Reading the news, you learn the bridge you crossed yesterday collapsed an hour after you drove over it. How do you feel?

ctx.s: 夜中[よなか]に誰[だれ]もいない部屋[へや]から足音[あしおと]がして、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなった}。
ctx.en: In the middle of the night I heard footsteps from an empty room, and a chill ran down my spine.

ctx.s: あのとき事故[じこ]に遭[あ]っていたらと思[おも]うと、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなる}。
ctx.en: When I think about what would have happened if I had been in that accident, it sends a shiver down my spine.

ctx.s: 「これ、本当[ほんとう]にあった話[はなし]なんだって。」「やめてよ、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなる}じゃない。」
ctx.en: "They say this really happened." "Stop it, you're giving me the creeps."

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]が隣[となり]の家[いえ]に住[す]んでいたと知[し]り、住民[じゅうみん]たちは{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなる}思[おも]いをした。
ctx.en: Learning that the culprit had lived next door, the residents felt a chill of horror.

ctx.s: データが全部[ぜんぶ]消[き]えていたかもしれないと気[き]づいて、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなった}。
ctx.en: When I realised all the data could have been wiped out, I went cold.

ctx.s: その小説[しょうせつ]は、読[よ]み終[お]えてから{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなる}ような結末[けつまつ]だった。
ctx.en: The novel had the kind of ending that leaves you chilled once you have finished it.

bad.s: 今朝[けさ]は気温[きおん]が低[ひく]くて、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: it was so cold this morning that I felt chilly)
bad.why: The chill is one of fear, not of temperature. For being cold, just say samukatta.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の歌声[うたごえ]があまりに美[うつく]しくて、{背筋[せすじ]が寒[さむ]くなった}。
bad.en: (meant: her singing was so beautiful it gave me goosebumps)
bad.why: It is only for fear or horror. Being thrilled or moved is torihada ga tatsu.

cards.mean: a last-ditch stand with no way to retreat
cards.lit: a battle formation with its back to the water: no room to fall back

story.text: In the wars that founded the Han dynasty, the Han general Han Xin attacked the larger army of Zhao. Against the usual rules of warfare he drew up his troops with a river at their backs, so they could not run. Knowing there was no retreat, his soldiers fought desperately, while a hidden force seized the Zhao camp, and Han Xin won a famous victory.
story.source: Sima Qian, Records of the Grand Historian (史記), biography of Han Xin (淮陰侯列伝)

use.how: A noun: 背水の陣で臨む, 背水の陣を敷く, or 背水の陣だ. Said of oneself or others committing to a do-or-die effort with no fallback.

near.diff: 腹をくくる is making up your mind to face something; 背水の陣 is the situation of having no way back, often one you set up on purpose.
正念場 is the decisive moment that tests you; 背水の陣 is the stance of fighting with every retreat cut off.

cards.cue: A runner quits her job, sells her car and moves abroad to train full-time: if she misses this Olympics, she has nothing to go back to.

ctx.s: 今年[ことし]落[お]ちたらもう後[あと]がない。{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で試験[しけん]に臨[のぞ]む。
ctx.en: If I fail this year, there's no next time. I'm going into the exam with my back to the wall.

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めて店[みせ]を開[ひら]いたのだから、まさに{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}だ。
ctx.en: He quit his company to open the shop, so it's truly do or die.

ctx.s: 「貯金[ちょきん]を全部[ぜんぶ]使[つか]うの？」「うん、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}を敷[し]くつもり。」
ctx.en: "You're using all your savings?" "Yes, I'm burning my bridges."

ctx.s: 二連敗[にれんぱい]したチームは、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で第三戦[だいさんせん]を迎[むか]えた。
ctx.en: After two straight defeats, the team went into the third game with no margin left.

ctx.s: 業績[ぎょうせき]不振[ふしん]が続[つづ]く同社[どうしゃ]は、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で新製品[しんせいひん]を投入[とうにゅう]した。
ctx.en: With poor results continuing, the company launched its new product as a last-ditch bid.

ctx.s: 引退[いんたい]をかけた{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}の試合[しあい]で、彼[かれ]は見事[みごと]に勝[か]った。
ctx.en: In a do-or-die match with his career on the line, he won brilliantly.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で、川[かわ]のそばでのんびりバーベキューをした。
bad.en: (meant: today we had a relaxed barbecue by the river)
bad.why: It is not about being near water; it means a desperate stand with no retreat, which a relaxed day out is the opposite of.

bad.s: 失敗[しっぱい]してもまた来年[らいねん]受[う]ければいいので、{背水[はいすい]の陣[じん]}で気楽[きらく]に挑戦[ちょうせん]する。
bad.en: (meant: I can always retake it next year, so I'll take it easy)
bad.why: The whole point is that there is no second chance. If you can try again, it is not a last stand with your back to the river.

cards.mean: speaking bluntly without mincing words
cards.lit: not putting a cloth over one's teeth: words come out bare, not wrapped or softened

use.how: Before a noun about speech: 歯に衣着せぬ物言い, 歯に衣着せぬ発言. Adverbial form 歯に衣着せずに言う. Can be admiring or wary, depending on context.

near.diff: 口が悪い is a habit of rude, harsh language; 歯に衣着せぬ is frankness, saying the plain truth without softening it, and may be admired.
身も蓋もない criticises a remark so blunt it leaves nothing to say; 歯に衣着せぬ describes a person's frank way of speaking.

cards.cue: A TV commentator is famous for telling ministers to their face exactly what is wrong with their policies, without any polite cushioning.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}人[ひと]で、何[なん]でもはっきり言[い]う。
ctx.en: My grandmother doesn't mince words; she says everything straight out.

ctx.s: あの評論家[ひょうろんか]は{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}物言[ものい]いで人気[にんき]がある。
ctx.en: That critic is popular for his outspoken way of talking.

ctx.s: 「遠慮[えんりょ]しないで、{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せず}に意見[いけん]を言[い]ってください。」
ctx.en: "Don't hold back. Please give me your opinion frankly."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}質問[しつもん]に、社長[しゃちょう]は思[おも]わず苦笑[くしょう]した。
ctx.en: At the newcomer's blunt question, the president couldn't help a wry smile.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}発言[はつげん]は、ときどき周[まわ]りをひやりとさせる。
ctx.en: Her unvarnished remarks sometimes make the people around her nervous.

ctx.s: 監督[かんとく]は会見[かいけん]で、選手[せんしゅ]たちの準備[じゅんび]不足[ぶそく]を{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せず}批判[ひはん]した。
ctx.en: At the press conference the coach bluntly criticised his players' lack of preparation.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}人[ひと]なので、いつも遠回[とおまわ]しに丁寧[ていねい]に話[はな]す。
bad.en: (meant: he is careful, so he always speaks politely and indirectly)
bad.why: It means the opposite: speaking frankly with nothing softened. Indirect, careful speech is tōmawashi na iikata.

bad.s: その政治家[せいじか]は{歯[は]に衣[きぬ]着[き]せぬ}嘘[うそ]を平気[へいき]でつく。
bad.en: (meant: that politician tells shameless lies without blinking)
bad.why: It praises or notes frankness, saying what one really thinks; it cannot describe lying. For shameless lies, say heiki de uso o tsuku.

cards.mean: to put a brake on a trend
cards.lit: to put on the brake: a wheel chock or brake that stops something from rolling on

use.how: Takes に: 人口減少に歯止めをかける. Said of curbing an unwelcome trend (decline, rising costs, excess). Intransitive form 歯止めがかかる / かからない.

near.diff: 待ったをかける halts a specific plan or action; 歯止めをかける curbs an ongoing trend such as falling sales or rising prices.
拍車をかける speeds a trend up; 歯止めをかける slows or stops it. They are opposites.

cards.cue: The town has lost residents every year for twenty years. The new mayor promises measures to finally stop the decline.

ctx.s: 使[つか]いすぎに{歯止[はど]めをかける}ため、カードを家[いえ]に置[お]いてきた。
ctx.en: To stop myself from overspending, I left my card at home.

ctx.s: 政府[せいふ]は少子化[しょうしか]に{歯止[はど]めをかけよう}と、様々[さまざま]な対策[たいさく]を打[う]ち出[だ]した。
ctx.en: The government announced various measures to halt the falling birth rate.

ctx.s: 値上[ねあ]げが続[つづ]き、物価[ぶっか]の上昇[じょうしょう]に{歯止[はど]めがかからない}。
ctx.en: Prices keep going up, and nothing is stopping the rise.

ctx.s: 「このままだと赤字[あかじ]がふくらむ一方[いっぽう]だ。どこかで{歯止[はど]めをかけない}と。」
ctx.en: "At this rate the deficit will only keep growing. We have to put a stop to it somewhere."

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい監督[かんとく]の就任[しゅうにん]で、チームの連敗[れんぱい]にようやく{歯止[はど]めがかかった}。
ctx.en: With the new coach's arrival, the team's losing streak was finally halted.

ctx.s: 森林[しんりん]の減少[げんしょう]に{歯止[はど]めをかける}には、国際的[こくさいてき]な協力[きょうりょく]が欠[か]かせない。
ctx.en: International cooperation is essential to check the loss of forests.

bad.s: 赤信号[あかしんごう]だったので、自転車[じてんしゃ]に{歯止[はど]めをかけた}。
bad.en: (meant: the light was red, so I braked my bicycle)
bad.why: As an idiom it curbs a trend, not a vehicle. To brake a bike, say burēki o kaketa.

bad.s: 好調[こうちょう]な売[う]り上[あ]げにさらに{歯止[はど]めをかけて}、もっと伸[の]ばしたい。
bad.en: (meant: we want to push our strong sales even higher)
bad.why: It stops a trend; it cannot boost one. To accelerate a trend, say hakusha o kakeru.

cards.mean: to marvel at someone's skill
cards.lit: to curl up one's tongue: so impressed that words fail you

use.how: Verb phrase, often 〜に舌を巻く or 舌を巻くほど. Said of being amazed at someone else's skill, talent or knowledge, often beyond what was expected.

near.diff: 目を見張る is being struck by anything remarkable, a sight or a change; 舌を巻く is admiration specifically for someone's ability.
頭が下がる is respect for someone's effort or attitude; 舌を巻く is amazement at their skill.

cards.cue: A ten-year-old at the chess club beats the club champion in twenty moves. The grown-ups watching can only shake their heads in admiration.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の料理[りょうり]の腕前[うでまえ]には、プロも{舌[した]を巻[ま]く}。

ctx.en: The judges were astonished by a performance you'd never think came from a primary schoolchild.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の交渉[こうしょう]のうまさに、ベテランの先輩[せんぱい]も{舌[した]を巻[ま]いていた}。
ctx.en: Even the veteran senior colleagues were in awe of how well the newcomer negotiated.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{舌[した]を巻[ま]く}ほど歴史[れきし]に詳[くわ]しい。
ctx.en: Her knowledge of history is astonishing.

ctx.s: 記者[きしゃ]たちは、通訳[つうやく]なしで質問[しつもん]に答[こた]える選手[せんしゅ]の語学力[ごがくりょく]に{舌[した]を巻[ま]いた}。
ctx.en: The reporters marvelled at the athlete's language skills as he answered their questions without an interpreter.

bad.en: (meant: this ramen was so good I smacked my lips)

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の失礼[しつれい]な態度[たいど]には{舌[した]を巻[ま]いた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was dumbfounded by his rude behaviour)

cards.mean: to feel stifled by a tense atmosphere
cards.lit: one's breath gets blocked: as if the air in the room were too thick to breathe

use.how: Predicate about a place, a relationship or an atmosphere that feels oppressive: 息が詰まりそうだ, 息が詰まるような沈黙. Often with ような or そう.

near.diff: 息を呑む is a sudden gasp at something surprising or beautiful; 息が詰まる is the lasting, suffocating feeling of a tense or oppressive situation.
間が持たない is the awkwardness of not knowing what to say to fill time; 息が詰まる is feeling suffocated by pressure or strictness.

cards.cue: Your new boss watches every keystroke, nobody in the office talks, and even the coffee break is silent. Describe how you feel there.

ctx.s: 狭[せま]い部屋[へや]に一日中[いちにちじゅう]こもっていると、{息[いき]が詰[つ]まる}。
ctx.en: Staying shut up in a small room all day is stifling.

ctx.s: 規則[きそく]だらけの寮[りょう]生活[せいかつ]に、{息[いき]が詰[つ]まりそう}だった。
ctx.en: I felt I would suffocate in that dormitory life full of rules.

ctx.s: 「毎日[まいにち]親[おや]に監視[かんし]されてて、{息[いき]が詰[つ]まる}よ。」
ctx.en: "My parents watch my every move, and I can't breathe."

ctx.s: 会議室[かいぎしつ]には{息[いき]が詰[つ]まる}ような沈黙[ちんもく]が流[なが]れていた。
ctx.en: A stifling silence hung over the meeting room.

ctx.en: Feeling stifled by city life, he moved to the countryside.

ctx.s: 三人[さんにん]の面接官[めんせつかん]ににらまれて、{息[いき]が詰[つ]まる}思[おも]いだった。

bad.en: (meant: the view from the summit was so beautiful it took my breath away)
bad.why: It is the stifled feeling of pressure, not wonder. For a breathtaking sight, say iki o nomu.

bad.s: 温泉[おんせん]でのんびりして、やっと{息[いき]が詰[つ]まった}。
bad.en: (meant: relaxing at the hot spring, I could finally breathe easy)

cards.mean: to come back to life, to make a comeback
cards.lit: to breathe again: a person who had stopped breathing starts to breathe once more

use.how: Intransitive verb phrase about a person regaining breath, or a business, town, team or custom reviving after nearly dying out: 商店街が息を吹き返した.

near.diff: 軌道に乗る is something new getting going smoothly; 息を吹き返す is something that was nearly dead coming back to life.
日の目を見る is something hidden finally becoming known; 息を吹き返す is something failing reviving.

cards.cue: An old shopping street was almost all shuttered, but after young owners opened cafés there, it is crowded again on weekends.

ctx.s: 古[ふる]いレコードが若者[わかもの]の間[あいだ]で人気[にんき]になり、{息[いき]を吹[ふ]き返[かえ]して}いる。
ctx.en: Old vinyl records have become popular with young people and are coming back to life.

ctx.s: 救急隊員[きゅうきゅうたいいん]の手当[てあ]てで、おぼれた子[こ]どもは{息[いき]を吹[ふ]き返[かえ]した}。
ctx.en: Thanks to the paramedics' treatment, the child who had nearly drowned started breathing again.

ctx.s: 観光客[かんこうきゃく]が戻[もど]り、さびれていた温泉街[おんせんがい]が{息[いき]を吹[ふ]き返[かえ]した}。
ctx.en: With tourists returning, the run-down hot-spring town has come back to life.

ctx.s: 「あの会社[かいしゃ]、倒産[とうさん]寸前[すんぜん]だったのに、ヒット商品[しょうひん]で{息[いき]を吹[ふ]き返[かえ]した}らしいよ。」
ctx.en: "That company was on the verge of bankruptcy, but I hear a hit product brought it back."

ctx.s: ゴールが決[き]まると、劣勢[れっせい]だったチームは一気[いっき]に{息[いき]を吹[ふ]き返[かえ]した}。
ctx.en: Once that goal went in, the team that had been on the back foot suddenly came alive.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]は途絶[とだ]えた祭[まつ]りが、若者[わかもの]たちの手[て]で{息[いき]を吹[ふ]き返[かえ]そう}としている。

bad.en: (meant: after the marathon I caught my breath on a bench)

cards.mean: to harden one's heart for someone's own good
cards.lit: to turn one's heart into an ogre: make a kind heart deliberately harsh

use.how: Usually 心を鬼にして + a strict act (叱る, 断る, 突き放す). Said of someone who is kind by nature choosing to be strict because it is good for the other person.

near.diff: 血も涙もない condemns a person as truly heartless; 心を鬼にする is a caring person acting strict on purpose, for the other's sake.

cards.cue: Your grown son keeps asking for money instead of looking for work. You love him, but this time you refuse so that he learns to stand on his own.

ctx.en: Only as an adult did I understand that my mother had pushed me away out of tough love.

bad.en: (meant: the bullies cruelly enjoyed teasing a weaker child)

bad.s: うちの部長[ぶちょう]は{心[こころ]を鬼[おに]にする}人[ひと]で、誰[だれ]にも同情[どうじょう]しない。
bad.en: (meant: our manager is a heartless man with no sympathy for anyone)

cards.mean: to mend one's ways and start afresh
cards.lit: to swap out one's heart: take out the bad one and put in a new one

use.how: Usually 心を入れ替えて + a new behaviour (頑張る, 真面目に働く). Said of someone giving up a bad attitude or habit, often after a scolding or failure.

near.diff: 足を洗う is quitting a bad line of work or way of life; 心を入れ替える is a change of attitude, being more serious or diligent from now on.
気を取り直す is pulling yourself together after a disappointment; 心を入れ替える is reforming after behaving badly.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]に厳[きび]しく叱[しか]られて、彼[かれ]はすっかり{心[こころ]を入[い]れ替[か]えた}。

bad.en: (meant: after the explanation I changed my mind and agreed to the plan)

bad.s: 雨[あめ]の日[ひ]は好[す]きな音楽[おんがく]を聴[き]いて{心[こころ]を入[い]れ替[か]える}。
bad.en: (meant: on rainy days I listen to music I like to change my mood)

cards.mean: freely, with nothing weighing on one's mind
cards.lit: without leaving anything set down in the heart: no worry or obligation left behind

bad.en: (meant: he carelessly forgot his homework)

bad.en: (meant: my homework is done, so now I feel completely at ease)
bad.why: It is an adverb and must modify a verb (kokoro okinaku asoberu); it cannot be a predicate with da. Say hotto shite iru.

cards.mean: cold-blooded and heartless
cards.lit: having neither blood nor tears: no warmth and no pity in them

use.how: Before a noun (血も涙もない人, 血も涙もないやり方) or as a predicate. Condemns a person or act that shows no compassion for those who suffer.

near.diff: 心を鬼にする is being strict on purpose for someone's good while still caring; 血も涙もない means having no compassion at all.

cards.cue: A landlord evicts an elderly tenant in midwinter because the rent was one day late, without listening to a word. How do the neighbours describe him?

ctx.s: 物語[ものがたり]の悪役[あくやく]は、村人[むらびと]から最後[さいご]の米[こめ]まで奪[うば]う{血[ち]も涙[なみだ]もない}男[おとこ]だった。

ctx.en: Even the businessman the public called heartless had a side to him that cared deeply for his family.

bad.s: 転[ころ]んだけど、{血[ち]も涙[なみだ]もなかった}よ。
bad.en: (meant: I fell over, but I didn't bleed or cry)

bad.s: あの外科医[げかい]は手術中[しゅじゅつちゅう]、{血[ち]も涙[なみだ]もない}ほど冷静[れいせい]で頼[たよ]もしい。
bad.en: (meant: that surgeon is admirably calm and steady during operations)
bad.why: It is a harsh condemnation of cruelty, never praise for composure. Say ochitsuite iru or reisei da.

cards.mean: hot-blooded and quick to fight
cards.lit: having a lot of blood in one: too much heat to stay calm

use.how: Describes a person's temperament, often young men: 血の気が多い若者. Says they get worked up and pick fights easily; mildly critical or wry.

near.diff: 気が短い is being impatient and irritable; 血の気が多い is being fiery and ready to argue or fight.

ctx.s: 若[わか]い頃[ころ]の父[ちち]は{血[ち]の気[け]が多[おお]く}、よく先輩[せんぱい]とぶつかっていたらしい。
ctx.en: When he was young, my father was apparently hot-tempered and often clashed with his seniors.

cards.mean: to search frantically

ctx.en: The police are frantically trying to track down the culprit.

cards.mean: to slack off chatting when one should be working
cards.lit: to sell oil

story.text: As the expression is traditionally explained, in the Edo period peddlers went door to door selling hair oil. The oil was thick and dripped slowly from the measuring ladle into the customer's container, so the sellers chatted with their customers while they waited. To onlookers they seemed to be gossiping instead of working, and 'selling oil' came to mean idling away time that should be spent on work.

use.how: Used of someone idling or chatting during work or an errand, often teasing: どこで油を売ってたの？ / 油を売ってないで戻れ.

near.diff: 道草を食う is stopping off on the way somewhere; 油を売る is wasting time that should go to work, typically chatting.

ctx.s: 無断[むだん]で車[くるま]を使[つか]ったことがばれて、兄[あに]は祖父[そふ]に{油[あぶら]を絞[しぼ]られた}らしい。

ctx.s: 宝[たから]くじで少[すこ]し当[あ]たったことに{味[あじ]をしめて}、彼[かれ]は毎月[まいつき]買[か]い続[つづ]けている。

ctx.s: 初[はじ]めてのフリーマーケットでよく売[う]れたことに{味[あじ]をしめ}、毎月[まいつき]出店[しゅってん]している。
ctx.en: Things sold so well at her first flea market that she has run a stall every month since.

ctx.s: 前回[ぜんかい]のセールで{味[あじ]をしめた}客[きゃく]が、今回[こんかい]も朝[あさ]から並[なら]んでいる。
ctx.en: Customers who did well at the last sale are queueing again from early morning.

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]は最初[さいしょ]の詐欺[さぎ]が成功[せいこう]したことに{味[あじ]をしめた}らしく、同[おな]じ手口[てぐち]を繰[く]り返[かえ]した。
ctx.en: Encouraged, it seems, by the success of his first scam, the culprit used the same trick again and again.

bad.s: スープは塩[しお]と醤油[しょうゆ]で{味[あじ]をしめた}。
bad.en: (meant: I seasoned the soup with salt and soy sauce)
bad.why: It is not about cooking. Seasoning is aji o tsukeru or aji o totonoeru.

bad.s: 一度[いちど]失敗[しっぱい]したことに{味[あじ]をしめて}、二度[にど]とやらなかった。
bad.en: (meant: I learned from failing once and never did it again)
bad.why: It means a success makes you want to repeat it, the opposite. Learning from failure is koriru: ichido no shippai ni korite.

cards.mean: to stir up debate on an issue
cards.lit: to throw a single stone (into still water), sending ripples outward

use.how: 〜に一石を投じる, of a statement, work or proposal that challenges an accepted view or a settled practice and starts people discussing it. Typical of news and essays.

near.diff: 水を差す dampens a plan or a good mood; 一石を投じる raises a question that gets people debating.

cards.cue: A young researcher's paper questions a theory everyone in the field had taken for granted, and now journals are full of responses. What did the paper do?

ctx.s: その論文[ろんぶん]は、従来[じゅうらい]の定説[ていせつ]に{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じた}。
ctx.en: The paper challenged the established theory and set off a debate.

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]で誰[だれ]も疑[うたが]わなかった前提[ぜんてい]に、新入社員[しんにゅうしゃいん]が{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じた}。
ctx.en: A new employee questioned an assumption no one in the meeting had ever doubted.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の発言[はつげん]は、長時間労働[ちょうじかんろうどう]の問題[もんだい]に{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じる}ものだった。
ctx.en: Her remarks raised questions that put the problem of long working hours up for discussion.

ctx.s: 新人監督[しんじんかんとく]の作品[さくひん]が、映画界[えいがかい]に{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じた}と話題[わだい]になっている。
ctx.en: People are saying the new director's film has shaken up the film world and got everyone talking.

ctx.s: 一人[ひとり]の保護者[ほごしゃ]の投書[とうしょ]が、校則[こうそく]の見直[みなお]しに{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じた}。
ctx.en: One parent's letter started a real discussion about revising the school rules.

ctx.s: 「この記事[きじ]で、地域[ちいき]の教育[きょういく]のあり方[かた]に{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じたい}と考[かんが]えています。」
ctx.en: "With this article I hope to spark a debate about how education is done in our region."

bad.s: 二人[ふたり]の喧嘩[けんか]に{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じて}、もっと仲[なか]を悪[わる]くしてしまった。
bad.en: (meant: I made their quarrel even worse)
bad.why: Making a bad situation worse is hi ni abura o sosogu. Isseki o toujiru is raising a question about a public issue.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は友達[ともだち]の話[はなし]に{一石[いっせき]を投[とう]じて}、みんなを笑[わら]わせた。
bad.en: (meant: he chipped in with a joke and made everyone laugh)
bad.why: It is a weighty, mostly written phrase for challenging accepted views, not for a light remark in a chat.

cards.mean: to set oneself clearly apart from
cards.lit: to draw a single line: marking a clear boundary between oneself and others

use.how: 〜とは一線を画す, often before a noun: 他社とは一線を画したサービス. Says something is clearly different in kind from the rest, usually in its favour.

near.diff: 一線を越える is crossing a line that should not be crossed; 一線を画す is drawing a clear distinction.

cards.cue: A new ramen shop's broth is nothing like the usual soy or pork-bone styles; critics say it belongs in a category of its own. How do they describe it?

ctx.s: この店[みせ]のラーメンは、ほかの店[みせ]とは{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]す}味[あじ]だ。
ctx.en: This shop's ramen tastes like nothing else around.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の作品[さくひん]は、従来[じゅうらい]のアニメとは{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]している}。
ctx.en: His work stands clearly apart from conventional anime.

ctx.s: 「あのバンド、デビュー当時[とうじ]からほかとは{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]して}たよね。」
ctx.en: "That band was in a different league from the rest right from their debut, wasn't it?"

ctx.s: 当社[とうしゃ]は、価格[かかく]だけを競[きそ]う他社[たしゃ]とは{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]した}サービスを目指[めざ]しています。
ctx.en: We aim to offer a service clearly distinct from competitors who compete on price alone.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は流行[りゅうこう]を追[お]う人々[ひとびと]とは{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]し}、自分[じぶん]の好[す]きな服[ふく]だけを着[き]ている。
ctx.en: She keeps herself apart from those who chase trends and wears only the clothes she likes.

ctx.s: 研究者[けんきゅうしゃ]として、彼[かれ]は根拠[こんきょ]のない噂[うわさ]とは常[つね]に{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]して}きた。
ctx.en: As a scientist, he has always kept a clear distance from unfounded rumours.

bad.s: 体育[たいいく]の先生[せんせい]が、校庭[こうてい]にチョークで{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]した}。
bad.en: (meant: the PE teacher drew a line on the playground in chalk)
bad.why: It is never a literal line. To draw a line on the ground, say sen o hiita.

bad.s: 友人[ゆうじん]の冗談[じょうだん]は{一線[いっせん]を画[かく]して}、相手[あいて]を怒[おこ]らせた。
bad.en: (meant: my friend's joke crossed the line and made the other person angry)
bad.why: Crossing a line is issen o koeru. Issen o kakusu means standing clearly apart from something.

cards.mean: a cut above, one step ahead
cards.lit: one rank higher (the counter 'mai' here counts ranks, as on a ranking list): just a notch above the other side

use.how: Always comparing two sides: AのほうがBより一枚上手だ, 相手が一枚上手だった. Says one side has a slight edge in skill or cunning, often in a contest of wits.

near.diff: 一目置く is respecting someone as better than you; 一枚上手 describes the side that is slightly ahead.

cards.cue: You set up a clever April Fool's prank on your sister, but she saw it coming and turned it back on you. Admit who won.

ctx.s: 将棋[しょうぎ]では、兄[あに]のほうが僕[ぼく]より{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だ。
ctx.en: At shogi, my older brother is a notch better than me.

ctx.s: 「いたずらを仕掛[しか]けたつもりが、妹[いもうと]のほうが{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だったよ。」
ctx.en: "I thought I was pranking my sister, but she was one step ahead of me."

ctx.s: 交渉[こうしょう]では相手[あいて]が{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}で、こちらの条件[じょうけん]はほとんど通[とお]らなかった。
ctx.en: The other side outmanoeuvred us in the negotiations, and hardly any of our terms got through.

ctx.s: 決勝[けっしょう]では、経験[けいけん]で{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}のベテランが勝[か]った。
ctx.en: In the final, the veteran, who had the edge in experience, won.

ctx.s: 逃[に]げ切[き]れると思[おも]っていた詐欺師[さぎし]より、刑事[けいじ]のほうが{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だった。
ctx.en: The con man thought he'd get away, but the detective was one step ahead of him.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]を出[だ]し抜[ぬ]こうなんて無理[むり]だよ。いつも{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}なんだから。」
ctx.en: "There's no way you'll outsmart her. She's always a step ahead."

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}にピアノを弾[ひ]く。
bad.en: (meant: he plays the piano skilfully)
bad.why: It is not an adverb of skill (here the kanji are read uwate, not jouzu). It only compares two sides: kare no hou ga ichimai uwate da.

bad.s: 世界[せかい]チャンピオンは、素人[しろうと]の僕[ぼく]より{一枚[いちまい]上手[うわて]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the world champion is vastly better than an amateur like me)
bad.why: It means a slight edge between near-equals. For a huge gap, say ashimoto ni mo oyobanai or kaku ga chigau.

cards.mean: to be outsmarted in an exchange
cards.lit: to have one full point taken: to be scored on cleanly, as in a martial-arts bout

story.text: In kendo and judo, ippon is a clean, decisive point awarded when a technique lands fully. To have ippon taken is to be scored on cleanly by your opponent. The word moved from the dojo into conversation: when someone's quick remark or clever move leaves you with no answer, they have taken a point off you.

use.how: Usually past, as a good-humoured concession: これは一本取られた. Said when someone's clever remark or move gets the better of you.

near.diff: 一枚上手 says someone is generally a level above you; 一本取られる is one moment where a clever remark or move gets the better of you.

cards.cue: Your seven-year-old points out that you also leave vegetables on your plate. You have no answer, so you laugh and concede.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもに「パパだって野菜[やさい]を残[のこ]してるよ」と言[い]われ、{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られた}。
ctx.en: My kid said, "You leave your vegetables too, Dad," and I had no comeback.

ctx.s: 「いやあ、これは{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られました}な」と部長[ぶちょう]は笑[わら]った。
ctx.en: "Well, you've got me there," the manager said with a laugh.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は孫[まご]のなぞなぞに答[こた]えられず、「{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られた}なあ」と頭[あたま]をかいた。
ctx.en: Unable to answer his grandchild's riddle, Grandpa scratched his head and said, "You've beaten me there."

ctx.s: 皮肉[ひにく]を言[い]ったつもりが見事[みごと]に切[き]り返[かえ]されて、{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られて}しまった。
ctx.en: I meant it as a dig, but he turned it neatly back on me and I was the one left speechless.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の鋭[するど]い質問[しつもん]に、講師[こうし]は「{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られましたね}」と苦笑[くしょう]した。
ctx.en: Faced with the new recruit's sharp question, the instructor gave a wry smile: "You've caught me out."

ctx.s: まさか小学生[しょうがくせい]に{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られる}とは思[おも]わなかった。
ctx.en: I never thought a primary-school kid would get the better of me.

bad.s: 詐欺[さぎ]に遭[あ]って、百万円[ひゃくまんえん]も{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られた}。
bad.en: (meant: I was swindled out of a million yen)
bad.why: It is a light concession that someone outwitted you in talk or play, not being robbed or cheated. Say damashitorareta.

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]で上司[じょうし]を言[い]い負[ま]かして、{一本[いっぽん]取[と]られた}。
bad.en: (meant: I won the argument against my boss)
bad.why: Torareru means you were the one scored on. When you outwit someone, say ippon totta.

cards.mean: an instant and willing yes
cards.lit: a two-fold reply: answering "yes, yes" straight away

use.how: Mostly 二つ返事で + verb (引き受ける, 承知する): agreeing at once and gladly to a request or offer. Also 二つ返事だ.

cards.cue: You ask a friend to help you move house on Saturday, and before you even finish asking, they say yes, happily.

ctx.s: 友達[ともだち]に引[ひ]っ越[こ]しの手伝[てつだ]いを頼[たの]んだら、{二[ふた]つ返事[へんじ]}でオーケーしてくれた。
ctx.en: When I asked a friend to help me move, they said yes right away.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は私[わたし]の企画[きかく]に{二[ふた]つ返事[へんじ]}で賛成[さんせい]した。
ctx.en: The department head agreed to my proposal without a moment's hesitation.

ctx.s: 「好[す]きな歌手[かしゅ]のライブに誘[さそ]われたら、そりゃ{二[ふた]つ返事[へんじ]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "If someone invites me to my favourite singer's concert, of course it's an instant yes."

ctx.s: 町内会[ちょうないかい]の役員[やくいん]を頼[たの]まれた父[ちち]は、珍[めずら]しく{二[ふた]つ返事[へんじ]}で引[ひ]き受[う]けた。
ctx.en: Asked to serve on the neighbourhood committee, my father, unusually for him, accepted on the spot.

ctx.en: The conditions were too strict for me to just say yes straight away.

ctx.en: I'm the type who says yes the moment I'm asked, so I'm always busy.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は私[わたし]の誘[さそ]いを{二[ふた]つ返事[へんじ]}で断[ことわ]った。
bad.en: (meant: he turned down my invitation at once)
bad.why: Futatsu henji is always a willing yes. A quick refusal is sokuza ni kotowatta.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は賛成[さんせい]とも反対[はんたい]とも言[い]わず、{二[ふた]つ返事[へんじ]}をした。
bad.en: (meant: the manager gave a vague, two-sided answer)
bad.why: The 'two' is 'yes, yes', not two possible answers. A noncommittal reply is aimai na henji.

cards.mean: to take every precaution to ensure success
cards.lit: to aim for complete soundness: to resolve that nothing be left lacking

use.how: Verb phrase, often with に for the area covered: 安全に万全を期す, 万全を期して臨む. Said of careful preparation in work, official or public statements.

near.diff: 手を尽くす is trying every possible means, often once trouble has come; 万全を期す is preparing carefully in advance so that nothing goes wrong.

cards.cue: A company spokesperson promises that every safety check for tomorrow's festival has been prepared with the utmost care.

ctx.s: 大事[だいじ]な試合[しあい]に向[む]けて、体調[たいちょう]管理[かんり]に{万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]して}いる。
ctx.en: With the big match coming up, I'm taking every care to stay in top condition.

ctx.s: {万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]す}ため、データのバックアップを二重[にじゅう]に取[と]っておいた。
ctx.en: To be completely safe, I made two backups of the data.

ctx.s: 「念[ねん]のため、もう一度[いちど]確認[かくにん]しましょう。{万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]したい}ので。」
ctx.en: "Let's check once more, just in case. I want to leave nothing to chance."

ctx.s: 当日[とうじつ]は会場[かいじょう]の警備[けいび]に{万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]して}まいります。
ctx.en: On the day, we will spare no effort to ensure the venue's security.

ctx.s: 大雪[おおゆき]の予報[よほう]を受[う]け、鉄道[てつどう]会社[がいしゃ]は除雪[じょせつ]に{万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]す}としている。
ctx.en: Following the heavy-snow forecast, the railway company says it is fully prepared to clear the lines.

ctx.s: {万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]した}つもりだったが、思[おも]わぬところでミスが出[で]た。
ctx.en: I thought I had covered everything, but a mistake turned up where I least expected it.
