bad.en: (meant: the exam result was perfect)
bad.why: It describes the care taken in preparing, not a perfect outcome. A perfect result is kanpeki datta.

bad.s: 明日[あした]晴[は]れるように、{万全[ばんぜん]を期[き]して}います。
bad.en: (meant: I'm hoping it will be sunny tomorrow)
bad.why: It means you yourself prepare so that nothing is lacking, which no one can do for the weather. Hoping for sun is hareru you ni negau.

cards.mean: to settle once and for all who is right
cards.lit: to mark off white from black: to decide which side is which

use.how: Verb phrase, often volitional or with たい／べきだ: 白黒をつけよう. Forcing a clear verdict on who is right in a dispute; を is often dropped in speech.

cards.cue: Two brothers have argued for a week over who broke the TV. One finally says it's time to decide, clearly, which of them is to blame.

ctx.s: 「どっちが正[ただ]しいか、今日[きょう]こそ{白黒[しろくろ]をつけよう}。」
ctx.en: "Today we're going to settle which of us is right."

ctx.s: 兄弟[きょうだい]は、どちらがゲームが上手[うま]いか{白黒[しろくろ]をつける}ため、もう一回[いっかい]勝負[しょうぶ]した。
ctx.en: To settle which of them was better at the game, the brothers played one more round.

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の家[いえ]との土地[とち]の境界[きょうかい]争[あらそ]いは、裁判[さいばん]で{白黒[しろくろ]をつける}ことになった。
ctx.en: The boundary dispute with the neighbours is going to be settled in court.

ctx.s: 「何[なん]でも{白黒[しろくろ]をつけたがる}のは、君[きみ]の悪[わる]い癖[くせ]だよ。」
ctx.en: "Always needing to decide who's right and who's wrong is a bad habit of yours."

ctx.s: 夫婦[ふうふ]げんかは、無理[むり]に{白黒[しろくろ]をつけない}ほうがうまくいくこともある。
ctx.en: With marital quarrels, it sometimes works better not to force a verdict on who was right.

ctx.s: 疑惑[ぎわく]について{白黒[しろくろ]をつけるべき}だと、記者[きしゃ]は会見[かいけん]で迫[せま]った。
ctx.en: At the press conference, a reporter pressed for the allegations to be settled one way or the other.

bad.s: 古[ふる]い写真[しゃしん]のように見[み]せたくて、画像[がぞう]に{白黒[しろくろ]をつけた}。
bad.en: (meant: I made the picture black and white to look old)
bad.why: It is about settling who is right, not colour. To make an image monochrome, say shirokuro ni shita.

bad.s: 議論[ぎろん]は平行線[へいこうせん]だったので、{白黒[しろくろ]をつけて}お互[たが]いの意見[いけん]を尊重[そんちょう]することにした。
bad.en: (meant: we agreed to disagree and respect each other's views)
bad.why: It means forcing a clear verdict on who is right; agreeing to disagree is the opposite of that.

cards.mean: to look on someone coldly with disapproval
cards.lit: to look at someone with white eyes: the cold sideways glance that shows the whites

story.text: Ruan Ji, one of the Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove in third-century China, is said to have met people he despised with the whites of his eyes and people he liked with the dark of his eyes. This is the source of the Chinese term 'white eye' for a scornful look, which survives in the Japanese written word hakuganshi, an equivalent of this phrase.
story.source: 『晋書』阮籍伝 (Book of Jin, biography of Ruan Ji)

use.how: Often passive: 周りから白い目で見られる. Describes the cold, disapproving attitude of others, often society or a group, toward someone's behaviour.

near.diff: 後ろ指を指される is being talked about behind your back; 白い目で見る is the cold, open disapproval people show you.
目くじらを立てる is getting worked up over small faults; 白い目で見る is a cold, shunning attitude, not angry fussing.

cards.cue: Someone takes a loud phone call on a quiet train, and the other passengers turn and give them cold looks.

ctx.s: 電車[でんしゃ]で大声[おおごえ]で電話[でんわ]していたら、周[まわ]りの人[ひと]に{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]られた}。
ctx.en: When I talked loudly on the phone on the train, the people around me gave me dirty looks.

ctx.s: 「そんな{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]ないで}よ。ちゃんと理由[りゆう]があるんだから。」
ctx.en: "Don't look at me like that. I have a good reason."

ctx.s: 遅刻[ちこく]ばかりする彼[かれ]は、同僚[どうりょう]から{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]られて}いる。
ctx.en: He is always late, so his colleagues regard him coldly.

ctx.s: 以前[いぜん]は、男性[だんせい]が育休[いくきゅう]を取[と]ると{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]られる}こともあった。
ctx.en: In the past, men who took paternity leave were sometimes frowned upon.

ctx.s: 村[むら]の人々[ひとびと]は、都会[とかい]から来[き]た若者[わかもの]を初[はじ]めは{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]て}いた。
ctx.en: At first the villagers looked coldly on the young newcomer from the city.

ctx.s: 罪[つみ]を償[つぐな]った人[ひと]を、いつまでも{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]る}のはどうだろうか。
ctx.en: Is it right to keep shunning someone who has paid for their crime?

bad.s: あまりに驚[おどろ]いて、彼[かれ]の顔[かお]を{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]た}。
bad.en: (meant: I stared at his face in astonishment)
bad.why: It shows cold disapproval, not surprise. Staring wide-eyed in surprise is me o maruku suru.

bad.s: 赤[あか]ちゃんが{白[しろ]い目[め]で見[み]つめて}いて、とてもかわいい。
bad.en: (meant: the baby is gazing with innocent, pure eyes)
bad.why: 'White' here is not purity; the phrase is a cold, scornful look and cannot describe an innocent gaze.

cards.mean: to scrap a plan and start over
cards.lit: to return it to a blank sheet of paper

use.how: Transitive, said of plans, proposals and agreements: 計画を白紙に戻す. Passive 白紙に戻される and intransitive 白紙に戻る are common in news.

near.diff: 振り出しに戻る is ending up back at the start, often against your will; 白紙に戻す is deliberately cancelling a plan or agreement.
水に流す is forgiving a past quarrel or wrong; 白紙に戻す cancels a plan or agreement, not a grudge.

cards.cue: After months of planning, the city council cancels the new stadium project entirely so that it can start again from nothing.

ctx.s: 予算[よさん]が足[た]りず、旅行[りょこう]の計画[けいかく]を{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]した}。
ctx.en: We didn't have enough money, so we scrapped the travel plans.

ctx.s: 「一度[いちど]{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]して}、最初[さいしょ]から考[かんが]え直[なお]そう。」
ctx.en: "Let's wipe the slate clean and rethink it from the beginning."

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]は結婚[けっこん]の話[はなし]をいったん{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]す}ことにした。
ctx.en: The couple decided to call off their marriage plans for the time being.

ctx.s: 市[し]は住民[じゅうみん]の反対[はんたい]を受[う]けて、駅前[えきまえ]の再開発[さいかいはつ]案[あん]を{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]す}と発表[はっぴょう]した。
ctx.en: In the face of residents' opposition, the city announced it was scrapping the station-area redevelopment plan.

ctx.s: 両社[りょうしゃ]の合併[がっぺい]は、条件[じょうけん]が折[お]り合[あ]わず{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]された}。
ctx.en: The merger of the two companies was called off when they couldn't agree on terms.

ctx.s: 「ここまで進[すす]めてきたのに、今[いま]さら全部[ぜんぶ]{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]す}んですか？」
ctx.en: "We've come this far, and now you want to throw it all out and start again?"

bad.s: 昔[むかし]のけんかのことは、もう{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]そう}。
bad.en: (meant: let's forgive and forget our old quarrel)
bad.why: It cancels plans or agreements, not grudges. Forgiving a past quarrel is mizu ni nagasu.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の最中[さいちゅう]に緊張[きんちょう]して、頭[あたま]が{白紙[はくし]に戻[もど]った}。
bad.en: (meant: my mind went blank from nerves in the middle of the exam)
bad.why: It is about scrapping a plan, not the mind. A blank mind is atama ga masshiro ni naru.

cards.mean: to hone one's skills
cards.lit: to polish one's arm, where the arm stands for skill

use.how: Transitive phrase, often with the skill named: 料理の腕を磨く. Said of working steadily to improve a craft, sport or professional skill.

near.diff: 手に職をつける is learning a trade so you can earn a living; 腕を磨く is getting better at a skill you already practise.

cards.cue: A young baker spends five years in bakeries in France, working to become better and better at the craft.

ctx.s: 料理[りょうり]の{腕[うで]を磨[みが]く}ために、毎日[まいにち]お弁当[べんとう]を作[つく]っている。
ctx.en: I make a packed lunch every day to improve my cooking.

ctx.s: 「プロになりたいなら、もっと{腕[うで]を磨[みが]かない}とね。」
ctx.en: "If you want to go pro, you'll have to sharpen your skills a lot more."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はフランスで五年間[ごねんかん]修業[しゅぎょう]し、パン職人[しょくにん]として{腕[うで]を磨[みが]いた}。
ctx.en: He trained in France for five years and honed his craft as a baker.

ctx.s: 大会[たいかい]に向[む]けて、チームは練習[れんしゅう]試合[じあい]で{腕[うで]を磨[みが]いて}いる。
ctx.en: Ahead of the tournament, the team is sharpening its skills in practice matches.

ctx.s: 将棋[しょうぎ]の{腕[うで]を磨[みが]く}には、どんな勉強[べんきょう]が効果的[こうかてき]ですか。
ctx.en: What kind of study works best for getting better at shogi?

ctx.s: 地方[ちほう]の病院[びょういん]で{腕[うで]を磨[みが]いた}外科医[げかい]が、東京[とうきょう]に戻[もど]ってきた。
ctx.en: A surgeon who honed his skills at a regional hospital has come back to Tokyo.

bad.s: 毎日[まいにち]ジムで{腕[うで]を磨[みが]いて}、太[ふと]い腕[うで]になった。
bad.en: (meant: I worked out my arms at the gym every day and built them up)
bad.why: Ude here means skill, not the arm's muscles. Building up your arms is ude o kitaeru.

bad.s: もっと優[やさ]しい人[ひと]になるために、{腕[うで]を磨[みが]いて}いる。
bad.en: (meant: I'm working on becoming a kinder person)
bad.why: Ude is a practical skill or technique, not character. Improving yourself as a person is ningen o migaku.

cards.mean: to be itching to show what one can do
cards.lit: one's arm rings out: it hums with eagerness to be put to use

use.how: Said by a skilled person, or of one, before a challenge: 腕が鳴るなあ. Also before a noun: 腕が鳴る仕事.

near.diff: 胸が躍る is any thrill of anticipation; 腕が鳴る is eagerness to use your own skill on a challenge that is coming.

cards.cue: A veteran carpenter learns he will restore a centuries-old temple and can hardly wait to get his tools on it.

ctx.s: 久[ひさ]しぶりの試合[しあい]だ。{腕[うで]が鳴[な]る}なあ。
ctx.en: It's my first match in ages. I can't wait to get out there.

ctx.s: 「次[つぎ]の相手[あいて]は去年[きょねん]の優勝[ゆうしょう]チームだって？それは{腕[うで]が鳴[な]る}ね。」
ctx.en: "Our next opponents are last year's champions? Now that's a challenge I'm itching for."

ctx.s: 「難[むずか]しい注文[ちゅうもん]ほど{腕[うで]が鳴[な]る}んですよ」と職人[しょくにん]は笑[わら]った。
ctx.en: "The harder the order, the more I want to get my hands on it," the craftsman said with a smile.

ctx.s: 大[おお]きな案件[あんけん]を任[まか]されて、エンジニアたちは{腕[うで]が鳴[な]る}思[おも]いだった。
ctx.en: Handed a major project, the engineers were raring to show what they could do.

ctx.s: 腕[うで]のいい大工[だいく]にとって、古[ふる]いお寺[てら]の修理[しゅうり]は{腕[うで]が鳴[な]る}仕事[しごと]だ。
ctx.en: For a skilled carpenter, restoring an old temple is a job to relish.

ctx.s: 料理[りょうり]大会[たいかい]の決勝[けっしょう]を明日[あした]に控[ひか]え、{腕[うで]が鳴[な]って}仕方[しかた]がない。
ctx.en: With the cooking contest final tomorrow, I'm dying to show what I can do.

bad.s: 重[おも]い荷物[にもつ]を運[はこ]んだら、{腕[うで]が鳴[な]って}痛[いた]い。
bad.en: (meant: my arms are aching after carrying heavy bags)
bad.why: It is eagerness to use one's skill, not a physical sensation. Sore arms are ude ga itai.

bad.s: 明日[あした]はサッカーの試合[しあい]を観客席[かんきゃくせき]で見[み]るので、{腕[うで]が鳴[な]る}。
bad.en: (meant: I'm excited to watch the football match from the stands tomorrow)
bad.why: It is about your own skill being put to use. Looking forward to watching is tanoshimi da or wakuwaku suru.

cards.mean: to look on enviously, unable to act
cards.lit: to watch with a finger in one's mouth, like a child staring at what it can't have

use.how: Usually 指をくわえて見ている (だけ／わけにはいかない): standing by enviously or helplessly while others gain. Often a call to act.

near.diff: 手も足も出ない is being powerless against something too strong; 指をくわえて見る stresses standing by while others get what you want.

cards.cue: A rival shop is winning over your customers one by one, and you tell your staff you will not just stand by and watch it happen.

ctx.s: お金[かね]がなくて、友達[ともだち]が新[あたら]しいゲームで遊[あそ]ぶのを{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]て}いた。
ctx.en: I had no money, so I could only watch enviously while my friends played the new game.

ctx.s: 「このまま{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]て}いるつもり？今[いま]動[うご]かないと間[ま]に合[あ]わないよ。」
ctx.en: "Are you just going to stand there and watch? If you don't act now, it'll be too late."

ctx.s: 補欠[ほけつ]の彼[かれ]は、仲間[なかま]が活躍[かつやく]するのをベンチで{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]て}いた。
ctx.en: As a substitute, he could only look on from the bench as his teammates shone.

ctx.s: 売[う]り切[き]れで、ほかの客[きゃく]が限定品[げんていひん]を買[か]うのを{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]る}しかなかった。
ctx.en: It sold out, and all I could do was watch other customers buy the limited edition.

ctx.s: ライバル会社[がいしゃ]に客[きゃく]を奪[うば]われるのを、{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]て}いるわけにはいかない。
ctx.en: We can't just sit back and watch our rival steal our customers.

ctx.s: 商店街[しょうてんがい]が寂[さび]れていくのを{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]て}いられず、若者[わかもの]たちが立[た]ち上[あ]がった。
ctx.en: Unwilling to stand by as the shopping street declined, the young people took action.

bad.s: 面白[おもしろ]い映画[えいが]だったので、最後[さいご]まで{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]た}。
bad.en: (meant: the film was so good I watched it intently to the end)
bad.why: It means watching enviously and doing nothing, not watching with absorption. Say kuiiru you ni mita.

bad.s: 息子[むすこ]の発表[はっぴょう]を、私[わたし]は誇[ほこ]らしく{指[ゆび]をくわえて見[み]て}いた。
bad.en: (meant: I watched my son's presentation proudly)
bad.why: The phrase carries envy and helplessness, so it clashes with pride. Say hokorashiku mimamotte ita.

cards.r: うしろゆびをさされる
cards.mean: to be criticised behind one's back
cards.lit: to have fingers pointed at one's back

use.how: Almost always passive, about conduct others would condemn: 後ろ指を指されるようなことはしていない, 後ろ指を指されない生き方.

near.diff: 白い目で見る is cold disapproval shown openly; 後ろ指を指される is being condemned in whispers behind your back.

cards.cue: Your mother always told you to live so honestly that the neighbours would never have reason to whisper about you.

ctx.s: 人[ひと]に{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]される}ようなことは、何[なに]もしていません。
ctx.en: I have done nothing that anyone could whisper about.

ctx.s: 「そんなことをしたら、近所[きんじょ]で{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]される}よ。」
ctx.en: "If you do that, the neighbours will talk about you behind your back."

ctx.s: 母[はは]はいつも「{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]されない}生[い]き方[かた]をしなさい」と言[い]っていた。
ctx.en: My mother always said, "Live in such a way that no one can point a finger at you."

ctx.s: 不正[ふせい]が明[あき]らかになり、彼[かれ]は町中[まちじゅう]の人[ひと]から{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]される}ようになった。
ctx.en: Once the fraud came to light, the whole town began to talk about him behind his back.

ctx.s: 親[おや]の借金[しゃっきん]のせいで{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]された}子[こ]ども時代[じだい]を、彼女[かのじょ]は今[いま]も忘[わす]れない。
ctx.en: She still remembers a childhood of being whispered about because of her parents' debts.

ctx.s: 決[き]まりを守[まも]って堂々[どうどう]としていれば、{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]される}心配[しんぱい]はない。
ctx.en: If you follow the rules and stand tall, there's no need to worry about people talking behind your back.

bad.s: 道[みち]を聞[き]いたら、駅[えき]の方向[ほうこう]を{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]された}。
bad.en: (meant: when I asked the way, someone pointed behind me toward the station)
bad.why: It is never literal pointing. It means being condemned in gossip; for directions, say yubisashite oshiete kureta.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はとても親切[しんせつ]なので、みんなに{後[うし]ろ指[ゆび]を指[さ]されて}いる。
bad.en: (meant: he is so kind that everyone speaks well of him)
bad.why: It is always condemnation, never praise. To be well spoken of is hyouban ga ii.

cards.mean: to slip up and give oneself away
cards.lit: to let one's tail show, like a fox or tanuki in human disguise whose tail pokes out

use.how: Predicate with the deceiver or culprit as subject: 犯人がついに尻尾を出した. Often negative: なかなか尻尾を出さない. Only about hidden lies or wrongdoing.

near.diff: ぼろが出る is hidden weaknesses or ignorance showing; 尻尾を出す is a concealed lie or misdeed being given away by a slip.
尻尾をつかむ is said of the investigator who gets the proof; 尻尾を出す is said of the culprit who lets it slip.

cards.cue: For months a cashier covered every trace of the missing money, until he carelessly mentions a figure only the thief could know.

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]はとうとう{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]した}。
ctx.en: The culprit finally gave himself away.

ctx.s: 「あの人[ひと]、怪[あや]しいよね。」「うん、でもなかなか{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]さない}んだ。」
ctx.en: "That guy is suspicious, isn't he?" "Yeah, but he never slips up."

ctx.s: 嘘[うそ]を重[かさ]ねていれば、いつか話[はなし]の辻褄[つじつま]が合[あ]わなくなって{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]す}ものだ。
ctx.en: If you keep piling up lies, sooner or later your story stops adding up and you give yourself away.

ctx.s: 経費[けいひ]を水増[みずま]ししていた社員[しゃいん]は、日付[ひづけ]の合[あ]わない領収書[りょうしゅうしょ]を提出[ていしゅつ]して{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]した}。
ctx.en: The employee who had been padding his expenses gave himself away by handing in a receipt with the wrong date.

ctx.s: その詐欺師[さぎし]は用心深[ようじんぶか]く、警察[けいさつ]の前[まえ]では決[けっ]して{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]さなかった}。
ctx.en: The con man was cautious and never let anything slip in front of the police.

ctx.s: 刑事[けいじ]は、容疑者[ようぎしゃ]が{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]す}のをじっと待[ま]った。
ctx.en: The detective waited patiently for the suspect to give himself away.

bad.s: 初[はじ]めての発表[はっぴょう]で緊張[きんちょう]して、{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]して}しまった。
bad.en: (meant: I was nervous at my first presentation and made a mistake)
bad.why: It means a hidden lie or misdeed being exposed by a slip. An honest blunder is just a mistake (misu o shita, shippai shita).

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は正直[しょうじき]に{尻尾[しっぽ]を出[だ]して}、自分[じぶん]のミスを認[みと]めた。
bad.en: (meant: she honestly owned up and admitted her mistake)
bad.why: It is an unintended slip, never a willing confession. To own up is to admit it honestly (shōjiki ni mitometa).

cards.mean: to turn tail and run
cards.lit: to tuck one's tail between one's legs, like a dog that has lost a fight

use.how: Almost always 尻尾を巻いて逃げる, also 退散する or 撤退する. Mocks someone who backs off in fear before a stronger opponent.

near.diff: 逃げ腰 is a hesitant attitude of wanting to back out; 尻尾を巻く is actually fleeing, beaten or scared off.

cards.cue: The loudmouth who has been challenging everyone at the bar sees the real champion walk in, and scurries out the back door.

ctx.s: 先輩[せんぱい]に強[つよ]く言[い]い返[かえ]されると、彼[かれ]は{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}逃[に]げていった。
ctx.en: When his senior answered back sharply, he turned tail and ran.

ctx.s: 「相手[あいて]が強[つよ]いからって、{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}逃[に]げるつもり？」
ctx.en: "Are you going to turn tail and run just because they're strong?"

ctx.s: 威勢[いせい]のいいことを言[い]っていた男[おとこ]たちは、警察[けいさつ]が来[く]ると{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}退散[たいさん]した。
ctx.en: The men who had been talking so tough beat a hasty retreat the moment the police arrived.

ctx.s: ここで{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いたら}、一生[いっしょう]後悔[こうかい]する。
ctx.en: If I turn tail now, I'll regret it for the rest of my life.

ctx.s: 大手[おおて]が参入[さんにゅう]してくると、小[ちい]さな業者[ぎょうしゃ]は{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}撤退[てったい]するしかなかった。
ctx.en: When the big companies moved in, the small firms had no choice but to pull out with their tails between their legs.

ctx.s: 挑戦者[ちょうせんしゃ]は王者[おうじゃ]の気迫[きはく]に押[お]され、{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}リングを降[お]りた。
ctx.en: Overwhelmed by the champion's ferocity, the challenger slunk out of the ring.

bad.s: 試合[しあい]に勝[か]って、選手[せんしゅ]たちは{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}喜[よろこ]んだ。
bad.en: (meant: the players won the match and jumped for joy)
bad.why: The tail is tucked in fear and defeat, not wagged for joy. For delight say they were overjoyed (ōyorokobi shita).

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]が長引[ながび]いたので、{尻尾[しっぽ]を巻[ま]いて}先[さき]に帰[かえ]った。
bad.en: (meant: the meeting dragged on, so I quietly left early)
bad.why: It means fleeing a stronger opponent in fear. Quietly slipping out early is just leaving early (kossori kaetta).

cards.mean: to find proof of someone's wrongdoing
cards.lit: to grab the tail of a disguised fox, proving what it really is

use.how: The investigator is the subject: 警察が犯人の尻尾をつかんだ. Often potential negative: なかなか尻尾がつかめない.

near.diff: 尻尾を出す is the culprit's slip; 尻尾をつかむ is the other side, the one who catches it and gets the proof.

cards.cue: After months of suspicion, an auditor finally finds the doctored invoice that proves the manager has been stealing.

ctx.s: 警察[けいさつ]はついに犯人[はんにん]の{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかんだ}。
ctx.en: The police finally got the proof they needed on the culprit.

ctx.s: 「あいつが怪[あや]しいのはわかってるけど、なかなか{尻尾[しっぽ]がつかめない}んだよ。」
ctx.en: "I know he's up to something, but I just can't pin anything on him."

ctx.s: 「次[つぎ]に会[あ]うときに会話[かいわ]を録音[ろくおん]すれば、{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかめる}かもしれない。」
ctx.en: "If we record the conversation next time we meet him, we might get the evidence on him."

ctx.s: 監視[かんし]カメラの映像[えいぞう]が、窃盗犯[せっとうはん]の{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかむ}決[き]め手[て]になった。
ctx.en: The security camera footage was what finally nailed the thief.

ctx.s: 探偵[たんてい]は相手[あいて]に気付[きづ]かれないよう、慎重[しんちょう]に{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかもう}とした。
ctx.en: The private detective tried carefully to catch the man out without being noticed.

ctx.s: 帳簿[ちょうぼ]の数字[すうじ]を一[ひと]つずつ照[て]らし合[あ]わせて、記者[きしゃ]はようやく横領[おうりょう]の{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかんだ}。
ctx.en: By checking the figures in the books one by one, the reporter at last found proof of the embezzlement.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]の説明[せつめい]を聞[き]いて、やっと問題[もんだい]の{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかんだ}。
bad.en: (meant: after the teacher's explanation I finally got a handle on the problem)
bad.why: It means catching proof of someone's misdeed. To get a grip on a problem you find a lead or the knack (itoguchi, kotsu o tsukamu).

bad.s: 犯人[はんにん]はうっかり{尻尾[しっぽ]をつかんで}、捕[つか]まった。
bad.en: (meant: the culprit carelessly gave himself away and was caught)
bad.why: The one who grabs the tail is the investigator. A culprit who slips up shows his tail (shippo o dasu).

cards.mean: (of a wife) to boss her husband around
cards.lit: to sit on someone as if he were a floor cushion

use.how: Wife as subject: 妻が夫を尻に敷く, or very often the husband in the passive: 奥さんの尻に敷かれている. Light teasing, not a serious charge.

near.diff: かかあ天下 is a noun for a household where the wife rules; 尻に敷く is the verb for her doing it, usually in the passive.

cards.cue: At a family dinner your uncle reaches for a third beer, catches his wife's eye, and puts the glass back down without a word.

ctx.en: My grandfather was famously stubborn outside, but at home my grandmother ran the show.

bad.en: (meant: my father is domineering and bosses my mother around)
bad.why: It is said of a wife ruling her husband and cannot be turned round. A husband who rules the home is teishu kanpaku.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は部下[ぶか]を{尻[しり]に敷[し]いて}、無理[むり]な残業[ざんぎょう]をさせている。
bad.en: (meant: the manager pushes his staff around and makes them work unreasonable overtime)

cards.mean: to take a lesson firmly to heart
cards.lit: to engrave something on one's liver, the organ once seen as the seat of the spirit

use.how: Object is a lesson, warning or advice: 失敗を肝に銘じる. Common in apologies and resolutions: 肝に銘じます, 肝に銘じておけ.

near.diff: 心に刻む keeps a moving memory or words close to one's heart; 肝に銘じる fixes a lesson or warning so as to act on it.

cards.cue: Your careless mistake nearly caused an accident. Your supervisor warns you, and you bow and promise you will never forget the lesson.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]のこの言葉[ことば]を、{肝[きも]に銘[めい]じて}おきます。
ctx.en: I will take these words of yours firmly to heart.

ctx.s: 「今回[こんかい]の失敗[しっぱい]を{肝[きも]に銘[めい]じて}、二度[にど]と同[おな]じミスはしません。」

ctx.en: Skip the safety checks and you get a major accident. Everyone should take that firmly to heart.

ctx.en: I still keep my grandfather's rule, "Whatever you do, never borrow money," firmly in mind.

ctx.en: "Once you lose a customer's trust, it never comes back. Don't you forget it," the manager said.

ctx.s: このたびのご指摘[してき]を{肝[きも]に銘[めい]じ}、再発[さいはつ]防止[ぼうし]に努[つと]めてまいります。
ctx.en: We take your criticism to heart and will do our utmost to prevent this from happening again.

bad.s: 楽[たの]しかった旅行[りょこう]の思[おも]い出[で]を{肝[きも]に銘[めい]じた}。
bad.en: (meant: I treasured the happy memories of the trip)
bad.why: It is for lessons and warnings you must act on, not fond memories. Treasured memories are engraved on the heart (kokoro ni kizamu).

bad.s: 明日[あした]の会議[かいぎ]の時間[じかん]を{肝[きも]に銘[めい]じて}、手帳[てちょう]に書[か]いた。
bad.en: (meant: I made a note of tomorrow's meeting time in my planner)
bad.why: Far too solemn for remembering a plain fact like a meeting time. Just say you made a note of it (memo shita).

cards.mean: to have nerves of steel
cards.lit: one's liver, the seat of courage, sits firmly in place and will not be shaken

use.how: Describes a person's lasting trait, usually as 肝が据わっている or before a noun: 肝の据わった人. Admires calm under pressure.

near.diff: 度胸がある is having the nerve to dare something; 肝が据わる stresses unshakeable composure that nothing can rattle.
図太い is thick-skinned and shameless, usually a criticism; 肝が据わる is admiring.

cards.cue: A rookie nurse stays perfectly calm when a patient collapses in the waiting room, and directs everyone while the veterans freeze.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は若[わか]いのに{肝[きも]が据[す]わって}いる。
ctx.en: She's young, but she has nerves of steel.

ctx.s: 大勢[おおぜい]の前[まえ]でも全然[ぜんぜん]緊張[きんちょう]しないなんて、{肝[きも]が据[す]わってる}ね。
ctx.en: You don't get nervous at all in front of a crowd? You're really unflappable.

ctx.en: During the earthquake, the store manager guided the customers out with perfect composure.

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]なのに社長[しゃちょう]に堂々[どうどう]と意見[いけん]するとは、なかなか{肝[きも]が据[す]わった}やつだ。
ctx.en: A newcomer calmly giving the company president his opinion to his face? That kid has real nerve.

ctx.en: "How can you stay so calm?" "Maybe I take after my mother and just don't rattle easily."

bad.s: この本棚[ほんだな]は重[おも]くて{肝[きも]が据[す]わって}いるから、地震[じしん]でも倒[たお]れない。
bad.en: (meant: this bookcase is heavy and steady, so it won't fall over in an earthquake)
bad.why: It describes a person's courage and composure, never how steady an object is. A bookcase that will not tip is antei shite iru.

bad.s: 怖[こわ]い映画[えいが]を見[み]て、{肝[きも]が据[す]わった}。
bad.en: (meant: watching the horror film scared me stiff)
bad.why: It means calm courage, the opposite of fright. To get a terrible scare is kimo o hiyasu, or simply zotto shita.

cards.mean: to astound, to take someone's breath away
cards.lit: to pull out someone's liver; the do- at the front is an emphatic prefix, as in do-mannaka (dead centre)

use.how: The amazing thing or person is subject: 観客の度肝を抜く; the amazed person uses the passive: 度肝を抜かれた. For something huge, bold or spectacular.

near.diff: 目を丸くする is the wide-eyed look of a surprised person, often mild; 度肝を抜く is the overwhelming impact of something bold or spectacular.

bad.s: 突然[とつぜん]の訃報[ふほう]に{度肝[どぎも]を抜[ぬ]かれて}、涙[なみだ]が止[と]まらなかった。
bad.en: (meant: I was shocked by the sudden news of his death and couldn't stop crying)

cards.mean: to frown in disapproval of others' conduct
cards.lit: to draw one's eyebrows together into a frown

bad.en: (meant: the department head flew into a rage and shouted at his staff)

cards.mean: to straighten up and act with integrity
cards.lit: to straighten one's collar and sit up properly, as before someone one respects

cards.r: さいふのひもをしめる
cards.mean: to tighten the purse strings
cards.lit: to pull tight the drawstring of a pouch-style purse so no money gets out

cards.mean: a pittance, a tiny amount
cards.lit: a sparrow's tears: the tears of a tiny bird, almost nothing at all

use.how: A noun phrase, usually 雀の涙だ or 雀の涙ほどの X. Said of an amount, mostly money (pay, bonus, interest, compensation), that is disappointingly small.

cards.cue: Your company announces the year-end bonus, and when you see the figure, it would barely pay for one dinner out.

ctx.en: This year's bonus was a pittance.

cards.mean: a tiny patch of land
cards.lit: a cat's forehead: a cat's brow is so narrow there is hardly any room on it

ctx.en: A little café went up on a tiny plot of land in front of the station.

ctx.s: ベランダは{猫[ねこ]の額[ひたい]}ほどだが、鉢植[はちう]えを並[なら]べて楽[たの]しんでいる。
ctx.en: The balcony is tiny, but I enjoy lining it with potted plants.

bad.s: 新[あたら]しい会社[かいしゃ]の給料[きゅうりょう]は{猫[ねこ]の額[ひたい]}ほどだ。
bad.en: (meant: the pay at my new company is tiny)
bad.why: Neko no hitai is only for land or space. A tiny sum of money is suzume no namida.

bad.s: 「先生[せんせい]のお宅[たく]の庭[にわ]は{猫[ねこ]の額[ひたい]}ですね。」
bad.en: (meant, as a compliment: your garden is so cosy, sir)
bad.why: It belittles the space. Said of your own land it is modest; said to the owner about theirs it is rude.

cards.mean: on terrible terms, at daggers drawn
cards.lit: the relationship of the dog and the monkey, two animals said to fight whenever they meet

use.how: AとBは犬猿の仲だ, or Aとは犬猿の仲だ. Describes a lasting mutual hostility between two people or groups, not a single quarrel.

near.diff: 水と油 means two people or things just do not mix or fit together; 犬猿の仲 means they are openly hostile to each other.

cards.cue: Two colleagues have refused to speak to each other for years, and any meeting with both of them turns into a fight.

ctx.s: あの二人[ふたり]は{犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}だ。
ctx.en: Those two can't stand each other.

ctx.s: 兄[あに]と私[わたし]は子[こ]どもの頃[ころ]から{犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}だった。
ctx.en: My older brother and I have been at each other's throats since we were kids.

ctx.s: 「営業部[えいぎょうぶ]と開発部[かいはつぶ]って、仲[なか]が悪[わる]いの？」「うん、{犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "Do sales and development not get along?" "No, they're at daggers drawn."

ctx.s: 隣[となり]の家[いえ]とは、土地[とち]の境界[きょうかい]のことで揉[も]めて以来[いらい]、{犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}だ。
ctx.en: Ever since we fell out with the neighbours over the property line, we've been on terrible terms.

ctx.s: {犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}で知[し]られる二人[ふたり]の俳優[はいゆう]が、映画[えいが]で共演[きょうえん]することになった。
ctx.en: Two actors famous for hating each other are going to star together in a film.

ctx.s: かつて{犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}だった二[ふた]つのチームが、今回[こんかい]は手[て]を組[く]んだ。
ctx.en: Two teams that were once bitter enemies have joined forces this time.

bad.s: {犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}の二人[ふたり]は、毎日[まいにち]一緒[いっしょ]にお昼[ひる]を食[た]べている。
bad.en: (meant: the two inseparable friends have lunch together every day)
bad.why: It means the two are bitter enemies, never close friends. Inseparable friends are dai no nakayoshi.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は私[わたし]に{犬猿[けんえん]の仲[なか]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: he and I are on terrible terms)
bad.why: It names a mutual relationship: kare to watashi wa, or kare to wa, ken'en no naka da. It cannot take ni like an attitude.

cards.mean: trapped like a rat, with no way out
cards.lit: a rat caught in a sack: it can run about inside, but there is no way out

use.how: X は袋の鼠だ, X を袋の鼠にする. Said, often by the pursuer, of someone cornered with every escape cut off: a criminal, an enemy, a piece in a game.

near.diff: 八方塞がり is a situation where every option is blocked; 袋の鼠 is someone physically cornered by pursuers.

cards.cue: The police have sealed every exit of the building where the thief is hiding; there is nowhere left for him to run.

ctx.s: 出口[でぐち]はふさがれた。犯人[はんにん]はもう{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}だ。
ctx.en: The exits are blocked. The culprit is trapped now.

ctx.s: 警察[けいさつ]に囲[かこ]まれ、男[おとこ]は{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}になった。
ctx.en: Surrounded by the police, the man was trapped with no way out.

ctx.s: 「裏口[うらぐち]も押[お]さえたぞ。これで奴[やつ]は{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}だ！」
ctx.en: "We've got the back door covered too. Now he's cornered!"

ctx.s: 鬼[おに]ごっこで行[い]き止[ど]まりに逃[に]げ込[こ]んだ弟[おとうと]は、{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}だった。
ctx.en: Playing tag, my little brother ran into a dead end and was trapped.

ctx.s: 敵[てき]を谷[たに]に誘[さそ]い込[こ]んで{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}にする作戦[さくせん]だ。
ctx.en: The plan is to lure the enemy into the valley and trap them there.

ctx.s: 将棋[しょうぎ]の終盤[しゅうばん]、相手[あいて]の王[おう]は逃[に]げ道[みち]を失[うしな]い、{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}同然[どうぜん]だった。
ctx.en: Late in the shogi game, the opponent's king had lost every escape route and was as good as trapped.

bad.s: 今週[こんしゅう]は仕事[しごと]が忙[いそが]しくて、{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: I'm swamped with work this week)
bad.why: It means being cornered by pursuers with no escape, not being busy. For being swamped, say isogashikute taihen da.

bad.s: 週末[しゅうまつ]はいつも家[いえ]で{袋[ふくろ]の鼠[ねずみ]}になっている。
bad.en: (meant: I always stay holed up at home at weekends)
bad.why: Staying in by choice is not being trapped; fukuro no nezumi needs someone closing in. Staying in is ie ni komotte iru.

cards.mean: (of a business) to be deserted, with no customers
cards.lit: the cuckoo is calling: a lonely bird call heard in quiet, empty places, here in an empty shop

use.how: Usually 閑古鳥が鳴いている. Said of a shop, restaurant, hotel or attraction that has few or no customers or visitors, not of people.

near.diff: 火の車 says money is desperately short; 閑古鳥が鳴く says a place has no customers or visitors.

cards.cue: You walk past a café at lunchtime: the staff stand around with nothing to do and every table is empty.

ctx.s: あの店[みせ]はいつも{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]いている}。
ctx.en: That shop is always deserted.

ctx.s: 「新[あたら]しいレストラン、どう？」「平日[へいじつ]は{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]いてる}よ。」
ctx.en: "How's the new restaurant doing?" "On weekdays there's hardly a customer."

ctx.s: 郊外[こうがい]に大型[おおがた]スーパーができて、商店街[しょうてんがい]は{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]く}ようになった。
ctx.en: Since a big supermarket opened out of town, the shopping street has been deserted.

ctx.s: シーズンオフの温泉街[おんせんがい]には、{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]いていた}。
ctx.en: Off-season, the hot-spring town was deserted.

ctx.s: 開店[かいてん]当初[とうしょ]は{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]いていた}が、口[くち]コミで客[きゃく]が増[ふ]えた。
ctx.en: At first nobody came, but customers grew through word of mouth.

ctx.s: 値上[ねあ]げで客[きゃく]が離[はな]れ、映画館[えいがかん]は{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]く}始末[しまつ]だ。
ctx.en: Prices went up, customers stayed away, and now the cinema is practically empty.

bad.s: 引[ひ]っ越[こ]したばかりで友達[ともだち]がいなくて、{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]いている}。
bad.en: (meant: I've just moved and have no friends, so I'm lonely)
bad.why: It describes a business or place without customers, not a lonely person. For loneliness, say sabishii.

bad.s: 夜[よる]の住宅街[じゅうたくがい]は{閑古鳥[かんこどり]が鳴[な]いて}、静[しず]かで住[す]みやすい。
bad.en: (meant: the residential area is quiet at night and pleasant to live in)
bad.why: It means a place that needs customers is failing to get them, so it is never praise for peace and quiet.

cards.r: むしのいどころがわるい
cards.mean: in a bad mood and easily irritated
cards.lit: the bug inside is sitting in a bad spot, from the old idea that a bug in the body stirs one's moods

use.how: Xは虫の居所が悪い: X is in a temporary bad mood and snaps at small things. Mostly said of someone else, often with らしい, みたい or のか.

near.diff: 虫が好かない is an instinctive dislike of a particular person; 虫の居所が悪い is a passing bad mood that makes someone touchy with everyone.

cards.cue: Your usually easygoing boss snapped at you over a typo this morning, and colleagues tell you to ask for leave tomorrow instead.

ctx.s: 今日[きょう]の部長[ぶちょう]は{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]い}。
ctx.en: The department head is in a foul mood today.

ctx.s: 「今[いま]話[はな]しかけないほうがいいよ。{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]い}みたいだから。」
ctx.en: "Better not talk to him now. He seems to be in a bad mood."

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]かった}のか、些細[ささい]なことで怒鳴[どな]った。
ctx.en: My father must have been in a bad mood; he shouted over nothing.

ctx.s: 「ごめん、さっきは{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]くて}、きつく言[い]っちゃった。」
ctx.en: "Sorry, I was in a bad mood earlier and I spoke harshly."

ctx.s: 普段[ふだん]は優[やさ]しい先生[せんせい]も、その日[ひ]は{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]かった}らしい。
ctx.en: Our teacher is usually kind, but that day she was apparently out of sorts.

ctx.s: 誰[だれ]にでも{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]い}日[ひ]はあるから、気[き]にしなくていいよ。
ctx.en: Everyone has days when they're irritable, so don't let it bother you.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は生[う]まれつき{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]い}人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he's a bad-tempered person by nature)
bad.why: It is a passing mood on a particular day, not a lasting character. A bad-tempered person is okorippoi hito.

bad.s: あの人[ひと]はなんとなく{虫[むし]の居所[いどころ]が悪[わる]い}から、話[はな]したくない。
bad.en: (meant: I just don't like that person, so I don't want to talk to them)
bad.why: An instinctive dislike of someone is mushi ga sukanai. This idiom describes the mood of the irritable person themselves.

cards.mean: laying the groundwork by sounding people out
cards.lit: going round the roots: preparing a tree's roots before it is moved

story.text: Nemawashi began as a gardening term. Before a large tree is transplanted, the gardener digs around the trunk and cuts back the thick roots well before the move, so that the tree grows fine new roots close in and survives the move. The word was borrowed for quietly preparing the people involved before a plan is formally proposed.
story.source: Japanese gardening term for preparing a tree for transplanting

use.how: A noun: 根回しをする, Xに根回しする, 根回しが必要だ. Quiet, informal consultation with the people concerned before a formal decision; it can hint at backroom dealing.

near.diff: 下準備 is any preparation of things or materials; 根回し is preparing people, winning their agreement in advance.

cards.cue: Before Friday's meeting, you visit each department head one by one to explain your proposal and win their support in private.

ctx.s: 会議[かいぎ]の前[まえ]に{根[ね]回[まわ]し}をしておこう。
ctx.en: Let's lay the groundwork before the meeting.

ctx.s: 「この件[けん]、社長[しゃちょう]にはもう{根[ね]回[まわ]し}してある？」
ctx.en: "Have you already sounded out the president on this?"

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]への{根[ね]回[まわ]し}が足[た]りなかったせいで、企画[きかく]は通[とお]らなかった。
ctx.en: The plan was rejected because we hadn't done enough groundwork with the department head.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しいルールを導入[どうにゅう]するには、各部署[かくぶしょ]への{根[ね]回[まわ]し}が欠[か]かせない。
ctx.en: To introduce a new rule, you have to get every department on board beforehand.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{根[ね]回[まわ]し}がうまいので、どんな提案[ていあん]もすんなり決[き]まる。
ctx.en: He's so good at working on people beforehand that all his proposals go through smoothly.

ctx.s: 事前[じぜん]の{根[ね]回[まわ]し}もなく会議[かいぎ]で突然[とつぜん]提案[ていあん]したら、全員[ぜんいん]に反対[はんたい]された。
ctx.en: I sprang the proposal at the meeting without any groundwork, and everyone opposed it.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の前[まえ]にしっかり{根[ね]回[まわ]し}して、教科書[きょうかしょ]を全部[ぜんぶ]読[よ]んだ。
bad.en: (meant: I prepared thoroughly for the exam and read the whole textbook)
bad.why: Nemawashi is winning people over before a decision, not studying or preparing materials. Exam study is shiken benkyou.

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]で決[き]まったことを、後[あと]で全員[ぜんいん]に{根[ね]回[まわ]し}した。
bad.en: (meant: afterwards I informed everyone of what the meeting decided)
bad.why: Nemawashi happens before a decision, to win support. Passing on a decision afterwards is tsutaeru or houkoku suru.

cards.mean: to give in under strain, to cry uncle
cards.lit: to let out a cry: the sound you make when you can bear no more

use.how: Xに音を上げる: to give up or say you can't take it under hardship (training, heat, work). Often negative: 音を上げない. Here 音 is read ね, not おと.

near.diff: 弱音を吐く is voicing discouragement or complaints, possibly while carrying on; 音を上げる is actually giving in.

cards.cue: On the third day of a brutal fitness camp, a participant declares he can't take any more and packs his bag to go home.

ctx.s: 練習[れんしゅう]がきつくて、新入部員[しんにゅうぶいん]はすぐに{音[ね]を上[あ]げた}。
ctx.en: Practice was so hard that the new club members gave up straight away.

ctx.s: 「もう{音[ね]を上[あ]げた}の？まだ始[はじ]まったばかりだよ。」
ctx.en: "Giving up already? We've only just started."

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]はどんなに厳[きび]しい仕事[しごと]でも、決[けっ]して{音[ね]を上[あ]げない}。
ctx.en: However tough the job, he never throws in the towel.

ctx.s: 今年[ことし]の暑[あつ]さに{音[ね]を上[あ]げて}、ついにエアコンを買[か]った。
ctx.en: I couldn't take this year's heat any more and finally bought an air conditioner.

ctx.s: 毎晩[まいばん]の夜泣[よな]きに、さすがの母[はは]も{音[ね]を上[あ]げそう}だった。
ctx.en: With the baby crying every night, even my tough mother was close to breaking.

ctx.s: 三日[みっか]で{音[ね]を上[あ]げる}と思[おも]われていたが、彼女[かのじょ]は一年[いちねん]続[つづ]けた。
ctx.en: Everyone thought she'd quit within three days, but she kept it up for a year.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]りそうなので、ピクニックは{音[ね]を上[あ]げた}。
bad.en: (meant: it looked like rain, so we called off the picnic)
bad.why: It means breaking under strain or hardship, not a calm decision to cancel. Calling something off is chuushi ni suru.

bad.s: 合格[ごうかく]の知[し]らせに、嬉[うれ]しくて{音[ね]を上[あ]げた}。
bad.en: (meant: I cried out with joy at the news that I'd passed)
bad.why: It is the cry of someone who can't bear any more, never a cry of joy. Shouting for joy is kansei o ageru.

cards.mean: to let someone else take the credit
cards.lit: to let someone else hold the flowers: you step back so they get the glory

use.how: Xに花を持たせる: out of consideration, you let X win or take the credit, often when you could have had it. Also 花を持たせてもらう from the receiver's side.

near.diff: 顔を立てる protects someone's dignity or standing; 花を持たせる goes further and hands them the win or the credit.

cards.cue: You did most of the work on a project, but at the presentation you let your junior colleague announce the results and receive the applause.

ctx.s: 「今回[こんかい]は後輩[こうはい]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせて}あげようよ。」
ctx.en: "Let's let our junior have the glory this time."

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は将棋[しょうぎ]でわざと負[ま]けて、孫[まご]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせた}。
ctx.en: Grandfather lost at shogi on purpose to let his grandson win.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は自分[じぶん]のアイデアだったのに、部下[ぶか]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせた}。
ctx.en: It was the manager's own idea, yet he gave the credit to his subordinate.

ctx.s: 引退[いんたい]する先輩[せんぱい]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせる}ため、最後[さいご]のシュートを譲[ゆず]った。
ctx.en: To give the retiring senior player a moment of glory, I let him take the final shot.

ctx.s: 発表会[はっぴょうかい]では主役[しゅやく]を新人[しんじん]に任[まか]せて、{花[はな]を持[も]たせる}ことにした。
ctx.en: At the recital we decided to give the lead role to the newcomer and let her shine.

ctx.s: あの試合[しあい]は、先輩[せんぱい]が僕[ぼく]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせて}くれたんだと思[おも]う。
ctx.en: I think my senior let me win that match.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は私[わたし]の手柄[てがら]を奪[うば]って、自分[じぶん]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせた}。
bad.en: (meant: he stole my credit and took the glory himself)
bad.why: It means generously yielding credit to someone else. Taking another's credit is tegara o yokodori suru.

bad.s: 母[はは]の日[ひ]に、母[はは]に{花[はな]を持[も]たせた}。
bad.en: (meant: I gave my mother flowers on Mother's Day)
bad.why: Giving flowers is hana o okuru or hana o ageru. Hana o motaseru is heard as letting someone take the credit.

cards.mean: something or someone far out of one's reach
cards.lit: a flower on a high peak: you can see it and admire it, but you cannot climb up to pick it

use.how: Xは(私には)高嶺の花だ. Said of something or someone you admire and want but cannot hope to get: a luxury item, a home, a person you have a crush on.

ctx.s: あのブランドのバッグは、私[わたし]には{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だ。
ctx.en: That designer bag is way out of my reach.

ctx.s: 「都心[としん]のマンションなんて、{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だよ。」
ctx.en: "A flat in central Tokyo? That's just a dream."

ctx.s: クラスで一番[いちばん]人気[にんき]の彼女[かのじょ]は、僕[ぼく]にとって{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だった。
ctx.en: The most popular girl in class was completely out of my league.

ctx.s: 一度[いちど]は乗[の]ってみたいけれど、ファーストクラスは{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だ。
ctx.en: I'd love to fly first class once, but it's far beyond my means.

ctx.s: かつては{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だった海外旅行[かいがいりょこう]も、今[いま]では身近[みぢか]になった。
ctx.en: Travelling abroad, once out of reach for most people, is now commonplace.

ctx.s: 社内[しゃない]の{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}と言[い]われていた先輩[せんぱい]が、結婚[けっこん]を発表[はっぴょう]した。
ctx.en: The colleague everyone at work considered out of their league announced her marriage.

bad.s: やっと買[か]った新車[しんしゃ]は、私[わたし]の{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: the new car I finally bought is my pride and joy)
bad.why: It is something out of reach; once you own it, it no longer is. A car you are proud of is jiman no kuruma.

bad.s: この数学[すうがく]の問題[もんだい]は難[むずか]しすぎて、{高嶺[たかね]の花[はな]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: this maths problem is too hard for me to solve)
bad.why: It is for something you desire and admire, not a task that is too hard. A problem beyond you is te ni oenai.

cards.mean: to dawdle on the way
cards.lit: to eat the grass by the road, like a horse that keeps stopping to graze instead of walking on

use.how: Predicate with the dawdler as subject, about lingering on the way somewhere you should go straight to: 帰りに道草を食う. Often a scolding or a wry admission.

near.diff: 寄り道 is simply stopping off somewhere on the way; 道草を食う stresses the time idled away when you should have come straight.

cards.cue: Your son should have been home from school an hour ago. He finally walks in after hanging around the park with his friends.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもが学校[がっこう]の帰[かえ]りに{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]って}、なかなか帰[かえ]ってこない。
ctx.en: My kid is dawdling on the way home from school and still isn't back.

ctx.s: 「どこで{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]ってたの}？もう七時[しちじ]よ。」
ctx.en: "Where have you been dawdling? It's already seven."

ctx.s: 本屋[ほんや]で{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]った}せいで、約束[やくそく]の時間[じかん]に遅[おく]れてしまった。
ctx.en: I lingered in a bookshop on the way and ended up late for the appointment.

ctx.s: お使[つか]いを頼[たの]まれたら、{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]わずに}まっすぐ帰[かえ]ってきなさい。
ctx.en: When you're sent on an errand, come straight back without dawdling.

ctx.s: 配達[はいたつ]の途中[とちゅう]で{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]う}ことは、規則[きそく]で禁止[きんし]されている。
ctx.en: Dawdling in the middle of a delivery round is against the rules.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は大学[だいがく]を出[で]てから少[すこ]し{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]って}、三十歳[さんじゅっさい]で教師[きょうし]になった。
ctx.en: After university he took a bit of a detour in life and became a teacher at thirty.

bad.s: 渋滞[じゅうたい]に巻[ま]き込[こ]まれて、二時間[にじかん]も{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]った}。
bad.en: (meant: I was stuck in a traffic jam for two hours)
bad.why: It means lingering by your own choice. Being held up against your will is ashidome o kuu, or juutai ni hamaru for traffic.

bad.s: 母[はは]に頼[たの]まれて、郵便局[ゆうびんきょく]に{道草[みちくさ]を食[く]って}から帰[かえ]った。
bad.en: (meant: I stopped at the post office, as my mother asked, before coming home)
bad.why: An errand you were asked to run is not idle dawdling, and the idiom takes no destination. Say yuubinkyoku ni yotte kara.

cards.mean: to ride a wave of success
cards.lit: to ride on a wave, carried forward by its force like a surfer

use.how: Predicate, often 波に乗っている: said of a person, team or business whose run of success keeps carrying it forward. Also 時代の波に乗る, to ride a trend.

near.diff: 調子に乗る is getting carried away and cocky, a criticism; 波に乗る is having real momentum.
軌道に乗る is a project settling into running smoothly; 波に乗る is riding a run of success or a trend.

cards.cue: A small startup's first app took off, the second sold even better, and now everything it launches seems to succeed.

ctx.s: 今[いま]のチームは{波[なみ]に乗[の]っていて}、五連勝中[ごれんしょうちゅう]だ。
ctx.en: The team is on a roll right now, with five straight wins.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]、{波[なみ]に乗[の]ってる}ね。」「うん、仕事[しごと]も恋愛[れんあい]も順調[じゅんちょう]なんだ。」
ctx.en: "You're on a roll lately." "Yeah, work and love are both going well."

ctx.s: あの会社[かいしゃ]はネット通販[つうはん]の{波[なみ]に乗[の]って}急成長[きゅうせいちょう]した。
ctx.en: That company grew rapidly by riding the wave of online shopping.

ctx.s: 一点目[いってんめ]が入[はい]ってからは、チーム全体[ぜんたい]が{波[なみ]に乗[の]った}。
ctx.en: Once the first goal went in, the whole team found its momentum.

ctx.s: デビュー曲[きょく]がヒットすると、彼女[かのじょ]はその{波[なみ]に乗[の]って}次々[つぎつぎ]と新曲[しんきょく]を出[だ]した。
ctx.en: When her debut song became a hit, she rode that wave and released one new song after another.

ctx.s: せっかく{波[なみ]に乗[の]りかけた}のに、けがで休[やす]むことになった。
ctx.en: Just when I was starting to get on a roll, an injury forced me to sit out.

bad.s: 不景気[ふけいき]の{波[なみ]に乗[の]って}、会社[かいしゃ]が倒産[とうさん]した。
bad.en: (meant: swept away by the recession, the company went bankrupt)
bad.why: It means being carried on to success. Being overwhelmed by a wave of hard times is nami ni nomareru.

bad.s: 少[すこ]し褒[ほ]められたくらいで{波[なみ]に乗[の]る}なよ。
bad.en: (meant: don't get cocky just because you got a little praise)
bad.why: Getting cocky is choushi ni noru. Nami ni noru is having real momentum, not something you scold someone for.

cards.mean: (of finances) desperately tight
cards.lit: a cart of fire: a budget as agonising as riding a burning cart

story.text: The phrase is the native Japanese reading of the Buddhist word kasha, the burning cart in which the wardens of hell carry sinners off to torment. Riding it is unending agony, and that agony came to stand for the constant pain of a household that cannot make ends meet.
story.source: Buddhist term kasha, the fiery cart of hell

use.how: Predicate with だ about money: 家計は火の車だ, 台所は火の車. Said of a household's or a business's finances, often wryly about one's own.

near.diff: 金欠 is a casual word for being short of cash yourself; 火の車 describes the finances of a household or business as desperately strained.

cards.cue: With a new baby, rising rent and only one salary, a couple can barely pay the bills each month. How do they describe their finances?

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもが三人[さんにん]もいて、うちの家計[かけい]はいつも{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}だ。
ctx.en: With three kids, our household budget is always stretched to breaking point.

ctx.s: 「旅行[りょこう]、行[い]かない？」「無理[むり]。引[ひ]っ越[こ]したばかりで、うちは今[いま]{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}なんだ。」
ctx.en: "Want to go on a trip?" "Can't. We've just moved, and money is really tight at home right now."

ctx.s: 売[う]り上[あ]げが落[お]ち込[こ]み、店[みせ]の経営[けいえい]は{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}になった。
ctx.en: Sales slumped and the shop's finances got desperate.

ctx.s: 祖母[そぼ]は、戦後[せんご]の{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}の暮[く]らしを笑[わら]って話[はな]してくれた。
ctx.en: My grandmother laughed as she told me about her hand-to-mouth life after the war.

ctx.s: 外[そと]からは派手[はで]に見[み]えるが、あの会社[かいしゃ]の内情[ないじょう]は{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}らしい。
ctx.en: It looks flashy from outside, but apparently that company's finances are in dire straits.

ctx.s: 住宅[じゅうたく]ローンと学費[がくひ]が重[かさ]なって、我[わ]が家[や]の台所[だいどころ]は{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}です。
ctx.en: With the mortgage and school fees coming at once, our household budget is in desperate shape.

bad.s: 締[し]め切[き]り前[まえ]で、毎日[まいにち]仕事[しごと]が{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: with the deadline coming, work is hectic every day)
bad.why: It is only about money. For being swamped with work say me ga mawaru hodo isogashii.

bad.s: 父[ちち]は顔[かお]を真[ま]っ赤[か]にして{火[ひ]の車[くるま]}のように怒[おこ]った。
bad.en: (meant: my father went red in the face and raged like fire)
bad.why: The fire is the torment of poverty, not anger. For a furious outburst say kankan ni okotta.

cards.r: ひをみるよりあきらか
cards.mean: as clear as day
cards.lit: clearer than looking at a fire: as plain as a blaze in front of your eyes

story.text: The image is traced to the Chinese Book of Documents. In the chapter Pan Geng, the king addressing his officials says, "I see it as plainly as one looks at a fire." Japanese built on this to say that something is even clearer than looking at fire.

use.how: Predicate in …のは火を見るより明らかだ, about a result or fact anyone can foresee, often a bad one: 失敗するのは火を見るより明らかだ.

near.diff: 一目瞭然 is what one glance at a chart or a room makes plain; 火を見るより明らか is mostly an outcome anyone can foresee.

cards.cue: Your friend plans to run a marathon next week without any training. You say there is no doubt at all how that will end.

ctx.s: 練習[れんしゅう]もしないで出[で]たら、負[ま]けるのは{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}だ。
ctx.en: If you go in without practising, it's as clear as day that you'll lose.

ctx.s: このまま値上[ねあ]げを続[つづ]ければ、客[きゃく]が離[はな]れるのは{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}です。
ctx.en: If we keep raising prices like this, it's plain as day that customers will leave.

ctx.s: ゲームばかりして勉強[べんきょう]しない弟[おとうと]が、試験[しけん]で苦労[くろう]するのは{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}だった。
ctx.en: It was obvious that my brother, who did nothing but play games, would struggle in the exams.

ctx.s: 結果[けっか]は{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}なのに、なぜ誰[だれ]も止[と]めなかったのか。
ctx.en: The outcome was plain as day, so why did nobody stop it?

ctx.s: このまま残業[ざんぎょう]が続[つづ]けば、社員[しゃいん]が倒[たお]れるのは{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}で、すぐに人[ひと]を増[ふ]やすべきだ。
ctx.en: If this overtime goes on, it's perfectly obvious staff will collapse; we should hire more people right away.

ctx.s: 子[こ]どもが減[へ]り続[つづ]ければ、地方[ちほう]の学校[がっこう]が消[き]えていくのは{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}である。
ctx.en: If the number of children keeps falling, it is evident that rural schools will disappear.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は雲[くも]ひとつなく、空[そら]が{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}だ。
bad.en: (meant: there isn't a cloud today and the sky is crystal clear)
bad.why: It says a fact or outcome is beyond doubt, not that anything looks bright. For a clear sky say sora ga sumikitte iru.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]の説明[せつめい]は{火[ひ]を見[み]るより明[あき]らか}で、とてもわかりやすかった。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher's explanation was very clear and easy to follow)
bad.why: It says a conclusion is obvious, not that an explanation is easy to follow. Say setsumei ga meikai datta.

cards.mean: to face harsh criticism
cards.lit: the wind hits hard, like a lone tree on an exposed hill taking the full force of the wind

use.how: Predicate with the target marked by への or に対する: 会社への風当たりが強い. Said of ongoing criticism and pressure from the public, the media or those around someone.

near.diff: 批判を浴びる is being criticised over one incident; 風当たりが強い is a continuing climate of hostility toward someone.
肩身が狭い is feeling ashamed and small among others; 風当たりが強い is the pressure itself coming from outside.

cards.cue: After a scandal, a company faces angry headlines, complaints online and pressure from shareholders, week after week.

ctx.s: 不祥事[ふしょうじ]が続[つづ]いて、会社[かいしゃ]への{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]く}なっている。
ctx.en: After a string of scandals, criticism of the company is getting fiercer.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい監督[かんとく]は負[ま]けが続[つづ]き、ファンからの{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]い}。
ctx.en: The new manager keeps losing, and the fans are giving him a hard time.

ctx.s: 「社長[しゃちょう]の息子[むすこ]だと、{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]い}んじゃない？」「うん、何[なに]をしても言[い]われるよ。」
ctx.en: "Being the president's son, don't you get a lot of flak?" "Yeah, whatever I do, people talk."

ctx.s: 運賃[うんちん]の値上[ねあ]げを発表[はっぴょう]した鉄道会社[てつどうがいしゃ]に対[たい]する{風当[かぜあ]たりは強[つよ]い}。
ctx.en: The railway company that announced the fare rise is facing heavy criticism.

ctx.s: 最近[さいきん]は、たばこを吸[す]う人[ひと]への{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]い}。
ctx.en: These days smokers face a lot of disapproval.

ctx.s: 前例[ぜんれい]のない挑戦[ちょうせん]をすれば、{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]い}のは覚悟[かくご]の上[うえ]だ。
ctx.en: If you try something unprecedented, you go in braced for plenty of flak.

bad.s: 新曲[しんきょく]が大[だい]ヒットして、ファンからの{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]い}。
bad.en: (meant: the new song is a huge hit and the fans are strongly behind us)
bad.why: Kazeatari is hostile pressure, never support. For strong backing say fan kara no shiji ga atsui.

bad.s: 部長[ぶちょう]は誰[だれ]に対[たい]しても{風当[かぜあ]たりが強[つよ]い}人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: the manager is harsh with everyone)
bad.why: Kazeatari is the pressure a person receives, not what they dish out. Someone harsh with others is atari ga kitsui or kibishii.

cards.mean: to outwit by doing the opposite of what is expected
cards.lit: to get at the reverse side: to strike where an opponent is not guarding

use.how: Takes the person outwitted: 相手の裏をかく, or passive 裏をかかれる. Said of games, sport, crime and business, where one side reads and foils the other's expectations.

near.diff: 出し抜く is getting ahead of others by acting first or on the sly; 裏をかく is beating someone by doing the opposite of what they expect.
裏切る is betraying someone's trust; 裏をかく is outsmarting an opponent, with no trust broken.

cards.cue: Everyone expected the penalty taker to shoot to the left, as he always does. He calmly shot to the right instead and scored.

ctx.s: 「次[つぎ]はグーを出[だ]すと思[おも]ったでしょ。」「やられた、{裏[うら]をかかれた}！」
ctx.en: "You thought I'd throw rock next, didn't you?" "Argh, you caught me out!"

ctx.s: 左[ひだり]を狙[ねら]うと見[み]せかけて、キーパーの{裏[うら]をかいて}右[みぎ]に決[き]めた。
ctx.en: He made as if to aim left, wrong-footed the keeper and put it in on the right.

ctx.s: 犯人[はんにん]は警察[けいさつ]の{裏[うら]をかいて}、正面[しょうめん]から堂々[どうどう]と逃[に]げた。
ctx.en: The criminal outwitted the police and walked boldly out the front.

ctx.s: 慎重[しんちょう]な彼[かれ]がまさか{裏[うら]をかかれる}とは、誰[だれ]も思[おも]わなかった。
ctx.en: No one imagined that someone as careful as he was could be outfoxed.

ctx.s: 将棋[しょうぎ]の名人[めいじん]は、相手[あいて]の{裏[うら]をかく}一手[いって]で形勢[けいせい]を逆転[ぎゃくてん]した。
ctx.en: The shogi master turned the game around with a move his opponent never saw coming.

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]は毎年[まいとし]同[おな]じ形式[けいしき]だったが、今年[ことし]は{裏[うら]をかかれて}全[まった]く違[ちが]う問題[もんだい]が出[で]た。
ctx.en: The exam had the same format every year, but this year they caught us out with completely different questions.

bad.s: 長年[ながねん]の親友[しんゆう]の{裏[うら]をかいて}、秘密[ひみつ]をみんなにばらした。
bad.en: (meant: I betrayed my old friend and told everyone the secret)
bad.why: It is outsmarting an opponent's expectations, not breaking a friend's trust. Betrayal is uragiru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の言葉[ことば]の{裏[うら]をかいて}、本当[ほんとう]の気持[きも]ちを探[さぐ]った。
bad.en: (meant: I read between the lines of what he said to find his real feelings)
bad.why: Reading the hidden meaning behind words is kotoba no ura o yomu. Ura o kaku is acting against expectations to beat someone.

cards.mean: unconventional, breaking the mould
cards.lit: breaking the form: going beyond the set forms (kata) that an art or craft hands down

use.how: Na-adjective or noun: 型破りな発想, 型破りの人物. Describes people, ideas and methods that ignore convention, usually with admiration.

near.diff: 常識外れ criticises behaviour that lacks common sense; 型破り describes a bold break with convention, usually admired.

cards.cue: A new head chef serves traditional kaiseki dishes in a completely new order and style, and critics call it bold and fresh.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は{型破[かたやぶ]り}な先生[せんせい]で、授業[じゅぎょう]を外[そと]でやることもある。
ctx.en: He's an unconventional teacher who sometimes holds class outdoors.

ctx.s: 「あの監督[かんとく]の作戦[さくせん]、{型破[かたやぶ]り}だね。」「うん、でも結果[けっか]は出[だ]してる。」
ctx.en: "That coach's tactics are really unorthodox." "Yeah, but he gets results."

ctx.s: 新人[しんじん]の{型破[かたやぶ]り}な企画[きかく]が、会議[かいぎ]で一番[いちばん]の評価[ひょうか]を得[え]た。
ctx.en: A newcomer's unconventional proposal got the highest marks at the meeting.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]は{型破[かたやぶ]り}な経営[けいえい]で、小[ちい]さな町工場[まちこうば]を世界的[せかいてき]な企業[きぎょう]に育[そだ]てた。
ctx.en: With unconventional management, the president grew a small local workshop into a global company.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は当時[とうじ]としては{型破[かたやぶ]り}な人[ひと]で、六十歳[ろくじゅっさい]で大学[だいがく]に入[はい]った。
ctx.en: My grandfather was unconventional for his time: he started university at sixty.

ctx.s: 伝統[でんとう]を学[まな]び尽[つ]くした上[うえ]での{型破[かたやぶ]り}だからこそ、彼[かれ]の舞台[ぶたい]は高[たか]く評価[ひょうか]されている。
ctx.en: His stage work is highly praised precisely because he breaks the mould only after mastering the tradition.

bad.s: 雨[あめ]のせいで、せっかくの計画[けいかく]が{型破[かたやぶ]り}になった。
bad.en: (meant: the rain ruined our carefully made plans)
bad.why: It is a bold break with convention, not a ruin. A spoiled plan is dainashi ni natta.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は友達[ともだち]との約束[やくそく]を{型破[かたやぶ]り}した。
bad.en: (meant: he broke his promise to his friend)
bad.why: Katayaburi is a noun and na-adjective, not a verb taking an object. Breaking a promise is yakusoku o yabutta.

cards.mean: (of a complaint) aimed at the wrong person
cards.lit: the wrong gate: calling at the gate of a house other than the one you mean

use.how: Predicate with だ, or before の/な: 私に文句を言うのはお門違いだ. Rejects a complaint, request or expectation aimed at someone who is not responsible.

near.diff: 見当違い is any guess or judgement that misses the mark; お門違い is directing blame or a request at the wrong person.

cards.cue: A customer shouts at the shop's part-time cleaner about the head office's new prices, which the cleaner had nothing to do with.

ctx.s: 決[き]めたのは部長[ぶちょう]なんだから、私[わたし]に文句[もんく]を言[い]うのは{お門違[かどちが]い}だよ。
ctx.en: It was the department head who decided, so complaining to me is barking up the wrong tree.

ctx.s: 「なんで止[と]めてくれなかったの？」「私[わたし]を責[せ]めるのは{お門違[かどちが]い}でしょう。」
ctx.en: "Why didn't you stop me?" "Don't blame me; I'm not the one responsible."

ctx.s: 法律[ほうりつ]の相談[そうだん]なら、医者[いしゃ]の私[わたし]に聞[き]くのは{お門違[かどちが]い}ですよ。
ctx.en: If it's legal advice you want, asking me, a doctor, is going to the wrong person.

ctx.s: 店員[てんいん]に怒鳴[どな]っても、それは{お門違[かどちが]い}の怒[いか]りだ。
ctx.en: Yelling at the shop assistant is anger aimed at the wrong person.

ctx.s: 家庭[かてい]のしつけまで学校[がっこう]に求[もと]めるのは{お門違[かどちが]い}だという意見[いけん]もある。
ctx.en: Some argue that expecting schools to handle children's upbringing at home is looking in the wrong place.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は自分[じぶん]の失敗[しっぱい]を棚[たな]に上[あ]げて、{お門違[かどちが]い}な批判[ひはん]を部下[ぶか]にぶつけた。
ctx.en: Ignoring his own mistake, he aimed misplaced criticism at his subordinates.

bad.s: 私[わたし]と兄[あに]は、音楽[おんがく]の好[この]みが{お門違[かどちが]い}だ。
bad.en: (meant: my brother and I have different tastes in music)
bad.why: It does not mean 'different'; it says blame or a request is aimed at the wrong person. For differing tastes say konomi ga chigau.

bad.s: ぼんやりしていて、{お門違[かどちが]い}の駅[えき]で降[お]りてしまった。
bad.en: (meant: I wasn't paying attention and got off at the wrong station)
bad.why: Today it is used for blame or requests sent to the wrong person, not for getting a place wrong. Say chigau eki de orita.

cards.mean: a guess that hits someone's secret exactly
cards.lit: the bull's-eye: the black dot at the very centre of a target

story.text: In archery, zuboshi is the name of the black dot at the centre of the target, the spot every archer aims for. To hit it is to hit exactly what you aimed at, and from there the word came to mean a guess that lands squarely on what someone was trying to hide.
story.source: Japanese archery term for the centre of the target

use.how: As 図星だ (that hit home), 図星を指す (to guess someone's secret) or 図星を指される (to be found out). Said about someone's hidden feelings, motives or situation.

near.diff: 的を射る praises a remark that grasps the point of an issue; 図星 is guessing exactly what someone was hiding.

cards.cue: Your friend insists she isn't upset, and you say, "You're jealous, aren't you?" She goes red and says nothing.

ctx.s: 「もしかして、寝坊[ねぼう]した？」「…{図星[ずぼし]}です。」
ctx.en: "Did you oversleep, by any chance?" "...Guilty as charged."

ctx.s: 「好[す]きな人[ひと]がいるんでしょう？」と聞[き]かれ、{図星[ずぼし]}だったので顔[かお]が赤[あか]くなった。
ctx.en: When I was asked, "There's someone you like, isn't there?", it was spot on, and I went red.

ctx.s: 急[きゅう]に怒[おこ]り出[だ]したところを見[み]ると、どうやら{図星[ずぼし]}だったらしい。
ctx.en: Judging by how suddenly he got angry, I seem to have hit the nail on the head.

ctx.s: 「本当[ほんとう]は行[い]きたくないんでしょ。」と母[はは]に{図星[ずぼし]を指[さ]され}、私[わたし]は黙[だま]ってしまった。
ctx.en: "You don't really want to go, do you?" My mother had seen right through me, and I fell silent.

ctx.s: 占[うらな]い師[し]の言葉[ことば]がことごとく{図星[ずぼし]}で、少[すこ]し怖[こわ]くなった。
ctx.en: Everything the fortune-teller said hit home, and I got a little scared.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は勘[かん]が鋭[するど]く、僕[ぼく]が何[なに]か隠[かく]していると、すぐに{図星[ずぼし]を指[さ]して}くる。
ctx.en: She has sharp intuition: whenever I'm hiding something, she guesses exactly what it is straight away.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の推測[すいそく]は{図星[ずぼし]}で、全然[ぜんぜん]違[ちが]っていた。
bad.en: (meant: his guess was way off)
bad.why: Zuboshi means the guess hit exactly. A guess that misses is kentouchigai or matohazure.

bad.s: 僕[ぼく]は彼女[かのじょ]の気持[きも]ちを{図星[ずぼし]した}。
bad.en: (meant: I guessed her feelings exactly)
bad.why: Zuboshi is a noun and cannot take suru. Say zuboshi o sashita, or kimochi o iiateta.

cards.mean: in rapid-fire succession
cards.lit: quick at fitting the next arrow: an archer notching another arrow the moment the last one flies

use.how: Adverb 矢継ぎ早に or before の: 矢継ぎ早に質問する, 矢継ぎ早の指示. Said of questions, orders or measures coming one after another with no pause.

near.diff: 次々 is one after another at any pace; 矢継ぎ早 stresses that there is no pause between them, often overwhelmingly.

cards.cue: At the press conference reporters fire one question after another at the coach, never letting him finish a single answer.

ctx.s: 記者[きしゃ]たちは監督[かんとく]に{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]に}質問[しつもん]を浴[あ]びせた。
ctx.en: The reporters fired question after question at the coach.

ctx.s: 「ちょっと待[ま]って、そんなに{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]に}言[い]われても覚[おぼ]えられないよ。」
ctx.en: "Hold on, I can't remember it all if you rattle things off that fast."

ctx.s: 面接官[めんせつかん]から{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]に}聞[き]かれて、頭[あたま]が真[ま]っ白[しろ]になった。
ctx.en: The interviewer hit me with question after question, and my mind went blank.

ctx.s: 店長[てんちょう]の{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]の}指示[しじ]に、新人[しんじん]はついていけなかった。
ctx.en: The new employee couldn't keep up with the manager's rapid-fire instructions.

ctx.s: 久[ひさ]しぶりに帰省[きせい]すると、祖母[そぼ]から近況[きんきょう]を{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]に}尋[たず]ねられた。
ctx.en: When I went home for the first time in ages, my grandmother peppered me with questions about my life.

ctx.s: 新社長[しんしゃちょう]は就任[しゅうにん]するなり、{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]に}改革[かいかく]を打[う]ち出[だ]した。
ctx.en: The moment the new president took office, he rolled out one reform after another.

bad.s: 遅刻[ちこく]しそうだったので、駅[えき]まで{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]に}走[はし]った。
bad.en: (meant: I was about to be late, so I ran to the station as fast as I could)
bad.why: It is for many things coming one after another, not one fast action. Say zensokuryoku de hashitta.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は何[なん]でもすぐ決[き]めたがる{矢継[やつ]ぎ早[ばや]な}人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he's an impatient person who wants to decide everything at once)
bad.why: It describes a rapid series of questions or actions, not a person's character. An impatient person is sekkachi na hito.

cards.mean: to work oneself to the bone
cards.lit: to grind one's own body into powder

use.how: Mostly 身を粉にして + 働く / 尽くす: long, tireless, self-sacrificing labour, usually for others. Said with respect, often of parents.

near.diff: 骨を折る is taking trouble over one task or for someone's sake; 身を粉にする is grinding labour kept up over a long time.

cards.cue: Your grandmother ran a shop for forty years, open from dawn to night with no holidays, so her children could go to school.

ctx.s: 母[はは]は家族[かぞく]のために{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}働[はたら]いた。
ctx.en: My mother worked herself to the bone for the family.

ctx.s: 「{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}働[はたら]いても、給料[きゅうりょう]はちっとも上[あ]がらない。」
ctx.en: "However hard I slave away, my pay never goes up."

ctx.s: 父[ちち]は{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}働[はたら]き、私[わたし]たち三人[さんにん]を大学[だいがく]に行[い]かせてくれた。
ctx.en: My father worked himself to the bone and put the three of us through university.

ctx.s: 祖父[そふ]は戦後[せんご]、町[まち]の復興[ふっこう]のために{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}尽[つ]くした。
ctx.en: After the war, my grandfather wore himself out working to rebuild the town.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は被災地[ひさいち]で、{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}支援[しえん]活動[かつどう]を続[つづ]けた。
ctx.en: In the disaster zone she kept up the relief work, never sparing herself.

ctx.s: 会社[かいしゃ]のために{身[み]を粉[こ]にする}時代[じだい]は、もう終[お]わったのかもしれない。
ctx.en: The days of wearing yourself out for the company may already be over.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は週末[しゅうまつ]、{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}遊[あそ]んだ。
bad.en: (meant: he played as hard as he could at the weekend)
bad.why: It is self-sacrificing toil, for work or for others. Using it for having fun sounds absurd.

bad.s: 昨日[きのう]は三十分[さんじゅっぷん]だけ{身[み]を粉[こ]にして}勉強[べんきょう]した。
bad.en: (meant: yesterday I studied hard for half an hour)
bad.why: It describes exhausting, self-sacrificing toil over a long stretch. Half an hour of study is far too small for it.

cards.mean: so blunt that all nuance and tact are lost
cards.lit: neither the body of the box nor its lid: nothing left to hold or cover the contents

use.how: それを言ったら身も蓋もない / 身も蓋もない言い方: a remark so bald that it leaves no tact, hope or charm, even if it is true. A mild complaint.

near.diff: 元も子もない is losing everything you had gained; 身も蓋もない is putting something so bluntly that nothing tactful is left.

cards.cue: A friend dreams of becoming an actor, and his uncle says flatly that only looks and connections matter in that business.

ctx.s: 「それを言[い]ったら{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}よ。」
ctx.en: "Well, if you put it that bluntly, there's nothing left to say."

ctx.s: 「顔[かお]がいい人[ひと]が得[とく]をする」なんて、{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}話[はなし]だ。
ctx.en: "Good-looking people come out ahead": what a brutally blunt thing to say.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]の{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}言[い]い方[かた]に、学生[がくせい]たちは黙[だま]ってしまった。
ctx.en: The students fell silent at the teacher's blunt way of putting it.

ctx.s: 「結局[けっきょく]はお金[かね]」と言[い]えば{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}が、それが本音[ほんね]だ。
ctx.en: Saying "in the end it's about money" sounds crude, but that's the honest truth.

ctx.s: 恋愛[れんあい]小説[しょうせつ]の結末[けつまつ]を「ただの勘違[かんちが]い」とまとめるのは{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}。
ctx.en: Summing up the ending of a love story as "just a misunderstanding" takes all the romance out of it.

ctx.s: その評論家[ひょうろんか]は、人気[にんき]作品[さくひん]を{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もなく}切[き]り捨[す]てた。
ctx.en: The critic dismissed the popular work with bald, tactless bluntness.

bad.s: 無理[むり]をして体[からだ]を壊[こわ]したら{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}。
bad.en: (meant: if you overdo it and ruin your health, you lose everything)
bad.why: That is moto mo ko mo nai. Mi mo futa mo nai is about something said too bluntly, not about losing what you had.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{身[み]も蓋[ふた]もない}人[ひと]なので、とても信頼[しんらい]できる。
bad.en: (meant: he is refreshingly frank, so I trust him)
bad.why: It complains that bluntness has killed all tact. It is never praise for honesty.

cards.mean: to take the lead in organising something
cards.lit: to take the ondo: to be the one who plays or sings the first phrase that the others follow

story.text: In gagaku, Japan's court music, the ondo was the lead wind player, who played the opening phrase alone before the rest of the ensemble came in. The word later came to mean the lead singer in group folk songs, who sings the first line so that everyone else can follow. To take the ondo is to start the others off together.

use.how: Xの音頭を取る / 音頭を取って: to be the one who gets a group started on a joint action. Very common: 乾杯の音頭を取る.

near.diff: 先頭に立つ is being out in front and leading by example; 音頭を取る is calling a group together and starting them off.

cards.cue: At the year-end party, the most senior person raises a glass and says a few words so that everyone can drink together.

ctx.s: 部長[ぶちょう]が乾杯[かんぱい]の{音頭[おんど]を取[と]った}。
ctx.en: The department head led the toast.

ctx.s: 「では、田中[たなか]さんに乾杯[かんぱい]の{音頭[おんど]を取[と]って}いただきます。」
ctx.en: "And now, Mr Tanaka will lead us in a toast."

ctx.s: 町内会長[ちょうないかいちょう]が{音頭[おんど]を取[と]って}、川[かわ]のごみ拾[ひろ]いが始[はじ]まった。
ctx.en: With the head of the neighbourhood association taking the lead, a river litter clean-up got going.

ctx.s: 「誰[だれ]かが{音頭[おんど]を取[と]らない}と、同窓会[どうそうかい]なんて開[ひら]けないよ。」
ctx.en: "Unless someone takes charge of organising it, a class reunion will never happen."

ctx.s: その運動[うんどう]は、地元[じもと]の高校生[こうこうせい]たちが{音頭[おんど]を取[と]る}形[かたち]で広[ひろ]がった。
ctx.en: The movement spread, with local high-school students leading the way.

ctx.s: 政府[せいふ]が{音頭[おんど]を取[と]り}、各社[かくしゃ]が共同[きょうどう]で研究[けんきゅう]を進[すす]めている。
ctx.en: With the government spearheading it, the companies are carrying out joint research.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]はマラソンで最初[さいしょ]から{音頭[おんど]を取[と]った}。
bad.en: (meant: he led the marathon from the start)
bad.why: It means getting a group to act together, not being in front of the others in a race.

bad.s: 休[やす]みの日[ひ]に、一人[ひとり]で部屋[へや]の掃除[そうじ]の{音頭[おんど]を取[と]った}。
bad.en: (meant: on my day off I took charge of cleaning my room by myself)
bad.why: It means starting a group off on something together. With no one else involved there is nobody to lead.

cards.mean: to get in first, to forestall
cards.lit: to play sente: to make the first move on the board

story.text: In go and shogi, sente is the player who moves first, and also a move the opponent is forced to answer. The player who plays sente holds the initiative and makes the other side respond. Everyday Japanese borrowed the image: to make your move before a rival or a problem can make theirs.

use.how: 先手を打つ / 先手を打って～する: acting early on purpose to head off a rival or a problem. Passive: ライバルに先手を打たれた.

near.diff: 先を越す is just getting there before someone; 先手を打つ is a deliberate early move to block a rival or a problem.

cards.cue: Hearing that a competitor will cut prices next month, a shop lowers its own prices this week.

ctx.s: 渋滞[じゅうたい]を予想[よそう]して、{先手[せんて]を打[う]って}早[はや]めに家[いえ]を出[で]た。
ctx.en: Expecting traffic jams, I got ahead of them and left home early.

ctx.s: 「文句[もんく]を言[い]われる前[まえ]に、{先手[せんて]を打[う]って}謝[あやま]っておこう。」
ctx.en: "Let's get in first and apologise before they complain."

ctx.s: 「値上[ねあ]げの噂[うわさ]があるから、{先手[せんて]を打[う]って}今[いま]のうちに買[か]っておく。」
ctx.en: "There's talk of a price rise, so I'm getting ahead of it and buying now."

ctx.s: ライバル会社[がいしゃ]に{先手[せんて]を打[う]たれて}、新商品[しんしょうひん]の話題[わだい]をさらわれた。
ctx.en: A rival company got in first and stole all the attention from our new product.

ctx.s: 市[し]は大雨[おおあめ]に備[そな]え、{先手[せんて]を打[う]って}避難所[ひなんじょ]を開[ひら]いた。
ctx.en: Ahead of the heavy rain, the city opened its shelters in advance.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{先手[せんて]を打[う]って}、出[で]そうな質問[しつもん]への答[こた]えを資料[しりょう]に入[い]れておいた。
ctx.en: She forestalled them by putting answers to the likely questions into her handout.

bad.s: 問題[もんだい]が起[お]きてから、すぐに{先手[せんて]を打[う]った}。
bad.en: (meant: once the problem happened, I acted quickly)
bad.why: Sente means acting before the trouble or the rival moves. Reacting after the fact is the opposite: gote ni mawaru.

bad.s: 今朝[けさ]は一番[いちばん]に{先手[せんて]を打[う]って}駅[えき]に着[つ]いた。
bad.en: (meant: this morning I got to the station first)
bad.why: Simply arriving before others is not it. It means a deliberate early move made to block a rival or a problem.

cards.mean: to fall behind and be left reacting
cards.lit: to end up as gote, the second player, who can only answer the other's moves

story.text: In go and shogi, gote is the player who moves second, and more broadly the side forced to answer the opponent's moves instead of following its own plan. To fall into gote is to lose the initiative. The phrase passed into everyday speech for anyone left scrambling to respond to events.

use.how: Usually 対応が後手に回る / 後手に回った: criticism of a response that came too late, common in news about governments and companies.

near.diff: 出遅れる is simply starting late; 後手に回る is being forced to react to events you failed to get ahead of.

cards.cue: A storm was forecast for days, but the town only started piling up sandbags once the river was already overflowing.

ctx.s: 準備[じゅんび]が遅[おく]れて、すべてが{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]った}。
ctx.en: Our preparations were late, and we were reacting to everything from then on.

ctx.s: 「相手[あいて]の出方[でかた]を待[ま]っていたら、{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]る}ぞ。」
ctx.en: "If we wait to see what they do, we'll be on the back foot."

ctx.s: 政府[せいふ]の対応[たいおう]が{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]り}、批判[ひはん]が高[たか]まった。
ctx.en: The government's response lagged behind events, and criticism grew.

ctx.s: 苦情[くじょう]への対応[たいおう]が{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]らない}よう、窓口[まどぐち]を増[ふ]やした。
ctx.en: We opened more help desks so that we wouldn't fall behind on complaints.

ctx.s: 「最近[さいきん]、仕事[しごと]が{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]って}ばかりで、毎日[まいにち]追[お]われている。」
ctx.en: "Lately I'm always behind at work, chasing after things every day."

ctx.s: 客[きゃく]が急[きゅう]に増[ふ]え、店[みせ]の準備[じゅんび]は完全[かんぜん]に{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]った}。
ctx.en: Customers suddenly poured in, and the shop's preparations fell completely behind.

bad.s: 列[れつ]が長[なが]くて、私[わたし]は{後手[ごて]に回[まわ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the line was long, so I ended up at the back)
bad.why: It is not about a physical position. It means being forced to react to events instead of getting ahead of them.

bad.s: 会社[かいしゃ]の対応[たいおう]が{後手[ごて]を回[まわ]った}。
bad.en: (meant: the company's response fell behind)
bad.why: The fixed form takes ni: gote ni mawaru. Gote o mawaru is ungrammatical.

cards.mean: being turned away at the door
cards.lit: being sent off in front of the gate, without being let inside

use.how: 門前払いだった / 門前払いされる / 門前払いを食う / 門前払いにする: refused outright without a hearing. Said of visitors, proposals, and lawsuits.

near.diff: 相手にされない is being ignored or not taken seriously; 門前払い is being refused at the first step, without even a hearing.

cards.cue: You travel to a company to pitch your idea, and the receptionist sends you away without letting you see anyone.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]に会[あ]いに行[い]ったが、{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}だった。
ctx.en: I went to see the company president, but I was turned away at the door.

ctx.s: 「約束[やくそく]なしで行[い]っても、{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}されるだけだよ。」
ctx.en: "If you go without an appointment, they'll just send you away."

ctx.s: せっかく来[き]てくれた人[ひと]を、{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}するわけにはいかない。
ctx.en: We can't just turn away someone who has come all this way.

ctx.s: 企画書[きかくしょ]を持[も]ち込[こ]んだが、中身[なかみ]も見[み]ずに{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}にされた。
ctx.en: I brought in my proposal, but they sent me off without even looking at it.

ctx.s: その記者[きしゃ]は、取材先[しゅざいさき]で何度[なんど]も{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}を食[く]った。
ctx.en: The reporter was turned away again and again by the people he wanted to interview.

ctx.s: 裁判所[さいばんしょ]は訴[うった]えの中身[なかみ]を審理[しんり]せず、{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}にした。
ctx.en: The court threw the case out without examining its merits.

bad.s: 面接[めんせつ]で一時間[いちじかん]話[はなし]を聞[き]いてもらったが、結局[けっきょく]{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}された。
bad.en: (meant: they heard me out for an hour but turned me down)
bad.why: It means being refused before you get any hearing. After an hour-long interview you were simply turned down.

bad.s: 店[みせ]に入[はい]ろうとしたら、{門前払[もんぜんばら]い}した。
bad.en: (meant: when I tried to go into the shop, I was turned away)
bad.why: Monzenbarai suru is what the one refusing does. When you are turned away, say monzenbarai sareta or monzenbarai o kutta.

cards.mean: to feel too awkward or intimidated to visit
cards.lit: the threshold is high: the door sill of someone's house feels hard to step over

use.how: Xの家は敷居が高い: traditionally, you hesitate to visit someone you have wronged or neglected. Now also used of a place that feels too posh to enter; some see that as a misuse.

near.diff: 足が遠のく is simply visiting less and less over time; 敷居が高い is feeling it hard to go because of guilt or intimidation.
ハードルが高い is any goal that feels hard to reach; 敷居が高い is about going to a particular person or place.

cards.cue: Years ago you borrowed money from an old friend and never paid it back; now you would feel too ashamed to drop by their house.

ctx.s: 借[か]りたお金[かね]をまだ返[かえ]していないので、彼[かれ]の家[いえ]は{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]い}。
ctx.en: I still haven't paid back the money I borrowed, so I feel too awkward to go to his house.

ctx.s: 「ずっと連絡[れんらく]してなかったから、実家[じっか]はちょっと{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]くて}……。」
ctx.en: "I haven't been in touch for ages, so going back to my parents' place feels a bit awkward..."

ctx.s: 卒業[そつぎょう]してから一度[いちど]も顔[かお]を出[だ]していないので、恩師[おんし]の研究室[けんきゅうしつ]は{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]い}。
ctx.en: I haven't shown my face once since graduating, so I feel awkward about visiting my old professor's lab.

ctx.s: 店長[てんちょう]と喧嘩[けんか]して以来[いらい]、あの店[みせ]は{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]く}なった。
ctx.en: Since I argued with the manager, I've felt too uncomfortable to go back to that shop.

ctx.s: 何年[なんねん]も年賀状[ねんがじょう]を出[だ]さずにいたら、叔母[おば]の家[いえ]はすっかり{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]く}なってしまった。
ctx.en: After years of not sending New Year cards, I now feel far too awkward to visit my aunt.

ctx.s: 高級[こうきゅう]な料亭[りょうてい]は{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]い}と思[おも]われがちだが、昼[ひる]なら気軽[きがる]に入[はい]れる。
ctx.en: Upmarket Japanese restaurants tend to seem intimidating, but at lunchtime you can walk in easily.

bad.s: あの人[ひと]は{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]い}から、誰[だれ]とも話[はな]さない。
bad.en: (meant: that person is stuck-up and talks to nobody)
bad.why: It describes your own reluctance to visit a place or person, not someone's arrogance. For that, say otakaku tomatte iru.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は恋人[こいびと]選[えら]びの{敷居[しきい]が高[たか]い}。
bad.en: (meant: she is very picky about boyfriends)
bad.why: It is not about having high standards. For being choosy, say risō ga takai.

cards.mean: (of a friend) distant, holding back
cards.lit: tasting of water: thin and watery, without the flavour you expected

use.how: Said to or about someone close: 水臭いなあ / 水臭いこと言うなよ. A warm complaint that a friend or relative is being too formal or kept something to themselves.

near.diff: よそよそしい describes cold, distant behaviour in general; 水臭い is a friendly complaint that someone close is needlessly holding back.

cards.cue: Your best friend moved house last weekend and only told you afterwards, saying they didn't want to bother you.

ctx.s: 「引[ひ]っ越[こ]すなら言[い]ってよ。{水臭[みずくさ]い}なあ。」
ctx.en: "You should have told me you were moving. Why keep it from me?"

ctx.s: 「お礼[れい]なんていいよ。そんな{水臭[みずくさ]い}こと言[い]うなって。」
ctx.en: "No need to thank me. Don't be so formal with me."

cards.r: いたくもかゆくもない

ctx.en: Insults like that don't bother me one bit.

bad.en: (meant: politely, your feedback causes me no trouble)

cards.mean: a superfluous addition
cards.lit: snake's feet: legs drawn onto a snake that never needed them

story.text: In the state of Chu, some servants were given a single cup of wine, too little to share, so they agreed that whoever drew a snake first would drink it. One man finished first and, cup in hand, began adding feet. Before he was done another man finished his snake, took the cup and said: a snake has no feet, so yours is not a snake.
story.source: 『戦国策』斉策 (Strategies of the Warring States)

use.how: Noun: 蛇足だ / 蛇足になる / 蛇足を加える. Also the humble preface 蛇足ですが, before a remark that may be unnecessary.

near.diff: 無用の長物 is a thing that is useless and in the way; 蛇足 is an extra part tacked onto something already complete.

bad.en: (meant: I added an extra paragraph to the report)

cards.mean: (of a worry) to turn out groundless
cards.lit: to end as the worry of the man of Qi: a fear that the sky might fall

story.text: A man of the small state of Qi was so afraid that the sky would fall and the earth would give way that he could neither sleep nor eat. Someone went to reassure him, explaining that the sky is only gathered air and the earth only piled-up soil, so there is nothing to collapse, and the man was greatly relieved. His needless fear, 'the worry of the man of Qi', gave Japanese the word kiyū.

use.how: Subject is a worry or fear, looked back on: 心配は杞憂に終わった. Also as a hope: 杞憂に終わればいいが (I hope my worry proves groundless).

near.diff: 取り越し苦労 is the act of worrying ahead of time; 杞憂に終わる reports that such a worry turned out to be unfounded.
胸をなで下ろす is the relief a person feels; 杞憂に終わる says the feared thing never happened.

cards.cue: For weeks you feared the new boss would cut your team, but she ended up praising it and adding staff. Your fear proved...

cards.mean: a gateway to success in a field
cards.lit: climbing the Dragon Gate: the rapids that turn a carp into a dragon

story.text: The Dragon Gate (ryūmon) was a stretch of violent rapids on the Yellow River. It was said that great fish gathered below it but few could swim up, and one that did turned into a dragon (in Japan the fish is told as a carp). In the Later Han, being received by the respected official Li Ying was so great an honour that people called it 'climbing the Dragon Gate'. Hence a hard test whose passing opens the way to success.

use.how: Noun, usually in AはBの登竜門だ, where A is a contest, award or exam and B a career: 新人作家の登竜門. Not used of people.

near.diff: 関門 is any barrier to get through; 登竜門 is a test whose passing launches a career or brings recognition.
白羽の矢が立つ is being picked out by others; 登竜門 is the contest or test through which one makes one's name.

ctx.s: このコンクールは若手[わかて]ピアニストの{登竜門[とうりゅうもん]}だ。
ctx.en: This competition is the gateway to success for young pianists.
