cards.mean: to incur the wrath of a superior
cards.lit: to touch the reversed scale under a dragon's throat

story.text: Han Feizi wrote that a dragon is gentle enough to be tamed and ridden, but under its throat grows one scale, a foot across, that lies the wrong way. Anyone who touches it is killed. A ruler, he warned, has such a scale too, and an adviser who can avoid touching it has almost succeeded in persuading him.

use.how: Verb phrase: [someone powerful]の逆鱗に触れる. The subject is the person or act that provoked the anger: 社長の逆鱗に触れて左遷された.

琴線に触れる means deeply moving someone; 逆鱗に触れる means enraging them. Learners mix them up because both use 触れる.

cards.cue: A junior employee publicly mocked the company founder's pet project, and the founder, furious, transferred him to a remote branch.

ctx.en: The young retainer incurred the lord's wrath and was driven from the castle.

cards.mean: the heart-wrenching pain of a hard choice
cards.lit: a feeling like one's bowels being torn apart

story.text: When the general Huan Wen was sailing through the Three Gorges, one of his men caught a baby monkey. Its mother ran along the bank crying for more than a hundred li, then leapt onto the boat and died. When her belly was opened, her intestines were found torn to pieces. Huan Wen, angered, dismissed the man.

near.diff: 胸が痛む is pain or sympathy at any sad thing; 断腸の思い is the agony of making a painful choice or parting yourself.
Close in feeling, but 断腸の思い is the set phrase for announcing a hard decision: 断腸の思いで決断した.

bad.en: (meant: we won the match and were overjoyed)

bad.why: Despite the image of torn bowels, it describes emotional pain, not a physical stomach ache.

cards.mean: the crucial moment, the moment of truth
cards.lit: the scene where one's true self must show

story.text: In kabuki and jōruri puppet theatre, the shōnenba (also written with the characters for 'true nature scene') was the most important scene of a role, where the lead actor had to bring out the true nature of the character. From the theatre the word spread to mean any crucial point where a person must show what they are made of.

use.how: Noun, typically ここからが正念場だ or 正念場を迎える. A decisive stretch that calls for full effort; often still ahead or under way.

near.diff: 土壇場 is the last moment with no time left, often with a sudden reversal; 正念場 is the decisive stretch where you must hold firm and give everything.
大詰め is simply the final stage of a process; 正念場 stresses that this is the make-or-break test of one's strength.

ctx.en: He felt that whether he could hold on now was the moment of truth in his life.

bad.en: (meant: I jumped onto the train at the last second before it left)

bad.en: (meant: today is my day off, a good time to relax at home)
bad.why: It names a hard, make-or-break moment demanding effort, not a chance or a good time for something easy.

cards.mean: at the very last moment
cards.lit: the earth mound of the execution ground

story.text: In the Edo period, beheadings were carried out on a dotan, a mound of piled earth built at the execution ground, and the place was called the dotanba. Since a person brought there had no way out, the word came to mean the very last moment, when nothing more can be done.

use.how: Noun, mostly 土壇場で (at the last moment) with a reversal, cancellation or change: 土壇場で逆転した, 土壇場になって断られた. Also 土壇場に追い込まれる.

near.diff: 正念場 is a decisive stretch that demands effort; 土壇場 is the final instant, where things are suddenly overturned or cancelled.
大詰め is the closing stage of a process, calm and planned; 土壇場 is the desperate last moment, often with a surprise.

cards.mean: the final stage
cards.lit: the grand final act of a play

story.text: In kabuki, the last act of the first play on the day's programme (the ichibanme kyōgen) was called the ōzume. From the theatre, the word passed into everyday speech for the last stage of any process, such as talks, an investigation or a season.

near.diff: 土壇場 is the desperate last instant, usually with a surprise; 大詰め is just the closing stage of an orderly process.
正念場 stresses a decisive test of strength; 大詰め says only that the end of the process is near.

cards.mean: an upset, an unexpected result

use.how: Predicate with a quality or resource as subject (経験, 金, 体力, 実力): 最後は経験がものを言う. Often ものを言うのは…だ.

ctx.s: マラソンの後半[こうはん]は、体力[たいりょく]が{ものを言[い]う}。
ctx.en: In the second half of a marathon, stamina is what counts.

ctx.s: 「こういう時[とき]は、やっぱり経験[けいけん]が{ものを言[い]う}ね。」
ctx.en: "In a situation like this, experience really makes the difference."

ctx.s: 結局[けっきょく]、最後[さいご]に{ものを言[い]った}のは毎日[まいにち]の練習[れんしゅう]だった。
ctx.en: In the end, what decided it was the daily practice.

ctx.s: この世界[せかい]では、学歴[がくれき]より実力[じつりょく]が{ものを言[い]う}。
ctx.en: In this world, ability counts for more than qualifications.

ctx.s: 選挙[せんきょ]では、地元[じもと]での人脈[じんみゃく]が{ものを言[い]う}らしい。
ctx.en: In elections, local connections apparently carry the day.

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]本番[ほんばん]では、それまでの積[つ]み重[かさ]ねが{ものを言[い]います}。
ctx.en: In the exam itself, it's the work you've built up until then that counts.

bad.s: この時計[とけい]は祖父[そふ]の形見[かたみ]なので、私[わたし]には{ものを言[い]う}。
bad.en: (meant: this watch matters to me because it was my grandfather's)
bad.why: It says a factor decides an outcome, such as a game, exam or deal, not that something is precious to you. Say watashi ni wa taisetsu da.

bad.s: この仕事[しごと]では経験[けいけん]を{ものを言[い]う}。
bad.en: (meant: in this job, experience is what counts)
bad.why: The deciding factor is the subject, marked with ga: keiken ga mono o iu. The phrase already has its own o and cannot take another object.

cards.mean: that saves a lot of explaining
cards.lit: the talk is quick: things can be settled fast because no long explanation is needed

use.how: Predicate, often それなら話が早い or …ほうが話が早い, when the other person already knows or agrees, or when a direct route skips the explaining.

near.diff: 話が違う protests that things are not as agreed; 話が早い welcomes that things can move quickly without explanation.

cards.cue: You start explaining a plan to a client, and she says she has already read the proposal and agrees with it. Relieved, you say this makes everything simpler. What phrase fits?

ctx.s: 「もう資料[しりょう]を読[よ]んだの？それなら{話[はなし]が早[はや]い}。」

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は事情[じじょう]を全部[ぜんぶ]知[し]っているから、{話[はなし]が早[はや]かった}。
ctx.en: She already knew the whole situation, so things went quickly.

ctx.s: 「君[きみ]も賛成[さんせい]してくれるなら{話[はなし]が早[はや]い}。さっそく始[はじ]めよう。」

ctx.s: 同[おな]じ業界[ぎょうかい]の人[ひと]だと、説明[せつめい]がいらないので{話[はなし]が早[はや]い}。

ctx.s: 電話[でんわ]で話[はな]すより、会[あ]って見[み]せたほうが{話[はなし]が早[はや]い}でしょう。
ctx.en: Rather than talking on the phone, it'll be quicker to meet and show you.

bad.s: あの先生[せんせい]は{話[はなし]が早[はや]くて}、聞[き]き取[と]れない。
bad.en: (meant: that teacher talks so fast I can't catch it)
bad.why: It is not about speaking speed. Someone who talks fast is hayakuchi da or hanasu no ga hayai.

bad.s: 会議[かいぎ]が三時間[さんじかん]も続[つづ]いて、{話[はなし]が早[はや]かった}。
bad.en: (meant: the meeting went on for three hours, it was so long)
bad.why: It means things are settled quickly with little explaining, the reverse of a long meeting. Say hanashi ga nagakatta.

cards.mean: to be deeply grateful for a favour
cards.lit: to wear the kindness: to carry the favour one received on oneself, like a garment

use.how: Said by the person helped, mostly as 恩に着るよ to a friend or equal for a real favour, or 恩に着るから when begging one. Not for a formal thank-you letter.

near.diff: 恩に着せる is to make others feel they owe you for your help; 恩に着る is to feel grateful yourself for help received.

cards.cue: Your friend cancels her weekend plans to help you move flat at short notice. Wanting to show how much you owe her, what do you say?

ctx.s: 「お金[かね]を貸[か]してくれて本当[ほんとう]に助[たす]かった。{恩[おん]に着[き]る}よ。」

ctx.en: He bowed his head and said, "I'll pay you back for this. I'm truly grateful."

ctx.s: 「夜中[よなか]に車[くるま]で迎[むか]えに来[き]てくれたの？{恩[おん]に着[き]る}わ。」
ctx.en: "You came to pick me up by car in the middle of the night? I really owe you."

ctx.s: 「推薦状[すいせんじょう]を書[か]いてもらえるなら、{恩[おん]に着[き]ます}。」
ctx.en: "If you'd write me a reference, I'd be deeply grateful."

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は小[ちい]さな親切[しんせつ]をすぐ{恩[おん]に着[き]る}から嫌[きら]われる。
bad.en: (meant: he's disliked because he makes people feel they owe him for every small kindness)
bad.why: That is on ni kiseru. On ni kiru is the grateful feeling of the one who was helped, which is never a fault.

bad.s: 拝啓[はいけい]　先日[せんじつ]はお世話[せわ]になり、{恩[おん]に着[き]ます}。
bad.en: (meant: Dear Sir, thank you for your help the other day)
bad.why: Wrong register: it is a personal, spoken expression. A formal letter says makoto ni arigatou gozaimashita.

cards.mean: to repay kindness with harm
cards.lit: to pay back a kindness with an injury, as if one's benefactor were an enemy

use.how: Predicate or 恩を仇で返すような + noun, condemning someone who harms the person who helped them. Can be said of oneself in regret: 恩を仇で返してしまった.

cards.cue: A man took in his friend's son, trained him and gave him a job; the young man then stole the firm's clients and left. How do people describe what he did?

ctx.s: 助[たす]けてくれた人[ひと]をだますなんて、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]す}ことだ。
ctx.en: Cheating the person who helped you is repaying kindness with harm.

ctx.s: 育[そだ]ててもらった会社[かいしゃ]の秘密[ひみつ]を売[う]るとは、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]す}行為[こうい]だ。
ctx.en: Selling the secrets of the company that trained you is biting the hand that fed you.

ctx.s: 「泊[と]めてあげたのに物[もの]を盗[ぬす]むなんて、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]された}気分[きぶん]だよ。」
ctx.en: "I put him up, and he stole from me. I feel stabbed in the back."

ctx.s: お世話[せわ]になった先生[せんせい]の悪口[わるぐち]を言[い]いふらし、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]して}しまったと後悔[こうかい]している。
ctx.en: I spread nasty talk about the teacher who had done so much for me, and I regret repaying his kindness with harm.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は、拾[ひろ]ってくれた監督[かんとく]を公[おおやけ]に批判[ひはん]し、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]した}と言[い]われた。
ctx.en: He publicly criticised the manager who had given him his chance, and people said he'd repaid kindness with harm.

ctx.s: {恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]す}ような真似[まね]だけはするなと、父[ちち]に言[い]われた。
ctx.en: My father told me never to do anything that repays kindness with harm.

bad.s: お世話[せわ]になった先輩[せんぱい]に、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]そう}とプレゼントを贈[おく]った。
bad.en: (meant: I sent a gift to the senior colleague who helped me, to repay the favour)
bad.why: Ada is harm, so this means repaying with injury. Repaying a kindness properly is on o kaesu or ongaeshi o suru.

bad.s: 知[し]らない男[おとこ]が、{恩[おん]を仇[あだ]で返[かえ]して}私[わたし]の財布[さいふ]を盗[ぬす]んだ。
bad.en: (meant: a stranger stole my wallet)
bad.why: It needs a prior kindness from the victim. A stranger who owed you nothing has no on to betray; he simply stole.

cards.mean: to work at something without a break
cards.lit: to pack in one's kon (stamina, as in konki, perseverance): to pour concentration into a task without letting up

use.how: Predicate for intense, unbroken work at a desk-type task. Very often in a caring warning: あまり根を詰めないでね. Note the reading こん, not ね.

near.diff: 寝る間も惜しむ is giving up sleep for days or weeks; 根を詰める is unbroken concentration in a stretch of work, and is often warned against.

cards.cue: Your flatmate has been hunched over her thesis since morning without a break, and it is now evening. You bring her tea and tell her not to overdo it. What phrase fits?

ctx.s: 「あまり{根[こん]を詰[つ]めない}で、少[すこ]し休[やす]んだら？」
ctx.en: "Don't push yourself so hard. Why not take a little break?"

ctx.s: 朝[あさ]から{根[こん]を詰[つ]めて}作業[さぎょう]したので、目[め]が疲[つか]れた。
ctx.en: I've been working flat out since morning, so my eyes are tired.

ctx.s: {根[こん]を詰[つ]め}すぎると、かえって効率[こうりつ]が下[さ]がる。
ctx.en: If you work too hard without a break, you actually get less done.

ctx.s: 「そんなに{根[こん]を詰[つ]めて}、体[からだ]を壊[こわ]さないでよ。」
ctx.en: "Working that hard without a break — don't make yourself ill."

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は午後[ごご]の間[あいだ]ずっと{根[こん]を詰[つ]めて}、ドレスの刺繍[ししゅう]をしていた。
ctx.en: She spent the whole afternoon bent over the dress's embroidery without a break.

ctx.s: 細[こま]かい修復[しゅうふく]作業[さぎょう]は{根[こん]を詰[つ]める}ので、一時間[いちじかん]ごとに休憩[きゅうけい]を取[と]る。
ctx.en: Fine restoration work takes such intense concentration that we take a break every hour.

bad.s: 今日[きょう]は{根[こん]を詰[つ]めて}、一日中[いちにちじゅう]ソファでのんびりした。
bad.en: (meant: I took it easy on the sofa all day)
bad.why: It means working hard without letting up, the opposite of lounging. For a relaxing day, say nonbiri sugoshita.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は昔[むかし]のことをまだ{根[こん]を詰[つ]めて}いる。
bad.en: (meant: he still holds a grudge about the past)
bad.why: Confusion with ne ni motsu (to hold a grudge). Kon o tsumeru is about effort and concentration, not grudges.

cards.mean: to begrudge even the time for sleep
cards.lit: to grudge even the time spent sleeping, so that hours of sleep go into the work instead

use.how: Almost always 寝る間も惜しんで + verb of effort (勉強する, 働く, 練習する), describing devotion over days or weeks. Often admiring.

near.diff: 身を粉にする is wearing oneself out labouring, often for others; 寝る間も惜しむ stresses cutting sleep to make time.

cards.cue: For three months before the bar exam, she studied late into every night and got up before dawn, sleeping only a few hours. How do you describe her effort?

ctx.s: 試験[しけん]前[まえ]、兄[あに]は{寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんで}勉強[べんきょう]した。
ctx.en: Before the exam, my brother studied so hard he barely slept.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は{寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんで}ピアノの練習[れんしゅう]を続[つづ]けた。
ctx.en: She kept practising the piano, grudging even the hours she spent asleep.

ctx.s: 「あの頃[ころ]は{寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんで}、毎晩[まいばん]明[あ]け方[がた]まで働[はたら]いたなあ。」
ctx.en: "Back then I grudged myself sleep and worked until dawn every night."

ctx.s: 創業者[そうぎょうしゃ]は{寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんで}製品[せいひん]の開発[かいはつ]に打[う]ち込[こ]んだという。
ctx.en: The founder is said to have thrown himself into developing the product, giving up sleep to do it.

ctx.s: 面白[おもしろ]い小説[しょうせつ]に夢中[むちゅう]になり、{寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんで}読[よ]んだ。
ctx.en: I was so absorbed in the gripping novel that I read it at the expense of sleep.

ctx.s: {寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しむ}ほどの努力[どりょく]があったからこそ、今[いま]の成功[せいこう]がある。
ctx.en: It's precisely because of effort so intense he begrudged himself sleep that he is successful now.

bad.s: 心配[しんぱい]で、昨夜[さくや]は{寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I was so worried I couldn't sleep last night)
bad.why: It is choosing to give up sleep for something you are devoted to, not insomnia. For worry, say shinpai de nemurenakatta.

bad.s: {寝[ね]る間[ま]も惜[お]しんで}、五分[ごふん]でメールを一通[いっつう]書[か]いた。
bad.en: (meant: I worked hard and wrote one email in five minutes)
bad.why: It describes sustained effort over nights, days or weeks. A five-minute task cannot cost you any sleep.

cards.mean: to finally see the light of day
cards.lit: to see the light of the sun: something kept in the dark comes out into daylight

use.how: Said of a work, plan, talent or effort that was hidden or ignored and is finally published or recognised: 原稿がようやく日の目を見た. Often negative: 日の目を見ずに終わる.

near.diff: 芽が出る is a person's career finally starting to succeed; 日の目を見る is a work, plan or effort finally coming out into public view.

cards.cue: A song recorded forty years ago sat forgotten in a studio vault. This year it is finally released.

ctx.en: Old photos that had been lying in a storeroom are going to be shown at an exhibition.

ctx.s: 「この企画[きかく]、いつか{日[ひ]の目[め]を見[み]る}と思[おも]う？」
ctx.en: "Do you think this project will ever actually happen?"

ctx.s: 予算[よさん]がつかず、その計画[けいかく]は結局[けっきょく]{日[ひ]の目[め]を見[み]ない}まま終[お]わった。
ctx.en: It never got funding, and in the end the plan died without ever seeing the light of day.

ctx.s: 無名[むめい]の時代[じだい]に録音[ろくおん]された曲[きょく]が、彼[かれ]の死後[しご]に{日[ひ]の目[め]を見[み]た}。
ctx.en: Songs he recorded while still unknown were released after his death.

ctx.s: 長年[ながねん]裏方[うらかた]として支[ささ]えてきた彼女[かのじょ]の仕事[しごと]が、ついに{日[ひ]の目[め]を見[み]る}時[とき]が来[き]た。

bad.en: (meant: the popular singer had another hit this year)

cards.mean: shrewder or more capable than one looks
cards.lit: cannot be left in the corner: too able to be ignored

near.diff: 抜け目がない says someone never misses a chance, often with a hint of calculation; 隅に置けない is warm surprise that someone is more than they seemed.

cards.cue: Your shy, quiet coworker turns out to have been dating someone for a year, and nobody had a clue. You tease them admiringly.

ctx.s: 「え、もう彼女[かのじょ]がいるの？{隅[すみ]に置[お]けない}なあ」
ctx.en: "What, you've already got a girlfriend? You're a dark horse!"

ctx.s: 大人[おとな]しい田中[たなか]さんが、実[じつ]はプロ並[な]みに歌[うた]がうまいなんて、{隅[すみ]に置[お]けない}ね。
ctx.en: Quiet Mr Tanaka actually sings like a pro? There's more to him than meets the eye.

ctx.s: いつもぼんやりしている新人[しんじん]が大口[おおぐち]の契約[けいやく]を取[と]ってくるとは、{隅[すみ]に置[お]けない}やつだ。
ctx.en: Our rookie always seems half asleep, and he lands a big contract? Don't underestimate that one.

ctx.en: "What, you speak three languages? You're full of surprises."

ctx.s: うちの祖母[そぼ]はスマホで株[かぶ]の取引[とりひき]までしていて、なかなか{隅[すみ]に置[お]けない}。
ctx.en: My grandmother even trades shares on her phone. She's sharper than you'd think.

ctx.s: 頼[たよ]りなさそうに見[み]えた彼[かれ]が、交渉[こうしょう]をあっさりまとめた。{隅[すみ]に置[お]けない}男[おとこ]だ。

bad.en: (meant: that Nobel-winning professor is a formidable researcher)

cards.mean: a bond one cannot shake off
cards.lit: a rotten tie: a connection gone stale that still will not break

near.diff: 切っても切れない describes a close, inseparable bond, usually positively; 腐れ縁 is a tie you half wish you could escape, or pretend to.

ctx.en: "You two get on well." "Nah, we're just stuck with each other."

ctx.s: 何度[なんど]も喧嘩[けんか]別[わか]れしたのに、なぜかまた一緒[いっしょ]に働[はたら]いている。{腐[くさ]れ縁[えん]}というやつだ。
ctx.en: We've fallen out and split up so many times, yet somehow we're working together again. Some ties just won't break.

ctx.s: あのバンドの二人[ふたり]は、解散[かいさん]と再結成[さいけっせい]を繰[く]り返[かえ]す{腐[くさ]れ縁[えん]}で知[し]られている。
ctx.en: The two in that band are known for a love-hate partnership, splitting up and reuniting again and again.

ctx.s: 別[わか]れようと思[おも]いながら、ずるずると{腐[くさ]れ縁[えん]}を続[つづ]けている。

bad.en: (meant: I hit it off right away with someone I met at yesterday's party)

bad.en: (meant: we are deeply grateful for our long relationship with your company)

cards.mean: to grow tired of waiting

cards.mean: having started, one must see it through
cards.lit: a boat you have already got into and pushed off in: you cannot step off midstream

cards.mean: to come to someone's rescue in a tight spot

cards.r: もとのさやにおさまる

cards.r: じゅうばこのすみをつつく

ctx.s: 強豪[きょうごう]と言[い]われた相手[あいて]は意外[いがい]に弱[よわ]く、選手[せんしゅ]たちは{拍子抜[ひょうしぬ]けした}様子[ようす]だった。

bad.en: (meant: I was devastated when my beloved grandmother died)

bad.en: (meant: I practised every day, so losing the match was a big disappointment)

cards.mean: stuck for a way to fill the silence
cards.lit: the gap won't hold: an empty pause in the talk that you cannot keep filled

use.how: Said when there is too much empty time with someone, usually a silence in conversation, and you don't know how to fill it: 二人だと間が持たない.

near.diff: 間が悪い is bad timing, arriving at the wrong moment; 間が持たない is being unable to fill an awkward stretch of silence or time.

bad.en: (meant: I overslept, missed the train and was late)

cards.mean: without a moment's delay
cards.lit: without leaving room for a single hair: no gap at all between one thing and the next

story.text: The phrase comes from a Chinese expression meaning 'the gap does not admit a hair'. In a Han-dynasty memorial, the official Mei Cheng warned the King of Wu, who was drifting towards rebellion, that his position was like a huge weight hung by a single thread over a bottomless abyss: the space between safety and ruin was too narrow to fit a hair. Japanese took the phrase over to mean a reaction that follows with no gap at all. Note the reading: kan, hatsu, not kanpatsu.
story.source: Mei Cheng's memorial remonstrating with the King of Wu (Han dynasty China)

use.how: Adverbial, with or without に, before the reaction: 間髪を入れず答えた. Said of a response that follows instantly on a trigger.

near.diff: すかさず is the everyday word for seizing the moment to respond; 間髪を入れず is more vivid and a little more bookish, stressing that there was no gap at all.

cards.cue: The teacher had barely finished asking who wanted the last cookie when every child shouted 'Me!' How did they answer?

ctx.en: When the new product was announced, the rival company immediately announced a price cut.

bad.s: メールをもらってから、{間髪[かんはつ]を入[い]れず}三日後[みっかご]に返事[へんじ]をした。
bad.en: (meant: I replied promptly, three days after the email)
bad.why: It means no gap at all between trigger and reaction; three days later is not without a moment's delay. Say hayame ni henji o shita.

cards.mean: shrewd, never missing a chance
cards.lit: to have no gaps or slips: nothing ever gets past one

use.how: Predicate or before a noun (抜け目のない人); adverb 抜け目なく. Said of someone quick to spot and take every advantage, often with wry admiration.

near.diff: ちゃっかり is light and colloquial, about grabbing a benefit on one occasion; 抜け目がない describes a person who reliably spots every advantage.

bad.en: (meant: he is scatterbrained, so he often forgets things)

cards.mean: to stand head and shoulders above the rest
cards.lit: to rise out of the crowd: to stand clear of the whole group

use.how: Mostly 群を抜いて + adjective (群を抜いて速い), 群を抜いた + noun, or 群を抜いている. Said of someone or something clearly best among many.

near.diff: 頭角を現す is the moment someone begins to stand out and rise; 群を抜く states that they already clearly outdo the rest.

cards.mean: acting as if one owns the place
cards.lit: a 'this is mine' face: the look of someone treating what is not theirs as their own

use.how: Usually 我が物顔で or 我が物顔に + verb (歩く, 使う, 振る舞う). Criticises someone treating a shared or someone else's space as their own.

near.diff: 大きな顔をする is acting self-important towards people; 我が物顔 is treating a place or thing that is not yours as if it were.

cards.mean: on a completely different scale

ctx.en: "Her knowledge is amazing." "Yeah, she's in a different league from us."

cards.mean: to gain experience by doing it many times

cards.t: 足を向けて寝られない

ctx.s: 誰[だれ]もが落[お]ちると思[おも]っていた彼[かれ]が首席[しゅせき]だと聞[き]き、皆[みな]{狐[きつね]につままれた}ようだった。
ctx.en: When we heard that he, whom everyone expected to fail, had come top, we were all dumbfounded.

bad.s: 数学[すうがく]の問題[もんだい]が難[むずか]しすぎて、{狐[きつね]につままれた}。
bad.en: (meant: the maths problem was too hard and I was stumped)
bad.why: It is for being dazed by something strange that should not have happened, not for a hard question. Say te mo ashi mo denakatta.

bad.s: 詐欺師[さぎし]に{狐[きつね]につままれて}、お金[かね]を取[と]られた。
bad.en: (meant: I was swindled out of my money by a con man)
bad.why: It describes bewilderment, not actually being cheated by someone. Say damasarete okane o torareta.

cards.mean: unusually meek and quiet in unfamiliar company
cards.lit: a borrowed cat: a cat taken into a strange house sits stiff and silent

use.how: Usually 借りてきた猫のように/みたいに おとなしい. Said, often teasingly, of someone normally lively who goes quiet in an unfamiliar place or company.

near.diff: 猫をかぶる is deliberately hiding one's true nature behind a meek front; 借りてきた猫 is being genuinely subdued by strange surroundings.

cards.cue: Your normally loud nephew sits stiff and silent all afternoon at a relative's house he has never visited before. How do you describe him?

ctx.s: いつもうるさい息子[むすこ]が、親戚[しんせき]の家[いえ]では{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}のようにおとなしかった。
ctx.en: My usually noisy son was as meek as a lamb at our relatives' house.

ctx.s: 普段[ふだん]は元気[げんき]な彼[かれ]も、新[あたら]しいクラスでは{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}みたいだ。
ctx.en: He's normally full of energy, but in his new class he's barely made a sound.

ctx.s: 「どうしたの、{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}みたいに黙[だま]っちゃって」と友達[ともだち]にからかわれた。
ctx.en: "What's up with you, sitting there all quiet and shy?" my friend teased.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]の両親[りょうしん]に初[はじ]めて会[あ]った日[ひ]、僕[ぼく]はまるで{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}だった。
ctx.en: The day I first met my girlfriend's parents, I hardly said a word.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の前[まえ]に出[で]ると、口[くち]の達者[たっしゃ]な部長[ぶちょう]も{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}のようになる。
ctx.en: In front of the company president, even our silver-tongued manager goes meek and quiet.

ctx.s: 合宿[がっしゅく]の初日[しょにち]、一年生[いちねんせい]たちは{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}のようだったが、夜[よる]には打[う]ち解[と]けた。
ctx.en: On the first day of training camp the first-years were timid and silent, but by evening they had relaxed.

bad.s: 彼女[かのじょ]は生[う]まれつき{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}のように静[しず]かな人[ひと]だ。
bad.en: (meant: she has always been a quiet person by nature)
bad.why: It describes an unusual change in an unfamiliar setting, not someone's permanent quiet personality.

bad.s: 知[し]らない家[いえ]で、子[こ]どもたちは{借[か]りてきた猫[ねこ]}のように暴[あば]れ回[まわ]った。
bad.en: (meant: in the strange house the children ran wild)
bad.why: The borrowed cat is still and timid. It means unusually meek, never wild or restless.

cards.mean: a decisive word from the person in charge
cards.lit: one call of the crane: a single cry that rises above the chatter of a thousand sparrows

use.how: A noun, usually Xの鶴の一声で決まる. Said of a boss, elder or leader whose one word ends a debate; sometimes wry about top-down decisions.

cards.cue: The committee argued over the new logo for two hours; then the company president said 'Blue', and the matter was closed.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}で、新[あたら]しい企画[きかく]が決[き]まった。
ctx.en: One word from the president, and the new project was settled.

ctx.s: 長[なが]い議論[ぎろん]も、会長[かいちょう]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}であっさり終[お]わった。
ctx.en: The long debate ended abruptly with a single word from the chairman.

ctx.s: 家族旅行[かぞくりょこう]の行[い]き先[さき]は、祖父[そふ]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}で沖縄[おきなわ]に決[き]まった。
ctx.en: Grandpa had the final say, and our family trip was fixed for Okinawa.

ctx.s: 「結局[けっきょく]、監督[かんとく]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}で決[き]まるんだよ」と選手[せんしゅ]たちは肩[かた]をすくめた。
ctx.en: "In the end it's whatever the manager says," the players shrugged.

ctx.s: 反対意見[はんたいいけん]も多[おお]かったが、市長[しちょう]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}で計画[けいかく]は進[すす]められた。
ctx.en: There was plenty of opposition, but the mayor's word carried the plan forward.

ctx.s: この会社[かいしゃ]では、何[なに]を決[き]めるにも創業者[そうぎょうしゃ]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}が必要[ひつよう]だ。
ctx.en: In this company, nothing gets decided without the founder's say-so.

bad.s: 合唱団[がっしょうだん]の先生[せんせい]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}は、とても美[うつく]しかった。
bad.en: (meant: the choir teacher's singing voice was very beautiful)
bad.why: It is not about the sound of a voice. It is the decisive word of someone with authority.

bad.s: 新入社員[しんにゅうしゃいん]の私[わたし]の{鶴[つる]の一声[ひとこえ]}で、会議[かいぎ]の結論[けつろん]が決[き]まった。
bad.en: (meant: my comment as a new recruit decided the meeting)
bad.why: Only someone with power or seniority can give it; a junior's remark that happens to sway people is not one.

cards.mean: to dislike someone for no clear reason
cards.lit: the bug inside does not like it: an old way of speaking of feelings as stirred by a creature within

use.how: Xは虫が好かない, or before a noun as 虫の好かない人. Said of a person, or their manner, you feel an instinctive aversion to, often with どうも or 何となく.

near.diff: 反りが合わない is two people failing to get along; 虫が好かない is one person's gut dislike of another.
気に食わない is displeasure at something specific; 虫が好かない is a dislike you cannot really explain.

cards.cue: You've met your new neighbour twice; he is polite and has done nothing wrong, yet something about him rubs you the wrong way.

ctx.s: 理由[りゆう]はないけど、あの人[ひと]はどうも{虫[むし]が好[す]かない}。
ctx.en: There's no reason for it, but I just don't like that person.

ctx.s: 初対面[しょたいめん]のときから、彼[かれ]のことは何[なん]となく{虫[むし]が好[す]かなかった}。
ctx.en: From the moment I met him, something about him put me off.

ctx.s: 「悪[わる]い人[ひと]じゃないんだけど、{虫[むし]が好[す]かない}んだよね」
ctx.en: "He's not a bad guy, but I just can't warm to him."

ctx.s: 母[はは]は姉[あね]の婚約者[こんやくしゃ]について、なぜか{虫[むし]が好[す]かない}と言[い]う。
ctx.en: For some reason my mother says she just doesn't take to my sister's fiancé.

ctx.s: あの店員[てんいん]には、どこか{虫[むし]の好[す]かない}ところがある。
ctx.en: There's something about that shop assistant that rubs me the wrong way.

ctx.s: {虫[むし]の好[す]かない}相手[あいて]とも、仕事[しごと]なら笑顔[えがお]で付[つ]き合[あ]わなければならない。
ctx.en: At work you have to smile and get along even with people you instinctively dislike.

bad.s: 私[わたし]は{虫[むし]が好[す]かない}ので、夏[なつ]のキャンプは苦手[にがて]だ。
bad.en: (meant: I don't like insects, so I hate summer camping)
bad.why: The bug is a figure for one's feelings; the phrase is about disliking a person. For insects say mushi ga kirai.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]とは{虫[むし]が好[す]いて}、すぐに仲良[なかよ]くなった。
bad.en: (meant: we hit it off and quickly became friends)
bad.why: It is used only in the negative. For instant liking say ki ga au or uma ga au.

cards.mean: asking prying questions about every detail
cards.lit: digging out the roots, and the leaves too: getting at every last bit of something

use.how: An adverb before 聞く or 尋ねる: 根掘り葉掘り聞かれる. Describes nosy, persistent questioning, usually from the annoyed side.

near.diff: 首を突っ込む is meddling in matters that are not yours; 根掘り葉掘り describes the manner of asking: question after prying question.

cards.cue: At a family dinner your aunt keeps firing questions: where your partner works, what they earn, why you aren't engaged yet.

ctx.s: 母[はは]に、彼氏[かれし]のことを{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}聞[き]かれた。
ctx.en: My mother grilled me about my boyfriend.

ctx.s: 「そんなに{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}聞[き]かないでよ」
ctx.en: "Stop asking me so many nosy questions!"

ctx.s: 初対面[しょたいめん]なのに、年収[ねんしゅう]まで{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}聞[き]いてくる人[ひと]がいた。
ctx.en: Someone I'd just met pried into everything, right down to my salary.

ctx.s: 同窓会[どうそうかい]で仕事[しごと]や結婚[けっこん]のことを{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}聞[き]かれて、疲[つか]れてしまった。
ctx.en: At the reunion I was quizzed about my job and marriage until I was worn out.

ctx.s: 記者[きしゃ]たちは、選手[せんしゅ]の私生活[しせいかつ]について{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}尋[たず]ねた。
ctx.en: The reporters pried into every corner of the player's private life.

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]で前[まえ]の会社[かいしゃ]を辞[や]めた理由[りゆう]を{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}聞[き]かれ、答[こた]えに困[こま]った。
ctx.en: At the interview they probed every detail of why I left my last job, and I struggled to answer.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]は文法[ぶんぽう]を{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}説明[せつめい]してくれた。
bad.en: (meant: the teacher explained the grammar in thorough detail)
bad.why: It describes prying questions, not a thorough explanation, and it is not praise. Say kuwashiku setsumei shite kureta.

bad.s: 週末[しゅうまつ]は庭[にわ]の雑草[ざっそう]を{根掘[ねほ]り葉掘[はほ]り}抜[ぬ]いた。
bad.en: (meant: at the weekend I pulled up every weed in the garden)
bad.why: It is used only of nosy questioning, never of actual digging or weeding.

cards.mean: to gamble on what will come up in an exam
cards.lit: to stake on 'the mountain': to bet everything on one guessed spot

use.how: Usually about tests: 山をかけて勉強する, 山をかけたところが出た/外れた. Often written ヤマをかける; also used of guessing interview questions.

cards.cue: With one night left before the history exam, you study only the Meiji period and hope that is what the test asks about.

ctx.s: テストで{山[やま]をかけたら}、見事[みごと]に当[あ]たった。
ctx.en: I gambled on what would be on the test, and I guessed right.

ctx.s: 「どこに{山[やま]をかける}？」「やっぱり第三章[だいさんしょう]かな」
ctx.en: "What are you betting will come up?" "Chapter three, I reckon."

ctx.s: {山[やま]をかけた}ところが全然[ぜんぜん]出[で]なくて、散々[さんざん]だった。
ctx.en: None of the parts I'd bet on came up, and it was a disaster.

ctx.s: 時間[じかん]がないので、出[で]そうな問題[もんだい]に{山[やま]をかけて}勉強[べんきょう]した。
ctx.en: Short of time, I just studied the questions I guessed were likely to come up.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はいつも{山[やま]をかけて}ばかりで、まじめに全部[ぜんぶ]復習[ふくしゅう]しない。
ctx.en: My brother always just gambles on a few topics and never revises everything properly.

ctx.s: 面接[めんせつ]で聞[き]かれそうな質問[しつもん]に{山[やま]をかけて}、答[こた]えを準備[じゅんび]した。
ctx.en: I guessed which questions the interviewers were likely to ask and prepared answers for those.

bad.s: 夏休[なつやす]みに家族[かぞく]で{山[やま]をかけて}、富士山[ふじさん]に登[のぼ]った。
bad.en: (meant: we went on a mountain trip in the summer and climbed Mount Fuji)
bad.why: It has nothing to do with real mountains. It means betting on which topics will come up.

bad.s: 試験[しけん]の範囲[はんい]を全部[ぜんぶ]しっかり{山[やま]をかけて}勉強[べんきょう]した。
bad.en: (meant: I studied the whole syllabus thoroughly)
bad.why: It means gambling on a few likely topics instead of covering everything, the opposite of thorough study.

cards.mean: (of a crowd) utterly hushed
cards.lit: as if water had been sprinkled on the ground: the dust settles and everything goes still

use.how: Adverbial 水を打ったように静まり返る/静かになる, or 水を打ったような静けさ. Said of a room or crowd full of people that suddenly falls silent.

near.diff: 鳴りを潜める is someone lying low and keeping quiet over a period; 水を打ったよう is a crowd falling silent in one moment.

cards.cue: The band walks on stage and an audience of two thousand chattering people instantly falls completely silent.

ctx.s: 先生[せんせい]が入[はい]ってくると、教室[きょうしつ]は{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}静[しず]かになった。
ctx.en: When the teacher came in, the classroom went completely silent.

ctx.s: 「さっきまであんなに騒[さわ]がしかったのに、急[きゅう]に{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}静[しず]かになったね。」
ctx.en: "It was so noisy a moment ago, and suddenly it's gone dead quiet."

ctx.s: 演奏[えんそう]が始[はじ]まると、ざわついていたホールが{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}静[しず]まった。
ctx.en: When the performance began, the buzzing hall fell utterly silent.

ctx.s: 合格者[ごうかくしゃ]の名前[なまえ]が読[よ]み上[あ]げられる瞬間[しゅんかん]、体育館[たいいくかん]は{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}静[しず]まり返[かえ]った。
ctx.en: The moment the names of those who passed were read out, the gym went completely still.

ctx.s: 黙祷[もくとう]の合図[あいず]で、満員[まんいん]の球場[きゅうじょう]が{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}静[しず]まり返[かえ]った。
ctx.en: At the signal for a moment of silence, the packed stadium fell utterly silent.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]が辞任[じにん]を告[つ]げると、会議室[かいぎしつ]は{水[みず]を打[う]ったような}静[しず]けさに包[つつ]まれた。
ctx.en: When the president announced his resignation, a deep hush fell over the meeting room.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]は{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}静[しず]かな性格[せいかく]だ。
bad.en: (meant: he has a very quiet personality)
bad.why: It describes a crowd or room suddenly falling silent, not a person's character. A quiet person is otonashii or monoshizuka.

bad.s: 試合[しあい]に勝[か]って、観客[かんきゃく]は{水[みず]を打[う]ったように}大喜[おおよろこ]びした。
bad.en: (meant: the crowd erupted with joy all at once)
bad.why: It only ever means a hush. A crowd erupting in joy is the opposite; say issei ni waita.

cards.mean: to pull far ahead of a rival
cards.lit: to open up water between you and a rival, like the gap between two boats in a race

use.how: X に(大きく)水をあける, or passive 水をあけられる for the one left behind. Said of competitors: firms, teams, athletes, colleagues.

near.diff: 水を差す is spoiling someone's mood or plans; 水をあける is building a big lead over a rival.

cards.cue: Two firms launched rival phones in the same year; three years later one sells five times as many as the other.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]は二位[にい]の選手[せんしゅ]に大[おお]きく{水[みず]をあけて}ゴールした。
ctx.en: He crossed the finish line far ahead of the runner-up.

ctx.s: 「このままだと、ライバル校[こう]に{水[みず]をあけられる}ぞ。」
ctx.en: "At this rate, our rival school is going to leave us far behind."

ctx.s: 新製品[しんせいひん]のヒットで、うちの会社[かいしゃ]は他社[たしゃ]に{水[みず]をあけた}。
ctx.en: Thanks to the hit new product, our company has pulled well ahead of its competitors.

ctx.s: 首位[しゅい]のチームは、二位[にい]に大[おお]きく{水[みず]をあけて}独走[どくそう]している。
ctx.en: The top team has opened up a huge lead over second place and is running away with it.

ctx.s: 入社[にゅうしゃ]した時[とき]は同[おな]じだった同期[どうき]に、いつの間[ま]にか{水[みず]をあけられて}しまった。
ctx.en: We started at the company on an equal footing, but before I knew it my peer had left me far behind.

ctx.s: 電気[でんき]自動車[じどうしゃ]の分野[ぶんや]では、海外[かいがい]メーカーに{水[みず]をあけられて}いるのが現状[げんじょう]だ。
ctx.en: In electric cars, the current situation is that foreign makers are well ahead of us.

bad.en: (meant: we won, edging ahead by one point)
bad.why: It means a wide, clear lead. A one-point win is the opposite; say itten-sa de serikatta.

bad.s: 友達[ともだち]と喧嘩[けんか]して、少[すこ]し{水[みず]をあけた}。
bad.en: (meant: after a fight, I kept my distance from my friend)
bad.why: It is about a lead over a competitor, not emotional distance. Keeping away from someone is kyori o oita.

cards.mean: vague and impossible to pin down
cards.lit: like trying to grab a cloud with your hand: there is nothing solid to hold

use.how: Almost always 雲をつかむような話/もの, or predicate 雲をつかむようだ. Said of a plan, request or search with nothing concrete to go on.

near.diff: 狐につままれる is being baffled by something that just happened; 雲をつかむよう is a plan or task too vague to get a grip on.

cards.cue: A client asks you to 'make the brand feel more alive' but cannot say what that means, for whom, or by when.

ctx.s: 彼[かれ]の計画[けいかく]は{雲[くも]をつかむような}話[はなし]で、具体性[ぐたいせい]がまったくない。
ctx.en: His plan is all vague talk with nothing concrete in it.

ctx.s: 「何[なに]か面白[おもしろ]いことがしたい」だけでは、{雲[くも]をつかむような}話[はなし]だよ。
ctx.en: "Just saying 'I want to do something interesting' is far too vague."

ctx.s: 「題名[だいめい]も作者[さくしゃ]もわからない青[あお]い本[ほん]？それは{雲[くも]をつかむような}ものだね。」
ctx.en: "A blue book, and you don't know the title or the author? That's next to impossible to track down."

ctx.s: 手[て]がかりが何[なに]もなく、{雲[くも]をつかむような}捜査[そうさ]が続[つづ]いた。
ctx.en: With no leads at all, the investigation dragged on with nothing to get hold of.

ctx.s: 上司[じょうし]の指示[しじ]はいつも{雲[くも]をつかむようで}、部下[ぶか]は困[こま]っている。
ctx.en: The boss's instructions are always so vague that his staff don't know what to do.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい仕事[しごと]は、最初[さいしょ]は{雲[くも]をつかむような}感[かん]じで、何[なに]から始[はじ]めればいいかわからなかった。
ctx.en: At first the new job felt so nebulous that I had no idea where to start.

bad.s: 駅前[えきまえ]に{雲[くも]をつかむように}高[たか]いビルが建[た]った。
bad.en: (meant: a sky-high building went up by the station)
bad.why: It is about vagueness, not height. A towering building is ten o tsuku yo na biru.

bad.s: 彼[かれ]の説明[せつめい]は{雲[くも]をつかんだ}。
bad.en: (meant: his explanation was vague)
bad.why: The fixed form is kumo o tsukamu yo na / yo da. The plain past tsukanda just says he grabbed a cloud.

cards.mean: to take the blame to protect others
cards.lit: to let mud be poured over your own head so that others stay clean

use.how: Verb phrase, often 自ら泥をかぶる. Said of someone who willingly takes the blame or the unpleasant role for a subordinate, a team or an organisation.

near.diff: 濡れ衣を着せる is pinning blame on an innocent person against their will; 泥をかぶる is choosing to take the blame yourself.

cards.cue: A launch failed because of a junior's error, but the team leader faces the client alone and says it was all their own call.

ctx.s: 部下[ぶか]のミスだったが、課長[かちょう]が{泥[どろ]をかぶって}謝[あやま]った。
ctx.en: It was a subordinate's mistake, but the section chief took the blame and apologised.

ctx.s: 「今回[こんかい]は俺[おれ]が{泥[どろ]をかぶる}から、お前[まえ]は何[なに]も言[い]うな。」
ctx.en: "I'll take the fall this time, so don't you say a word."

ctx.s: 誰[だれ]かが{泥[どろ]をかぶらなければ}、この問題[もんだい]は片付[かたづ]かない。
ctx.en: Unless someone takes the blame, this problem won't be settled.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]は会社[かいしゃ]を守[まも]るため、自[みずか]ら{泥[どろ]をかぶって}辞任[じにん]した。
ctx.en: To protect the company, the president took the blame on himself and resigned.

ctx.s: 彼女[かのじょ]はいつもチームのために{泥[どろ]をかぶる}、損[そん]な役回[やくまわ]りだ。
ctx.en: She always ends up in the thankless role of taking the blame for the team.

ctx.s: 「どうして君[きみ]が{泥[どろ]をかぶる}必要[ひつよう]があるの？悪[わる]いのは彼[かれ]でしょう。」
ctx.en: "Why should you take the blame? He's the one at fault."

bad.s: 自分[じぶん]のミスがばれて、上司[じょうし]に叱[しか]られ{泥[どろ]をかぶった}。
bad.en: (meant: my own mistake came out and I got told off)

bad.en: (meant: he broke his promise and shamed me)
bad.why: Shaming someone is kao ni doro o nuru. Doro o kaburu is about taking blame yourself and takes no target.

cards.mean: to stand in the line of fire for criticism
cards.lit: to stand at the front line facing the enemy's arrows

use.how: Usually 批判/非難の矢面に立つ, or passive 矢面に立たされる. Said of the person who directly faces criticism, questions or anger.

near.diff: 槍玉に挙げる is others singling someone out to attack; 矢面に立つ is the position of the one who faces the attack head-on.
風当たりが強い describes how strong the criticism is; 矢面に立つ names who stands at the front receiving it.

cards.cue: After a data leak, the company spokesperson must face hours of angry questions from reporters on live TV.

ctx.en: After the accident, the head of PR stood in the line of fire of public criticism.

ctx.s: 「記者[きしゃ]会見[かいけん]では、私[わたし]が{矢面[やおもて]に立[た]ちます}。」
ctx.en: "I'll be the one to face the reporters at the press conference."

ctx.s: 値上[ねあ]げを決[き]めたのは本社[ほんしゃ]なのに、客[きゃく]の不満[ふまん]の{矢面[やおもて]に立[た]たされる}のは店員[てんいん]だ。
ctx.en: Head office decided on the price rise, but it's the shop staff who have to face the customers' complaints.

ctx.s: 負[ま]けが続[つづ]き、監督[かんとく]はファンの非難[ひなん]の{矢面[やおもて]に立[た]って}いる。
ctx.en: After a run of defeats, the manager is bearing the brunt of the fans' anger.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい制度[せいど]への反発[はんぱつ]が強[つよ]く、担当者[たんとうしゃ]の彼[かれ]が{矢面[やおもて]に立[た]つ}ことになった。
ctx.en: Opposition to the new system was strong, and as the person in charge he ended up facing it head-on.

ctx.s: 苦情[くじょう]の窓口[まどぐち]は、毎日[まいにち]客[きゃく]の怒[いか]りの{矢面[やおもて]に立[た]つ}仕事[しごと]だ。
ctx.en: Working the complaints desk means facing customers' anger every single day.

bad.en: (meant: he was showered with applause)
bad.why: It is only for facing criticism or attack. Being applauded is hakushu o abita.

bad.s: 運動会[うんどうかい]で、弟[おとうと]は行進[こうしん]の{矢面[やおもて]に立[た]った}。
bad.en: (meant: my brother led the parade at sports day)
bad.why: It does not mean being at the front of a line. Leading a parade is sento ni tatta.

cards.mean: to just not get along with someone
cards.lit: the curve of a sword blade does not match its scabbard, so it will not slide in

use.how: X と反りが合わない. Said of two people, often a boss, colleague or in-law, whose temperaments just do not fit, as a lasting state.

near.diff: 気が合う is the everyday positive, getting on well; 反りが合わない is the set negative, a lasting clash of temperament.

cards.cue: You and a coworker are both competent and polite, yet every project together grates: you have simply never clicked.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい上司[じょうし]とは、どうも{反[そ]りが合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: I just don't get along with my new boss.

ctx.s: 「あの二人[ふたり]、昔[むかし]から{反[そ]りが合[あ]わない}みたいだね。」
ctx.en: "Those two seem to have never got on, even from way back."

ctx.s: 能力[のうりょく]は認[みと]めているが、彼[かれ]とは性格[せいかく]的[てき]に{反[そ]りが合[あ]わない}。
ctx.en: I respect his ability, but our personalities just don't mesh.

ctx.s: 嫌[きら]いなわけではないけれど、なぜか{反[そ]りが合[あ]わない}人[ひと]っているよね。
ctx.en: There are people you don't dislike, yet somehow you just can't get along with.

ctx.en: I couldn't get along with my mother-in-law, so we decided to live separately.

bad.en: (meant: this sofa doesn't suit the room)

bad.en: (meant: my husband and I disagreed once this morning)
bad.why: It is a lasting mismatch between people, not a single disagreement. One argument is iken ga awanakatta.

cards.mean: a third party profiting from a quarrel
cards.lit: the fisherman's gain

story.text: The state of Zhao was about to attack Yan. Su Dai, sent by Yan, told the King of Zhao: a clam opened its shell to sun itself and a snipe pecked at it, so the clam snapped shut on the bird's beak. Neither would let go, each sure the other would die first, and a passing fisherman caught them both. If Zhao and Yan wear each other out, he said, Qin will be that fisherman. The king called off the attack.
story.source: Zhan Guo Ce (戦国策), Strategies of Yan

use.how: A noun, usually 漁夫の利を得る/占める. Said of a third party who gains because two others are busy fighting each other.

near.diff: 一石二鳥 is getting two benefits from one action; 漁夫の利 is a bystander profiting from two others' fight.

cards.cue: Two big supermarkets wage a price war until both are exhausted, and a small newcomer quietly takes their customers.

ctx.en: While the two of them were arguing, a third person walked off with the prize.

ctx.s: 兄[あに]と姉[あね]がケーキを取[と]り合[あ]っているうちに、弟[おとうと]が食[た]べてしまった。まさに{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}だ。
ctx.en: While my older brother and sister fought over the cake, the youngest ate it. A textbook case of the bystander winning.

ctx.s: 「上位[じょうい]の二[に]チームが潰[つぶ]し合[あ]えば、うちが{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}を得[え]られるかもしれない。」
ctx.en: "If the top two teams knock each other out, we might be the ones who profit."

ctx.s: 二人[ふたり]の先輩[せんぱい]がリーダーの座[ざ]を争[あらそ]った結果[けっか]、{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}で私[わたし]が選[えら]ばれた。
ctx.en: Two seniors fought over the leader's post, and in the end I was chosen, the one who gained from their fight.

ctx.s: 大手[おおて]二社[にしゃ]の値下[ねさ]げ競争[きょうそう]で、新興[しんこう]企業[きぎょう]が{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}を占[し]めた。
ctx.en: In the price war between the two big firms, a young start-up reaped the benefits.

ctx.s: 「この裁判[さいばん]で一番[いちばん]得[とく]をするのは誰[だれ]？」「結局[けっきょく]、{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}を得[え]るのは弁護士[べんごし]だよ。」
ctx.en: "Who comes out best from this lawsuit?" "In the end it's the lawyers who profit from the fight."

bad.s: 毎日[まいにち]練習[れんしゅう]して、試合[しあい]で{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}を得[え]た。
bad.en: (meant: I practised every day and won the match)
bad.why: It is gain that falls to a bystander from others' quarrel, not a reward earned by your own effort.

bad.s: 散歩[さんぽ]は運動[うんどう]にも気分[きぶん]転換[てんかん]にもなる。{漁夫[ぎょふ]の利[り]}だ。
bad.en: (meant: walking is exercise and a change of mood at once)
bad.why: Two benefits from one action is isseki nicho. Gyofu no ri needs two parties fighting and a third who profits.

cards.mean: unstoppable momentum
cards.lit: the force of splitting bamboo: once the first joints give, the whole stalk splits by itself

story.text: When the Jin dynasty was conquering the state of Wu, some officers urged waiting for winter, since summer was near with its rains, floods and sickness. The general Du Yu refused: the army's might was at its height, he said, like splitting bamboo, where after the first few joints the rest open up on the blade by themselves. He pressed on, and Wu soon fell.
story.source: Book of Jin (晋書), biography of Du Yu

use.how: Usually 破竹の勢いで勝ち進む/連勝する, or predicate 破竹の勢いだ. Said of a team, army, person or firm winning or advancing one success after another.

near.diff: 飛ぶ鳥を落とす勢い is power and influence at its peak; 破竹の勢い is the momentum of winning one victory after another.

ctx.s: 決勝[けっしょう]まで{破竹[はちく]の勢[いきお]い}だった高校[こうこう]が、最後[さいご]にまさかの敗戦[はいせん]を喫[きっ]した。
ctx.en: The high school that had swept all before it right up to the final suffered a shock defeat at the last.

bad.s: 大型[おおがた]の台風[たいふう]が{破竹[はちく]の勢[いきお]い}で近[ちか]づいている。
bad.en: (meant: a big typhoon is approaching fast)

bad.en: (meant: he was starving and wolfed down his food)

cards.mean: to call a halt to a plan
cards.lit: to call out 'wait!' and stop the play

story.text: The phrase comes from the call 'matta!' (wait!). In sumo, a wrestler who is not ready can hold back at the initial charge and the start is redone; in shogi and go, a player who regrets a move asks for a 'matta' to take it back. From this call that stops play, the phrase came to mean stepping in to halt any plan already under way.

use.how: X に待ったをかける, or intransitive X に待ったがかかる. Said of someone, often with authority, stopping another person's plan or project that is in motion.

near.diff: 水を差す is dampening enthusiasm or spoiling a mood; 待ったをかける is actually stopping a plan from going ahead.

cards.cue: The board is about to sign a huge contract when the legal team steps in and insists everything stop until it reviews the terms.

ctx.s: 社長[しゃちょう]が「もう一度[いちど]考[かんが]えよう」と、新[あたら]しい計画[けいかく]に{待[ま]ったをかけた}。

ctx.s: 「その発注[はっちゅう]、いったん{待[ま]ったをかけて}もいいですか。」
ctx.en: "Could we put a stop to that order for now?"

bad.why: It has nothing to do with waiting for someone. Keeping a person waiting is mataseta.

bad.en: (meant: I was tired, so I paused my studying and went to bed)
bad.why: It is stepping in to stop someone else's plan, not pausing your own activity. Say benkyo o chudan shite.

cards.mean: brazen-faced, shameless
cards.lit: the skin of one's mug is thick: nothing makes them blush

use.how: Predicate (面の皮が厚い) or before a noun (面の皮の厚い人). A blunt insult for someone who does shameless things without a trace of embarrassment.

near.diff: 図々しい is the everyday adjective for pushy or cheeky; 面の皮が厚い is a rougher, more cutting idiom for utter shamelessness.

near.diff: 矢面に立つ is standing in front and taking the criticism yourself; 槍玉に挙げる is what the critics do when they pick out a target.

bad.en: (meant: the teacher singled out the top student for praise)

bad.en: (meant: to protect the team, the section chief stepped forward to take the criticism)
bad.why: Taking the blows yourself is yaomote ni tatsu. Yaridama ni ageru needs an attacker and a separate target.

cards.mean: to nod off while sitting up

ctx.en: The person next to me on the train is nodding off.

ctx.en: My section chief caught me nodding off in the middle of the meeting.

ctx.s: 長[なが]い講演[こうえん]の後半[こうはん]、会場[かいじょう]のあちこちで{船[ふね]を漕[こ]ぐ}姿[すがた]が見[み]られた。
ctx.en: In the second half of the long talk, people could be seen nodding off all over the hall.

bad.s: 疲[つか]れていたので、ベッドで朝[あさ]まで{船[ふね]を漕[こ]いだ}。
bad.en: (meant: I was tired, so I slept in bed till morning)
bad.why: It is only the nodding doze of someone sitting up, not real sleep lying down. Say gussuri nemutta.

bad.s: 「眠[ねむ]くなってきたから、そろそろ{船[ふね]を漕[こ]いで}きます。」
bad.en: (meant: I'm getting sleepy, so I'll go and take a nap)
bad.why: Nobody does it on purpose; it describes unintended dozing as seen from outside. For a planned nap say hirune shite kimasu.

cards.mean: to round on someone angrily
cards.lit: to come at someone as if to bite: lunging forward with angry words

use.how: Xに食ってかかる: to confront someone with fierce, angry protest, often someone with more authority. Used to narrate the scene: 審判に食ってかかった.

near.diff: 突っかかる suggests picking fights or needling someone, often over small things; 食ってかかる is a fierce, head-on angry protest in the moment.

cards.cue: When the referee shows him a yellow card, the striker storms up to him shouting that it was never a foul.

ctx.s: 弟[おとうと]はゲームを取[と]り上[あ]げられて、母[はは]に{食[く]ってかかった}。
ctx.en: When his game was taken away, my little brother lashed out angrily at our mother.

ctx.en: "If you go at the referee like that, you'll get sent off."

ctx.s: 評価[ひょうか]の説明[せつめい]を聞[き]くなり、彼女[かのじょ]は声[こえ]を荒[あら]げて上司[じょうし]に{食[く]ってかかった}。
ctx.en: The moment she heard the reasons for her evaluation, she raised her voice and rounded on her boss.

ctx.s: 「なんで私[わたし]のせいなの！」と、妹[いもうと]はすごい剣幕[けんまく]で{食[く]ってかかって}きた。
ctx.en: "Why is it my fault?!" my sister snapped, coming at me furiously.

ctx.s: 記者[きしゃ]の失礼[しつれい]な質問[しつもん]に、選手[せんしゅ]は思[おも]わず{食[く]ってかかった}。
ctx.en: At the reporter's rude question, the athlete couldn't help rounding on him.

ctx.s: いつもは穏[おだ]やかな父[ちち]が、店員[てんいん]に{食[く]ってかかる}のを初[はじ]めて見[み]た。
ctx.en: For the first time, I saw my usually mild father angrily confront a shop clerk.

bad.s: お腹[なか]が空[す]いていたので、ラーメンに{食[く]ってかかった}。
bad.en: (meant: I was hungry, so I dug into my ramen)
bad.why: Despite kuu, it has nothing to do with eating; it is angry protest aimed at a person. Say raamen ni gattsuita.

bad.s: 先生[せんせい]に質問[しつもん]があったので、授業[じゅぎょう]の後[あと]に{食[く]ってかかった}。
bad.en: (meant: I had a question, so I went up to the teacher after class)
bad.why: It always means angry, aggressive confrontation. Going politely to ask a question is shitsumon shi ni itta.

cards.mean: to get the short end of the stick
cards.lit: to eat the share: to be the one left swallowing the bad portion

use.how: Xが割を食う: someone ends up bearing a loss or burden because of a rule, a decision or other people. Often 割を食うのは…だ.

near.diff: 損をする is any loss; 割を食う stresses losing out unfairly because of others or because of how things were set up.

ctx.s: 「いつも{割[わり]を食[く]う}のは真面目[まじめ]な人[ひと]だ。」

ctx.s: 「急[きゅう]な予定変更[よていへんこう]で{割[わり]を食[く]う}のは、現場[げんば]のスタッフなんですよ。」
ctx.en: "When plans change suddenly, it's the staff on site who pay for it."

ctx.s: 駅前[えきまえ]に大[おお]きな店[みせ]ができて、昔[むかし]からの小[ちい]さな商店[しょうてん]が{割[わり]を食[く]って}いる。
ctx.en: Since a big store opened by the station, the old small shops have been losing out.

ctx.s: 新[あたら]しい制度[せいど]では、パートで働[はたら]く人[ひと]が{割[わり]を食[く]う}形[かたち]になった。

bad.en: (meant: I won the lottery and came out ahead)

bad.en: (meant: I've cut the pizza into four, so let's each eat our share)
bad.why: It never means eating a portion of food; it means bearing an unfair loss. Say hitokire zutsu tabeyou.

cards.mean: to be thrown into a panic
cards.lit: to eat bubbles: picture someone gulping and sputtering in a sudden fluster

use.how: Usually 泡を食って + action (逃げる, 飛び出す): someone is so startled by something sudden that they act in a hurried, flustered way.

near.diff: 慌てる is the everyday word for being flustered; 泡を食う is more vivid, for a sudden shock that sends someone scrambling.

bad.en: (meant: I've been worried about the exam all week)
bad.why: It is a sudden startled reaction, not lasting worry. For a week of anxiety say zutto shinpai shite iru.

bad.en: (meant: I drank the beer too fast and got a mouthful of foam)
bad.why: The idiom only means panicking; it is never about actual foam. Say awa ga kuchi ni haitta.

cards.mean: to go quiet, to lie low
cards.lit: to hide one's sound: to fall silent and keep still

use.how: Xが鳴りを潜める / 鳴りを潜めている: a person, group or trend that used to be loud or active has gone quiet, often with the hint it may return.

cards.mean: in great demand, sought by many
cards.lit: many pulling hands: lots of people reaching out to draw you to their side

bad.en: (meant: nobody helped, and there was far too much work)

cards.mean: (of a story) to grow in the retelling

cards.mean: unable to stand by and watch any longer

cards.r: はれものにさわるよう

bad.en: (meant: the nurse was so warmly gentle with me, I was really grateful)

bad.en: (meant: he is a touchy person)
